The tell: does the leader point you toward your own authority, or does he make you more dependent on his? Real elders make you less dependent on them over time. Predatory ones make you more dependent. The retreat pitch immediately after a vulnerable ceremony is a classic capture move.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — "S" CHECK: "When did I last check in with my own people — not this circle, not this leader, but MY people?"
scenarios.darkTitle: How To Spot A Predatory Men's Leader
scenarios.dark: Red flags in any men's circle context: leader claims special access to masculine truth others don't have, members are discouraged from talking about the group with outsiders, doubts about the leader are framed as your ego or fear, sexual or financial exploitation of members happens but stays quiet, ex-members are characterized as weak for leaving. Real elders welcome your questions, encourage outside relationships, and become less central to you over time as you become more connected to yourself.
scenarios.move: Receive genuine value. Take the pitch home. Verify with people outside the circle before spending anything.
scenarios.say: That sounds powerful — I need to sit with it before I commit. Can I reach you in a week?
scenarios.truth: Real brotherhood points you toward your own authority. Predatory brotherhood points you toward theirs.

scenarios.hook: THE PROMOTER'S GOT A DEAL FOR YOU
scenarios.archetype: Promoter Exploitation / Access Used as Control
scenarios.who: The promoter or "connector" who offers access — backstage, bookings, exposure — in exchange for labor, money, or loyalty that goes one direction. Common target: male artists, DJs, and performers hungry for the next level.
scenarios.scene: He can get you on a bigger stage. He knows the right people. He wants to manage you — no contract yet, "let's feel this out." Three events later you've promoted his parties for free, paid your own travel, given him 30% of your merch "until you're established," and performed at two events where you were never paid what was agreed. The bigger stage keeps being three months away.
tells: Handshake deals with no contract — "we're family, we don't need paperwork"
Money and labor flow toward him; opportunity stays perpetually in the future
Raises the stakes of questioning him — "after everything I've done for you"
Isolates you from other industry contacts — "those people don't understand your vision"
scenarios.happening: Access is currency in the music and festival world and predatory promoters know exactly how to use it. The pattern: create genuine-feeling opportunity, establish dependency before paperwork, extract labor while the opportunity stays always ahead. The "family" framing removes the business structure that would protect you. Contracts are not distrust — they're what makes relationships honest.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — "A" CHECK: "Who controls my access to the next level — and what is that actually costing me?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Get It In Writing — Every Time
scenarios.dark: Every booking, management agreement, revenue share — in writing, signed, before you show up. A basic performance contract covers: fee, payment timeline, cancellation terms, what you're responsible for. Music attorneys offer one-time consultations. Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts offers free/low-cost help. A legitimate promoter will have no problem signing. The ones who resist paperwork are the ones the paperwork was designed to protect you from.
scenarios.move: Opportunity is real. Opportunity without a contract is a liability. Get it in writing or keep walking.
scenarios.say: I'm interested — let's put the basics in writing so we're both protected. I can send you a simple agreement tonight.
scenarios.truth: Any promoter who won't sign a contract is telling you what the deal actually is.

scenarios.archetype: Reputation Threats / Social Smear Campaigns
scenarios.who: The person who threatens or executes damage to your reputation on the festival circuit when you push back, question them, or simply stop complying. Common in promoter relationships, crew dynamics, and romantic situations gone sour.
scenarios.scene: You stopped promoting for the promoter who wasn't paying you and the next week three festival Facebook groups had posts about you being "unreliable" and "difficult to work with." You didn't do anything wrong. But the narrative is already in circulation on the circuit and your next event inquiries have gone quiet. The people spreading it are the same people who weren't paying you.
tells: Implicit or explicit threats to "ruin you" on the circuit if you push back
Negative characterizations of you begin circulating after you exercise independence
Your professional contacts become suddenly distant without clear reason
The people spreading the narrative are the same people you had a dispute with
scenarios.happening: Reputation threats are a control mechanism that works specifically because the festival circuit is small and relationship-driven. The goal is to make the cost of pushing back higher than the cost of compliance. It often works. The counter is documenting everything before the dispute escalates, building independent relationships that don't run through the person threatening you, and proactively communicating your version of events to people who matter to you.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — "S" CHECK: "Have I documented this situation in writing so I have something to point to?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Documentation Is Your Defense
scenarios.dark: Before any dispute escalates: screenshot every agreement, every payment confirmation, every communication. If payments are owed: send a written demand via email with terms attached — this creates a legal paper trail. If reputation damage is happening: keep records of what's being said, where, and when. Defamation (false statements presented as fact that damage your reputation) is actionable. Most predatory promoters rely on targets being too embarrassed or too tired to document. Document anyway.
scenarios.move: Build independent circuit relationships. Document everything. Your reputation is built over time — one smear campaign doesn't end it.
scenarios.say: "I'm going to communicate directly with the people who matter to me about what actually happened."
scenarios.truth: Your reputation is yours. It was built by your actual work. One person's narrative doesn't own it.

scenarios.archetype: Camp Obligation / Manufactured Debt to the Group
scenarios.who: The camp structure where housing, infrastructure, and event access are provided in exchange for vague "contribution" that expands over time to include labor, money, silence about what happens inside the group.
scenarios.scene: The camp was incredible — shade structure, kitchen, generator, solid location. "We just ask that everyone contributes to community." Week 1: set up shifts. Week 2: purchasing supplies. Week 3: managing other members. Month 3: you're running operations for the camp and still paying your entry fee and you're not sure exactly how you got here, but leaving now feels like abandoning something you've built.
tells: Contribution expectations vague at start and expand with each event
Access to camp infrastructure tied to your continued compliance
"After everything this camp has given you" appears when you express. a limit
Camp leadership is not accountable in the same ways regular members are
scenarios.happening: Camp debt works the same way gifter debt does — at a larger scale with a group enforcement mechanism. The contributions feel small individually but accumulate. The belonging feels real and the infrastructure is genuinely valuable. The tell is whether the arrangement is reciprocal and defined. Real community has terms both parties can articulate. When your contributions keep expanding and the camp's contributions stay stable — you're working, not belonging.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — "S" CHECK: "When did I last actually talk to people outside this camp — my own people?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Calculate Your Actual Camp Cost
scenarios.dark: Write this down: (1) Entry fees and membership costs, (2) Hours of your labor at your hourly rate, (3) Cash contributions to camp expenses, (4) Value of any goods or services you provided. Compare to: what this event would cost you as an independent attendee with a solo ticket and your own setup. If the camp costs you more in total than going independently — you are paying for the privilege of working for them. Name that clearly before committing to another season.
scenarios.move: Define the terms before you commit. Expanding terms after commitment is pressure, not negotiation.
scenarios.say: I need to understand what's expected specifically before I commit to another season.
scenarios.truth: Community costs should be mutual, defined, and agreed to in advance. Everything else is just uncompensated labor.

scenarios.archetype: Legal, Otherwise, and How to Spot Undercovers
scenarios.who: Transactions at festivals — substances, goods, services, tickets — carry real legal risk. Undercover officers work festivals and look exactly like attendees. This page is about navigating that reality with eyes open.
scenarios.scene: He's in full kandi, wristbands up both arms, talking knowledgeably about the lineup, vibing completely with the crowd. He finds you and opens a conversation about what you're looking for. Everything about him reads as a fellow festie. He seems genuinely connected. He asks for your number. He says to meet him near the back of the camping area in twenty minutes. Something about the sequence feels slightly scripted.
tells: They approach YOU to buy or sell — not the other way around
Unusual interest in quantities, prices, or whether you know "anyone else who's looking"
Wants to meet somewhere private or away from the crowd to transact
Pushes for a quick decision or seems vaguely impatient with your hesitation
scenarios.happening: Undercover officers at festivals are specifically trained to blend in and are often very good at it. The behavioral tells are in the transaction pattern itself, not the appearance: they initiate, they guide you toward isolation, they want specificity about quantities, and they push pace. You are never obligated to complete any transaction. "Actually I'm good" ends it without incident. Never follow anyone to an isolated location for any transaction regardless of what's being offered.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — “A” CHECK: “Who has access to my decisions in this transaction — and do I know enough about this person to be doing this at all?” — if the answer is no, the deal isn’t worth what it’s about to cost you.
scenarios.darkTitle: If You're Approached By Police Or Arrested
scenarios.dark: Know this before the festival: (1) You have the right to remain silent — use it. "I'd like to speak with a lawyer" is the only thing you say. (2) You can ask if you're being detained or are free to go — if free to go, go. (3) Do not consent to a search — you can decline without it being suspicious. (4) Write down badge numbers and officer names as soon as possible. (5) Contact a lawyer or the National Lawyers Guild (nlg.org) which has observer programs at many festivals. Good Samaritan laws protect people seeking overdose help in most states — use them.
scenarios.move: "Actually I'm good" ends any transaction. Walk toward people. Never go somewhere isolated for any deal.
scenarios.say: "Actually I'm good" — then walk. No elaboration. No explanation. Just go.
scenarios.truth: The festival is not worth your freedom. No transaction is worth your freedom.

scenarios.archetype: Getting Out of Any Situation Without Drama
scenarios.who: Men are socialized to stay in uncomfortable situations because leaving reads as weakness. It's not. Knowing when and how to exit — a crew, a deal, a tent, a transaction — is one of the most important skills you'll use this weekend.
scenarios.scene: You're in a situation that feels wrong and the voice in your head is running through reasons to stay: it'd be rude to leave, you don't want to make it weird, maybe you're just being paranoid, the crew will think you can't handle it. None of those reasons are about your safety. All of them are about managing other people's opinions of you. Those are not the same thing.
tells: "I need to find my camp" works everywhere and requires zero explanation
Code word system with your crew before the festival: one text = come get me
Festival Rangers are there for uncomfortable situations — not just medical emergencies
You don't have to explain yourself. You don't have to make it clean. You can just go.
scenarios.happening: The difficulty of leaving is almost always manufactured — by social pressure, by sunk cost thinking, by not wanting to be the one who breaks the vibe. Men specifically are socialized to read the desire to leave as cowardice rather than wisdom. It is wisdom. Your body knows when something is off before your brain has fully processed it. The moment leaving feels complicated is the moment leaving becomes most important.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — "S" CHECK: "When did I last actually check in with my squad — my actual people, not this new crew?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Safety Infrastructure Before You Arrive
scenarios.dark: Before gates open: set a daily check-in time with at least one friend outside whatever crew you end up in. Pick a meeting spot your whole group knows. Establish a code word. Write two emergency numbers in pen on your arm. Download an offline festival map. Know where the medical tent and Harm Reduction tent are. Know where the Ranger station is. These feel like overkill until the one time they're not.
scenarios.move: Stand up. Say "I'm out." Walk. Managing their feelings about your departure is not your job.
scenarios.say: "I need to bounce — catch you later." Then go. No elaboration needed.
scenarios.truth: Knowing when to leave and actually leaving is a skill. Practice it.

scenarios.archetype: The Page Every Man Needs To Read
scenarios.who: This is not an accusation. This is the page that makes you genuinely safer to be around — which is what most of you actually want. The festival world needs men who understand this.
scenarios.scene: She's been dancing near you all night and the energy has felt reciprocal. You've talked a few times, she laughed, she touched your arm once. You're reading it as interest. You might be right. You might also be reading into it through a haze of MDMA and wishful thinking. Before you make a move: the way to know if someone wants what you're offering is to ask. Out loud. With words. "Can I kiss you?" takes two seconds and changes everything about what happens next.
tells: Altered states mean consent needs to be MORE explicit, not less — not less
Someone who is very high or dissociating cannot give consent — even if they seem willing
Offering substances to someone you're attracted to is a power dynamic — be honest about that
"She was into it" is not the same as "she said yes" — only one of these is consent
scenarios.happening: Festival environments amplify everything — including the ways men unconsciously push past ambiguity because the cost of being wrong feels low and the reward of being right feels high. Altered states, dark spaces, PLUR culture, and the "anything goes" vibe create conditions where consent gets murky fast. It doesn't have to. Two words — "is this okay?" — asked clearly and genuinely, change the entire dynamic.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — “B” CHECK: “What is my body — and hers — actually saying right now, separate from what I want the answer to be?” — ask out loud rather than guessing. The men who ask are the ones people want to be around.
scenarios.darkTitle: If Something Happened That Shouldn't Have
scenarios.dark: If you crossed a line — even accidentally, even while altered, even if you're not sure — the courageous thing is to acknowledge it. Not to yourself in private. To the person affected. "I'm not sure if what happened last night was okay for you — I want to check in" is a sentence that can change someone's entire recovery. RAINN has resources for people who have caused harm as well as those harmed (rainn.org). Accountability is not the end. It is the beginning of being someone people can actually trust.
scenarios.move: Ask with words. Receive the answer with grace. The yes you get after asking clearly is the only one that counts.
scenarios.say: "Hey — I'm feeling a connection with you. Can I kiss you?" Then respect whatever comes next.
scenarios.truth: The men who ask are the ones people want to be around. Be that man.

scenarios.archetype: When You're the One With Access or Status
scenarios.who: If you're a camp lead, a promoter, a performer, a veteran with a big network, or simply the one who controls the substances, the ride, or the access — you have power. This page is about what you do with it.
scenarios.scene: You run a camp that people want to be part of. You have connections, good substances, a reputation. People come to you. People want things from you. Some of them are also in vulnerable positions — first-timers, people new to the scene, people who are deep in an altered state. Your position means your "yes" is more weighted and your "no" is harder for some people to hear. That's not bad. It's a responsibility.
tells: People in your orbit may feel unable to say no to you — even when they want to
Offering substances, access, or opportunity creates a power dynamic regardless of intent
Your "just joking" or "just testing" reads differently to people with less power than you
Silence from someone in your camp or crew is not consent — it may be fear
scenarios.happening: Power differentials exist whether you acknowledge them or not. Camp leads, veterans, performers, and access holders in festival culture have real leverage over people who want what they have. That leverage doesn't disappear because the environment is loving or because your intentions are good. The question is not whether you have power. The question is whether you're using it in ways that leave people genuinely free to choose.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — "B" CHECK: "Are the people in my orbit genuinely free to say no to me — and do they know that?"
scenarios.darkTitle: What Responsible Leadership Looks Like
scenarios.dark: In your camp, your crew, your circle: explicitly state that people are free to leave any situation, any time, no explanation needed, with no social cost. Model this by not reacting poorly when someone does leave. Don't make your substances, your connections, or your space feel conditional on compliance with your preferences. Check in with people who seem quiet or withdrawn rather than assuming they're fine. The test of good leadership is whether the people in your orbit are more themselves at the end of the weekend, not less.
scenarios.move: Use your access to create freedom for people in your orbit, not dependency on you.
scenarios.say: [To your camp]: "Everyone here is free to leave any situation at any time, no questions asked. That includes leaving this camp."
scenarios.truth: The best leaders in this community are the ones people feel most free around. Build that.

scenarios.archetype: Bystander Activation for Men
scenarios.who: At some point this weekend you will see something that doesn't look right. A woman in a situation she didn't choose. A person too out of it to be alone. A transaction that has setup written all over it. What you do in that moment matters.
scenarios.scene: You're walking between stages and you see a woman sitting with a guy who seems agitated. Her body language is closed. He's leaning into her space. You don't want to assume. You don't want to make it weird. You're not sure it's anything. But something caught. This is the moment. This is the one that either you act on or you walk past. Those are the only two options.
tells: THE DIRECT APPROACH: walk over like you know her — "Hey! There you are! Come on, everyone's looking for you"
THE RESOURCE APPROACH: find a Ranger or Harm Reduction worker, describe what and where
THE BUDDY APPROACH: position yourself nearby and make conversation with both until the dynamic shifts
You do NOT need to confront anyone — that is not required and not always safe
scenarios.happening: Men specifically have a role in bystander intervention that's often underused. A man appearing who "knows" the woman in a tense situation changes the social calculus immediately — it creates an out without confrontation. You don't have to be the hero. You have to be the person who showed up. The most effective interventions are the quiet ones. Walk over. Be a familiar face. Give someone an exit.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — “S” CHECK: “Is someone in my squad or nearby in a situation that doesn’t look right? What would I want someone to do if it were me?” — do that.
scenarios.darkTitle: When A Friend Discloses Something Happened To Them
scenarios.dark: Men rarely know what to do when a friend discloses assault or harassment. Here's what actually helps: listen without judgment, believe them without interrogating the details, ask what they need rather than assuming, don't push them toward reporting if they're not ready. What doesn't help: "are you sure that's what happened," "what were you doing there," immediately offering to "handle it" in ways that remove their agency. Their experience is theirs to process on their timeline. Your job is to show up and stay.
scenarios.move: See something, do something. You don't have to be the hero. You just have to show up.
scenarios.say: [Natural, easy]: "Hey! There you are! Come on, everyone's at the stage." Then walk with her.
scenarios.truth: The community is only as safe as what we each do in the moment we see something.

scenarios.archetype: Mental Health & Crisis Support at Festivals
scenarios.who: Sometimes the festival brings up things that were already there. Sometimes the substances take someone somewhere dark. Sometimes it's exhaustion and overwhelm and feeling completely alone in a crowd of thousands. This page is for knowing what to do in those moments.
scenarios.scene: Your campmate has been in his tent since Saturday afternoon. He came out once, looked off, said he was fine, went back in. It's Sunday morning. You've knocked twice. He said he's okay but something in his voice sounds wrong. You don't want to be dramatic. You also know him and this isn't normal. The moment you're sitting with right now — do you go back and check on him again, or do you leave it?
tells: Withdrawal from the festival when they came to engage — especially sudden
Saying they're fine in a way that doesn't match their voice or energy
Not eating, not sleeping, not coming out — for hours longer than exhaustion explains
Saying things that sound like goodbye or that they shouldn't have come
scenarios.happening: Festival environments can precipitate real mental health crises — substance effects, sleep deprivation, emotional openness that surfaces difficult things, and the isolation that can exist inside a crowd. Men are specifically at risk of not receiving support because "I'm fine" is the expected answer and people accept it. If your gut says something is wrong, knock again. Ask directly. "Are you actually okay?" delivered with real eye contact is a different question than "you okay?"
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — "B" CHECK: "What is my gut actually saying about this situation — and am I acting on it?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Crisis Resources At Festivals
scenarios.dark: Zendo Project (zendoproject.org) specializes in difficult psychedelic experiences and is present at many festivals — they can help with everything from bad trips to deeper crisis. Festival medical tents handle mental health crises — this is not just for physical injuries. Crisis Text Line: text HOME to 741741 — works where voice calls feel too hard. 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988, available 24/7. If someone is in immediate danger, get festival medical or call 911. Staying with someone in crisis until help arrives is the most important thing you can do.
scenarios.move: Knock again. Ask directly. Stay with them. Get help if needed. That's the whole protocol.
scenarios.say: Hey — I'm asking for real. Are you actually okay? Because I'm not going anywhere until I know.
scenarios.truth: Checking on your people is not being dramatic. It's being a real friend.

scenarios.hook: IT HAPPENED TO YOU AND YOU HAVE NO WORDS FOR IT
scenarios.archetype: The Thing Men Are Not Supposed To Be Able To Have Happen
scenarios.who: Nobody. This page is about you, and about the specific reason you have not said anything about the thing that happened on Saturday.
scenarios.scene: You were extremely drunk or extremely high or both. You do not have all of it. You have enough of it. And every time you get close to describing it, some part of your head supplies the sentence that men cannot really have this happen, or that you should have wanted it, or that people would laugh — and you put it back down, and it has now been four months.
tells: You have not told anyone, and the reason is how it would sound
You keep landing on “I should have been able to stop it”
You are performing fine, loudly, to specific people
Sleep, drinking, or temper have changed and you have attributed it elsewhere
You have described it once as a funny story and felt worse afterwards
You would recognize it instantly as assault if a friend described it to you
scenarios.happening: Sexual assault of men is substantially more common than the culture admits and substantially less reported, and the barrier is well documented: the expectation that a man could not be overpowered, the belief that arousal equals consent (it does not — it is a physiological response and it occurs during assaults), and the fear of being disbelieved or mocked. Incapacity is incapacity regardless of gender. If you could not consent, you did not, and nothing about your body's reactions, your size, or your enjoyment of the evening up to that point changes that.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — “B” CHECK: “If a mate described this exact thing to me, what would I call it?” You already know. Use your own answer.
scenarios.darkTitle: What The Silence Does Over Time
scenarios.dark: The untreated course of this is fairly predictable and it is why the page is here rather than in a footnote: undisclosed assault in men shows up later as drinking, as anger, as an inability to be touched, as a relationship that ends without either party understanding why, and in the worst cases as suicidality — and by then it is several years downstream and nobody connects it to a weekend nobody was told about. The single intervention that changes the trajectory is telling one person. Not the group, not a public account, one person: a specialist line, a GP, a therapist, or the one friend you already know would not make it a joke. Male survivors' services exist in every country and they exist because there are many, many of you.
scenarios.move: Tell one person this month. Choose a helpline first if choosing a friend feels impossible — it is anonymous, they have heard it, and saying it out loud once breaks the thing that shame relies on. If it was recent, a forensic examination is available to men too, and in most places without a police report.
scenarios.say: Something happened at a festival and I haven't told anyone and I think I need to say it out loud once. I don't need you to do anything about it.
scenarios.truth: You could not consent, so you did not. That sentence does not have a different version for men.

scenarios.archetype: The Recruit / Being Used As Muscle
scenarios.who: The camp lead, the promoter, or the guy with the arrangement, who has looked at you and seen an asset rather than a person. Flattering about it. Specific about what he needs and vague about what it involves.
scenarios.scene: He says you have a presence, that people listen to you, that he needs someone who can stand at the gate of the camp and turn people away. Then it is someone to have a word with a bloke who has been a problem. Then it is someone to come along to a conversation at the far end of the site, and you are eleven minutes into a walk before you have properly asked what this conversation is.
tells: Recruited for your size or presence rather than for judgement or skill
The task keeps growing and was never described in full
No role, no training, no authority, and no radio
You would be the one physically present if it goes wrong
He is not coming, or is coming and standing behind you
Nobody has mentioned who is liable if somebody gets hurt
scenarios.happening: Untrained physical intervention is the fastest route to a criminal charge at a festival, and men get recruited into it constantly because presence reads as competence. The person asking transfers every risk to you — legal, physical and reputational — while keeping the authority and the benefit. Real security is trained, licensed, insured and radio-connected for exactly these reasons. Being big is not a qualification, it is an appearance, and it is the thing that makes you the most useful available person to put between someone else and a problem.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — “A” CHECK: “What exactly am I being asked to do, and who is responsible if it goes wrong?” If either answer is fuzzy, that fuzziness is the arrangement.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Are The One In The Footage
scenarios.dark: Picture the aftermath rather than the moment. There is phone footage, and it starts thirty seconds in, and in every frame of it the large man doing something physical is you. The person who asked is not in shot. He was not there, he did not instruct anything, and his account afterwards will be that you took it upon yourself. This is precisely how men end up arrested at festivals for other people's disputes, and it is why the answer is not a braver version of yes. Getting a trained person is not cowardice; it is the only version of this that ends with you not being the defendant.
scenarios.move: Decline the physical role and supply the actual one: get security or the duty manager, be a visible witness, film from a distance, stay with the person who is at risk. Presence without contact is genuinely useful and is not a criminal offence.
scenarios.say: I'm not putting hands on anyone — that's a job for someone licensed. I'll come and stand there, and I'll get a radio, but I'm not the muscle.
scenarios.truth: Being the biggest bloke available is not a job description. It is just who they will name afterwards.

scenarios.hook: ARE YOU GOING TO DO SOMETHING ABOUT IT
scenarios.archetype: The Goad / Being Walked Into A Fight
scenarios.who: Someone who wants this. Sometimes drunk and stupid, sometimes practised and calm, occasionally a pair working together — one to provoke and one to film. Has picked you because you responded to the first line rather than to the fifth.
scenarios.scene: He has been at it for ten minutes. The comments started about the queue and are now about the woman you came with, and there are people watching, and he is asking whether you are going to do something about it in a tone that is doing exactly what it is designed to do. Your hands have already made the decision. There are two phones up.
tells: Escalates in public and specifically wants an audience
Moves to insults about the people you are with, because that works
Closes distance while keeping his hands visible and low
Somebody nearby is filming and started before anything happened
He is calmer than the situation warrants
You are being asked a question whose only wrong answer is engaging
scenarios.happening: The provocation is the technique and the fight is the product. It produces a clip, a reputation, a claim of self-defence, or occasionally a legal position — and in every version of it the person who throws first is the person who loses, legally and practically. At a festival the additional problem is the ground: a single punch on hard standing, near a barrier, in the dark, after a night of drinking, is how people acquire a conviction or a headline. The people who do this are good at it and have done it before, which is why it feels so specifically calibrated to you.
scenarios.check: B.A.S.S. — “S” CHECK: “Is this a threat, or a performance aimed at getting a reaction?” A real threat closes on you. A performance keeps asking questions.
scenarios.darkTitle: One Punch Is The Whole Rest Of It
scenarios.dark: The arithmetic is unforgiving and worth knowing while you are calm: a single punch that lands can kill somebody who falls badly, and campaigns in several countries exist for precisely that reason. The likeliest outcomes in descending order are that you are removed and lose your ticket, that you are arrested, that somebody is seriously hurt, or that you are the one on the ground. What is on the other side of not engaging is you being mildly embarrassed in front of strangers you will never see again. Men lose careers and lives to a four-second decision made because leaving felt worse than staying, and it never does the next morning.
scenarios.move: Turn your body side-on, keep your hands open and visible, say nothing that answers the question, and move toward people and light. Take the group with you. Report it to security with a description — that is the response that costs him something and costs you nothing.
scenarios.say: Nah, you're alright, mate. — [to your group, walking] We're going. Come on.
scenarios.truth: He is offering you the chance to lose everything in front of an audience. Declining an invitation is not losing a fight.

guides.intro: For every first festival — the guide nobody hands you at the gate.

checks.name: Real Vs Performance
checks.desc: That person seems amazing. They might be. Real = consistent over time. Performance = whatever the weekend needs it to be.

checks.name: Ask Before You Take
checks.desc: Anything going into your body — test it first, know what it is, start small, have a sober friend who knows what you took.

checks.name: Verify Your Exit
checks.desc: Do you know where your camp is right now? Can you get there without help? Fix that before you need it.

checks.name: Everyone Is A Stranger
checks.desc: The veteran who's been coming for 10 years is still a stranger to you. Warmth is not safety. Both can be true.

outline.desc: How they specifically target first-timers
How the environment itself gets used against you
What veteran dependency actually looks like
How to have the best first festival AND stay safe
Finding your real people vs being collected

sentences: Warmth is not the same as safety.
I don't know this person as well as it feels like I do.
Going slowly doesn't mean missing out. It means staying in the game.
I can be open AND have limits. These have always been compatible.

scenarios.archetype: The Veteran Who Makes You Dependent
scenarios.who: The 10-year veteran who adopts you at the gate. Knows every shortcut, every camp, every artist. Makes themselves completely indispensable — and then uses that indispensability to keep you close, compliant, and grateful.
scenarios.scene: You're overwhelmed at the gate — it's bigger than you imagined and your signal is patchy. He appears: eleven years of attendance, knows everyone, perfect camp set up. He walks you in, introduces you to people, knows where everything is. By Day 2 you haven't made a single independent decision about your weekend. By Day 3 when he makes a move you're not comfortable with, saying no feels like losing your entire festival infrastructure.
tells: Makes himself the essential navigator of your experience from the first hour
Festival information — layout, resources, schedule — held close rather than shared freely
Your independence inside the festival decreases over time rather than growing
Any desire to explore alone is gently discouraged as unsafe or naive
scenarios.happening: The "guide" setup mimics genuine mentorship so closely. Real guides give you information and independence. Predatory guides give you access that requires them. The test is simple: after 48 hours with a real mentor, you know more about how to navigate independently. After 48 hours with a predatory guide, you know less — because your navigation runs through them.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “V” CHECK: “Can I get to my camp, the medical tent, and the exit right now without asking him?” — if not, you’re not being guided, you’re being kept.
scenarios.darkTitle: Build Your Own Map In The First Two Hours
scenarios.dark: When you arrive, before anything else, find these four things independently: (1) your camp location with a physical landmark, (2) nearest medical or Harm Reduction tent, (3) nearest Ranger station, (4) two exit points. Do this with your own group, not with a stranger who volunteered to help. Text your camp location to someone not at the festival. Takes 20 minutes and means you never have to depend on a stranger to get home.
scenarios.move: Accept genuine help. Build your own navigation as fast as possible. Independence is the goal.
scenarios.say: Thanks for showing me around — can you point me toward the Harm Reduction tent so I know where it is?
scenarios.truth: A real guide makes you less dependent on them over time. Watch for that.

scenarios.archetype: Pedestal Ploy / The Special Exception
scenarios.who: The one who singles you out as unusually ready, perceptive, or special for a first-timer. The compliment is real and lands hard. It also separates you from other first-timers — your most natural peer group — and attaches your self-image to their approval.
scenarios.scene: "Most people who come for the first time don't get it like you do. You're different." She says it looking right at you and it feels completely true. By the next day you're slightly embarrassed to hang out with the other first-timers because you've been coded as more evolved. You're spending all your time with her crowd — people you've known for 36 hours — and your actual friends are somewhere on the other side of the festival.
tells: "You're not like other first-timers" — your natural peer group gets gently dismissed
The compliment attaches your self-worth to their assessment
You start to distance yourself from your actual friends to match the identity being offered
Your status in their world depends on staying close to them
scenarios.happening: The pedestal ploy separates you from your natural support network by making that network feel beneath the version of yourself they're reflecting back. Other first-timers are your most reliable safety network this weekend. Anyone who positions themselves between you and that solidarity, however flatteringly, is removing your protection.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — "E" CHECK: "This person is still a stranger. Warmth and flattery are not the same thing as safety."
scenarios.darkTitle: Your First-Timer Peer Group Is Your Greatest Asset
scenarios.dark: Other first-timers are your most honest mirrors this weekend — people also navigating the overwhelm, also learning the culture, also figuring it out. The veteran who makes you feel above that is separating you from your strongest source of solidarity. First-timer meetups exist at many festivals — seek them out on Day 1. You don't have to figure this out alone AND you don't have to figure it out through someone who wants something from you.
scenarios.move: Receive the compliment. Stay with your people. Specialness that requires isolation isn't specialness.
scenarios.say: That means a lot — I'm gonna go check in with the people I came with. See you at the set tonight.
scenarios.truth: The people who came with you are your actual family this weekend. Don't let flattery move you away from them.

scenarios.archetype: The Substance Introduction Trap
scenarios.who: The person who introduces you to substances at your first festival — sometimes with genuine generosity, sometimes deliberately. Either way, they become the anchor of your experience, and how that goes shapes your whole weekend.
scenarios.scene: "You've never tried it? Oh you HAVE to — this is literally what the festival is for. Trust me, I've done this hundreds of times, I'll take care of you." You trust him. He seems experienced. You don't test it. You don't know your tolerance. You don't tell your friends what you took or when. Three hours later you're having the worst experience of your life in an unfamiliar place with a person you met 24 hours ago.
tells: Pressured or encouraged to try something new without informed consent and preparation
No discussion of what it is, how much, what to expect, or what your tolerances are
They position themselves as the expert and caretaker — dependency built in
You don't know what you took or when, so you can't get appropriate help if needed
scenarios.happening: First-time substance experiences in festival environments without preparation, testing, or a trusted sober support person are one of the highest-risk situations in the festie world. The person introducing you may have the best intentions and still set you up for a terrible experience. Informed consent means knowing what you're taking, what to expect, having tested it, having someone who knows what and when, and having the Harm Reduction tent location memorized.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “V” CHECK: “Can I get to my camp, the medical tent, and the exit right now without asking him?” — if not, slow down before the moment sweeps you somewhere you didn’t choose.
scenarios.darkTitle: First Time, Unknown Substance, Strangers
scenarios.dark: The highest-risk combination at any festival is a first-timer, an untested substance, and people who do not know your baseline. You have no tolerance, no reference point for what “too much” feels like in your own body, and nobody around you knows what you look like when you are fine. A dose calibrated to someone who has done this two hundred times is not calibrated to you, and the person handing it over is usually estimating rather than measuring. Add the part nobody mentions: the generous stranger who wants to be present for your first time is sometimes exactly that, and is sometimes someone who has learned that a person’s first experience is the easiest one to be in charge of. You are not obligated to make your first festival your first anything else. Test it, halve it, and be with someone who knew you before this weekend.
scenarios.move: Your first experience is yours to set the terms of. Test it, pace it, know your support.
scenarios.say: "I appreciate the offer — I want to make sure I've got my setup right first. Can you help me find the Harm Reduction tent?"
scenarios.truth: Your first time is not something to be swept into. It's something to prepare for.

scenarios.archetype: Hazing as Initiation / Social Proof Pressure
scenarios.clinical: Social Proof Exploitation / Informed Consent Bypass
scenarios.who: The framing that to be a real member of this community you need to do what the community does — and what the community does is whatever this particular person says it does. Your hesitation is framed as naivety or not being ready.
scenarios.scene: "Dude everyone does this here — it's part of the experience. If you don't try it you're not really at the festival, you're just watching it." You haven't slept properly in 36 hours, you're overwhelmed, you're trying to fit in with people who clearly know this world. The social cost of no feels higher than the cost of yes. So you say yes to something you didn't actually want.
tells: "Everyone does this" stated as fact — impossible to verify in the moment
Your hesitation framed as inexperience rather than a valid decision
The initiation happens when you're most overwhelmed and least resourced
Genuine community values invoked to override individual judgment
scenarios.happening: Social proof is one of the most powerful human decision-making shortcuts. First-timers have maximum social uncertainty and minimum local knowledge, making this especially effective. "Everyone does this" is almost never literally true. It's a frame that makes your hesitation seem like an outlier when it's actually just your judgment working correctly. Your hesitation is not naivety. It is your nervous system doing its job.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — "R" CHECK: "Is this real connection — or performance designed to get me to say yes to something?"
scenarios.darkTitle: What Real Festie Culture Actually Looks Like
scenarios.dark: Real festie culture: people share resources freely without expectation of return, consent is asked not assumed, no means no without negotiation, everyone looks out for everyone, harm reduction is celebrated not stigmatized, you can be exactly who you are without pressure to perform. If someone is using "festie culture" to pressure you into something you don't want — they're not representing the culture. They're using it as cover. Real culture includes your right to say no.
scenarios.move: Your hesitation is your nervous system working. It doesn't need to be overridden to prove you belong.
scenarios.say: I'm good for now — I'll figure out my own pace this weekend.
scenarios.truth: "Everyone does it" is a frame, not a fact. Your judgment is allowed to exist here.

scenarios.archetype: The Guardian Who Isn't / Exploiting Overwhelm
scenarios.who: The person who appears exactly when you're most overwhelmed, most lost, most in need of an anchor. Positions themselves as your safe harbor. Uses the relief you feel at being found to establish proximity and trust that then gets leveraged.
scenarios.scene: You got separated from your group Saturday night and your phone died. You're in the wrong part of the festival and you don't know how to get back. He appears — calm, oriented, kind. He walks you somewhere warm, gets you water, sits with you while your portable charger works. An hour later, when he suggests you stay in his camp rather than find your friends, the relief and gratitude are still running the show.
tells: Appears at peak vulnerability: separated, lost, depleted, frightened
Genuine help arrives first — establishing debt before asks are made
Relief and gratitude are still active when the actual ask comes
The suggested next step keeps you in their orbit rather than returning you to yours
scenarios.happening: The rescue hook targets the specific window when you're most resource-depleted and least capable of independent assessment. The help is often genuinely real — which makes the subsequent leverage feel confusing. Gratitude is a genuine human response to being helped. It is not a binding contract. You can thank someone sincerely for real help and still choose to go back to your own people afterward.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “V” CHECK: “Does this person’s help return me to my own people and navigation — or keep me needing them for the next thing too?” — real help ends. It doesn’t renew itself.
scenarios.darkTitle: Dead Phone = Highest Risk Window
scenarios.dark: A dead phone at a festival is one of the most dangerous situations for a first-timer. Before you're ever in this situation: carry a portable charger and keep it topped up. Write your camp location and two friends' numbers in ink on your arm before each day. Know your camp by a physical landmark — not just GPS. Establish a meeting spot your whole group knows. "If we get separated, meet at the big wooden arch at midnight." These are not paranoid. They are just good festie practice.
scenarios.move: Accept real help gratefully. Return to your own people as soon as you're able. Gratitude is not a contract.
scenarios.say: Thank you so much — that was genuinely kind. I'm going to try to find my camp now. Can you point me toward the Rangers?
scenarios.truth: Real help returns you to independence. Watch for that.

scenarios.archetype: Festival Time Distortion / False Familiarity
scenarios.who: Festivals do something strange to time — three days feels like three months. Someone you met 18 hours ago can feel like a person you've known forever. This is real. It is also one of the most consistently exploited features of the festival environment.
scenarios.scene: It's Saturday night and you feel like you've known these people your whole life. The person you've been spending time with feels like one of your closest friends. The intimacy feels earned. You've shared things you've never told people you've known for years. By Sunday when they ask for something you wouldn't normally agree to — a favor, money, something physical — the relationship feels real enough that saying no feels like a betrayal of something genuine.
tells: You feel closer to someone after 48 hours than to people you've known for years
The intimacy feels earned but was created by the environment, not time
Major decisions — financial, physical, logistical — being made in this accelerated time frame
The relationship feels too real to question, which makes you unwilling to slow down
scenarios.happening: Time compression is a documented psychological feature of festival environments — high novelty, altered states, emotional intensity, and social density all compress the felt experience of time. Genuine closeness can develop faster here. Manipulators who know this use the accelerated intimacy deliberately — sharing vulnerably, moving fast, creating the feeling of deep connection — then leveraging that feeling before you've had time to verify it with actual behavior patterns.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — "E" CHECK: "Everyone here is still a stranger to me — warmth and familiarity are not the same as safety."
scenarios.darkTitle: The 72-Hour Rule For First-Timers
scenarios.dark: Here's a simple rule for your first festival: no major decisions in the first 72 hours. That means: no lending significant money, no committing to ongoing arrangements with people you just met, no physical intimacy you haven't verified feeling comfortable about in a sober moment, no leaving the festival with someone you met there. This isn't about not having fun. It's about not making permanent decisions inside temporary conditions.
scenarios.move: Let the connection be real. Don't let the speed be set by the environment rather than you.
scenarios.say: "I'm feeling this — let's stay in touch after the festival and see what this looks like in the regular world."
scenarios.truth: Real connection survives the end of the festival. Manufactured connection requires the festival bubble to sustain it.

scenarios.archetype: Targeting You When You're Most Depleted
scenarios.who: First-time festival attendees experience overwhelm in predictable waves — and predators know exactly when those waves hit. Gates on Day 1, Sunday morning crash, the late-night disorientation period. These are the windows.
scenarios.scene: It's 3am Saturday and you're exhausted, slightly lost, slightly overwhelmed, and running on whatever you took six hours ago. Your friends are somewhere. Your phone is at 12%. Everything is loud and bright and moving and you feel suddenly very small. This is the window. This is when someone who's been watching for you will appear. And they will seem like exactly what you need.
tells: You're at peak overwhelm, exhaustion, or disorientation when they appear
Their offer feels exactly calibrated to what you need in that moment
You have less access to your own judgment than you would in any other context
The "help" requires proximity to them rather than returning you to your group
scenarios.happening: The overwhelm window is predictable and exploitable. Knowing when it's likely to hit — Day 1 arrival chaos, late Saturday night, Sunday morning crash — lets you build support into those specific moments rather than being surprised by them. Your most vulnerable moments don't have to be your least protected ones. That's what pre-planning your support infrastructure is for.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “A” CHECK: “Am I making decisions right now with the same judgment I’d have at 2pm on a Tuesday?” — if not, this isn’t the moment to decide anything.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Predicted Hard Moments At Your First Festival
scenarios.dark: Know these windows are coming: (1) First hour at the gate — overwhelming, plan to walk the grounds with your group before anything else. (2) Late Saturday night — peak exhaustion plus peak substances plus peak crowd. Have a buddy system. (3) Sunday morning — emotional crash, physical depletion, homesickness sometimes. Plan for rest. (4) Load-out day — tired, sad, vulnerable. Be careful about new "connections" in breakdown. Pre-planning support for these moments is what experienced festies do.
scenarios.move: Know your vulnerable windows. Pre-plan support for them. Don't make major decisions inside them.
scenarios.say: I need to find my camp and sleep — if I'm not better in the morning this can wait.
scenarios.truth: Decisions made at your most depleted are not your decisions. They're the depletion's decisions.

scenarios.hook: YOU DON'T NEED YOUR OLD FRIENDS HERE
scenarios.archetype: Social Network Replacement
scenarios.who: The gradual replacement of your actual people with their world. Your old friends become characterized as not on your level, not ready for this, not able to understand. Their crew becomes your crew. Their values become your values.
scenarios.scene: By Day 3 you've barely seen the people you drove up with. Every time you've mentioned them this weekend the veteran has had something slightly dismissive to say — "they seem pretty default world honestly," "they're not really engaging with the deeper experience." His people feel more real now. When your original friends text asking where you are, you feel vaguely embarrassed of them. That shift happened fast.
tells: Your existing friends characterized as less evolved, less open, less real
Their world and people become your primary social context over 48-72 hours
Your pre-festival identity starts to feel naive or lesser than your new festival self
Returning to your original group feels like a step backward
scenarios.happening: Social network replacement feels like growth from the inside. The tell is direction: genuine growth expands your world — you come back from a transformative experience and eventually bring your existing people along. Predatory replacement contracts your world — your existing people get smaller and your connection to this new person gets bigger. Your friends who drove up with you know your full self. They are not the problem.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — "E" CHECK: "My original people are still strangers to this person. My original people actually know me."
scenarios.darkTitle: Transformation Is Real — And It's Not Isolation
scenarios.dark: Festivals genuinely change people. Real transformation happens here. The difference between real transformation and predatory social replacement: real transformation makes you want to bring your people along on the journey, even if they're not ready yet. Predatory replacement makes your people feel like obstacles to your evolution. If you come home from your first festival and your existing friendships feel like a problem — not a growth edge, but a problem — talk to someone outside the festival context about what happened.
scenarios.move: Let the experience expand you. Don't let anyone use the expansion to replace your foundation.
scenarios.say: I need to go spend some time with the people I came with — I'll find you tomorrow.
scenarios.truth: Real growth makes your existing world bigger. It doesn't require deleting it.

scenarios.hook: LET ME SHOW YOU THE REAL FESTIVAL
scenarios.archetype: Access Bait / Exclusive Experience Manipulation
scenarios.who: The veteran who dangles exclusive access — the private camp, the backstage, the "real" experience that regular attendees don't get — as a hook for keeping you in their orbit and dependent on their gatekeeping.
scenarios.scene: "The main stages are for tourists. I'll show you the real festival — the private camps, the underground sets, the people who actually run this thing." By Day 2 you're spending all your time in his exclusive world and it IS more interesting. But you're also completely dependent on him for access to it, you've barely seen the artists you bought tickets to see, and your friends from home feel like they're at a different festival.
tells: The "real" festival is always exclusive and accessible only through them
Your original plans, interests, and friends become positioned as the lesser experience
Access to the exclusive world requires continued closeness and compliance
Independence is implicitly framed as missing out or being too naive to know better
scenarios.happening: Access bait works by making your existing festival experience feel inadequate while positioning the gatekeeper as the key to something better. Your original excitement about the festival — the artists you love, the things you planned — gets subtly devalued. This is manufactured inadequacy. The festival you bought a ticket to is real and full and complete. Anyone who makes you feel like you're missing it by not being in their exclusive world wants something from you.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — "R" CHECK: "Is this person showing me the festival or using the festival to show me I need them?"
scenarios.darkTitle: The Festival You Bought A Ticket To Is Complete
scenarios.dark: First-timers sometimes feel that the "real" experience is happening somewhere they're not. This is manufactured FOMO and it's extremely common. The sets you love, the art installations, the community stages, the random 3am campfire conversations — these are all real. The exclusive private camp is also real but it is not more real. Anyone who makes you feel like you're missing out unless you're with them is using FOMO as a control mechanism. You bought a ticket to a complete festival.
scenarios.move: Explore the whole festival through your own curiosity, not through someone else's selective access.
scenarios.say: Thanks for the tour — I'm going to go catch the set I've been looking forward to. I'll find you later.
scenarios.truth: The festival you bought a ticket to is complete. You don't need a guide to access your own experience.

scenarios.archetype: Camp Recruitment / The Cult Invite
scenarios.who: The camp that seems perfect — tight community, great infrastructure, welcoming energy — and actively recruits first-timers into a structure that is more controlling than it first appears.
scenarios.scene: The camp found you on Friday — fed you, gave you shade, made you feel like you'd found your people. By Saturday they're talking about next year, about the regional events in between, about the "camp family" that extends year-round. It all sounds beautiful. Then you start noticing: people don't really leave the camp, questioning the camp leadership is gently but clearly not done, and the "contribution" expectations are more extensive than you understood when you arrived.
tells: Camp leadership is not accountable in the same ways regular members are
Questioning camp norms or leadership is framed as not being a good fit
Leaving the camp during the festival is subtly discouraged
Commitment to the camp family extends far beyond the weekend without your full understanding
scenarios.happening: Tight community in festival culture is real and beautiful. It also exists on a spectrum that includes high-control groups using festie aesthetics. The tells are always the same: is leadership accountable or above questioning? Are members free to leave? Are contribution expectations defined and mutual? Is dissent welcomed or managed? Real community answers yes to all of these. High-control groups answer no.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “E” CHECK: “Am I free to leave this camp right now, without social cost?” — if that question makes you nervous to even ask, that nervousness is the answer.
scenarios.darkTitle: Real Community Vs High-Control Group — The Tells
scenarios.dark: Real community: leadership is accountable, people come and go freely, dissent is welcomed, contribution expectations are clear and mutual, the community makes you more yourself over time. High-control group: leadership is above questioning, leaving or questioning costs you socially, contribution expectations expand without renegotiation, the community makes you increasingly dependent on it rather than more independent. First-timers are specifically targeted by high-control camp cultures because you're looking for belonging and you don't yet have a reference point.
scenarios.move: Receive the belonging. Verify the freedom. You should be able to leave any camp any time without social consequence.
scenarios.say: This is a beautiful community — I'm going to float and explore a bit and come back. See you at dinner.
scenarios.truth: The community that is right for you will be just as welcoming when you return as when you arrived.

scenarios.archetype: Everything Nobody Tells You at the Gate
scenarios.who: This is the page that should have been in your ticket confirmation email. Practical, unsexy, completely essential. The people who have the best first festivals are the ones who built the infrastructure before they arrived.
scenarios.scene: The best festie veterans you'll meet this weekend have one thing in common: they've thought through what happens when things go sideways. Not because they expect the worst — because having a plan for the worst means you can fully relax into the best. Infrastructure isn't the opposite of magic. It's what makes the magic safe to fully inhabit.
tells: Fentanyl strips + reagent kit in your bag before you arrive — non-negotiable
Physical camp landmark memorized, not just GPS (landmarks survive dead phones)
Two numbers written in pen on your arm: your most reliable friend and your camp lead
Code word established with your group: one text = come find me, no questions asked
scenarios.happening: First festivals are overwhelming by design — enormous, multi-sensory, socially rich. That overwhelm is part of the magic. It's also what makes you most vulnerable to people who know how to exploit it. Every piece of infrastructure you build before you arrive is one less thing someone can use as leverage over you. Charged phone, known camp location, tested substances, trusted contacts: these are not the opposite of freedom. They are freedom.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — "A" CHECK: "Before I take anything: do I know what it is, have I tested it, and does someone sober know?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Harm Reduction Tents — Use Them, They're For You
scenarios.dark: Harm Reduction tents and festival medical staff are not the police. They are specifically there to help without judgment and with confidentiality. They have: free fentanyl test strips and reagent kits, a safe quiet space if you're overwhelmed, trained support for difficult experiences (bad trips, emotional crises), and naloxone for opioid emergencies. You can walk in and say "I took something and I'm not okay" and receive help. That is exactly what they are there for.
scenarios.move: Build the infrastructure. Then put the phone down and be fully in it. That's the move.
scenarios.say: Before we go in — does everyone know where camp is and have the code word?
scenarios.truth: The festies who have the most fun are the ones who planned for when they couldn't plan.

scenarios.hook: BUYING AND SELLING AT YOUR FIRST FEST
scenarios.archetype: Legal Risk, Undercovers, and How to Navigate Safely
scenarios.who: Transactions at festivals — tickets, substances, goods, services — carry real legal risk that first-timers often underestimate. Undercover officers work festivals and look exactly like attendees. This page is about navigating that with eyes open.
scenarios.scene: He's got full kandi, wristbands up both arms, knows the lineup, vibing completely. He finds you and asks if you're looking for anything. He seems like just another attendee. He has the energy of someone who belongs here completely. Something about the sequence of the conversation — the way he guides it, the specificity of his questions — feels slightly scripted. You can't articulate why. But something is off.
tells: They approach YOU rather than you finding them through organic conversation
Unusual interest in quantities or whether you know "anyone else who might be interested"
Wants to meet somewhere private or away from the crowd for any transaction
Something about the interaction feels slightly rehearsed — you can't put your finger on it
scenarios.happening: Undercover officers at festivals are specifically trained to blend in and they're often very good at it. The tells are in the transaction pattern itself: they initiate, they guide toward isolation, they want specificity about quantities, they push pace. You are never obligated to complete any transaction. "Actually I'm good" ends it without incident. Never follow anyone to an isolated location for any reason.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — "A" CHECK: "Am I proceeding with this because I actually want to — or because saying no feels awkward?"
scenarios.darkTitle: If You're Approached By Police Or Detained
scenarios.dark: Know this before you arrive: (1) You have the right to remain silent — use it. "I'd like to speak with a lawyer" is the only thing you say. (2) You can ask if you're being detained or free to go — if free to go, go. (3) You can decline to consent to a search. (4) Do not physically resist any police interaction. (5) Write down badge numbers as soon as possible. Good Samaritan laws protect people seeking help for overdose in most US states — always call for medical help in an overdose situation.
scenarios.move: "Actually I'm good" ends any transaction. Walk toward people. Never go somewhere isolated.
scenarios.say: "Actually I'm good" — then walk. No elaboration. No explanation.
scenarios.truth: No transaction at a festival is worth your freedom.

scenarios.hook: THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN BEING FOUND AND BEING COLLECTED
scenarios.archetype: Real Connection vs Being Recruited
scenarios.who: The festival world is full of people who will genuinely become part of your life and full of people who are collecting you. The difference is not always obvious in the moment. Here's how to tell.
scenarios.scene: Two different people approached you this weekend in a warm way. One of them has shared their food, pointed you toward things you love, introduced you to people without hovering, and seemed genuinely happy when you went off to explore independently. The other has kept you close, subtly steered you away from other people, and seems slightly off when you exercise independence. Same warm opening energy. Very different underlying dynamic.
tells: Real connection: glad when you explore independently, makes your world bigger
Real connection: introduces you to others without monitoring those relationships
Real connection: their warmth doesn't fluctuate based on your compliance
Collection: needs you close, subtly discourages independence, warmth fluctuates with compliance
scenarios.happening: The difference between genuine connection and being collected is not visible in the opening — it becomes visible in how the person responds to your independence. Genuine connectors are happy when you flourish without them. They celebrate your other connections. They don't need to be the center of your festival experience. Collectors need your orbit. They need your dependency. They need to be the source of your experience. Watch for that distinction over a full day.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “R” CHECK: “Is this person’s warmth consistent whether I’m being compliant or independent?” — that’s the whole test.
scenarios.darkTitle: How To Find Your Real Festival Family
scenarios.dark: Real festival family is found through shared experiences with no agenda: the spontaneous conversation at a water station, the people around you at a set who are moved by the same moment, the mutual help during a logistical challenge. It develops through repeated small interactions over the course of the festival where each person is free to come and go. It doesn't start with someone targeting you specifically or making you feel specially chosen. It starts with just being next to each other in the same experience.
scenarios.move: Notice how people respond when you exercise independence. That's the most honest information you'll get about them.
scenarios.say: "I'm going to go wander for a bit — I'll find you later." Then notice what happens.
scenarios.truth: Your real festival family will be just as glad to see you after you've been elsewhere. Watch for that.

scenarios.hook: LET ME SHOW YOU HOW THIS WORKS
scenarios.archetype: The Veteran Guide / Experience As A Leash
scenarios.who: Been coming for nine years. Knows the site, the shortcuts, the sound guy, the good stage at 2am. Attached himself at the gate and has been indispensable ever since, which is not the same as being kind.
scenarios.scene: He has been right about everything. The queue, the water point, the set you'd have missed. He is genuinely good company and the weekend is better for him. On Saturday your friends want to go to the far stage and he says they'll get lost, that they don't know this place, that you should stay with him — and you notice you are about to agree with somebody you met on Thursday over people you have known for years.
tells: Is the only route to information, and keeps it that way
Corrects or subtly mocks your own crew's plans
“You don't know this place yet” used to close down your decisions
Positions himself between you and the people you came with
Generous with access, but the access always runs through him
Reacts to you making independent plans as though it were a mistake he must fix
scenarios.happening: Every first-timer needs a guide and most veterans are exactly that — the scene runs on people cheerfully handing down what they know. The pattern to watch for is not helpfulness, it is exclusivity: a guide who wants you competent teaches you the site, and a guide who wants you dependent stays the site. Asymmetric knowledge is the lever, and at your first festival the asymmetry is total, which is why this is a first-timer's chapter. The test is direction of travel: by Sunday, do you know more, or do you need him more?
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “V” CHECK: “Could I get back to my own camp, right now, without him?” If the answer is no on day three, that is not experience. That is a leash.
scenarios.darkTitle: Competence Is What A Real Guide Gives You
scenarios.dark: The specific thing to watch is what he does with your own people. A veteran who separates a first-timer from the friends they arrived with — gently, reasonably, always with a practical justification — has done the single most consequential thing in this entire book, because every other protection you have is made of those people. It rarely looks like an instruction. It looks like a better plan, offered by someone who knows the site, at a moment when you cannot evaluate it. And it is worth knowing that the genuinely good veterans do the exact opposite: they teach you the map and then send you off with your mates, because the whole point was for you to be able to do this without them.
scenarios.move: Learn the site yourself on day one — walk it, pin your camp, find medical and the water points. Take the help and then go use it with your own crew. If someone objects to you being independent, that objection is the whole finding.
scenarios.say: Cheers, that's really useful — I'm going to go find the others and we'll try the far stage. Catch you later.
scenarios.truth: A real guide makes you not need them by Sunday. Watch which direction the weekend is travelling in.

scenarios.archetype: The Ticket That Does Not Scan
scenarios.who: A stranger outside the gate, or a friendly account in a resale group who has been messaging you for a fortnight. Plausible, apologetic, in a hurry, and about to be unreachable.
scenarios.scene: It sold out and this was the only way. The PDF looked real. The bank transfer went to a name slightly different from the account you were talking to, which he explained. You are now at the gate, four hundred miles from home, with your camping gear on your back, watching a scanner go red, and the number you have been messaging is no longer receiving messages.
tells: Bank transfer, crypto, or a friends-and-family payment — all irreversible
The account name does not match the person you have been talking to
Urgency about deciding, and a reason resale platforms cannot be used
A screenshot or PDF rather than a transfer through the official system
Price is below face value, or a surprisingly simple explanation for why
They want to meet outside the gate rather than transfer in advance
scenarios.happening: Ticket fraud spikes for sold-out events and targets first-timers because they do not know that the only safe routes are the official resale platform or a transfer inside the ticketing system — both of which make the fraud impossible rather than merely detectable. A PDF proves nothing: the same barcode can be sold to nine people and the first through the gate is the only one who gets in. Irreversible payment is the tell that matters most, because it is chosen for exactly that property, and because a card payment would have given you a chargeback.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “V” CHECK: “Is this going through the official resale system, and can I reverse the payment?” Two noes means it is not a ticket, it is a donation.
scenarios.darkTitle: Stranded Is The Second Problem
scenarios.dark: The money is not the worst of it. A first-timer at a rural gate with no ticket, no phone signal, no accommodation, a tent, and no way home until the coach on Monday is a genuinely vulnerable person, and there are people at every gate who understand that perfectly. Offers of somewhere to sleep, a way in, or a lift arrive quickly and some of them are exactly what they look like and some are not. So decide the fallback before you travel: what you do, who you call, and how you get home if you do not get in. Nobody expects to need that plan, and the people who needed it always wished they had made it.
scenarios.move: Buy from the official seller or the event's own resale platform. If you already have a private ticket, pay by card or a service with buyer protection, never by bank transfer, and verify the ticket through the ticketing company before you travel. Have a get-home plan and the money for it, kept separate.
scenarios.say: Happy to buy it if you transfer it through the official system — I don't do PDFs or bank transfers, I've been burned. — I'll pay by card with protection or not at all.
scenarios.truth: A screenshot is not a ticket. If the payment cannot be reversed, that is the reason they chose it.

scenarios.hook: MY PHONE'S DEAD AND I DON'T KNOW WHERE ANYONE IS
scenarios.archetype: The Predictable Crisis Nobody Plans For
scenarios.who: Not a person — the standard second evening of a first festival. Eighty thousand people, no signal, four percent battery, a camp that all looks the same, and the growing realization that you do not actually know where you are.
scenarios.scene: You got separated at the changeover. Your phone died twenty minutes ago. You cannot remember whether the camp is left or right of the big flag, all the flags look the same in the dark, and you have just discovered that you do not know a single person's phone number by heart because you have never needed to.
tells: No meeting point was ever agreed, because everyone assumed phones
You do not know anyone's number without your phone
Your camp has no distinguishing landmark you could describe
No power bank, and the charging tent has a two-hour queue
You have started walking to look for them, which makes it worse
You have been drinking, it is dark, and you are now alone
scenarios.happening: This is the single most common bad night at a first festival, and it is entirely preventable with about four minutes of Thursday planning. It matters beyond inconvenience because it produces exactly the state every predatory pattern in this guide needs: a visibly lost, overwhelmed, slightly drunk newcomer with no way to contact anyone, wandering a dark site. The help that arrives is usually genuine. The point is not to need to rely on whoever it happens to be.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “V” CHECK: “If my phone died right now, could I get back to my camp and reach my people?” That is a Thursday question with a Thursday answer.
scenarios.darkTitle: Lost And New Is The Target Profile
scenarios.dark: If you read only one line of this guide, read this one: the state described above is the exact profile that the approaches in the first nine pages of this guide are written for. Overwhelmed, isolated, uncontactable, unable to verify anything anybody tells you, and grateful to the first person who is kind. That is not an argument for being frightened of strangers, most of whom will genuinely help you. It is an argument for making sure that you are never in the position of having to take whatever help appears, because you have a meeting point, a written number, and a charged phone.
scenarios.move: On Thursday: agree a physical meeting point and a fallback time with your group, photograph your tent and a landmark near it, write two phone numbers and your camp location on paper in your pocket, and carry two charged power banks. If it happens anyway: go to the meeting point and stay there, or to welfare, and do not wander.
scenarios.say: Before we split up — if anyone loses everyone, the big oak by the water point, on the hour. Everyone got that? Write it on your arm.
scenarios.truth: Phones die at festivals. Plan for the version of the weekend where yours already has.

scenarios.archetype: Everything You Own In An Unlockable Bag
scenarios.who: Mostly opportunists working the campsites during headline sets, when the fields empty out and thousands of tents stand unattended for two hours. Occasionally someone who has been watching your camp specifically since Thursday.
scenarios.scene: Everyone said the campsite was safe and mostly it is and you believed it, so your passport, your bank card, your keys and your spare phone are in your tent, which is closed with a zip that a child could open, while you are a mile away watching the headliner along with everybody else in the field.
tells: Valuables kept in a tent, which is a bag, not a room
Nobody in your camp stays behind during the big sets
Your camp is on a main thoroughfare or at the edge
Someone unfamiliar has been friendly about which sets you are going to
No photographs of your gear, no serial numbers, no contents insurance
You are carrying every card you own rather than one
scenarios.happening: Campsite theft is almost entirely opportunistic and almost entirely timed — it happens during the headline sets, when the campsite is empty and nobody will be back for hours. The advice that the campsite is safe is broadly true and slightly dangerous, because it is true about people and not about opportunity. The practical loss is rarely the phone; it is the passport, the car keys, the bank cards and the house keys, which turn a stolen bag into a genuinely hard week rather than an annoying one.
scenarios.check: R.A.V.E. — “A” CHECK: “What is in my tent right now that I could not get home without?” Whatever that is should not be in there.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Keys Are Worse Than The Phone
scenarios.dark: Think past the value of the objects. Car keys taken from a tent mean somebody knows there is a vehicle in that car park and now has the means to open it. House keys plus a driving licence or an addressed letter in the same bag mean somebody has your address and your keys, and you are four hours from home and will not be back for two days.
