That is the version worth preventing, and it is prevented by separation rather than by security: cards, keys and documents split across your body, the car, and a locker, so that no single loss is catastrophic.
scenarios.move: Rent the locker — it is the best value item at any festival. Keep one bank card and a photo of your ID on you, leave the passport at home unless the event requires it, and never keep house keys and your address in the same place. Photograph your gear before you travel.
scenarios.say: I'm doing a locker for the cards and keys — anyone want to split one? — Someone's always at camp during the headliner, let's rota it.
scenarios.truth: A tent is a bag with a zip. Anything you cannot get home without does not live in a bag with a zip.

guides.intro: You do not need a substance to be here and you never did. This guide is about the people who need you to be the exception.

checks.name: Sober Is Not An Explanation You Owe
checks.desc: “I'm good” is a complete sentence. Anyone who requires the story behind it is asking for something other than information.

checks.name: Open Containers Are Not Yours
checks.desc: You do not accept a drink you did not watch being made. This is the same rule everyone should follow, and for you the consequences are larger.

checks.name: Being The Reliable One Has A Price
checks.desc: The sober friend gets handed everything. Care is a gift you choose, not a duty assigned to you because you are the one who remembers the night.

checks.name: Exit Before The Turn
checks.desc: Every night has an hour where it changes. Yours is earlier than theirs. Leaving early is not missing out, it is how you get the next twenty years of this.

checks.name: Relapse Is Not A Character Verdict
checks.desc: If it happens, it is a medical and practical event with a next step. It is not proof of anything about who you are — and shame is what keeps people from the next step.

outline.desc: The convincer, the spiked drink, sobriety as a target
Being assigned the care role, the FOMO squeeze, the hour the night turns
Engineered relapse as leverage, being outed, the shame spiral
The festival sober plan, drink discipline, the people you find first
Sober scene inside the scene — where it already exists and how to find it

sentences: “I'm good” is the whole sentence. There is no second half.
I pour it, I carry it, or I don't drink it.
I am not this group's designated adult unless I agreed to be.
I leave before the turn, and I am not apologizing for it.
If I slip, the next step is a phone call, not a verdict.

scenarios.archetype: The Convincer / Your Sobriety As Their Problem
scenarios.who: Usually not malicious. Frequently drunk. Genuinely believes he is being welcoming, and is also, underneath it, uncomfortable that somebody nearby is not doing what he is doing. Persistent in a way he would not be about anything else.
scenarios.scene: Fourth time tonight. He is holding it out again, doing the thing where he waggles it slightly, saying he is not trying to pressure you but it is a festival, and asking — warmly, in front of five people — what actually happened, like your sobriety is a story he is owed and the story will settle whether your no is reasonable.
tells: Asks more than once after a clear answer
Wants the reason, and frames your reason as the thing that would justify the no
Does it in front of an audience, so declining has a social cost
Reframes your boundary as a mood you could be talked out of
“Just this once”, “it's a festival”, “you're no fun like this”
Gets cold or wounded when the fourth no lands
scenarios.happening: The pressure is usually about him rather than about you — a person drinking heavily next to someone who is not is being handed an unwelcome mirror, and the fastest way to put the mirror down is to get you to join. That does not make it harmless. Repeated asking is how boundaries get worn rather than broken, and the reason-demand is the actual move: once you are explaining, you are in a negotiation, and negotiations have outcomes. You are not in a negotiation. The most effective response is also the most boring one, which is the same three words, at the same volume, indefinitely, with no new information added.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “S” CHECK: “Am I explaining?” The moment you start supplying reasons, you have accepted that your no needs approving. It does not.
scenarios.darkTitle: Some Of Them Know Exactly What You Are
scenarios.dark: Most of the people doing this are just drunk. A few are not, and the difference shows in what they do with the information once you give it. Someone who learns you are in recovery and keeps pushing is not being socially clumsy — they have been told there is a specific cost to you and have decided it is worth it, and a person who wants somebody impaired has just found the one person here whose impairment would come with built-in silence. This is why the reason is worth keeping to yourself in a crowd. Not shame — information discipline. Your recovery is not a secret; it is also not something to hand to a stranger who has already ignored three noes.
scenarios.move: Repeat the same three words with no escalation and no new content, and move your body — turn a shoulder, go get water, join a different conversation. Broken-record plus physical exit ends it faster than any argument, because there is nothing to push against.
scenarios.say: I'm good. — I'm good. — I'm good, mate. Anyway, has anyone seen Priya?
scenarios.truth: Your no does not improve with an explanation attached. “I'm good” is already the strongest version of it.

scenarios.archetype: The Handed Drink / Why This Rule Is Not Paranoia
scenarios.who: Anyone holding a cup you did not watch being filled. Usually a friend being kind. Occasionally not — and the second category is why the rule has to apply to the first, because you cannot tell them apart by looking.
scenarios.scene: Someone hands you a lemonade. They are being nice, they know you do not drink, they went and got it specially. Refusing it feels ungrateful and slightly insulting and like you are accusing a friend of something. It also costs nothing, and the alternative — a drink you cannot vouch for, in a body with no tolerance, in front of people who will later say you seemed fine — costs a great deal.
tells: A drink arriving already poured, that you did not see made
Insistence when you set it down or ask for a sealed one
Attention to whether and how much you are drinking it
“It's only soft” as an argument for skipping the rule
Someone treating the rule as an accusation rather than a policy
Any drink left unattended, including yours, including for a minute
scenarios.happening: The most common drink adulterant is alcohol added to something someone believes is soft, which matters enormously here: for a sober or in-recovery person that is not a lesser version of spiking, it is the specific harm. Zero tolerance means a small dose lands hard, and the aftermath is not only physical — it can register internally as a relapse, with all the shame that carries, even though nothing about it was chosen. The rule is the same one this whole book gives everyone: you pour it, you watch it poured, or you carry it sealed. The difference is that for you the failure mode includes losing your sense of your own recovery.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “O” CHECK: “Did I watch this being made, or open it myself?” If not, it is not a drink, it is an unknown.
scenarios.darkTitle: When It Registers As A Relapse
scenarios.dark: Here is the part worth having read in advance, because it matters in the hour it happens: if you are dosed without knowing, that is not a relapse. It is an assault. Your body may not distinguish, your recovery community's language may not distinguish, and at four in the morning you will absolutely not distinguish — which is exactly why a person who wanted you compliant and quiet would choose this method. The shame does the silencing for them. Decide now, while it is hypothetical: if it happens, the first call is to somebody in your recovery network and the second is to medical, and neither of those calls is a confession. Say it out loud once so the sober version of you has already made the ruling.
scenarios.move: Carry your own, sealed, and open it yourself. Decline anything handed to you already poured, cheerfully and as a blanket policy rather than as a judgment of the person offering. If you set a drink down, it is finished.
scenarios.say: Ah, cheers — I've got a weird rule where I only drink stuff I've opened myself, nothing personal. I'll grab one with you though.
scenarios.truth: Being dosed is not drinking. Decide that now, in daylight, so you are not deciding it at four in the morning.

scenarios.archetype: The Designated Adult / Care Assigned Rather Than Chosen
scenarios.who: The whole group, gradually and without a conversation. Because you are the one who is sober, you become the one with the keys, the map, the phone battery, the plan, the medical decisions, and everybody's emergency.
scenarios.scene: It is two in the morning and you are walking a stranger to medical because you are the only one upright enough to do it. This is the third night running. You came here for the music and you have seen about forty minutes of it, and somebody said earlier, as a compliment, that it is so good having you around because you always know what to do.
tells: You hold the keys, the cash, the phones, the plan — by default, never by agreement
Your sobriety is described as a resource the group has
You have not seen the sets you came for
Other people's medical decisions keep landing on you
Nobody has asked whether you want this role
Resenting it makes you feel like a bad friend, so you do not mention it
scenarios.happening: Care work assigned by default rather than agreement is a well-documented route to burnout, and the festival version is unusually total: you are the group's driver, medic, treasurer, and institutional memory simultaneously, at exactly the time of year you came to enjoy yourself. It matters more than it sounds. Resentment plus exhaustion plus not having had any of the thing you came for is a genuinely recognized relapse-risk combination, and it builds quietly because the role arrives as a compliment. Choosing to look after your people is one of the good things about being the sober one. Being silently conscripted is not the same act.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “B” CHECK: “Did I agree to this role, or was it assigned to me because I'm the one who'll remember?” Those produce the same behaviour and completely different costs.
scenarios.darkTitle: Resentment Is A Relapse Risk, Not A Character Flaw
scenarios.dark: The dangerous sequence is specific and it is worth being able to see coming: you do the caretaking, you miss the festival, you start resenting people you love, you feel guilty about the resentment because they are your friends and you chose this, and the guilt stops you saying any of it out loud. Depleted, resentful, isolated inside a group, and unable to name it — that is the state, and in recovery terms it is a familiar and serious one. Nobody engineered it. It assembled itself out of everyone's good intentions and the fact that you are reliable. The fix is a conversation on Tuesday, not heroism on Saturday.
scenarios.move: Rotate it explicitly before the event — a named driver, a named phone-holder, a named person on duty each night, sober or not. Then take the sets you came for and say so in advance so it is a plan rather than an abandonment.
scenarios.say: I'm not on duty tonight — I'm watching the whole set, phone on if it's an emergency. Who's got the keys? Let's actually rota this.
scenarios.truth: Being sober makes you capable of holding everyone. It does not make you responsible for it. Those are different sentences.

scenarios.hook: NOBODY NEEDS TO KNOW ABOUT THIS
scenarios.archetype: The Engineered Slip / Relapse As Leverage
scenarios.who: Someone who learned what your sobriety means to you and filed it. Manufactures the slip, or simply waits for one, and then becomes the only person who knows about it — which is the actual objective.
scenarios.scene: It happened. However it happened, it happened, and he was there, and now he is being extraordinarily kind about it. He says it stays between you. He says he understands, no judgment, everyone slips. He says it about four times over the next two days, in a way that is comforting the first time and something else by the fourth.
tells: Present for the slip, and unusually relaxed about it
Immediately frames it as a secret the two of you now share
Repeats the reassurance more often than reassurance requires
Discourages you from telling your sponsor, your partner, your people
Your recovery network is described as judgmental or as not understanding festivals
Small asks start arriving, and declining them feels newly complicated
scenarios.happening: A secret held by one other person is leverage whether or not anyone ever names it, and shame is the most reliable silencer there is because the person being controlled does the work themselves. This is why isolation from your recovery network is the tell to watch rather than any explicit threat — the threat is never made, it does not need to be. Coercive control research finds this shape consistently: cut the person off from the relationships that would give them a competing account of themselves, then be the only one who knows the worst thing. What makes recovery a target is simply that the worst thing is already pre-loaded and everyone knows how much it costs you.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “R” CHECK: “Is there something about me only one person here knows?” That is not intimacy. That is a holding.
scenarios.darkTitle: Disclosure Is How You Disarm It
scenarios.dark: The single move that ends this is the one that feels impossible: tell someone else. The leverage exists only while the information is scarce, and it evaporates the moment a second person knows — not because the slip stops mattering, but because he is no longer the only one holding it. Recovery communities are unusually good at exactly this; a slip disclosed is an ordinary event with a known next step, and everyone in your network has either had one or sat with somebody who did. The person telling you they will keep it between you is not protecting you from judgment. They are protecting the scarcity. Call your sponsor tonight, not when you feel ready — feeling ready is the thing the shame is preventing.
scenarios.move: Break the exclusivity immediately: tell one person in your recovery network today, before the story gets any older. Then treat the slip as a practical event with a next step — that is all it is — and put distance between you and whoever wanted to hold it.
scenarios.say: I'm telling my sponsor, so it's not staying between us — that's not how I do this. — [to your person] It happened Saturday. I'm okay. I wanted you to know before it got old.
scenarios.truth: A secret with one keeper is a lever. Hand it to a second person and it stops being one.

scenarios.archetype: Twenty Minutes That Hold All Weekend
scenarios.who: For anyone sober, in recovery, California sober, taking a break, or just not drinking this weekend. Made in advance, in a calm room, by a version of you who is not tired, lonely, or three days into a field.
scenarios.scene: Tuesday, twenty minutes, a notes app. Everything that will be hard on Saturday night is currently something you can solve in one line. On Saturday night it will not be, because the whole difficulty of Saturday night is that it takes away the part of you that makes plans.
tells: Your line, decided now: what you drink, what you never accept, what ends the night
The hour you leave — an actual time, set before you arrive
Two people on site who know you are sober and will not make it a thing
One person off-site who picks up at any hour, tested before you travel
The sober meetings on site, located Thursday — the Rats, the Phellowship, the sober camp
What you do if you slip: who you call, in what order. Written down.
scenarios.happening: Relapse prevention planning is the most evidence-backed piece of self-management in recovery, and its whole logic is pre-commitment — a decision made in a regulated state, handed to a depleted one, so the hard moment only requires following rather than deciding. A festival concentrates every known risk factor into seventy-two hours: sleep loss, crowds, availability, loneliness inside a group, and the specific ache of watching people you love have an experience you have chosen not to have. None of that means you should not go. It means you go with a plan, the way you would go anywhere else that mattered.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “E” CHECK: “Do I know what time I'm leaving tonight, and who I call if it gets hard?” Two answers, decided before you arrive.
scenarios.darkTitle: Write The Slip Plan While You Are Fine
scenarios.dark: Write the what-if-I-slip page now, while it is theoretical and slightly embarrassing to be writing. The reason is simple and it is the thing that kills people: after a slip, shame closes the exact channels you need, and the plan you did not write is not a plan you will invent at four in the morning while believing you are a fraud. Two names and an order of calls, written down on a Tuesday by someone who was fine, is a message from a version of you that your Saturday self will not be able to argue with. Nobody who writes that page is planning to use it. Everyone who needed it was glad it existed.
scenarios.move: Write the six lines. Send the off-site person a message before you travel so they know they are on. Find the sober meeting on Thursday, before you need it — walking in on Saturday when it is hard is a much bigger ask than walking in on Thursday when it is not.
scenarios.say: I'm out by one tonight, that's fixed. — You're my call this weekend if it gets hard, is that alright? I probably won't need it, I just want it arranged.
scenarios.truth: The plan is not a prediction. It is Tuesday-you leaving instructions for Saturday-you, who will not be able to work it out alone.

scenarios.hook: THERE ARE MORE OF US THAN YOU THINK
scenarios.archetype: The Sober Scene Inside The Scene
scenarios.who: The Wharf Rats with the yellow balloons. The Phellowship. The sober camp with the coffee urn. The Zendo volunteers. The ones who have been coming for thirty years and have not had a drink for twenty-five of them.
scenarios.scene: You assume you are the only one. You are not remotely the only one — there is a meeting on this site, probably daily, probably signposted with a yellow balloon or a hand-lettered board, and the people at it have been navigating exactly this weekend for longer than you have been alive. Most of them found it the same way, which is late, having assumed the same thing you are assuming.
tells: Yellow balloons at the back of the crowd — that is the Wharf Rats, and it is an invitation
A meeting board, a sober camp, a coffee urn where a bar would be
Harm reduction volunteers, a lot of whom are sober themselves
People who clock your soda and say nothing, which is the good sign
Real: nobody asks for your story as the price of entry
Real: you can go, say nothing, drink the coffee, and leave
scenarios.happening: Sober infrastructure inside festival culture is decades old and largely invisible unless you are looking for it — the Wharf Rats go back to the early eighties, the Phellowship not much later, and most large festivals now have something. The reason it matters more than any individual tactic in this guide is that isolation is the common factor underneath every pattern here: the convincer works on someone with no one to turn to, the assigned care role works on someone who does not know other sober people are around, and the engineered slip works on someone cut off from their network. Finding these people on Thursday removes the precondition for all three at once.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “B” CHECK: “Do I know where the sober meeting is on this site — today, not hypothetically?” Find it before you need it. That is the whole page.
scenarios.darkTitle: Isolation Is The Shared Precondition
scenarios.dark: Go back through this guide and the same thing is underneath every page. The convincer is only effective on somebody standing alone. The care role only becomes total when nobody else here is sober. The slip becomes leverage only when one person is the only one who knows. Every single mechanism requires you to be the exception in the room — which is exactly the belief you arrived with, and exactly the belief that a hand-lettered board at the back of the field disproves in about ninety seconds. Find them Thursday. Not because you are fragile, but because being findable is what makes the rest of this book mostly theoretical for you.
scenarios.move: Locate the meeting, the sober camp, or the balloons in your first few hours on site, and go once when things are fine. Tell two people in your group you are sober so it is ordinary rather than a revelation at a bad moment. Then have the weekend you came for.
scenarios.say: Any sober meeting on site this year? — Just so you know, I don't drink, it's not a whole thing, I'm just easier to find at the coffee than the bar.
scenarios.truth: You are not the only sober person at this festival. You are the only one who has not found the others yet, and that takes about ten minutes.

scenarios.archetype: Accidental Exposure / The Brownie, The Vape, The Shared Bottle
scenarios.who: Nobody hostile. A camp full of people who forgot, or who genuinely did not consider that the tray of brownies needed a label, or that the vape going round has more in it than nicotine.
scenarios.scene: You ate one thing from the communal table because you were starving and it was food. Forty minutes later you know. You are sitting in a camp chair doing arithmetic about whether this counts, whether you have to tell anyone, whether your sponsor will think you engineered it, and whether your sobriety date has just moved — and none of that arithmetic is helping with the part where you are currently high and did not agree to be.
tells: Unlabelled food on a communal table
A vape, joint or bottle passed round with no statement of contents
Nobody in the camp thinks to mention it because everybody else knows
A drink topped up rather than handed over
You are the only sober person and the camp has not adjusted anything
The first you hear of it is somebody laughing about it afterwards
scenarios.happening: Accidental ingestion at festivals is common and it is a labelling failure rather than an attack — which does not make it less serious for you. Edibles are the usual route because they are food-shaped and the onset is delayed enough that you have eaten it before anyone could have told you. The practical harm is real — being involuntarily altered removes your capacity in an environment where you are frequently the person others are relying on — and the internal harm can be larger, because it lands as a relapse in a body that cannot tell the difference.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “O” CHECK: “Do I know what is in this, from the person who made it?” Communal food counts. This is the rule the book gives everybody, applied to a plate.
scenarios.darkTitle: It Is Not A Relapse, And Decide That Now
scenarios.dark: Settle this in advance, in daylight, because at the time you will not be able to. Being dosed without agreeing to it is an exposure, not a use — there was no decision, so there is nothing to have relapsed from. Recovery frameworks vary in language but not in substance on this, and every sponsor you could call has fielded it. The danger is not the substance, it is the forty-eight hours afterwards, when shame says you are a fraud, that you must have known, that you cannot tell anyone — and that is the state that turns an accident into an actual return to use. Ring your person that night, not when you feel ready.
scenarios.move: Eat from your own supply at camp and ask about anything communal before it reaches your hand. Ask the camp once, openly, on Thursday to label things. If it happens: get somewhere safe with a person, hydrate, ride it out, and call your recovery contact the same day.
scenarios.say: Quick one before we settle in — I'm sober, so can we label anything with stuff in it? Doesn't have to be a whole thing, just a note on the tray.
scenarios.truth: You did not decide, so you did not relapse. Call your person the same night, before shame writes a different version.

scenarios.archetype: The Rotation / Declining The Same Thing Forty Times
scenarios.clinical: Repeated Refusal Fatigue / Social Ritual Pressure
scenarios.who: The circle itself. The joint, the bottle, the balloon, the vape — a physical object moving clockwise, arriving at you every few minutes, requiring a small public decision each time, for six hours.
scenarios.scene: It is not one refusal, it is the fortieth, and by the fortieth you have stopped saying anything and started doing the small hand movement, and somebody has noticed and said something kind about it which made it worse, and you are now thinking about leaving a fire you were enjoying because the geometry of the circle has made your sobriety the most visible thing about you all night.
tells: The object physically arrives at you on a loop
Each pass is a small public moment you have to handle
Somebody kindly announces your sobriety on your behalf
The circle re-forms around you in a way that makes leaving obvious
You are exhausted by evening and cannot say why
You have started avoiding fires you actually like
scenarios.happening: Refusal fatigue is real and underrated: the cost of any single no is negligible and the cost of forty is significant, particularly when each one happens in front of people and requires a micro-decision about tone. It is also the mechanism by which sober people quietly stop going to the parts of a festival they enjoy most, which produces exactly the isolation that everything else in this guide warns about. The circle is not doing anything to you. The geometry is doing it, and geometry can be changed.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “B” CHECK: “Am I avoiding somewhere I like because of the effort of being there?” That is the cost showing up, and it is fixable without leaving.
scenarios.darkTitle: Do Not Let It Push You Out
scenarios.dark: The outcome to prevent is not any single awkward pass, it is the slow withdrawal — skipping the fire, skipping the camp, spending the weekend at the edges, and ending up alone at a festival, which is the precondition for every pattern in this guide. That withdrawal is invisible while it happens because each individual decision is reasonable. If you find yourself three nights in and mostly on your own, that is not you being antisocial; it is forty small refusals adding up. Fix the mechanics rather than removing yourself: sit at the end of the arc, hold your own cup, and let one friend know to pass it over you.
scenarios.move: Change the geometry — sit at the end of the rotation rather than mid-circle, keep both hands busy with your own drink, and ask one friend to skip you so the object never arrives. Pre-empt once, lightly, at the start of the night, so nobody announces it for you later.
scenarios.say: Pass it over me all night, saves us both forty conversations. — [holding up your cup] I'm sorted, cheers.
scenarios.truth: Forty small refusals cost more than one big one. Move your chair rather than leaving the fire.

scenarios.archetype: The Medication Auditor / Policing Your Prescription
scenarios.who: Somebody in your own corner — a recovery acquaintance, a camp mate who is proud of you, occasionally someone with a strong opinion about a programme — who has appointed themselves the judge of whether your sobriety counts.
scenarios.scene: You take your prescribed medication in front of the camp, as you do every day, and somebody asks what it is. Then asks whether that is allowed. Then says, not unkindly, that they thought you were clean, and you find yourself standing in a field defending a prescription to a person with no medical training and considerable confidence.
tells: Being asked to justify a prescription socially
Talk of being properly clean, or real sobriety
Your psychiatric or substitution medication discussed as a loophole
Pressure to reduce or stop, from someone who is not your prescriber
You have started taking your meds privately to avoid the conversation
The same person is relaxed about their own caffeine, nicotine or painkillers
scenarios.happening: Medication-assisted treatment and psychiatric prescriptions are medicine, and the evidence for them is strong — but purity narratives inside some recovery cultures treat them as a compromised form of sobriety, and the result is people quietly skipping doses to stay socially legitimate. That is the actual harm here and it is a serious one: interrupted psychiatric medication at a festival, with no sleep and heavy sensory load, is a genuine risk of crisis, and interrupted substitution treatment carries a risk of return to use with reduced tolerance.
scenarios.check: S.O.B.E.R. — “R” CHECK: “Has my prescriber said this is fine?” That is the only opinion in this conversation that has any standing.
scenarios.darkTitle: Hiding Doses Is How This Hurts You
scenarios.dark: Watch for the behavioural tell rather than the argument: the moment you start taking your medication where nobody can see, you have accepted that it is shameful, and skipping becomes easy from there. That is the sequence that lands people in a medical tent on Sunday or in a crisis three weeks later, and it starts with one well-meaning question in a field. Your prescriber knows your history, knows what you are taking and knows why. Nobody in that circle does. If somebody keeps pushing after a flat answer, that is not concern about your recovery, it is a person who needs your compliance to feel right about their own framework.
scenarios.move: Answer once, flatly, and do not debate. Take your meds on schedule, in the open, on the same routine you use at home. Tell one person in your camp what they are and what to do if you are unwell, so the information exists somewhere useful.
scenarios.say: It's prescribed, my doctor's across it, and I'm not discussing the dose. — Setting an alarm for it, same as at home.
scenarios.truth: The only person qualified to audit your prescription is the one who wrote it. Take it in the open and on time.

guides.intro: The scene calls itself a family. This guide is about the weekends where that is completely true and the moments where it is not — and about having a plan for both.

checks.name: Read The Room Before It Reads You
checks.desc: Who is here, who is staff, who would be believed. Knowing the answer on Thursday is worth more than deciding it at two in the morning.

checks.name: Ownership Of Your Body And Your Hair
checks.desc: Nobody touches you without asking. Not your hair, not your skin, not for a photo. Being at a festival is not a waiver.

checks.name: Options That Do Not Assume Police
checks.desc: The standard escalation ladder ends at security and police. Yours may need to stop earlier. Build the ladder that is actually safe for you.

checks.name: Tokenizing Is An Opening Move
checks.desc: Exoticization, the compliment about your look, the fascination — these are approaches. Warmth aimed at a category is not warmth aimed at you.

checks.name: Solidarity Is Findable
checks.desc: Affinity camps, crews and regulars exist at nearly every festival. Finding them on day one changes the whole weekend.

outline.desc: Fetishization as an approach, tokenizing warmth, the collector
Hypervisibility, unsolicited touch, colorblind framing that erases what happened
Security called on you, being disbelieved, escalation routes that are not safe
The escalation ladder you can actually use, documentation, the anchor crew
Affinity space, real solidarity, and the festivals that get it right

sentences: Warmth aimed at a category is not warmth aimed at me.
Nobody touches my hair. There is no version of that question I owe a yes to.
My escalation plan does not have to end where the brochure says it ends.
If I am the only one here, that is information about the event, not about me.
I find my people on day one, not on the night I need them.

scenarios.archetype: The Collector / Fetishization As An Approach
scenarios.clinical: Racial Fetishization / Objectification as Opening Move
scenarios.who: Intense, immediate, and full of enthusiasm about a version of you he assembled before you spoke. Compliments a category. Has a type and tells you so as though it were a gift he is handing over.
scenarios.scene: He has been talking for four minutes and every single thing he has said has been about how you look, in language that keeps reaching for somewhere — a country, a continent, a word he clearly thinks is a compliment. He asks where you are really from. He tells you he has always wanted to be with someone like you. There is no point in this conversation where you have been a person with a name.
tells: Compliments a category rather than anything you chose, said, or made
“Where are you really from”, and a guess afterwards
Announces a preference for people like you as though it flatters you
Reaches for your hair, your skin, or a photo within minutes
Knows nothing about you and is nonetheless certain about you
Gets cold fast when you are ordinary rather than the thing he pictured
scenarios.happening: Fetishization does the same work as any other idealization in this book: it replaces a person with a symbol, and symbols are not allowed boundaries. It is also unusually efficient as an opening move, because it arrives disguised as enthusiastic admiration, which makes declining it look like you are the one being difficult. The practical tell is not the subject matter, it is the direction of attention — someone interested in you asks questions and updates on the answers; someone interested in a category delivers conclusions and does not update at all, because your actual self is not the point and is in fact slightly in the way.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “T” CHECK: “Has he asked me anything, or only told me things?” Interest asks. Collecting announces.
scenarios.darkTitle: Being A Type Means Being Interchangeable
scenarios.dark: The thing worth understanding early is what fetishization does to the aftermath. Somebody attracted to a category rather than a person has, by definition, no particular attachment to you — which means the ordinary brakes that come with actually knowing someone are not installed. It also gives him a ready explanation for anything that goes wrong: a misunderstanding, a cultural thing, you took it the wrong way. And if you raise it afterwards in a scene that prides itself on openness, you will frequently be met with the suggestion that he was just really into you and you have made it about race. That pre-built defense is part of why this approach gets used. None of it means you have to litigate it. You can simply leave a conversation that has never once been about you.
scenarios.move: Test it once, cheaply: give him a real detail about yourself that has nothing to do with how you look, and watch whether he picks it up or steers back. Then leave, without a verdict and without a debate — you are not obliged to prove it to him or to anyone standing nearby.
scenarios.say: I'm going to find my people — have a good one. — [if pressed] Not interested, mate. That's the whole answer.
scenarios.truth: Someone who wanted you would ask you something. You are allowed to walk away from an audition you never entered.

scenarios.archetype: The Reacher / Your Body As Public Property
scenarios.who: Frequently a stranger, frequently delighted, frequently already reaching while asking — which means the question was decorative. Often drunk, often a woman, often genuinely baffled that this lands badly.
scenarios.scene: Her hand is already in your hair. She is saying it is amazing and asking how you get it like that and whether it is all yours, and three people are watching and smiling, and the entire social weight of this moment is arranged so that the rude person in it would be you. You have about two seconds and the good options all cost something.
tells: Asks while already reaching, or does not ask at all
Treats your hair, skin, or features as a topic for public discussion
Does it in front of people, so objecting has an audience cost
“Is it real”, “how do you get it like that”, “I've never touched”
Wants a photo with you rather than of the moment
Reacts to a no as though you have been unkind to them
scenarios.happening: Unsolicited touching is a boundary violation regardless of intent, and the specific version aimed at Black women's hair is documented well enough to have prompted its own body of workplace and school policy. The mechanism at a festival is the environment: everyone is close, warm, uninhibited and touching each other constantly, which supplies a ready-made explanation for the contact and makes objecting feel like importing outside-world rules into a space that is supposed to be free of them. That framing is the problem. A culture of physical affection is consent-based or it is not a culture of affection, it is just a culture where some people get touched.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “O” CHECK: “Did the question stop the hand?” If the hand kept moving, it was not a question, and you owe it nothing.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Cost Is The Accumulation
scenarios.dark: Any one of these is small. The reason it belongs in a safety guide is what a weekend of them does: by Sunday you have absorbed forty small interactions in which your body was treated as a shared object and you were required to be gracious about each one, and that steady grinding down of your standing to say no is precisely the ground condition every predator in this book is looking for. Someone who has watched you accept unwanted contact all weekend, smiling, has learned something about you that they should not have been allowed to learn. Practising the flat no on the small stuff is not pettiness. It is keeping the muscle available for the night you need it.
scenarios.move: Block with your body rather than your words — step back and put a hand up before you speak. Then a flat, short sentence with no apology and no explanation, and move on immediately so there is no space for a discussion.
scenarios.say: No — don't touch my hair. — [flat, no smile, then turn away] Anyway. Have you seen where the water point is?
scenarios.truth: You are not a texture. A space that needs you to be gracious about being handled is not actually free for you.

scenarios.archetype: When The Escalation Route Points At You
scenarios.who: Someone in a dispute with you who has correctly worked out that involving staff is a move that costs them nothing and costs you a great deal. Sometimes deliberate. Sometimes just a person who reached for the phone without thinking about who would be believed.
scenarios.scene: There was an argument at your camp. It was nothing. Now there are two radios and a torch and the questions are coming at you rather than at the person who started it, and the specific thing you notice, standing there, is that everybody is being perfectly polite and the outcome has somehow already been decided before anybody asked you anything.
tells: Security arrives asking you the questions rather than asking everyone
The other party is treated as the reporter rather than as a participant
Your tone becomes the subject rather than what happened
Someone reaches for staff or police unusually fast over something small
You are asked to leave to resolve it while the other party stays
You are, or are close to, the only one of you in the immediate area
scenarios.happening: This book's standard advice is to escalate — tell a ranger, tell security, involve staff. That advice assumes the escalation route is neutral, and for a lot of readers it is not: the same call produces different outcomes depending on who is standing where, and a police involvement that resolves one person's evening can be a materially dangerous event for another. Saying so is not cynicism about festival staff, most of whom are decent and trying. It is the difference between a safety plan built for an average reader and one built for you. A plan that ignores this is not neutral — it is a plan that works for other people.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “O” CHECK: “If this escalates to staff, who does that help?” Ask it before the moment, because in the moment there is no time.
scenarios.darkTitle: Build A Ladder That Stops Where You Need It To
scenarios.dark: The practical version of this is not avoid all staff — it is have more rungs before that one, and know which specific humans they are. Camp leads, welfare, the harm-reduction tent, an artist liaison, a named accessibility or community lead: these are escalation routes that are generally safer and almost always more effective than a radio call, and they exist at nearly every festival. The other half is witnesses. The single biggest change in how one of these encounters goes is whether two other people are standing there, and the second biggest is whether somebody is recording. Neither requires a confrontation. Both require having thought about it before the torch is pointing at you, which is the entire reason this page exists.
scenarios.move: On arrival, get two names that are not security — welfare and a camp or community lead. In any dispute, get a witness beside you before it escalates, stay still and boring, and write it down immediately afterwards with the time and the names. Do not resolve it alone in the dark.
scenarios.say: I'm happy to talk about this with welfare present. — [to a friend] Stand here with me a minute, would you.
scenarios.truth: Escalation is a tool, not a reflex. Know which rung is safe for you before you need to climb.

scenarios.archetype: Building The Plan That Actually Fits You
scenarios.who: For anyone whose safety plan cannot be copied straight out of a generic guide — which, at some events, is most of the people reading this one.
scenarios.scene: Thursday afternoon, before anything has happened, while the site is calm and the people you would need are all findable and not busy. Twenty minutes now buys you the thing that is impossible to assemble at two in the morning with a torch in your face, which is a set of names and a route you already trust.
tells: Two named non-security contacts: welfare, and a camp or community lead
Two people on site who will physically stand next to you on request
One person off-site who expects a check-in and knows where you are
Your own transport, or a lift that is not in anybody else's control
A note app for time, place, names — written the same hour, not the next day
The affinity camp or crew, found on day one rather than on the bad night
scenarios.happening: Everything in this guide is cheaper to arrange in advance than to invent under pressure, and the reason is the same one that runs through this whole book: the moment is designed to be one where you cannot think. A prepared ladder converts a judgment call into a lookup. The witness rule does the most work of anything on that list — accounts of these encounters diverge sharply depending on whether anyone else was present, and a second person standing beside you changes both what happens and what can be said about it afterwards. None of this is about expecting trouble. It is the same logic as knowing where the medical tent is.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “R” CHECK: “Can I name my two non-security contacts right now?” If not, that is the twenty minutes, and it is best spent on Thursday.
scenarios.darkTitle: Write It The Same Hour
scenarios.dark: Documentation is the part people skip and the part that matters most, because these situations are decided later by whose account is more specific. A dated note written within the hour — time, location, names, what was actually said, who else was there — outperforms any amount of remembered detail weeks on, and it does not require anyone to find you credible in the moment. Send it to someone off-site so it exists outside this weekend and outside your own phone. It takes ninety seconds. Do it even when you are fairly sure nothing will come of it, because the cases where something does come of it are exactly the ones where you did not expect it to.
scenarios.move: Get your two non-security names in the first hour on site. Agree the stand-next-to-me signal with two friends. Write anything that happens down the same hour and send it off-site. Keep your own way home.
scenarios.say: Who's the welfare lead this year, and how do I reach them directly? — If I text you a pin, just come stand next to me, you don't have to say anything.
scenarios.truth: A plan built for the average reader is not built for you. Build yours on Thursday, out of real names.

scenarios.archetype: Affinity Space, And The Festivals That Get It Right
scenarios.who: The camp with the sound system and the good food that has been coming for eleven years. The crew who clocked you at the gate and nodded. The promoters and collectives who built something deliberately and did the work of making it real.
scenarios.scene: Saturday, and you have spent two days being the only one in every frame, doing the low-level arithmetic that costs more energy than anyone who does not do it understands. Then you walk past a camp and three people look up and one of them says come and eat something, and you feel your shoulders drop about two inches, and you had not registered they were up.
tells: Real: you are not explained, introduced as a demographic, or asked to represent
Real: you can be ordinary, annoying, or quiet with no change in standing
Real: people share practical information without ceremony — who is sound, who is not
Performative: your presence gets mentioned to other people as a credit
Performative: the event's diversity is discussed with you rather than built
Performative: you are the only one there and nobody has ever asked why
scenarios.happening: Affinity space is protective for reasons that are entirely practical rather than sentimental: it replaces hypervisibility with ordinariness, it supplies witnesses who do not need the situation explained to them, and it is where the informal warnings circulate — which promoter is sound, which crew to avoid, what happened last year. Every mechanism in this guide works better on someone isolated, and the fetishizer, the reacher and the weaponized report all operate most freely on a person with nobody standing near them. This is also the page where the scene deserves credit: there are collectives and festivals doing this properly, and they are findable.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “S” CHECK: “Have I found my people here, or am I still doing this alone?” Day one. Not the night it goes wrong.
scenarios.darkTitle: Shoulders Down Is Data
scenarios.dark: Worth naming plainly: the constant low-level vigilance has a cost, and because it is continuous it becomes invisible to the person paying it. You will not notice you have been braced all weekend until you stop, and the stopping is what tells you. That fatigue is not fragility and it is not you being difficult — it is the predictable result of running a background process everyone around you has switched off. It also degrades judgment, the same way sensory load and sleep loss do elsewhere in this book, which means finding the people who let you put it down is not a comfort measure. It is a safety measure, and it belongs on day one alongside knowing where medical is.
scenarios.move: Find the camp, the crew, or the collective on day one, before you need anything. Ask the regulars what they know — the informal information network is the best safety infrastructure at any festival. And go back to the events that actually built something, because they are the ones that respond to being supported.
scenarios.say: First time at this one — who's sound round here, and is there anything I should know? — Come find us at the camp with the blue flag, we're cooking Saturday.
scenarios.truth: You came for the music, not to be a subject of interest. Find the people who let you be ordinary, on day one.

scenarios.archetype: Your Culture Worn Around You / Appropriation As Ambience
scenarios.who: Not a predator. Hundreds of people, none of whom thought about it, wearing your grandmother's dress, a headdress, a bindi, a keffiyeh, a sacred pattern, as festival wear — and one person who will argue with you about it if you say anything.
scenarios.scene: You are walking to the second stage and you pass a war bonnet, two bindis and somebody's idea of a kimono, and you are doing the thing you always do, which is deciding forty separate times an hour whether to spend energy on it. Then somebody in your own camp asks you — warmly, as the resident expert — whether her outfit is okay, and now it is your job.
tells: Sacred or ceremonial items worn as decoration
You are asked to adjudicate, because you are the nearest person of colour
Objecting is treated as policing rather than as information
“It's appreciation” offered as though it settles the question
The energy cost is continuous and invisible to everyone around you
Somebody wants absolution more than they want an answer
scenarios.happening: This belongs in a safety guide for one reason: the cumulative cost. Any single instance is minor and arguable. Forty a day, every day, while also being asked to educate people about it, is a continuous background tax on the same attention you need for everything else in this guide, and depleted attention is the precondition every other pattern relies on. There is also a specific trap in being made the arbiter — once you are the person who rules on this, every conversation about it becomes work you did not agree to do, performed for an audience that wants reassurance rather than information.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “T” CHECK: “Am I being asked for information, or for permission?” Information is a conversation. Permission is a job, and you can decline it.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Are Not The Ethics Department
scenarios.dark: The sharpest version is the person who will not let it go until you approve. They are not asking what you think; they are looking for a member of the group to sign it off so that the discomfort goes away, and your reluctance reads to them as you being difficult rather than as you being tired. That is the moment to notice that a request for education has become an obligation to perform it, in public, for free, about your own culture, at a festival you paid to attend. You are allowed to hand it back. Declining to be the arbiter is not conceding the argument; it is refusing an unpaid role.
scenarios.move: Decide your own policy in advance and apply it without deliberating each time — most people pick one thing they will always say something about and let the rest go, and that is a legitimate and sustainable choice. Hand the adjudication back with a resource rather than a ruling.
scenarios.say: I'm not the person to green-light that, and I'd rather not be. Have a look up why it's a thing — there's loads written by people who actually want to explain it.
scenarios.truth: Deciding forty times a day whether to say something is the cost nobody else can see. Spend it on purpose, not by default.

scenarios.archetype: Assumed To Be The Dealer, The Staff, Or The Security
scenarios.who: Strangers, all weekend, who have decided what you are doing here before speaking to you. Sometimes it is a drinks order. Sometimes it is a bin bag handed to you. Sometimes it is somebody asking, very directly, what you are holding.
scenarios.scene: You are standing near the edge of a crowd, doing nothing, and a man comes up close and asks quietly what you have got. Then later somebody hands you an empty cup as though you were staff. Then somebody asks where the toilets are in the tone people use with stewards, and you are wearing exactly what everybody else is wearing.
tells: Approached about substances by strangers who have no reason to
Mistaken for staff, security or crew while in ordinary clothes
Spoken to in an instructional register by people who want service
Security attention that does not match what you are doing
It happens repeatedly, to you and not to the people you came with
Correcting it makes the other person embarrassed, and then annoyed
scenarios.happening: Each instance is small and the pattern is not, and there is a specific risk hiding inside the most common version. Being repeatedly approached about substances by strangers puts you in conversations about drugs, in public, that you did not initiate and did not want — and undercover officers work festivals. A person who is approached fifteen times a weekend has fifteen chances to be observed having exactly the wrong conversation, and the observation does not come with the context that you were approached rather than approaching.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “R” CHECK: “Am I in a conversation I did not start, about something I am not doing?” End it flatly and physically, not with an explanation.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Conversation You Did Not Start
scenarios.dark: This is where the misidentification stops being an indignity and becomes a legal exposure. The differential-enforcement problem from the security page applies directly: if a conversation about substances goes wrong, whose account gets believed is not a neutral question, and being the person who was standing there is a worse position than being the person who walked off. So the move is not wit and it is not a lecture about assumptions. It is ending the exchange in under three seconds and physically relocating, every time, no matter how tedious that becomes by Sunday — and having witnesses who can say you walked away.
scenarios.move: Two flat words and a step away. Do not engage, do not joke, do not correct at length. Stay near the people you came with, because the approaches drop off sharply when you are visibly in a group.
scenarios.say: Nothing, mate. — [stepping away] Not staff, sorry. — [to your group] That's the fourth one today, I'm sticking with you lot.
scenarios.truth: You did not start that conversation and you do not owe it a reply. Walking off is the whole technique.

scenarios.hook: IF YOUR STATUS IS THE RISK
scenarios.archetype: Immigration Status, Visas, And Why The Advice Changes
scenarios.who: For anyone whose worst-case outcome from any encounter with authority is not a fine or a night in a cell but a removal from the country, a visa consequence, or a family separation.
scenarios.scene: Everything else in this book says get help, tell security, make a report. For you, every one of those sentences has a second half nobody wrote down, and you have been quietly translating the whole guide as you read it. This page does the translating out loud.
tells: Any police contact carries a consequence unrelated to what happened
You avoid medical and welfare because you are unsure who they report to
You do not carry ID, or you carry documents you cannot afford to lose
Someone knows your status and has mentioned it more than once
A dispute would end with you being asked questions the other party will not be asked
No one at home knows exactly where you are this weekend
scenarios.happening: A safety guide that assumes a neutral escalation route is giving some readers a plan that raises their risk. Medical and welfare at festivals are generally not immigration functions and treating people is their job, but the calculation is legitimately different, and pretending otherwise is not kindness. The practical answer is the same as the escalation-ladder page, with more rungs: welfare, harm reduction, camp and community leads, artist liaison — all of which resolve most situations and none of which is a police interaction.
scenarios.check: R.O.O.T.S. — “O” CHECK: “What is my worst-case outcome from this escalation — not the average person's?” Plan from your answer, not from the generic one.
scenarios.darkTitle: Status As Leverage
scenarios.dark: The thing to watch for is somebody who knows and mentions it. Status is among the most effective coercive levers that exists — it needs no threat, it silences reporting completely, and it is why people in precarious immigration positions are targeted deliberately for unpaid work, for sexual coercion, and for keeping quiet about both. If somebody has brought up your status in a conversation that was about something else, that is not conversation, and you are not the first person they have done it to. Get advice from an immigration charity rather than from anyone in the situation, and get it before you need it.
scenarios.move: Know the non-police rungs by name before you need them. Carry a copy rather than an original document, and leave the original somewhere safe. Have one person off-site who knows where you are and who to call. Find an immigration advice line now and save the number, while nothing is happening.
scenarios.say: I'd rather handle this with welfare than with anyone else — can you get them? — [if your status is raised] We're not talking about that. What's actually the issue here?
scenarios.truth: The standard advice was written for somebody whose worst case is a fine. Build the version whose worst case is yours.

guides.intro: You brought your kids to the best place you know. This guide is the boring infrastructure that keeps it that way.

checks.name: Know Where They Are, By Name
checks.desc: Not “with the camp”. A named adult who has agreed, out loud, that they have your child right now and until when.

checks.name: Identify Them If They Are Lost
checks.desc: Wristband with your number, a photo taken each morning in that day's clothes, and a meeting point they can say back to you.

checks.name: No Adult Needs Private Time With Your Kid
checks.desc: Not to show them something, not for a lesson, not to be kind. The rule is simple because simple rules survive a friendly, trusted, well-liked exception.

outline.desc: The helpful adult, gifts and special attention, the camp everyone trusts
Diffused supervision, your own capacity, the festival's actual hazards
The lost-child kit, the handover rule, the family-field brief
Real village versus nobody actually watching

sentences: Someone is always named. “The camp” is not a person.
Photo every morning, number on the wrist, meeting point they can repeat back.
No adult needs to be alone with my child. There is no good version of that ask.
If I am too tired or too altered to parent, I say so and hand over to a named person.
A village with nobody named in it is not supervision, it is an assumption.

scenarios.archetype: The Beloved Camp Uncle / Access Through Trust
scenarios.who: Genuinely great with children, which is the difficult part of this page. Everybody's favourite. Has been coming for years, runs the games, remembers the kids' names between festivals, and is the first person anyone would defend.
scenarios.scene: Your daughter adores him. He does the face paint and the treasure hunt and he is the reason the family field is fun. He has started giving her small presents — a bracelet, a patch for her jacket — and asking for her specifically, and suggesting he take her to the workshop tent because you look tired, and the sentence forming in your head is that you would be insulting a good man to say no.
tells: Seeks time alone with a specific child, always with a good reason
Gives gifts or attention to one child rather than to all of them
Establishes secrets — small, harmless ones, framed as a shared joke
Prefers the company of children to that of adults at an adult event
Pushes past a soft no with warmth rather than pressure
Universally liked, which means raising anything has a social cost
scenarios.happening: Child sexual abuse is overwhelmingly committed by somebody the child and the family already know and trust, and the grooming literature describes a consistent sequence: access, then a special relationship with one child, then small secrets, then isolation. Every step looks like kindness and most of them, performed by most people, are kindness. That is exactly why safeguarding policy in every organization that works with children is built on rules about situations rather than judgments about people — because judging individuals is precisely what the pattern defeats, and because the people who are wrongly suspected and the people who are correctly suspected look identical from outside.
scenarios.check: K.I.N. — “N” CHECK: “Is an adult asking for time alone with my child?” The answer is no, every time, regardless of who is asking. The rule is the protection. Assessing the person is not.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Rule Exists So You Never Have To Judge
scenarios.dark: This is the hardest page in this book to write and to read, and the reason is that the overwhelming majority of beloved camp uncles are exactly what they appear to be — generous adults who like kids and make festivals magical. A blanket rule is not an accusation against any of them. It is a rule precisely because no parent can reliably tell, because the ones who cannot be told apart are the whole problem, and because a good man will not mind. That last part is the practical test: a genuinely safe adult hears “we don't do one-on-one” and says fine, of course, come along too. Only one kind of person argues with a safeguarding rule, and the argument is the finding.
scenarios.move: Make it a policy rather than a judgment, and say it out loud to the whole camp at the start so it is never about one person: no one-on-one, activities happen with two adults or in view. Then say yes to everything that meets the rule — the face paint, the treasure hunt, all of it.
scenarios.say: We do a two-adult rule for the kids, nothing personal to anyone — so yes to the workshop, and I'll walk over with you both.
scenarios.truth: Good adults are not offended by safeguarding rules. The rule protects them too, and the person who argues has told you something.

scenarios.hook: I THOUGHT HE WAS WITH YOU
scenarios.archetype: Diffused Supervision / The Camp Everybody Assumed
scenarios.who: Not a person — a structure. Eleven adults, four children, a shared camp, an unspoken sense that somebody is always around, and no moment at which anybody specifically agreed to be watching.
scenarios.scene: It is nine in the evening and somebody asks where Theo is and there is a pause, and in that pause four adults each realize they had assumed one of the others had him. He is almost certainly thirty metres away at the other fire. He almost certainly is. The forty seconds before you find him are the longest forty seconds of the year and nothing in the camp's arrangements was designed to prevent them.
tells: Supervision described as “the camp” rather than a named adult
No agreed handover — children move between adults without a word said
Nobody knows how many adults are currently drinking or dosed
No headcount, and no agreed time for one
Older children tasked with younger ones without that being decided
“Someone's always around” said as though it were a system
scenarios.happening: Diffusion of responsibility is one of the most robust findings in social psychology: the more people who could act, the less likely any given person is to act, and the more each assumes somebody else has. Applied to child supervision in a camp it produces a specific failure — not neglect, but a group of attentive adults each accurately believing the child is covered. Festivals add the aggravating factors: no fences, thousands of strangers, darkness, noise that swallows a shout, and a proportion of the adults present with reduced capacity. The fix is not more vigilance. It is a named person and a spoken handover, which converts an assumption into an agreement.
scenarios.check: K.I.N. — “K” CHECK: “Can I name the adult who has my child right now, and did they say yes out loud?” If the answer is a camp rather than a name, nobody has them.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Other Half Is Your Own Capacity
scenarios.dark: The part that is harder to say: the handover rule has to include you. A festival is one of the few places where a parent may be genuinely impaired — drinking, dosed, or simply forty hours short of sleep — and the moment where you most need to hand over is the moment you are least able to assess that you should. So the decision gets made in advance, sober, like a designated driver: who is on duty tonight, who is not drinking, and what the signal is for I am done, take over. Agreeing that on Thursday costs a five-minute conversation. Not agreeing it is how a child ends up nominally supervised by four adults, none of whom is currently able to drive.
scenarios.move: Run a nightly rota decided in advance: a named on-duty adult each evening who stays under, and a spoken handover every time a child changes hands — “you have Theo until eight”, answered out loud. Headcount at every set change.
scenarios.say: You've got Theo till eight — say it back to me. — I'm on duty tonight, so I'm not drinking; Mo's on tomorrow.
scenarios.truth: “I thought he was with you” is what four attentive adults say. A name and a time out loud is the only thing that prevents it.

scenarios.archetype: Ten Minutes On Thursday That You Will Never Regret
scenarios.clinical: Child Safety Preparation / Lost Child Protocol
scenarios.who: For everyone in the family field, every year, including the veterans who have done twelve of these and especially the ones who think their kid is too sensible to get lost.
scenarios.scene: The first ninety seconds of a missing child are the ones that matter, and they are ninety seconds in which you will be useless — heart rate through the roof, unable to remember what they were wearing, phone at four percent. Everything on this page exists so that a calm Thursday version of you has already done the thinking.
tells: Wristband with your mobile number, written fresh each morning
A photo of each child taken every morning, in that day's actual clothes
A meeting point they can say back to you, chosen and physically visited
The phrase: find a person with a radio, or a stall, or a mum with kids
Ear defenders, sun hat, water — the boring three that prevent most of it
Your phone charged, and a second adult's number on the band too
scenarios.happening: Lost children at festivals are common and almost always resolve in minutes, and the reason they resolve is infrastructure: wristbands with numbers, a welfare tent that does this constantly, and staff who are trained for it. The daily photo is the single highest-value item and the one almost nobody does — a described child is hard to search for and a photographed child in today's clothes is easy. Teaching who to approach matters as much as teaching not to wander: children told only about stranger danger will avoid the very adults most likely to help them, so name the categories instead — radio, stall, parent with kids.
scenarios.check: K.I.N. — “I” CHECK: “Wristband on, photo taken today, meeting point they can repeat?” Three things, every morning, before anything else.
scenarios.darkTitle: Ninety Seconds, And What To Do In Them
scenarios.dark: Have the protocol memorized because you will not be able to reason it out. One adult stays exactly where the child was last seen and does not move — children double back, and a moving parent and a moving child can search past each other for an hour. A second adult goes straight to welfare or the nearest radio and reports it immediately; there is no waiting period and nobody will think you are overreacting, because they do this several times a day. Show the photo. Give the wristband number so it can be called. Everyone else checks the last three places the child liked, not the whole site. Ninety seconds of the right actions beats twenty minutes of frantic ones.
scenarios.move: Do the three every morning — band, photo, meeting point — and walk the child to the welfare tent on Thursday so they have physically seen where it is. Agree the stay-put rule with the other adults now, before it is needed.
scenarios.say: If you can't find me: stay where you are and find someone with a radio, or a stall, or a mum with kids. Show them your wristband. Tell me the plan back?
scenarios.truth: Ten minutes on Thursday buys you the only ninety seconds that will ever matter. Do the photo — it is the one everybody skips.

scenarios.archetype: A Real Village Versus An Assumed One
scenarios.clinical: Authentic Collective Care vs Diffused Assumption
scenarios.who: The family field at its best, which is genuinely one of the great things this culture has built — kids running semi-feral in the safest possible way, raised for a weekend by twenty adults who all know them.
scenarios.scene: The real version is unmistakable once you have seen it. Adults who know which kid belongs to whom. Somebody bringing your child back with a comment about the face paint. A camp where the rota is on the whiteboard and nobody thinks that is uptight. Kids who can name four adults they are allowed to go to, because somebody sat down and taught them the four.
tells: Real: adults are named, rotas exist, handovers are spoken
Real: children can name the adults they may go to
Real: someone is always sober and everyone knows who
Real: the two-adult rule is stated openly and nobody is offended
Assumed: “someone's always around”, and no one is specifically
Assumed: raising a safeguarding point would make you the awkward one
scenarios.happening: The village is real and it works, and it works because of structure rather than in spite of it. The camps where children are genuinely safest are the ones that look, from outside, slightly over-organized: whiteboard, rota, named on-duty adult, an out-loud rule about one-on-one. That structure is what lets the freedom be real — kids roaming the family field all weekend, which is the thing you came for. The unstructured version produces the opposite: adults who feel responsible in general and therefore nobody responsible in particular, and a culture where the person who suggests a rota is the problem.
scenarios.check: K.I.N. — “K” CHECK: “Can every adult here name tonight's on-duty person, and can every kid name four adults they can go to?” Two questions, asked on Thursday.
scenarios.darkTitle: Be The One Who Says It First
scenarios.dark: Somebody has to say the rules out loud, and in a warm camp of old friends that feels enormously awkward — like importing suspicion into a place built on trust. Say them anyway, and say them on day one, to everyone, before anything has happened, because a rule introduced as general policy costs nothing and a rule introduced after a specific worry is an accusation. You will find that most of the camp is relieved. Parents are usually all quietly thinking it and each assuming they would be the uptight one, which is the same diffusion problem as the supervision gap, applied to speaking up.
scenarios.move: Call the five-minute family brief on Thursday: rota, on-duty adult, two-adult rule, meeting point, and the four adults each child may go to. Put it on a whiteboard. Then let them run.
scenarios.say: Quick family-camp thing before we all settle in — rota's on the board, on-duty's not drinking, no one-on-one with the kids, and let's make sure every kid can name four grown-ups they can go to.
scenarios.truth: The village is real, and it is made of names. A village where nobody is named is just a field with your child in it.

scenarios.archetype: Substances Within Reach Of A Child
scenarios.who: Your camp, and the eleven adults in it who are all lovely and none of whom is thinking about a four-year-old's sight lines.
scenarios.scene: There is a tin on the low table with something in it, and a half-drunk cider at child height, and a bag on a chair. Your daughter is four and everything at that height is, to her, food. She has been putting things in her mouth for four years and nobody in this camp has had to think about that for a decade.
tells: Edibles, powders or pills at or below adult-knee height
Unlabelled food on a shared table in a camp with kids in it
Half-finished drinks left within reach
Bags left open on chairs and in tent doorways
The camp has never explicitly discussed having children present
“She won't touch it” offered as the safety measure
scenarios.happening: Pediatric cannabis ingestion has risen sharply everywhere edibles have become common, and the reason is entirely mechanical: edibles look like sweets, a child's dose is a fraction of an adult's, and onset is delayed so the first sign is a small child who is unexpectedly unwell an hour later. At a festival the risk multiplies — more substances, more adults, more surfaces, and a medical tent rather than an emergency department. This is not a page about whether adults in your camp should use anything. It is a page about height.
scenarios.check: K.I.N. — “K” CHECK: “If I crouch to my child's eye level right now, what can I reach?” Do it literally. It is a different camp from down there.
scenarios.darkTitle: Tell The Medics What They Might Have Taken
scenarios.dark: The failure that turns this serious is not the ingestion, it is the hour afterwards. A small child who has eaten an edible presents as unusually drowsy and unsteady, and a parent who does not know what happened reports a child who seems sleepy — which is a completely different clinical picture from a possible ingestion, and gets a completely different response. So the instruction is blunt: if there is any possibility, say so immediately and say exactly what it might have been. Nobody at that medical tent is interested in getting anybody in trouble and they will tell you so, and the treatment depends entirely on knowing. Guessing wrong costs hours, and hours matter at that body weight.
scenarios.move: Run a waist-height rule as camp policy on day one — nothing above the ground and below the waist, everything in a closed bag in a tent. Label communal food. Do the crouch test yourself each morning, because camps drift by Saturday.
scenarios.say: Kids in camp this year, so can we keep everything above waist height and label the food? Not a judgement thing, just height. — [at medical] She may have eaten an edible, about an hour ago, I don't know how much.
scenarios.truth: Your camp is safe at adult eye level. Crouch down to three feet and look again.

scenarios.archetype: The Teenager At A Festival / A Completely Different Job
scenarios.clinical: Adolescent Supervision / Autonomy and Risk Calibration
scenarios.who: Your fourteen-to-seventeen-year-old, who is too old for the kids' field, too young for everything else, and now navigating a site full of adults, substances and sexual attention with a child's experience and an adult's height.
scenarios.scene: They want to go and watch a band with the two kids from the next camp and be back later, and that is a completely reasonable thing for a fifteen-year-old to want. It is also a fifteen-year-old, at night, in a crowd of adults, where nobody checks anybody's age for anything, and where a nineteen-year-old and a twenty-six-year-old will both read them as older than they are.
tells: Adults who take an unusual interest in your teenager specifically
An older new friend who appears and is vague about their age
Substances offered to them because they read as older
They have no meeting point, no charged phone and no agreed check-in
They will not tell you if something goes wrong, because of what they were doing
You have not said the one sentence that makes telling you possible
scenarios.happening: A teenager needs a different regime from both a child and an adult — real independence, because refusing it produces a teenager who lies, and real structure, because the environment contains things they have no experience of. The single highest-value item is not a rule, it is a disclosure guarantee. Adolescents decide whether to tell a parent about a bad situation almost entirely on their prediction of the reaction, so a teenager who believes they will be punished for being where they were will handle it alone, at night, at a festival. That is the outcome to prevent.
scenarios.check: K.I.N. — “K” CHECK: “Do they have a check-in time, a meeting point, and a promise from me that ringing costs them nothing?” Three things, agreed before they go anywhere.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Sentence That Actually Protects Them
scenarios.dark: Say this to them plainly, once, before the weekend: if anything goes wrong, whatever you were doing, ring me and I will not be angry and we will sort it out afterwards. Then keep it the first time it is used, over something small, because that is the test and they will run it. The alternative is a fifteen-year-old who has taken something, or is with somebody who will not let them leave, running the calculation about how much trouble they are in, and deciding to manage it themselves. Every safeguarding professional will tell you the same thing: the child who tells you is the one who thinks telling you is survivable.
scenarios.move: Give real autonomy with real structure — agreed zones, an hourly-ish check-in, a charged phone and a power bank, a meeting point, and the names of the friends they are with. Say the unconditional sentence and mean it. Tell them the two adult-world things nobody else will: watch your own drink, and an adult being very interested in you is a reason to leave.
scenarios.say: Here's the deal: go, have a great time, text me at ten and midnight. And whatever happens, whatever you were doing, ring me — I won't be angry, I'll just come. That's a promise, not a trap.
scenarios.truth: You cannot supervise a fifteen-year-old at a festival. You can be the person they are not afraid to ring, and that is worth more.

scenarios.hook: EARS, SUN AND THE LONG DAY
scenarios.archetype: The Three Physical Things That Actually Hurt Children Here
scenarios.clinical: Pediatric Environmental Protection / Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
scenarios.who: For every adult with a child at a festival. Nothing on this page involves another person. All of it is the environment, and all of it is preventable with items that cost less than a round of drinks.
scenarios.scene: The three things that send children to a festival medical tent are almost never dramatic: overheating, exhaustion, and the slow damage of a hundred decibels going into ears that are much more vulnerable than yours. None of it looks like an emergency while it is happening, which is precisely the problem.
tells: Ear defenders: not optional, and not just at the main stage
Shade, hat, high-factor sun cream reapplied — they will not ask
Water pushed on a schedule, because children under-report thirst
A real nap or quiet hour every day, in shade, with defenders off
Their own bag: snack, water, defenders, hat, a photo of you
Watch for the quiet child — that is the sign, not the crying one
scenarios.happening: Children's hearing is more vulnerable than adults' and noise damage is cumulative, permanent, and completely painless at the time, which is why nobody acts on it. Festival sound levels routinely sit where hearing protection is required in an occupational setting, and a child does not have to be at the rail to be exposed — a campsite within earshot of a stage is enough over three days. Heat and exhaustion are the other two, and both present quietly: a child who is overheating or depleted goes still and compliant rather than loud, which reads to a busy adult as a child who is finally settling down.
