scenarios.who: Mostly delighted, drunk, well-meaning people, arriving at a rate of roughly one every four minutes all weekend. Occasionally somebody who has worked out that distracting the dog is a way to get at you.
scenarios.scene: She is in her vest and she is working and a man crouches down in front of her going hey, hey gorgeous, clicking his fingers, and behind him two other people are also crouching, and one of them is offering her a chip. Your dog's whole job is to notice things about you and she has just spent forty seconds noticing him instead.
tells: Approaching, touching, feeding or calling a dog in a working vest
Continuing after being told she is working
Treating your no as unfriendliness rather than as a medical instruction
Using the dog as an opening to keep talking to you
Letting their own off-lead dog approach yours
Photographing her, or you, without asking
scenarios.happening: A distracted assistance dog is a disabled piece of equipment. An alert dog that misses a signal, a guide dog that loses the line, a mobility dog that breaks position — these are functional failures with real consequences, and a festival supplies distraction at a density found almost nowhere else. Feeding is the most dangerous version because it can make a working animal ill for the rest of the weekend, which removes your support entirely. The legal position in most places is clear that interference is not permitted; the practical position is that fifty people a day will do it anyway.
scenarios.check: A.C.C.E.S.S. — “C” CHECK: “Is my equipment currently able to do its job?” A dog is equipment while the vest is on, and this is the one piece of equipment strangers will touch without asking.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Dog As An Approach
scenarios.dark: There is a version of this that is not about the dog at all. An assistance animal is a guaranteed conversation starter with a person who cannot easily leave, and somebody who wants sustained access to you has an unlimited, socially approved reason to keep returning — asking after her, bringing her water, wanting a photo. It is the inspiration approach from earlier in this guide with a better cover story, and it is harder to refuse because refusing looks like you are being precious about a dog everybody can see is lovely. Watch for the person who comes back. Once is a stranger; the fourth time is a pattern.
scenarios.move: Put a bright DO NOT DISTRACT patch on the vest so the sentence is pre-said, and use a flat one-liner without a smile so it does not open a conversation. Keep her water and her food entirely under your control, and do not accept treats from anyone.
scenarios.say: She's working, please don't — and please don't feed her, it makes her ill. — [flat, turning away] Thanks.
scenarios.truth: She is not a pet this weekend. She is the reason you can be here, and a stranger's forty seconds of fun costs you her attention.

scenarios.archetype: Being Moved Without Consent / Terrain As A Trap
scenarios.who: Helpful, strong, and already reaching for your chair's handles or your arms. Genuinely trying to solve a problem — the mud, the step, the gap — that the event should have solved and did not.
scenarios.scene: The path has turned to mud and you are stuck, which was entirely predictable in October. Three men decide to help. Nobody asks how your chair lifts. Somebody takes the armrest, which is not a lifting point and now bends, and you are briefly airborne and entirely at the mercy of people who mean well and have no idea what they are doing, and your footplate is being used as a handle.
tells: Hands on you or your equipment before anyone asked
Lifting by armrests, footplates or wheels rather than the frame
“We've got you” said while you are trying to explain how it works
Being carried somewhere you did not agree to go
Terrain the event never made passable, treated as your problem
The offer of help proceeds regardless of your answer
scenarios.happening: Two failures stack here. The event's, which is that accessible routes are an obligation and mud is foreseeable; and the crowd's, which is that helping a disabled person is treated as something that does not require permission. Being lifted incorrectly causes real injuries to both people and to expensive, hard-to-replace equipment, and a chair damaged on Saturday cannot be repaired before Monday, which turns a bad moment into the end of your weekend and possibly your independence for weeks.
scenarios.check: A.C.C.E.S.S. — “E” CHECK: “Did I plan a route I can actually use, in this weather?” And in the moment: “Did anybody ask me before touching me?”
scenarios.darkTitle: Moved Is Not The Same As Helped
scenarios.dark: Underneath the practical risk is the one that matters more. A person who can be picked up and relocated by strangers without agreement has had their ability to leave taken away, and being carried somewhere you did not choose is the single most efficient way to isolate a disabled person — no coercion needed, no conversation, just a friendly group and a mud patch. Most of the time it is exactly what it looks like. The habit worth building is the one that holds in both cases: nobody moves you or your equipment without your instruction, and the instruction includes where you are going.
scenarios.move: Say stop first and instruct second — people follow clear instructions and freeze at arguments. Know your chair's actual lift points and say them out loud. Pre-plan hard-standing routes and ask the accessibility team about wet-weather alternatives on arrival, before the mud exists.
scenarios.say: Stop — hands off, please. If I want lifting I'll tell you where to hold. It's the frame here and here, and we're going to the hard path, not the tent.
scenarios.truth: Help you did not agree to is just being moved. You decide whether, how, and to where.

scenarios.hook: IF YOU CANNOT HEAR THE ANNOUNCEMENT
scenarios.archetype: Deaf And Hard-Of-Hearing At A Music Festival
scenarios.who: For Deaf and hard-of-hearing attendees, and for anyone whose hearing aids or implants have to survive four days of dust, rain and a hundred and ten decibels.
scenarios.scene: Every piece of safety information at a festival is delivered by tannoy: the weather warning, the stage closure, the evacuation route, the missing child, the thing that has just happened at the other end of the site. All of it is audio, all of it is over a distorted PA, and none of it reaches you. You will find out what happened when the crowd starts moving.
tells: Emergency and safety announcements are audio-only with no visual equivalent
No interpreter listed, and no text alert or app notification option
Staff default to talking louder rather than to writing it down
Your aids or processor have no dry storage, spare batteries, or backup
Nobody in your group has agreed a visual signal for we are leaving
You have not told welfare that you will not hear a tannoy
scenarios.happening: Deaf attendees are systematically excluded from the emergency information layer of an event, and that is a safety issue rather than an inclusion one — evacuation instructions, severe weather warnings and stage cancellations are all broadcast in the one modality you cannot receive. Most events will provide interpreters, text alerts or a welfare contact if asked in advance, and almost none provide them by default. The equipment problem is separate and severe: rain, dust and a dead battery are all far more likely here than at home, and a processor lost at a festival is a five-figure object in a field.
scenarios.check: A.C.C.E.S.S. — “A” CHECK: “How will I find out if something goes wrong on this site?” If the only answer is the tannoy, you have no route to emergency information.
scenarios.darkTitle: Evacuations Are Announced Out Loud
scenarios.dark: The scenario that matters is the rare one. A crowd evacuation, a severe weather call, a stage closure that redirects forty thousand people — these are announced by PA, once, urgently, and then everyone around you starts moving in a direction you do not understand for a reason you have not been told. Moving in a dense crowd without knowing why is how people get hurt. Arrange the alternative in advance, in writing: ask the event for text alerts, register with welfare so they know to find you, and agree a physical signal with your group that means leave now, follow me, no questions.
scenarios.move: Email the event before you travel about interpreters and text alerts. Register at welfare on arrival so somebody knows you will not hear a tannoy. Bring a dry box, spare batteries and a backup, and agree a visual emergency signal with your group.
scenarios.say: I'm Deaf and I won't hear announcements — can you register that at welfare and tell me how safety info gets out here? — [to your group] If we need to go, this signal. Don't explain, just do it and I'll follow.
scenarios.truth: The safety information at a festival is audio-only. Arrange your own channel before you need it, because there will be no time afterwards.

guides.intro: You hand your body to gravity, fire, and other people's hands. This guide is about who you hand it to.

checks.name: Fuel, Rig, And Gear Are Yours To Check
checks.desc: You inspect what you hang from, what you burn, and what you spin. Every time, personally. Nobody's feelings outrank that check.

checks.name: Lights Mean You Are Being Filmed
checks.desc: Assume a camera on every burn and every set. Decide what you consent to before you are lit, not after the clip is up.

checks.name: Overrides Are The Pattern
checks.desc: Spin injured, one more burn, skip the safety brief, it's fine. Watch who benefits from every override — it is almost never you.

checks.name: Who Holds You Is A Safety Decision
checks.desc: The rigger, the spotter, the safety, the base. That person holds your body. Choosing them is a technical decision, not a social one.

outline.desc: The teacher with access, the base who makes you dependent, gear as a gift with strings
Safety-third pressure, performing injured, adjustments that stop being technical
Rigging and safety as leverage, circle gatekeeping, image and footage control
The pre-burn check, the consent brief, the footage policy
Real jam culture versus a circle with an owner

sentences: I check my own gear. Every time. That is not distrust, that is the job.
The person who holds my weight is chosen for their competence, not their charm.
Being hurt is not a reason to perform. It is the reason not to.
My image is mine. Filming me is not the same as owning me.
A circle with a gatekeeper is not a jam.

scenarios.hook: I'LL TEACH YOU THE REAL STUFF
scenarios.archetype: The Mentor With A Waiting List / Skill Access As Currency
scenarios.who: Genuinely good, visibly senior, and the reason half this circle can do what they do. Teaches selectively. Makes it clear that being taught is a thing you are chosen for, and that the choosing is ongoing.
scenarios.scene: He has been doing this for fifteen years and the thing he does with a staff is the reason you started. He offers to work with you properly — not in the jam, at his camp, after, when it's quiet and there's space. The first session is the best hour of instruction you have ever had. The second session he corrects your stance with his hands and holds the correction slightly longer than the correction needs.
tells: Teaching happens privately and late rather than in open practice
Access to instruction is framed as being chosen, and is reviewable
Physical correction escalates in duration or location over sessions
Discourages you from training with others — they'll teach you bad habits
Mentions what he could do for your booking or your profile
The lesson quality is real, which is what makes leaving expensive
scenarios.happening: Skill is the currency in this scene and a person who controls access to it controls a great deal. The mechanism is the same as every other access trap in this book, but it has an unusual protection: the teaching is genuinely valuable, so the cost of walking away is real and everybody can see it. That asymmetry is what gets exploited. It is also why the correction-by-touch escalation works — in a discipline where hands-on adjustment is legitimate and constant, the line between instruction and testing is exactly where a person can operate while retaining deniability, and where you will second-guess yourself for weeks.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “O” CHECK: “Would this lesson be identical if it happened at 2pm in the open jam?” If the answer is no, the privacy is doing something the teaching does not need.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Adjustment That Tests You
scenarios.dark: The escalation is deliberately gradual and it is designed to be unreportable. A hand on the hip is technique. The same hand, a beat longer, is a test — and if you do not react, the next one is longer. Every individual step is defensible and the whole staircase is not, which is precisely why it is built in steps. Dance, martial arts, aerial, and acro have all documented this shape, and it works the same way here. The counter is not deciding where the line is in the moment, when you are mid-correction and unsure. It is deciding beforehand that instruction happens where people can see it, and treating any pressure to move it somewhere quieter as the finding rather than as a scheduling preference.
scenarios.move: Train in the open. Take instruction from at least two people so no single person is your route to progress. If a session has already moved somewhere private, bring someone — “my friend wants to watch” is unarguable and tells you a great deal by how it lands.
scenarios.say: I learn better in the jam — more eyes, more feedback. Can we do it there? I'll bring Kai, they've been wanting to work on the same thing.
scenarios.truth: A teacher worth having will teach you in daylight with people watching. The ones who need the room quiet are not protecting your focus.

scenarios.archetype: The Gear Gifter / Props With A Ledger
scenarios.who: Generous, well-equipped, and quick to notice what you cannot afford. Hands you a set of pro-grade props, a rig, a costume, a fire kit. Does not want anything for it, says so repeatedly, and mentions its value twice.
scenarios.scene: Your poi are entry-level and everyone knows it. He has a spare set of the ones you have been saving for — seven hundred dollars of them — and he wants you to have them, no, really, take them, he has three sets. Two weeks later there is an afterparty you do not want to go to and the sentence in your head, unprompted, is that he gave you the poi.
tells: The gift is expensive enough to be uncomfortable and given fast
Refusing is treated as an insult rather than a choice
Its value gets mentioned more than once, casually
Given in front of other people, so the generosity is witnessed
Followed within weeks by an ask that is hard to decline
Taking it back is floated, lightly, when you say no to something
scenarios.happening: Reciprocity is the strongest lever in the book — a received gift creates a felt obligation that operates below deliberation, and it does not care whether you asked for the gift or wanted it. Gift economy culture supercharges it, because the frame says a gift is pure, which removes your permission to be suspicious of one. Expensive gear is a particularly efficient version: it is high value, it is useful daily, it visibly improves your practice, and every time you use it you renew the debt. Most gifts in this scene are exactly what they look like. The tell is not generosity. It is generosity that arrives before the relationship has any other content.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “O” CHECK: “Would I be comfortable saying no to this person tomorrow?” If the gear makes that harder, the gear is doing something other than spinning.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Ledger Nobody Admits Exists
scenarios.dark: The damage is not the moment the ask arrives — it is the weeks before, when you quietly start being easier to be around. You stop raising the thing that bothered you. You go to the thing you did not want to go to. Nobody has threatened anything and there is nothing to report, and if you told a friend they would say he sounds nice. That self-editing in advance of a demand that has not been made is the whole mechanism, and it is the most reliably reported experience of people who later realized they had been managed. If you want to test it cheaply: decline something small this week and watch whether the temperature of the friendship changes.
scenarios.move: Price the gift and settle it — pay something, trade something, or return it. If none of that is possible, say out loud and early what the gift does not buy, which converts an unspoken ledger into a stated one and removes its power.
scenarios.say: These are amazing and I'm not comfortable with a gift this size — let me pay you half, or I'll take them as a loan for the season and get them back to you.
scenarios.truth: A real gift survives you saying no to the giver a week later. Test it early, while the test is cheap.

scenarios.archetype: The Culture That Jokes About The Thing That Kills You
scenarios.clinical: Normalized Risk / Social Override of Safety Protocol
scenarios.who: Not a person — a room. The collective eye-roll when someone asks for a safety brief. The laugh when you check your fuel. The lightly impatient veteran waiting while you do a rig inspection everybody else skipped.
scenarios.scene: You are about to burn. The safety is a guy you met an hour ago who is holding a duvetyne blanket like it is a beach towel, and when you ask whether he has done this before he says yeah, loads, and looks at his phone. The circle is waiting. Asking again in front of everyone would make you the difficult one. You have about four seconds to decide whether being the difficult one is worse than the other thing.
tells: Safety checks treated as a personality flaw rather than procedure
A designated safety who cannot describe what they would actually do
Fuel handled near lit tools, or depot uncovered
“Safety third” said in a context where it is not a joke
Nobody has asked who is calling stop, or what stop sounds like
The social cost of pausing is visibly higher than the cost of proceeding
scenarios.happening: Normalized deviance is the documented process by which a group repeatedly gets away with skipping a step until the skipped step becomes the standard. Every fire and aerial community runs on it to some degree, because the consequence is rare and the friction is constant, and the people most exposed are the newest — who have the least standing to pause and the most to lose by being seen as green. The joke is doing real work here: it pre-frames anyone who insists on the check as humorless, which means the insisting costs something, which means fewer people insist. That is not culture, it is a mechanism, and it runs whether or not anybody in the circle intends it.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “F” CHECK: “Have I personally checked my fuel, my depot, and my safety — by asking them what they would do?” Secondhand assurance is not a check.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Four Seconds
scenarios.dark: Burn injuries in this scene cluster around exactly this moment — not around difficult tricks, around skipped checks under social pressure with an audience waiting. The specific failure is almost always mundane: fuel too close, a depot uncovered, a safety who had never actually done it, nobody having agreed what the stop call was. And the reason it is mundane is the reason it is preventable. The four seconds of being the difficult one is the entire intervention. People who have been burned describe those four seconds with total clarity afterwards, every time — they remember deciding not to ask again. Ask again. The circle waits, and then forgets by morning, and you do not have a graft.
scenarios.move: Run your own check out loud, every time, in the same words, so it becomes your known habit rather than a comment on this circle: fuel, depot, safety, stop call. Ask the safety one question they have to answer — what do you do if my wick catches my sleeve? Their answer is the check.
scenarios.say: Quick one before I light — what's the stop call, and what do you do if it goes up my arm? Not being difficult, I just do this every time.
scenarios.truth: The circle's patience is not a safety system. Being briefly annoying is cheaper than being briefly on fire.

scenarios.hook: YOU'RE ON IN TWENTY, IT'S FINE
scenarios.archetype: The Show Must Go On / Performing Through Injury
scenarios.who: The organizer with a running order, the troupe lead with a headcount, and — most often — you, doing the arithmetic about letting people down and arriving at the wrong answer.
scenarios.scene: Your shoulder went on the last rehearsal and you can feel it in a way that is new. You are on in twenty. There is no understudy because there is never an understudy. The set is four minutes. Four minutes is nothing. You have already decided you are doing it, and you are now assembling reasons, which is a different mental activity from deciding and it is worth noticing that you are doing it.
tells: No cover, no contingency, and that is treated as normal
Your injury is reframed as a scheduling problem
“It's only four minutes” applied to a load-bearing body part
Someone else's disappointment is the thing being weighed, not the joint
You are assembling reasons rather than reaching a decision
Pulling out has a reputational price everyone can name
scenarios.happening: Performing-arts and circus injury research keeps finding the same thing: the significant injuries are disproportionately not freak accidents but re-injuries and compensations, sustained by people who continued while compromised. The economics drive it — no cover, no sick pay, gigs awarded by reputation, and a culture that reads reliability as showing up regardless. In a festival context it is sharper still, because the gig is often unpaid or trade, so you are risking a shoulder for a wristband and the thing keeping you in the air is not money but not wanting to be the person who dropped out.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “O” CHECK: “Am I deciding, or justifying?” If you are listing reasons, the decision already happened and it was not made by your judgment.
scenarios.darkTitle: What Four Minutes Costs
scenarios.dark: The ugly arithmetic is that four minutes of a compromised shoulder, rotator cuff, or ankle can end a practice you spent a decade building, and the people asking you to do it will have forgotten by the next event. Aerialists lose careers to exactly this. The second half is worse: performing impaired — injured, exhausted, or altered — also puts your base, your spotter, and anybody underneath you at risk, so the loyalty argument that got you into the air is actually pointing the other way. The culture that will pressure you to go on is the same culture that will not cover your physio. Decide accordingly.
scenarios.move: Set the rule before the season, not in the twenty minutes: a named list of injuries that mean you do not perform, agreed with yourself while nothing is at stake. Then it is a policy you are following rather than a judgment you are making under pressure.
scenarios.say: Shoulder's gone, so I'm out tonight — that's firm. I can still do the ground set or safety for someone else if that helps you fill it.
scenarios.truth: Nobody in that crowd will remember the set. You will be carrying the shoulder for thirty years.

scenarios.archetype: The Rigger Who Owns The Point / Life Safety As Leverage
scenarios.who: The one with the hardware, the certification everyone assumes he has, and the only ladder. Rigs for everybody. Decides whose point goes up, when, and how high. Has never been asked to show anything.
scenarios.scene: You want to fly and he is the only person here who can hang you. He is warm about it, competent-looking, and slightly dismissive when you ask what the anchor is rated to — he says he has been doing this since before you were spinning. Later he mentions, in the same warm voice, that some people get priority because they are part of the crew and you could be part of the crew.
tells: One person rigs everything and no second competent person exists on site
Deflects or jokes when asked about ratings, inspection, or load path
Rigging priority tracks social closeness rather than the running order
No written check, no second pair of eyes, no logbook
Access to flying is described as something you earn from him socially
Asking technical questions is treated as an insult rather than as normal
scenarios.happening: Aerial rigging is life safety — a single point failure is a fall from height — and the entire discipline's professional practice is built on redundancy, documentation, and independent inspection precisely because competence cannot be established by reputation. When a festival has one unsupervised rigger, two things are true at once: the technical risk is unmanaged, and a person now controls something people want badly enough to trade for. The second follows from the first. It is the accessible-platform pattern from the A.C.C.E.S.S. guide, with the stakes raised from a good view to your spine.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “W” CHECK: “Can this person tell me the load path and the rating, without irritation?” Competence explains itself. Only insecurity gets offended by the question.
scenarios.darkTitle: Two Failures Sharing One Cause
scenarios.dark: An unchecked rigger is both a fall risk and a coercion risk, and they are the same structural fact: nobody is watching, and the thing he controls is something you will trade for. That is how these situations run for years without a complaint — the people who could complain need the point, and the people who could check him were never appointed. If you take one thing from this page: a competent rigger will answer a technical question with relief, because it means somebody else in the room is thinking. The irritation is the signal. It means he has not been asked before, and that is the actual finding — not about him specifically, about the whole arrangement.
scenarios.move: Ask the three questions before you ever go up: what is the anchor, what is it rated to, and who checked it besides you. Do not fly on a point nobody but its own rigger has inspected. Find the second competent person on site on arrival — if there is not one, that is your answer about flying this weekend.
scenarios.say: Before I go up — what's the anchor and the rating, and who's your second pair of eyes on it? I ask everyone, it's not about you.
scenarios.truth: Redundancy is the whole discipline. A rig with one person and no check is not a rig, it is a bet.

scenarios.archetype: The Filmer / Your Body As Somebody Else's Content
scenarios.who: Always filming, often good at it, and operating on the assumption that a public performance is a public license. Sometimes a friend with a phone. Sometimes an account with two hundred thousand followers and a monetization deal.
scenarios.scene: You burned last night. This morning there is a clip of it on an account you have never heard of, forty thousand views, your face clearly visible, your name nowhere, a brand tagged in the caption. The comments are mostly about your body. Somebody has stitched it. You did not know a camera was there, and the account owner, when you message, is genuinely baffled that you are not pleased.
tells: Films without asking and treats performing as blanket consent
Cannot say where footage will end up or who else gets it
Credits the venue and the brand but not the performer
Reacts to a takedown request as though you are being ungrateful
Monetized account, unmonetized subject
Costume, aerial, and fire performers get framed body-first
scenarios.happening: Performing in public does not transfer your rights in your own image, and it never has — but the practical position is that enforcement is slow, cross-border, and expensive, so the operative protection is the one you set up in advance rather than the one you litigate afterwards. What makes this acute for flow and aerial performers is the combination of revealing costume, physical spectacle, and a distribution system that rewards exactly the framing you did not choose. The version that does real harm is not the friendly clip, it is the reposted one, where it travels without context, without your name, and often into spaces you would never have agreed to.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “L” CHECK: “Have I said, out loud, before I start, what I consent to being filmed and posted?” Silence gets read as a yes by people who wanted a yes.
scenarios.darkTitle: It Does Not Come Back Down
scenarios.dark: Once a clip is stitched, reposted, and mirrored, there is no version of this where you get it back. The realistic goal is containment, not removal — which is why the work is all front-loaded. State it before the burn, to the organizer and to anyone visibly filming, and get the organizer's media policy in writing when you agree to the gig. The second thing worth knowing is that this is often where a different kind of leverage starts: somebody holding footage of you, and mentioning it. Footage held over a performer is coercion, it is not a grey area, and the response is the same as for any other documentation threat — tell one person now, in writing, so the footage stops being a secret that can be spent.
scenarios.move: Set your policy before you are lit, in one sentence, to the organizer and the circle. Get the event's media terms in writing when you take the booking. Watermark or claim your own footage first so the canonical version is yours.
scenarios.say: Happy to be filmed, not happy to be posted without a tag — credit me or don't put it up. Who's your media lead so I can send them that in writing?
scenarios.truth: A performance is not a release. Saying so takes six seconds and it is the only part of this you control.

scenarios.archetype: The Check You Run Every Time, Out Loud
scenarios.who: For every fire, aerial, and prop performer, at every skill level. The veterans who have been hurt are the most rigorous people in any circle, and that is not a coincidence — it is what the injury taught them.
scenarios.scene: You are about to go. There is a circle waiting, a running order slipping, and a version of you that wants to skip this because everything looks fine and everything usually is. This page exists because “usually” is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence.
tells: Fuel: which fuel, how old, where is the depot, is it lidded and upwind
Tools: wicks sound, no loose hardware, chains and leaders intact
Body: hair tied, no synthetics, nothing loose, sober enough to be doing this
Safety: who, do they have duvetyne, can they say what they would do
Stop: what is the call, who can make it, does everyone know it
Rig: anchor, rating, second inspection, and a spotter who is watching you
scenarios.happening: Checklists work for the same reason in every high-consequence discipline: they take the decision out of the moment and out of the social context. Reading a list is not a judgment call and cannot be read as a comment on the people present, which is precisely what makes it survivable under an impatient circle. Saying it out loud does the second job — it makes the check public, which means the circle adjusts to it rather than you adjusting to the circle, and it quietly gives permission to the newer performer behind you who was not going to ask.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “F” CHECK: “Did I run all six, this time, for this burn?” Last burn's check does not cover this one. Fuel moves, safeties change, hardware fails between sets.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Check Is Also Social Cover
scenarios.dark: There is a second reason to do it out loud and it is not about fire. A performer who visibly runs their own checks, asks technical questions, and is comfortable being briefly annoying in front of a circle is a conspicuously bad target for every pattern in this guide — the mentor with the private lesson, the rigger who does not like being asked, the person who wants the footage. Not because it makes you unpleasant, but because all of those depend on you being someone who will not make a small public fuss to avoid an awkward moment. The checklist trains exactly that muscle, thirty seconds at a time, on something where you already know you are right.
scenarios.move: Run the six out loud, in the same order, every single time, until it is your known habit and the circle expects it. Teach it to the newest person there — that is how it becomes the culture rather than your quirk.
scenarios.say: Fuel, tools, body, safety, stop call, rig. — Right, what's the stop call tonight?
scenarios.truth: Every burned performer in this scene can tell you exactly which item they skipped. Run all six.

scenarios.archetype: Real Jam Culture Versus A Circle With An Owner
scenarios.clinical: Authentic Practice Space vs Gatekept Hierarchy
scenarios.who: The good version has no owner, teaches sideways, and lets terrible beginners take up space. The other version has a centre, and the centre is a person, and everyone's position is measured by distance from him.
scenarios.scene: Two circles at the same festival. In the first, a woman who has been spinning for twenty years spends eleven minutes helping somebody who picked up poi on Thursday, then goes back to her own practice and never mentions it again. In the second, everyone is subtly performing for one man at the edge, and when he leaves for ten minutes the energy of the whole circle changes, and everybody notices that it did.
tells: Real: beginners get space and nobody is ranked
Real: teaching flows in every direction, including upward
Real: you can leave, be bad, or sit out with no cost
Owned: one person's approval organizes the room
Owned: access to gear, instruction, or gigs routes through him
Owned: people describe the circle by his name
scenarios.happening: A practice circle is one of the genuinely great things this scene produces — skill transmitted for free, across ages and levels, because somebody once did it for you. It is also a structure with an obvious failure mode: circles with a centre concentrate access, and concentrated access is what every pattern in this guide runs on. The test is identical to the one in every other guide here, which is not an accident: can you decline, be unimpressive, or leave without it costing you? In a real jam the answer is yes and nobody registers it. In an owned one, everybody registers everything.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “W” CHECK: “If I sat out tonight and said nothing, would anything change for me here?” If sitting out has a price, this circle has an owner.
scenarios.darkTitle: When The Circle Is The Supply Chain
scenarios.dark: It gets serious when the circle is also where the gigs, the gear, and the instruction come from, because then leaving costs your practice and not just your evening. That is the configuration to watch for — not a charismatic person, which is normal and often lovely, but one person sitting across all of it at once. Everybody in that circle can feel it and nobody names it, because naming it is the thing that costs the most. If you are reading this and recognizing your own circle: the others already know, the conversation is easier than you think, and the fix is usually structural rather than confrontational. Two teachers. A second rigger. Somebody else who books.
scenarios.move: Keep your practice plural on purpose — more than one circle, more than one teacher, more than one route to a gig. Then hand skill downward for free, because a circle where everybody teaches cannot develop a centre.
scenarios.say: Come spin with us, we're rubbish and nobody cares. — Here, let me show you the grip, it took me a year to work out and it shouldn't have.
scenarios.truth: A jam that needs a specific person to be good is not a jam. It is an audience with props.

scenarios.archetype: The Base / Partner Acro And The Hands That Are Already On You
scenarios.clinical: Consent in Physical-Contact Disciplines / Positional Vulnerability
scenarios.who: Your base, your flyer, or the person spotting. The discipline requires hands on your ribs, hips and inner thighs, so the contact is legitimate, constant and unremarkable — which is the whole difficulty.
scenarios.scene: You are inverted with your entire weight on his hands and he adjusts his grip, and the adjustment goes somewhere that was not necessary for the position, and you are upside down four feet off the ground and the only thing keeping you there is the person who just did that. You come down. Neither of you says anything. He books you for the next jam.
tells: Grip adjustments that are not required by the position
New moves introduced without describing the contact first
Contact continues after you have landed and are stable
Objecting is framed as not trusting your base, which is a safety word here
Sessions move from open practice to private space
You come out of a wash feeling odd and cannot point to a single thing
scenarios.happening: Partner acro, aerial and any spotting discipline share a structural problem: consent to hold has to be given in advance and continuously, while the person giving it is frequently inverted, load-bearing, or in a position where objecting is physically unsafe. Every acro community that has addressed this has landed on the same protocol — name the contact before the move, no new contact mid-position, and trust means trusting the hold rather than trusting the person's intentions. The word trust is the thing to watch, because it is doing safety work and social work simultaneously and somebody can lean on the second to get the first.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “W” CHECK: “Was this contact named before the move started?” Unnamed contact is the finding, regardless of where it landed.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Cannot Object At Four Feet
scenarios.dark: The reason this is not like other unwanted contact is the physics. You cannot step back, you cannot pull away, and reacting sharply while inverted risks a genuine injury to both of you — so your body overrides the objection to keep you both safe, and afterwards you will read your own stillness as consent. It was not; it was self-preservation. This is exactly why the protocol lives before the move rather than during it, and why the right move afterwards is not to relitigate what happened in the air but to change the practice: named contact, open space, and a different base. You do not owe anybody an accusation to be allowed to stop flying with them.
scenarios.move: Agree the contact map before any new move, out loud, every time — where hands go, and where they do not. Practise in open space. Change base without explaining yourself; you never owe a reason for who holds your body.
scenarios.say: Before we try it — where are your hands going? Ribs and hips, nothing else, and tell me if that changes. — I'm going to work with Sam on this one, cheers.
scenarios.truth: Trust in acro means trusting the hold. It has never meant losing the right to say where the hands go.

scenarios.archetype: The Crowd / Performing Is Not Consent To Be Touched
scenarios.who: The crowd, at about one in the morning, drunk and delighted and not thinking — grabbing a hoop, stepping into a fire circle for a photograph, putting hands on a stilt-walker's legs, reaching for an aerialist's foot.
scenarios.scene: You are three minutes into a fire set and a man steps inside the circle to film himself next to you. He is about a metre from a lit wick moving at speed and he has no idea, and you now have to decide, mid-spin, whether to stop the set or keep going while somebody stands in the burn radius filming.
tells: People entering the performance space for photographs
Props grabbed, touched or stepped on mid-set
Costume, wings, stilts or rigging treated as public property
No safety perimeter, no marshal, and no marked boundary
Contact that would be obviously unacceptable if you were not performing
The venue treats crowd management as your problem
scenarios.happening: Performing in public gets read as an open invitation, and for fire and aerial that misreading is a physical danger to the audience as well as to you — a person inside a fire circle is inside a burn radius, and a grabbed hoop or a knocked stilt takes a performer down onto hard ground. The professional answer is that crowd management is the event's job and a perimeter is a condition of the booking, not a nicety. The individual answer is that you are allowed to stop, and stopping is safer than performing around an obstacle.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “O” CHECK: “Is there a real perimeter and somebody holding it?” If not, that is a condition to fix before you light, not a thing to absorb during.
scenarios.darkTitle: Stopping Is The Professional Response
scenarios.dark: The trained instinct is to keep going, because performers are conditioned that stopping is failure. Unlearn that one. A set continued around a member of the public standing in the burn radius ends, when it ends badly, with a burned stranger, an insurance claim, and a performer explaining why they did not stop — and the explanation will be that it would have been awkward. The second half of this belongs to the event: a perimeter and a marshal are a condition of booking for fire, and if a promoter will not provide them the correct answer is that you do not perform, not that you perform more carefully.
scenarios.move: Make the perimeter and a named marshal part of accepting the booking. Stop the set the moment the boundary is broken — kill it, say why, restart when it is clear. Agree a stop signal with your safety before you start.
scenarios.say: I need a marshal and a three-metre perimeter or I can't light — that's not negotiable for fire. — [stopping] Set's paused, mate, you're standing in the burn circle. Back behind the line and we'll go again.
scenarios.truth: You are working, not on display. A set that has to be performed around an obstacle is a set that should have stopped.

scenarios.hook: IT'S A GREAT LOOK FOR YOUR REEL
scenarios.archetype: The Unpaid Booking / Spectacle For Exposure
scenarios.clinical: Labor Exploitation / Exposure as Substitute Payment
scenarios.who: A promoter with a budget for sound, lights, security and bar staff, and a line about community for the people doing the dangerous thing in the middle of the field.
scenarios.scene: He wants three fire performers for the Saturday headline changeover. There is no fee. There are wristbands, and he says it in a way that makes the wristbands sound generous. He also mentions that a lot of people get seen at this one, and that the photographer is really good, and every single other trade at this event is being paid.
tells: Wristbands offered as the fee for skilled, insured, dangerous work
Every other supplier at the event is on a rate
No contract, no call time in writing, no fuel or travel budget
No mention of insurance, or an assumption that you carry it
“Exposure”, “the community”, “great for your reel”
The photographer is paid and you are not
scenarios.happening: Fire and aerial performance is skilled, insured, equipment-heavy, physically dangerous labour, and it is the single most reliably unpaid element of a festival's programme because performers love doing it and promoters know that. The comparison that settles it is on-site: the sound engineer, the bar staff, the security and the photographer are all on rates. If a budget exists for everyone who touches the event except the people doing the thing with fire in it, that is a decision rather than a constraint.
scenarios.check: F.L.O.W. — “L” CHECK: “Who else working this event is unpaid?” If the answer is only the performers, the budget is not the problem.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Insurance Question Is The Real One
scenarios.dark: The part that outlives the argument about money is liability. Unpaid, uncontracted, uninsured fire performance means that when somebody is burned — you, a colleague, or a member of the public who walked into the circle — there is no contract establishing who was responsible for the perimeter, no employer, and frequently no cover. Promoters who do not pay performers also, reliably, have not thought about any of that, and the person standing in the footage holding the lit tool is the one who will be answering for it. Ask about public liability in the first conversation. The answer tells you everything about the event's professionalism, before money is even discussed.
scenarios.move: Quote a rate like any other supplier and ask two questions early: what is the fee, and who carries public liability for this performance. Get the call time, perimeter and marshal in writing. Decline cheerfully and early rather than resentfully and late.
scenarios.say: My rate's [x] per performer plus fuel and travel. Also — who's carrying public liability for the fire, you or us? I need that confirmed before I commit.
scenarios.truth: Everyone else at this event is being paid. Your work is more dangerous than most of theirs, and a wristband is not a fee.

guides.intro: Your art is yours. Your body is yours. Your worth is not for sale.

checks.name: Contract First
checks.desc: Handshake deals are not deals. If it's not written, it's not real. Every wall, commission, collab — get it in writing.

checks.name: Rate Is Sacred
checks.desc: 'Exposure' doesn't pay rent. Know your rate before every conversation and don't negotiate it under pressure.

checks.name: Exit Clause
checks.desc: Can you leave this arrangement if it stops being okay? If the answer is no or complicated — that is the problem, not your hesitation.

checks.name: Art Stays Yours
checks.desc: Your image, your work, your process. Nobody photographs it, sells it, or claims credit without your explicit yes.

checks.name: Test The Room
checks.desc: Who's in your creative space while you work? Attention during creation is intimate. Not everyone watching has earned that access.

checks.name: Enough Is Enough
checks.desc: Burnout, boundary erosion, over-giving are the slow drain. You're allowed to stop.

outline.desc: Exposure traps, false collabs, the fan who won't leave
Substance vulnerability while working, validation weaponized
Camp walls that own you, credit theft, financial manipulation
Contracts, rates, saying no, protecting your work and rights
Real collab vs extraction — how to tell the difference

sentences: Exposure doesn't pay rent. A rate does.
Creating in public is not consent to be consumed in private.
My art is my labor. My labor has a price. I know what it is.
A collab without a contract is a favor waiting to be taken.

scenarios.archetype: The Exposure Promoter
scenarios.who: The promoter, organizer, or influencer who wants your art for their event and offers exposure instead of payment. The opportunity sounds real. The exposure rarely materializes. The art is already on their wall.
scenarios.scene: "We can't pay for the live painting but your work will be seen by 20,000 people this weekend and we'll tag you in everything — this could really launch you." You spend 16 hours creating something extraordinary on their main stage wall. The photos go everywhere — 40,000 likes. You get tagged in two of them. The painting stays on their wall. You leave with nothing except the work experience, which you already had.
tells: Payment replaced with "exposure," "experience," or future opportunity — all unquantifiable
The beneficiary of your labor is clearly defined; your benefit is vague and future-tense
No written agreement about tagging, credit, reproduction rights, or ownership
The ask comes under time pressure — event is this weekend, they need an answer now
scenarios.happening: Exposure is a real form of value in some contexts. It is also one of the most systematically used tools to extract free labor from artists. The test: would this person pay a photographer, sound engineer, or caterer in "exposure"? No — because those are recognized as labor. Live painting is also labor. The festival ecosystem has a long history of treating visual artists as ambient decoration. You are not decoration.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — "C" CHECK: "Is there a written agreement — or just a verbal promise that evaporates after the event?"
scenarios.darkTitle: The Live Painting Minimum Contract
scenarios.dark: Every engagement should have in writing: your fee or explicit agreement that this is donated (your choice, not their default), who owns the finished piece, photo/video rights and credit requirements, whether they can reproduce commercially, and what happens if they cancel. Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts (vlany.org) offers free legal help. A legitimate organizer will sign it. The ones who won't are telling you everything.
scenarios.move: Know your rate before every conversation. Exposure is a supplement, not a replacement.
scenarios.say: I'd love to be involved — my rate for a live painting is [X]. What's your budget?
scenarios.truth: Your art is your labor. Your labor has a price. You get to know what it is.

scenarios.archetype: The Collab That Becomes Unpaid Labor
scenarios.who: The person who wants to "collaborate" — which in practice means they contribute a concept or their presence while you contribute the actual skill, time, and materials. Credit gets split equally. Labor doesn't.
scenarios.scene: "I have this incredible vision — I can see it so clearly — I just need someone with your skills to bring it to life. We'd be equal partners." You spend the next day executing their vague concept with your specific technical ability, your materials, your time. The finished piece gets posted with both your names. Their 8,000 followers see it first. The caption says "our piece." When you mention the execution was entirely yours, the vibe goes cold.
tells: They bring concept or personality; you bring skill, time, materials, and execution
Credit proposed as 50/50 before any conversation about actual labor split
Pushback about contribution equity received as you being difficult or insecure
Their platform/following positioned as their "equal contribution"
scenarios.happening: Platform is not the same as labor. A concept is not the same as execution. In the art world these distinctions matter enormously for credit, compensation, and professional record. The collab frame is used to extract skilled labor under the cover of partnership. A genuine collaboration is one where both parties' contributions are named honestly and the credit reflects actual work.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — "A" CHECK: "Does my name appear clearly on this work in a way that reflects my actual contribution?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Photo And Video Credit — Non-Negotiable
scenarios.dark: Every time your work appears online, your name should appear in the caption — not just a tag that can be removed, a written credit. Before any event or collab, establish in writing: (1) all posts featuring your work credit you by name in the caption, (2) you receive advance notice before your work appears in any commercial context, (3) you retain rights to your own images of the work. Screenshot every post featuring your work.
scenarios.move: Define the contribution split before you start creating. If they can't have that conversation — that's your answer.
scenarios.say: I'm into the idea — let's talk about what each of us is actually bringing so we're clear on credit before we start.
scenarios.truth: Equal credit requires equal contribution. Concepts and execution are not the same thing.

scenarios.archetype: The Connector Who Wants a Cut of Everything
scenarios.who: The "connector" — not quite a manager, not quite a promoter — who positions themselves as the key to your next level of exposure and begins expecting ongoing commission on work they introduce you to, then on work they didn't introduce you to.
scenarios.scene: "I'm going to connect you with everyone this weekend — I know all the right people." He does introduce you to two legitimate leads. He also begins referring to himself as your "rep" in conversations with those leads and starts mentioning a 20% "arrangement" that you never agreed to. By the time you realize what's happening, the leads think he's already your manager.
tells: Introduces themselves as your "rep" or "manager" in conversations without your agreement
Commission expectations appear after introductions, not before — retroactively
Scope of what they expect commission on keeps expanding
You're now in a complicated position with leads who believe a deal exists
scenarios.happening: The parasitic middleman move works by creating facts on the ground before you've had a chance to define the relationship. By the time you understand what they're claiming, they're already representing you to the people who matter to you professionally. Clear, early conversation about what any assistance means in terms of compensation is the only protection. If someone introduces themselves as your representative without your agreement — correct it immediately and directly.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “C” CHECK: “Have I agreed to any representation arrangement — or is someone claiming one that was never actually agreed?” — a representative you never hired is telling you exactly who they are.
scenarios.darkTitle: Correcting False Representation
scenarios.dark: If someone is representing themselves as your manager or rep without your agreement: (1) Contact the leads directly and privately: "I want to clarify — [name] is not my manager/rep. I'm handling my own bookings." (2) Tell the person directly: "I haven't agreed to any representation arrangement and I need you to stop representing yourself that way." (3) Document this conversation in writing immediately after. False representation can create enforceable implied contracts in some jurisdictions — address it fast.
scenarios.move: Define every assistance relationship before it becomes a representation relationship.
scenarios.say: "I appreciate the intros — I want to be clear that I'm handling my own arrangements. Any intros are just that — intros, not representation."
scenarios.truth: Anyone who represents themselves as your representative before you've agreed to that is telling you who they are.

scenarios.hook: I JUST LOVE WATCHING YOU CREATE
scenarios.archetype: The Hoverer / The Fan Who Becomes a Fixture
scenarios.who: The person who camps near your workspace all weekend under the banner of admiration. Creating in public is inherently intimate — your focus makes you less boundaried — and predatory hovering exploits all of that.
scenarios.scene: He's been near your painting station since you set up. Brings you water. Makes comments about your process that show he's genuinely paying attention. It feels nice to be witnessed. By Sunday he feels like a fixture of your weekend — he knows your whole process, has opinions about your choices, offered to help break down. When he starts steering the direction of the piece and you redirect, he takes it personally. You feel like you owe him something.
tells: Presence near your workspace extends across the whole weekend without invitation
Witness role gradually becomes advisory role — opinions about your work appear uninvited
Small acts of service (water, help) build invisible debt over time
Redirecting their input or asking for space is received as rejection
scenarios.happening: Creating in public is an intimate act — you're in a focused, slightly vulnerable state. This is a window that predatory observers specifically exploit. Real appreciation respects the artist's process and follows their lead about interaction. Hovering that gradually expands into advisory territory, then into physical presence in your workspace, then into emotional debt — is not admiration. It's occupation disguised as appreciation.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — "T" CHECK: "Who is actually in my creative space right now — and did I invite them there?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Substances And Creative Work — The Vulnerability Window
scenarios.dark: Many live painters work with substances as part of their creative practice — completely valid. Your altered state while working is a specific vulnerability window. You're focused on the work, your social threat-detection is lower, and your boundaries are softer. People who offer substances to you while you're creating are not always doing it neutrally. Know what you're taking, test it before you're in the flow state, and have a trusted person in your orbit who is less altered than you while you work.
scenarios.move: Name your workspace boundaries clearly and early. "I go pretty internal while I work" is a complete sentence.
scenarios.say: I really appreciate the support — I need to be heads-down for a while. I'll find you when I come up for air.
scenarios.truth: Admiration that respects your process from a distance is real. Admiration that requires access to your workspace is not admiration.

scenarios.archetype: Sexual Attention as Artistic Validation
scenarios.who: The specific way sexual attention gets entangled with artistic recognition for visible artists. When someone's interest in your art and interest in your body arrive in the same package, receiving one without the other becomes complicated. That confusion is the tool.
scenarios.scene: He's been complimenting your work genuinely all weekend — knowledgeable, specific, clearly understands what you're doing. It feels good to be seen by someone who gets it. Saturday night he asks if you want to "continue the conversation" at his camp. When you decline he says "I guess I misread the creative energy between us." Suddenly the whole weekend of genuine-feeling artistic recognition has a retroactive question mark over it.
tells: Artistic interest and sexual interest arrive in the same package from the same person
Declining sexual interest causes withdrawal of artistic validation — they're linked
Retroactive reframing of the whole interaction when you say no
You start wondering which of your artistic connections this weekend were actually about your work
scenarios.happening: For visible artists — especially women creating in public — sexual attention and professional attention are frequently bundled together. Being seen as an artist is meaningful and the confusion of that with being desired is a specific manipulation: it makes you question your artistic worth every time you decline someone's sexual interest. Your art's validity is entirely separate from anyone's desire for you.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “T” CHECK: “Is the appreciation of my work actually about my work — or is it cover for something else entirely?” — your art being beautiful does not make your body available.
scenarios.darkTitle: Your Work Being Shared Is Not Your Body Being Available
scenarios.dark: Live painting is public art. Photographs of your work circulate. Your face and body are often in those photographs. None of this is consent for contact, pursuit, or sexual attention. If someone's engagement with images of your work has crossed into following, gathering information about you, or sexual fixation — that's stalking behavior regardless of the artistic frame around it. Screenshot. Block. Report. Document before you report.
scenarios.move: Receive genuine artistic recognition with full confidence. Decline sexual interest without apology. These are completely separate.
scenarios.say: I'm going to keep those two things separate — I'm glad you connected with the work. I'm not available for the rest.
scenarios.truth: Your art being beautiful does not make your body available. Full stop.

scenarios.hook: WE JUST NEED THIS ONE THING
scenarios.archetype: Scope Creep / Moving Goalposts on the Brief
scenarios.who: The commission or project that starts with a clear brief and expands, shifts, or escalates with each interaction — while the original agreed compensation stays fixed. Each change seems small. The cumulative impact is significant.
scenarios.scene: "We love the direction — can you also just add a panel on the left? And can the main figure be slightly different? And can you include our camp's logo somewhere subtle? And can you do a smaller companion piece for the kitchen?" Each ask arrives after the previous one is done, when you're already invested and it feels petty to push back on "just one more thing." You've delivered four times what was originally scoped for the original price.
tells: New requests arrive after previous work is completed and your investment is high
Each individual ask seems small and reasonable in isolation
Original compensation stays fixed as scope expands
Pushing back on changes is framed as being difficult or not collaborative
scenarios.happening: Scope creep in creative work is one of the most common forms of exploitation precisely because each individual expansion seems minor and the accumulated investment makes pushing back feel like losing everything. The professional protection is a written brief with explicit terms: this is what is included, this is what additional work costs. Changes to scope trigger a new conversation about compensation. Every time. Without apology.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “C” CHECK: “Is what I’m being asked to do now what I agreed to do — and is the compensation still matching the scope?” — if the ask has grown and the fee hasn’t, that gap is the whole story.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Change Order Conversation
scenarios.dark: "That's a new element that's outside the original scope — I'm happy to include it, my rate for additions is [X]." Say this every time a new request appears after the brief is agreed. You don't need to be apologetic or elaborate. A change order is a completely normal part of professional creative work. Clients who push back on this are clients who planned to expand scope without paying for it. That's your information about whether you want to work with them again.
scenarios.move: Changes to scope trigger a new compensation conversation. Every time. Without apology.
scenarios.say: That's a new element outside the original brief — happy to include it, my rate for additions is [X]. Want to proceed?
scenarios.truth: Your time and skill are finite. Scope creep is not creative collaboration — it's extraction in slow motion.

scenarios.hook: THE CAMP GAVE YOU A WALL
scenarios.archetype: Camp Ownership / The Wall With Strings
scenarios.who: The camp or art collective that offers you a wall, a stage, a platform — in exchange for labor, loyalty, compliance, or silence about what happens inside that space.
scenarios.scene: "We're giving you the main wall — that's a massive opportunity. We just need you to also help with camp setup, do a couple smaller pieces for the kitchen, and be around for our events as artist-in-residence." What started as one wall becomes three pieces, ten hours of camp labor, mandatory presence at events, and a growing sense that saying no to anything risks losing the whole opportunity. By Sunday you're exhausted and haven't made anything you actually wanted to make.
tells: The initial opportunity expands after you've committed — goalposts keep moving
The space or wall is used as leverage whenever you express a limit
"After everything we've given you" appears when you push back
Your artistic choices are subject to camp approval rather than your own vision
scenarios.happening: Offering a platform and then expanding the terms of accessing it is a classic exploitation structure — you've already committed, walking away means losing what you came for, and each small additional ask seems reasonable. This is scope creep as manipulation. A real artist-in-residence opportunity has defined terms before you arrive. If the terms are defined verbally and keep expanding in practice — you're not a resident artist. You're camp labor with an art cover story.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “E” CHECK: “Can I walk away from this arrangement right now without losing something I shouldn’t have had to risk in the first place?” — an undefined arrangement is a contract you’re signing in paint.
scenarios.darkTitle: Who Actually Owns The Finished Piece
scenarios.dark: When you paint on someone's wall, at someone's event, on someone's surface — who owns the finished work? Physical custody of a wall is not the same as copyright ownership of the art on it. Before you paint: establish in writing whether you retain reproduction rights to your own images of the work, whether the piece can be painted over without your consent, whether your name must accompany any reproduction, and whether they can sell images or prints. US Copyright Office (copyright.gov): your work is automatically copyrighted the moment you create it.
scenarios.move: Define the terms before you commit. Changing terms after commitment is pressure, not negotiation.
scenarios.say: I'm excited about the wall — can we nail down exactly what's included on both sides before I commit?
scenarios.truth: A platform with undefined terms is not an opportunity. It's a blank contract you're signing in paint.

scenarios.hook: WE'LL PAY YOU AFTER THE EVENT
scenarios.archetype: Payment Delays / Non-Payment for Creative Work
scenarios.who: Getting paid what you were promised, on the timeline agreed, is the baseline. It is also one of the most commonly violated terms for creative workers at festivals. The variations are endless. The pattern is always the same.
scenarios.scene: "The accounting is still getting sorted — payment will be in your account by end of month." End of month: "we had some unexpected costs, we're going to need to adjust the final payment." Or: you delivered the commission, the client went quiet, three weeks later you're following up for the third time. Or: the event was three months ago and the check that was "in the mail" has never arrived.
tells: Payment delayed past agreed date without prior communication
"Unexpected costs" or "accounting issues" appear after the work is delivered
Communication becomes vague or slow after the work is delivered
Each follow-up produces a new reason and a new timeline
scenarios.happening: Cash flow manipulation is a feature, not a bug, of predatory event economics. Your leverage decreases dramatically once you've delivered the work — which is why deposits exist. Get 50% before you start. Invoice immediately on delivery. Send written payment requests with your contract attached. Paper trail everything. Most non-payers rely on artists being too tired, too embarrassed, or too non-confrontational to pursue it. Pursue it.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — "C" CHECK: "Do I have a signed agreement with payment terms — so I have something to enforce?"
scenarios.darkTitle: When They Don't Pay — Your Options
scenarios.dark: Step 1: written demand email with contract attached, specific payment deadline (7-14 days). Step 2: small claims court handles disputes up to $10,000-$25,000 depending on state — filing fee usually under $100, you represent yourself. Step 3: for larger amounts, one attorney demand letter (often $150-300) frequently resolves it. Step 4: publicizing non-payment in artist and vendor communities is legal and effective — many predatory organizers rely on silence. Document everything before going public.
scenarios.move: 50% deposit before you start. Invoice immediately on delivery. Paper trail everything.
scenarios.say: Per our agreement, the remaining balance of [X] is due within 7 days. Please confirm receipt of this.
scenarios.truth: You created the work. You get paid what was agreed. This is not complicated and it is completely enforceable.

scenarios.archetype: Image and IP Theft / Unauthorized Reproduction
scenarios.who: Your designs, your process images, your finished work appearing on someone else's merchandise, social media, or promotional materials — without your permission, without credit, and often generating revenue for them while you receive nothing.
scenarios.scene: You find your work on a festival's merchandise table — a tote bag and two t-shirts featuring a painting you created for them two years ago. You were paid for the original painting. You were not paid for any reproduction rights. Nobody asked. When you bring it up you're told "but we paid for the painting" — as if payment for the original work included unlimited commercial reproduction rights forever. It didn't.
tells: Your work appearing on merchandise, promotional materials, or commercial contexts without notice
"We paid for the painting" used to justify unlimited reproduction rights
Your work appearing in advertising, sponsorship materials, or branded content
Digital versions of your work being sold, licensed, or reproduced without your knowledge
scenarios.happening: Payment for an original artwork does not transfer reproduction rights unless explicitly stated in writing. Copyright in the original work belongs to you. The buyer purchased the physical object — not the right to reproduce it commercially. This is not a gray area. It is copyright law. The protection is a written agreement before any commission that specifies exactly what rights the buyer receives and what they do not.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “A” CHECK: “Has anyone asked me in writing for permission to reproduce this work — or did they just assume they could?” — assumption is not permission, and it never comes with a check attached.
scenarios.darkTitle: Reproduction Rights — What To Include In Every Commission
scenarios.dark: Your commission agreement should specify: (1) what rights the buyer receives — typically "right to display the original artwork" only, (2) that all reproduction rights remain with the artist, (3) any commercial use (merchandise, advertising, print) requires a separate license with additional fee, (4) your name must appear with any digital reproduction. US Copyright registration ($65 at copyright.gov) gives you the ability to sue for statutory damages ($750-$30,000 per infringement) — making enforcement financially viable.
scenarios.move: Define reproduction rights in writing before any commission. Payment for the original piece is not payment for reproduction rights.
scenarios.say: Reproduction rights are separate from the original — if you'd like to use this work on merchandise we'll need a separate licensing agreement.
scenarios.truth: You created it. You own the right to reproduce it. Every commercial use requires your permission and your compensation.

scenarios.archetype: Rates, Rights, and Protecting What You Make
scenarios.who: This is the practical page. Rates, rights, contracts, credit. The unglamorous infrastructure that means you can keep making art without being slowly drained by every festival you attend.
scenarios.scene: The artists who thrive on the festival circuit long-term are not the ones who work hardest. They're the ones who figured out their value early, put it in writing consistently, and stopped apologizing for having a professional framework inside a culture that frames everything as family and love. You can love this community AND operate professionally within it.
tells: Know your day rate and piece rate before any conversation — not during it
Every engagement in writing: fee, deliverables, credit requirements, ownership, cancellation
Photograph your own work before, during, and after — your documentation is your record
Watermark your digital images before sharing widely online
scenarios.happening: Festival culture's "we're all family" framing is beautiful and also systematically used to remove the professional frameworks that protect artists. Family doesn't charge family. Family doesn't need contracts. Family gives freely. This creates the conditions for systematic exploitation of your labor. You can operate with full love for the community AND maintain professional clarity about how your work is valued. In fact, artists who know their worth make the community stronger by modeling that art has value.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “R” CHECK: “Is my rate for this engagement something I decided — or something that got decided around me?” — a rate you didn’t set is a rate someone else set, on purpose, in their favor.
scenarios.darkTitle: Resources For Artists
scenarios.dark: Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts (vlany.org): free/low-cost legal help on contracts, copyright, and disputes. US Copyright Office (copyright.gov): automatic copyright on creation, registration ($65) enables enforcement. Graphic Artists Guild Handbook — Pricing and Ethical Standards: industry reference for rates. CERF+ (cerfplus.org): emergency assistance for working craft artists facing crisis. Artists' legal clinics exist in most major cities — search "volunteer lawyers for the arts [your city]."
scenarios.move: Set your rate. Put it in writing. Say it out loud without apologizing. Repeat.
scenarios.say: My rate for live painting is [X] for the weekend. Does that work with your budget?
scenarios.truth: Knowing your worth and saying it out loud is not ego. It is what keeps you in the game.

scenarios.archetype: What Genuine Creative Partnership Actually Looks Like
scenarios.who: Real collabs exist. They're some of the best creative experiences in the festival world. Here's how they're different from the extractive version — so you can recognize and pursue the genuine ones.
scenarios.scene: She approaches you and says she's been watching your work and she does immersive sound installations and she thinks your visual language and her sonic language could be interesting together. "I'm not sure what it would look like — want to just experiment and see? No output pressure, no specific deliverable, just exploration. And if we make something we both want to show, we figure out the terms then." No agenda. No pitch. Just curiosity. That's different.
tells: Both parties' contributions are named honestly before work begins
Decision about whether to share the output happens AFTER creation — not before as leverage
Credit structure is proposed as a conversation, not a demand
The person is genuinely interested in you as an artist, not in what you can do for their project
scenarios.happening: Real collaboration is characterized by mutual curiosity, defined terms, and shared investment in the outcome. The distinction from extraction is visible in who carries the risk, who defines the terms, and whether both parties' contributions are named honestly. Real collaborators are comfortable with the credit conversation because they're not trying to hide the imbalance. Real collaborators celebrate each other's other work and connections rather than centralizing everything through themselves.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “A” CHECK: “Is this person interested in my whole artistic practice — or just in what my hands can do for their project?” — real collaborators want your voice. The fake ones just want your output.
scenarios.darkTitle: How To Propose A Real Collab
scenarios.dark: When you want to genuinely collaborate with another artist: (1) Express specific interest in their work and why you think your practices could be interesting together. (2) Propose exploration without a predetermined outcome or output obligation. (3) Agree on credit and ownership structure BEFORE you create anything you might want to share. (4) Be comfortable with "this didn't produce something we want to show" as a valid outcome. The best creative partnerships in the festival world start with this kind of honest, low-stakes curiosity.
scenarios.move: Pursue real collabs with full enthusiasm. Protect yourself from extraction with clear terms. Both can be true.
scenarios.say: "I'd love to explore this — before we create anything, let's agree on how we'd handle credit and ownership if something comes out of it worth sharing."
scenarios.truth: The real collabs are out there. Protect yourself from the fake ones so you have the energy to find them.

scenarios.archetype: Your Online Presence, Your Work, Your Safety
scenarios.who: Your digital presence as an artist at festivals creates specific vulnerabilities: your work being appropriated without credit, your images being used without consent, and your online presence being used to locate or contact you in ways you didn't invite.
scenarios.scene: Someone has been using your work without credit for three months. You've found it on their Etsy, their promotional materials, their social media. You've found your face — from a photo someone else took at a festival — being used in a "free creative" stock image collection. You've received DMs from a man who clearly knows your festival schedule, your booth location, and details about your process that feel like surveillance. Each thing is individually manageable. Together they paint a picture.
tells: Your work appearing online without credit or permission in commercial contexts
Photographs of you from festivals used in contexts you didn't authorize
Someone who seems to know your festival schedule, locations, and movements in detail
DMs that reference specific details about your process or whereabouts that weren't publicly shared
scenarios.happening: Digital exploitation of artists operates on multiple simultaneous tracks: IP theft (your work), image rights violations (your likeness), and stalking behavior (your location and schedule). Each track requires different tools. All of them require documentation. Screenshot everything that might be relevant before you report it — platforms remove content on reports and you lose your evidence if you don't capture it first.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — "A" CHECK: "Have I documented this situation before reporting it — do I have screenshots and dates?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Digital Safety Basics For Festival Artists
scenarios.dark: (1) Watermark your digital work — your name and website embedded in the image itself, not just the caption. (2) Use a dedicated email for professional inquiries — not your personal email. (3) Don't share your festival schedule publicly beyond the event you're at. (4) If you feel someone is tracking your location or movements: document it, tell a trusted person, contact festival security, and if it escalates contact local law enforcement (Stalking Prevention Awareness and Resource Center: stalkingawareness.org). (5) Your festival address, vehicle, and home location are private. Treat them that way.
scenarios.move: Watermark everything. Document anything concerning. Report before you think you should.
scenarios.say: [To festival security]: "Someone has been tracking my location and movements across events. I'd like to make a report."
scenarios.truth: Your online presence is an extension of your work. Protect it with the same intentionality you bring to your art.

scenarios.archetype: Over-Giving as a Control Dynamic
scenarios.who: The pressure to create publicly, generously, and constantly — for the community, for the vibe, for the love of it — while ignoring the reality that your creative capacity is finite and the constant demands on it are not always coming from a neutral place.
scenarios.scene: You came to the festival to create and you've made twelve pieces, done two free workshops, gifted four finished works, painted a wall for the camp, contributed to a collab you didn't really want to be part of, and helped three other artists with their setups. It's Sunday and you're empty. You feel proud and resentful simultaneously. You gave everything and you're not sure you gave it to the right people or the right places or even because you wanted to.
tells: Requests for your creative labor accumulate until you can't find your own work in your schedule
"For the community" is used to override your "I need to stop now"
Your giving is received as a baseline expectation rather than a choice
You feel proud and resentful simultaneously — the resentment is information
