scenarios.happening: Giving is a value in festival culture and creative communities. The shadow side is that it can be systematically exploited — where one person's generosity is treated as an extractable resource rather than a chosen gift. When the word "no" starts to feel selfish inside a community that calls itself loving, that community is using your values against you. Resentment is the signal that giving has crossed from chosen to coerced.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — "E" CHECK: "Enough is enough — am I still giving from abundance or am I giving from depletion?"
scenarios.darkTitle: What Sovereign Creative Giving Looks Like
scenarios.dark: Sovereign giving is giving from fullness — you have something to give, you choose to give it, and the giving leaves you replenished rather than depleted. The test: do you feel genuinely good after giving, or do you feel relief that the request has been satisfied? Relief is not generosity. Relief is appeasement. You are allowed to say: "I'm not available for this right now." You are allowed to charge for your time. You are allowed to choose what you make and for whom. These are not failures of community. They are the conditions that make sustainable community possible.
scenarios.move: Give from fullness. Stop when you're depleted. Resentment is information, not ingratitude.
scenarios.say: I'm not available for any more projects this weekend — I need to be protective of my own creative energy.
scenarios.truth: Your creative capacity is finite. Treating it like an unlimited public resource is not community. It's extraction.

scenarios.hook: WE RAN YOUR STUFF THROUGH A MODEL
scenarios.archetype: Your Style, Regenerated Without You
scenarios.who: A promoter, a brand, or a former client who has discovered they can get something that looks like your work without booking you — and who genuinely does not understand why you would object, because no file of yours was copied.
scenarios.scene: The poster for this year's event is unmistakably yours. The palette, the linework, the way you do figures. You did not make it. When you ask, they say they made it in-house, and then, cheerfully, that they used your last three pieces as references, and they say it as though that were a compliment rather than a description of what they did.
tells: Work that reproduces your recognizable style without your involvement
“In the style of”, or your name used as a prompt reference
A former client who stopped booking you and whose visuals did not change
Your live-painting footage or process shots used as training references
A contract clause licensing your work for “any purpose including machine learning”
They are baffled by your objection and cite that nothing was copied
scenarios.happening: Style is not protected the way a specific work is, which makes this legally murky and commercially devastating — a festival that can generate something close enough to your look does not need to book you, and the thing that made you employable becomes the thing that replaces you. The practical defence is therefore contractual and evidential rather than legal after the fact: what you license, to whom, for how long, and whether machine learning uses are excluded. Most artists have never read that clause and most event contracts now contain one.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “A” CHECK: “What exactly did I license, and does it exclude training and generation?” If you have never checked, assume it does not.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Clause You Signed In A Queue
scenarios.dark: Look at the media and artist agreements you have already signed, because the grabbing happens there rather than later. Perpetual, worldwide, sublicensable, all media now known or hereafter devised, for any purpose — that language predates all of this and covers it completely, and the artists most exposed are the ones who signed it years ago and never looked again. Add an exclusion in writing to every future agreement, register the significant pieces where registration exists in your country, and document your process with dated footage. Provenance is what you will have instead of a remedy.
scenarios.move: Add an explicit exclusion to every contract — no training, no generative reuse, no style derivation — and get it in the email even when you cannot get it in the document. Watermark and register key work. Keep dated process footage. Raise it once, in writing, with the actual decision-maker rather than publicly.
scenarios.say: My licence excludes any machine-learning or generative use, including style references — can you confirm that in writing before I invoice? — That poster is derived from my work. I'd like to talk about a fee or its removal.
scenarios.truth: They did not copy a file, they copied the decade. Put the exclusion in the contract, because there is no remedy afterwards.

scenarios.hook: IT'S FINE, THE TENT'S OPEN AT ONE END
scenarios.archetype: Solvents, Aerosols And Four Days In A Marquee
scenarios.who: The environment, plus a schedule that wants eight hours of live painting a day inside a structure designed to keep rain off rather than to move air.
scenarios.scene: You are spraying in a marquee with the sides down because it is raining. There are three other painters doing the same thing and a crowd standing in it watching, and by the fourth hour you have the headache you always get and have stopped noticing the smell, which is the part that should worry you most.
tells: Aerosols or solvents used in an enclosed or half-closed structure
You have stopped smelling it, which means saturation rather than safety
Headache, dizziness, nausea, or a sore throat by mid-afternoon
No respirator, or a dust mask being used as though it filtered vapour
The public standing in the same air with no ventilation plan
Consecutive long days, because the exposure is cumulative
scenarios.happening: Solvent and aerosol exposure is a genuine occupational hazard with cumulative effects on the nervous system and the airways, and live painting at festivals reproduces almost every condition that makes it worse: enclosed space, long consecutive days, no extraction, and no employer carrying a duty of care. The critical detail is that a dust mask does nothing against organic vapour — it is the wrong class of protection entirely, and it produces a false sense of safety that leads people to work longer in worse air.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “E” CHECK: “Can I smell it, and is air actually moving through here?” If you have stopped smelling it and nothing is moving, leave now rather than at the end of the piece.
scenarios.darkTitle: Acclimatization Is Not Tolerance
scenarios.dark: The dangerous signal is the one that feels like good news. When the smell fades you have not adapted, your olfactory receptors have saturated — and you are now breathing the same concentration with the warning system switched off, which is why people work through it and why the worst exposures happen to the most experienced painters on the longest days. Cumulative solvent exposure over years of festivals is a known occupational pattern and it does not announce itself. Buy the right cartridge respirator, insist on open sides, and take the piece outside when the rain stops.
scenarios.move: Carry an organic-vapour cartridge respirator, not a dust mask, and know when the cartridges expire. Insist on cross-ventilation as a condition of the pitch. Break outside every hour. Use water-based paint where the piece allows it, and keep the public out of the immediate air.
scenarios.say: I need the sides up on at least two walls or I can't spray in here — it's a vapour thing, not a preference. — Taking twenty outside, back at four.
scenarios.truth: When you stop smelling it, your warning system has failed, not the fumes. That is the moment to go outside.

scenarios.hook: I DON'T WANT TO PAINT THAT
scenarios.archetype: The Brief You Object To / Declining Without Burning The Circuit
scenarios.clinical: Creative Autonomy / Reputational Risk in Refusal
scenarios.who: A promoter, a brand or a camp with a brief that conflicts with something you actually hold — imagery you find appropriative, a sponsor you object to, a message you do not want your name on.
scenarios.scene: The brief lands and it is a good fee and there is a piece of it you cannot do: a symbol that is not yours to paint, or a brand you have publicly criticized, or a theme you think is straightforwardly bad. And the circuit is small, and saying no to this promoter means something for next season, and you are already assembling a version where you do it and put it in a different corner of your portfolio.
tells: The brief conflicts with something you would defend in public
You are negotiating with yourself rather than with them
The fee is doing the arguing
Nobody has offered a route to modify the brief
You are planning to leave it off your portfolio, which is the tell
You expect refusal to cost you future bookings
scenarios.happening: This is a live-painting problem more than a studio one, because you make the work in public, with your name on the pitch, in front of the audience whose opinion is your actual asset. A piece you are uncomfortable with is not a private compromise; it is a public statement made in your hand, photographed, and attributed to you for years. The practical question is rarely whether to refuse outright — most briefs have a component that can be changed — and the useful move is to separate the part you object to from the job and offer an alternative.
scenarios.check: C.R.E.A.T.E. — “T” CHECK: “Would I be happy for this to be the piece people associate with me?” Planning to leave it out of your portfolio is the answer arriving early.
scenarios.darkTitle: Refusing Well Is A Skill Worth Having
scenarios.dark: The real risk is not refusing, it is refusing badly — late, publicly, or with a moral framing that makes the promoter the villain in a small circuit where everybody talks. That is what costs bookings, and it is avoidable. Decline early, privately, warmly, with an alternative attached and no lecture, and you will usually keep the relationship and occasionally get the brief changed. Nobody is owed your explanation for why, and delivering one is what turns a professional no into an argument. The artists who last on a circuit are the ones who can say no in a single friendly sentence and still be booked the following year.
scenarios.move: Decline early and privately, name only the specific element, and offer a concrete alternative. Do not explain your ethics at length and do not go public. If the fee is genuinely tempting, ask for the brief to change rather than negotiating with yourself.
scenarios.say: Love the rest of it and I'm keen — the one thing I can't paint is [element], it's not mine to use. If you're happy with [alternative] in that space I'm in, and if not, no hard feelings, I'd still love to do next season.
scenarios.truth: You make your work in public with your name on it. A piece you would hide is a piece you should have declined.

guides.intro: You hold two things at once: a camera that gives you access, and a file that belongs to somebody else's life. This guide is about handling both honestly.

checks.name: License Is Not Implied By Location
checks.desc: Being in public is not consent to be published. Legality and ethics are different questions and only one of them protects the person in the frame.

checks.name: Everything You Shoot Is Someone's Monday
checks.desc: That frame outlives the weekend. Who sees it, where it lands, and what it costs them at work or at home is your call before you post, not theirs after.

checks.name: No Means Delete It Now, In Front Of Them
checks.desc: A withdrawal of consent is not a negotiation about a good shot. Delete it while they watch, and say you have.

checks.name: Sell Your Work, Not Your Rights
checks.desc: Unpaid, unlimited, perpetual, all media. Festival media contracts take everything by default and most shooters sign without reading.

outline.desc: Access as a lure, the shoot that becomes something else, exposure as payment
The frame you did not earn, altered subjects, the long lens
Footage held over people, rights grabs, the unpaid perpetual license
The consent practice, the delete rule, the contract you actually read
What you owe the people in your frames

sentences: Public is not permission. I ask, and I take a no without negotiating.
If somebody changes their mind, I delete it while they watch.
I do not shoot people who cannot currently tell me not to.
My rate is a rate. Exposure is not a currency I accept.
The file outlives the weekend. I act like it.

scenarios.archetype: The Camera As A Key / Access Offered In Trade
scenarios.clinical: Access Exploitation / Quid Pro Quo Grooming
scenarios.who: Has a laminate, a long lens, and an unusual amount of freedom of movement. Offers to shoot you, offers to get you in, offers to introduce you — and the offers arrive in a sequence that keeps having a next step.
scenarios.scene: He says your look is incredible and he wants to shoot you properly, and he can get you into the artist area because he shoots for them. The first shoot is professional and the pictures are genuinely the best you have ever had of yourself. The second one he suggests somewhere private for the light, and mentions the festival he shoots in the spring, and asks whether you would want to be involved with that.
tells: Access, introductions and opportunity all route through one person
Shoots move from public to private across sessions
Wardrobe or nudity is introduced gradually rather than agreed up front
The next opportunity is always just ahead and is always in his gift
No call sheet, no assistant, no third person, no written brief
The work is good, which is what makes the arrangement hard to leave
scenarios.happening: A camera is one of the most efficient access tools at a festival — it explains proximity, justifies attention, licenses photographing strangers, and moves through restricted space. Nearly everyone carrying one is doing the job. But the same properties make it attractive to someone who wants proximity for other reasons, and the pattern is the classic one from the modelling and music industries: real opportunity, real skill, real photographs, with each step requiring slightly more and each step justified by the last. The tell is not creepiness. It is the absence of the ordinary professional furniture — no brief, no third person, no rate, nothing in writing.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “E” CHECK: “Is there a third person, a written brief, and a stated rate?” Professionals have all three. Their absence is not informality, it is the design.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Photographs Are The Hold
scenarios.dark: The photographs themselves become the leverage, and that is often the point rather than a side effect. Once someone holds images of you — especially anything you agreed to when you were tired, altered, flattered, or halfway through a shoot you did not want to ruin — they hold something that can be released, hinted at, or simply remembered out loud. Nothing has to be threatened. If you are in this: the files existing is not the end of your options, and the fastest way to defuse a hold is to stop it being a secret — tell one person now, in writing, before anything is asked. A secret with two keepers is worth far less to the person holding it.
scenarios.move: Insist on the professional furniture: a written brief, a rate or a clear trade, a third person present, and no private locations for a first shoot. Bring somebody. Somebody wanting to shoot you properly will not mind an assistant; somebody wanting the room will mind a great deal, and that is your answer.
scenarios.say: Sounds great — I'll bring a friend, and can you send me a quick brief and what the usage is? I keep it all written down, it's just how I work.
scenarios.truth: A real photographer wants an assistant, a brief and a release. The ones who want the room empty are telling you what the shoot is for.

scenarios.hook: SHE WON'T MIND, SHE'S HAVING A GREAT TIME
scenarios.archetype: The Frame You Did Not Earn / Shooting The Incapacitated
scenarios.who: You, on a good night, with a great frame in front of you and a legal right to take it and a rationalization already forming. This page is aimed at the photographer, not at the subject.
scenarios.scene: It is four in the morning and she is beautiful and completely gone, sitting on the grass laughing at nothing with her top half off, and it is the best light of the entire weekend. Nobody would stop you. It is a public field. She is not in a position to object and will not remember either way, and you already know that is the reason the shot is available.
tells: The subject could not consent right now if you asked
You are relying on them not noticing rather than on them agreeing
The frame's value comes from their state rather than from the moment
Long lens, from distance, on someone who has not clocked you
You are constructing a justification before you have taken it
You would not show them the shot tomorrow and ask
scenarios.happening: Legality and ethics part company here completely. In most jurisdictions you may photograph people in public and publish it, and that permission is exactly why the profession needs a standard above it — the law is not doing the work of deciding whether a frame should exist. A person who is incapacitated cannot consent to being photographed any more than they can consent to anything else, and a photographer relying on their impairment has made the same move as everybody else in this book who waits for capacity to drop. The test is simple and it is the one the whole trade runs on: could you show them tomorrow, and would they say yes.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “L” CHECK: “Could this person consent right now if I asked?” If not, there is no frame here. The camera does not create a permission the situation does not contain.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Are The Risk On This Page
scenarios.dark: Most of this book is about somebody doing something to the reader. This page is the other way round, and it is in here because festival photography has a genuine, ongoing problem with it: the near-nude, the overwhelmed, the passed-out, the person in a crisis at the harm-reduction tent, shot at distance and posted as atmosphere. Those frames circulate for years. They cost people jobs, custody arrangements, and their sense of safety in a place they loved. The photographer is usually not malicious — they are a person who wanted a good shot and let the law answer an ethical question. Do not be that. Tomorrow-test every frame, and when a frame fails it, do not take it rather than not posting it, because files leak and drives get shared.
scenarios.move: Apply the tomorrow test before the shutter, not before the upload. If someone is impaired, in distress, or in a medical or harm-reduction context, put the camera down entirely — and if you have already shot it, delete it now rather than filing it.
scenarios.say: Not shooting that one. — [to a colleague] Mate, she's gone, leave it. Get the crowd instead.
scenarios.truth: The law says you may. The law is not your ethics, and a photograph of somebody's worst night outlives both of you.

scenarios.archetype: The Rights Grab / Unpaid, Unlimited, Perpetual
scenarios.who: The media accreditation form nobody reads, and the production manager who genuinely believes a wristband is payment because everybody has always said it is.
scenarios.scene: The accreditation form is four paragraphs and you are filling it in on your phone in a queue. One of those paragraphs assigns the festival a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free, sublicensable license to everything you shoot, in all media, for any purpose including advertising, with no credit obligation. You tick it because the gate opens in ten minutes and because everyone ticks it.
tells: “Perpetual”, “irrevocable”, “royalty-free”, “all media now known or hereafter devised”
Sublicensable — meaning sponsors and brands get your work too
No credit obligation, or credit at their discretion
Payment described as exposure, access, or a wristband
The form arrives at the gate, under time pressure, on a phone
No usage window, no territory limit, no carve-out for your own portfolio
scenarios.happening: Festival media terms are among the most aggressive rights grabs in working photography, and they are accepted almost universally because they are presented at the moment of least leverage — at the gate, in a queue, with the job about to start. The result is a marketing archive built for free out of freelancers' work, resold to sponsors, with no credit. This is the M.A.R.K.E.T. guide's exposure problem with a contract stapled to it, and the difference is that here you are signing away the asset itself rather than just working cheap. The good news is that these terms are usually negotiable, because the person holding the clipboard has never been asked.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “S” CHECK: “What exactly am I licensing, to whom, for how long?” Three answers before you tick. If you cannot state them, do not sign at the gate.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Signed Away The Archive, Not The Weekend
scenarios.dark: The cost is not this festival, it is the decade afterwards. A perpetual sublicensable license means the frame you shot at twenty-three can be sold to a drinks brand at thirty-three without a call, a credit or a fee, and you have no standing to object because you ticked a box in a queue. Shooters discover this years later when their own image turns up on a billboard for something they would never endorse. Ask for the form in advance, by email, before you travel. That one request — the most junior-sounding thing on this page — is the whole defense, because a term you negotiate on Tuesday is a term, and a term you meet at the gate is an ultimatum.
scenarios.move: Request the media terms by email before you commit to the trip. Propose a limited license: twelve months, editorial and social only, credit required, no sublicensing to sponsors, and you keep everything else. Most will accept, because almost nobody asks.
scenarios.say: Can you send the accreditation terms over before I book travel? I usually license twelve months editorial with credit rather than perpetual all-media — happy to work to that.
scenarios.truth: Exposure has never once paid an invoice. The license is the deal, and the gate is the worst place on earth to read one.

scenarios.archetype: How Working Photographers Actually Do This
scenarios.who: For every shooter, from the phone in the crowd to the one with the laminate. None of this slows you down after the first weekend, and all of it is what separates a photographer people trust from one they warn each other about.
scenarios.scene: The whole practice is four habits and they take about three seconds each. The reason to build them now is that the moment you need them — somebody upset, somebody's partner asking, somebody who saw themselves on an account — is not a moment when you want to be inventing a policy.
tells: Ask before, not after — a raised camera and a look is often enough
Say where it is going: personal, editorial, client, socials, with credit or not
If they are impaired, in distress, or with kids: no frame, no exceptions
If a no arrives later, delete it while they watch and tell them you have
Hand over a card or a handle so people can reach you
Never post a stranger's face with a caption that mocks them
scenarios.happening: Consent practice is what makes the difference between a photographer who gets access and one who gets asked to leave, and it compounds: people who have been treated well introduce you, tip you off, and let you shoot things nobody else gets to shoot. It is also the cheapest professional insurance available, because almost every media dispute at a festival starts with somebody who was photographed without being asked and had no way to reach the person who did it. Being findable is half the practice. Deleting on request is the other half, and it costs you one frame out of two thousand.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “N” CHECK: “If they asked me to delete this right now, would I do it without arguing?” If the answer is no, you are treating the file as more important than the person, and you will eventually be the story.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Delete Is The Whole Reputation
scenarios.dark: Deleting in front of somebody, immediately and without negotiation, is the single most reputationally valuable thing a festival photographer can do, and it is also the one most of them get wrong. The instinct is to explain — that it is a great shot, that you would not post it, that you shoot for the festival. Every word of that reads as a negotiation over whether their no counts, and it is remembered that way. Delete first. Say you have. Explain nothing. People talk to each other, and the photographers who become trusted in a scene are trusted for exactly this, not for their portfolio.
scenarios.move: Build the four habits until they are automatic, and put your handle on a sticker on your camera strap so anybody can find you afterwards. Practise the delete — do it once, cheerfully, and notice it costs you nothing.
scenarios.say: Mind if I grab one? It's for my own stuff, I'd tag you. — [later] Course, deleting it now, look — gone. All good.
scenarios.truth: One deleted frame costs you nothing. The reputation for deleting without arguing is worth more than any shot you will take this weekend.

scenarios.archetype: What You Owe The People In Your Frames
scenarios.who: You, at home on the Tuesday, with two thousand frames and a deadline and no one watching what you select.
scenarios.scene: There is a frame in there of somebody mid-breakdown at the edge of a crowd, and it is the best photograph you took all weekend. It says something true about the whole event. Nobody would ever know who they are except everyone who knows them, which at a festival of this size is probably four hundred people.
tells: Would this person be fine with their employer, family or ex seeing this
Are they identifiable to people who know them, even if not to strangers
Are they in a medical, harm-reduction, welfare or crisis context
Is anybody in the frame a minor, and is anybody outed by it
Would you be comfortable sending it to them before you post it
Is this frame about the festival, or about them specifically
scenarios.happening: Selection is where the ethics actually live — the shutter is a reflex, the edit is a decision made with time and without pressure, and that is the moment you are accountable for. Festival crowds contain people who are not out, people whose employers do not know they are here, people in custody disputes, people in recovery, people who are somewhere they told someone else they were not. None of that is visible in the frame and all of it is downstream of your upload. You cannot check for every case, which is exactly why the general rules exist: no crisis contexts, no minors without a parent's yes, no identifiable faces in compromising states, and send it to them first when you are unsure.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “E” CHECK: “Am I willing to send this to the person in it before it goes up?” If not, that reluctance is the answer, and you already know what it means.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Best Frame Is Usually The One To Kill
scenarios.dark: The photographs that do the most damage are almost never the careless ones — they are the excellent ones, because those are the ones that travel. A brilliant frame of somebody at their worst gets shared precisely as far as it is good, and the person in it spends a year meeting it. If you shoot festivals for long enough you will take a frame that is genuinely the best work of your career and should never be published, and what you do with that frame is the whole of your professional character. Nobody will ever know you killed it. That is rather the point.
scenarios.move: Make the edit a separate session with the rules in front of you, not a scroll at 1am. When a frame is strong and you are unsure, send it to the subject and let them decide — most say yes, and the ones who say no are the ones that would have been the problem.
scenarios.say: Hey — took this of you on Saturday, think it's a great shot. Only posting it if you're happy, no hard feelings either way.
scenarios.truth: Your best photograph is not automatically a photograph you are allowed to publish. The edit is where you find out what kind of photographer you are.

scenarios.hook: ALONE, AT NIGHT, WITH FOUR GRAND OF GEAR
scenarios.archetype: The Photographer As The Target
scenarios.who: Whoever has been watching the person with the obvious camera bag walk back to the media tent alone at three in the morning for the third night running, on the same route, at roughly the same time.
scenarios.scene: You shot the headliner, you are carrying two bodies and three lenses, and the walk back to the car park goes through the dark bit behind the production compound because it is quicker. You do this every night. You have never thought about it, because you are thinking about the edit.
tells: The same route, the same time, alone, every night
Visible high-value equipment and no discreet bag
Working at the crowd's edges and in unlit areas by the nature of the job
Head in the camera — the one posture that removes your situational awareness
Nobody knows your route or when you are due back
Somebody has been unusually interested in what you are carrying
scenarios.happening: Photographers occupy the highest-risk position at a festival and almost never think of themselves as at risk: they carry the most valuable and most portable items on site, they work alone at night by necessity, they are in the unlit margins rather than in the crowd, and the job itself requires them to spend long stretches with one eye in a viewfinder and no awareness of what is behind them. The equipment loss is the visible risk. Being followed to a vehicle in an unlit car park at three in the morning is the one that matters more.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “E” CHECK: “Does anybody know my route and my ETA tonight?” If the answer is no, and it is the same route as last night, that is two problems rather than one.
scenarios.darkTitle: Vary The Route, Tell Somebody The Time
scenarios.dark: The pattern is what does it. Somebody who wants your gear does not need to find you; they need to watch you once and then wait in the right place the following night, and a photographer is the most predictable person on a festival site — same stages, same pits, same exit, same hour. Two changes remove almost all of it, and neither costs anything: alter the route and the timing, and have a named person expecting you with a time. The gear is insured. Being alone in an unlit car park at three in the morning with somebody who has been planning it since Friday is not.
scenarios.move: Vary your route and your times. Use an unbranded bag. Walk out with someone — another shooter, crew, security — and agree an ETA with a named person each night. Insure the kit properly and keep serial numbers and photographs.
scenarios.say: Walking out at half two — anyone going the same way? — [message] Heading to the car park now, back at the hotel by three, I'll text when I'm in.
scenarios.truth: You are the most predictable, most valuable and least accompanied person on this site. Change two of those three tonight.

scenarios.hook: THERE ARE KIDS IN THAT FRAME
scenarios.archetype: Photographing Children At A Public Event
scenarios.clinical: Child Safeguarding / Image Consent for Minors
scenarios.who: You, in the family field, where the light is good and the pictures are genuinely lovely and every single one of them has a safeguarding dimension you are responsible for.
scenarios.scene: A child on someone's shoulders at golden hour with her hands in the air is one of the great festival photographs and you have a clear shot of it. You do not know her, you have not spoken to her parents, and in about four hours you will be deciding whether to put a recognizable image of somebody else's child on a public account.
tells: A recognizable minor, no parent asked
The frame would identify them to anyone who knows them
You are relying on the setting being public as your permission
A child in distress, undressed, or in a medical context
You have no written consent and are about to publish commercially
You would not be comfortable if a stranger did this to your own child
scenarios.happening: Photographing children is the one area of event photography where the legal position and the professional standard diverge most sharply. In most public settings it is not unlawful, and every festival's media policy, every safeguarding lead, and every reputable agency nevertheless requires parental consent for identifiable minors — because the risk is not to you, it is to a child whose image you are putting into circulation without anyone who is responsible for them having agreed. Custody arrangements, safeguarding orders and families who are not findable are all invisible from behind a lens.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “L” CHECK: “Has a parent said yes, by name, to this specific use?” Public setting is not permission where a child is concerned.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Cannot See The Reason It Matters
scenarios.dark: The specific families this hurts are the ones you cannot identify from where you are standing: a child in a custody dispute whose location must not be public, a family with a safeguarding order, a parent who has moved away from someone. A photograph of a child geotagged at a named festival on a public account can undo arrangements that took years to build, and the photographer will never learn that they did it. That is the whole argument for asking, and it is why the standard is consent rather than judgement — you are not in a position to assess the risk, so you do not get to decide it is low.
scenarios.move: Ask the parent before you shoot, and get a name and a contact if you intend to publish. Default to backs of heads, crowd-scale, or unidentifiable framing in family areas. Never shoot a child in distress or in a medical context. If in doubt, send it to the parent and let them decide.
scenarios.say: Lovely moment — do you mind if I take it? I'd only post it if you're happy, and I'll send it to you either way. Can I grab your number?
scenarios.truth: A public field is not consent for somebody else's child. Ask the parent, or shoot the back of the head.

scenarios.hook: TAKE IT DOWN OR I'LL MAKE IT A THING
scenarios.archetype: The Subject Who Turns / Demands, Threats And Pile-Ons
scenarios.who: Someone in a frame you published — sometimes with an entirely legitimate grievance you should act on immediately, sometimes escalating to demands for money, and occasionally mobilizing a pile-on that arrives before you have read the first message.
scenarios.scene: The message says take it down. You took it at a public stage, you asked at the time, and you have the reply. The second message says you owe them money for using their image. The third says they have screenshotted your account and people are going to hear about this, and by the morning there are forty comments on a photograph of somebody else entirely.
tells: A takedown request — which you should simply honour, immediately
A demand for payment attached to the takedown
Threats about your reputation rather than about the image
Claims that shift each time you answer them
Public escalation before any private conversation
You have no record of the consent you actually obtained
scenarios.happening: Two different things arrive in the same inbox and telling them apart is the whole skill. A person asking for their image to come down is exercising something you should grant without argument, whatever the law says and whatever you paid to be there — that is the profession's own standard and it is also the cheapest possible resolution. A demand for money, or a threat about your reputation, is a different transaction, and the correct response to that one is not negotiation but documentation.
scenarios.check: L.E.N.S. — “N” CHECK: “Is this a request to remove, or a demand for something else?” Remove instantly for the first. Do not pay the second.
scenarios.darkTitle: Delete First, Document Everything
scenarios.dark: The sequence that keeps photographers out of trouble is counterintuitive: comply completely and immediately on the takedown, and only then deal with the rest. Arguing about whether you were entitled to publish is the thing that converts a two-minute fix into a public campaign, because to everyone watching you are the person with the camera refusing to delete a picture. Take it down, say you have, apologize for the distress without conceding any claim, and keep every message. And build the thing that makes all of this short next time: a consent log, with a name, a date and what was agreed, which turns a he-said-she-said into a record.
scenarios.move: Remove it immediately and say so. Do not pay, do not argue the law, do not respond publicly. Screenshot everything with timestamps. Keep a consent log from now on so the next one is a thirty-second conversation.
scenarios.say: It's down — removed as soon as I saw your message, and I'm sorry it upset you. I'm not able to pay anything, but the image is gone and it won't be used again.
scenarios.truth: Take it down first and sort out who was right afterwards. The photograph was never worth the week.

guides.intro: You work on people at their most open. This guide is about protecting them, and protecting you — and about the practitioners who use the same door.

checks.name: Hands Need Spoken Permission
checks.desc: Every session, every new area, out loud, before contact. A body on your table has not pre-agreed to anything it has not heard described.

checks.name: Evidence Of Training, Or Say So
checks.desc: Name your actual qualification and its actual limits. Borrowed authority is the first move of every false practitioner in this scene.

checks.name: Altered States Cannot Consent Forward
checks.desc: A yes given before a state cannot cover what happens inside it, and a yes given during one is not a yes. This is the whole line.

checks.name: Leave The Dual Relationship Alone
checks.desc: Client, then lover, then integrator, then landlord. Every role you add removes one exit they had.

outline.desc: Borrowed credentials, the lineage that cannot be checked, recruitment of the vulnerable
Consent inside altered states, scope creep, the session that keeps extending
Dual relationships, integration dependency, silencing through spiritual framing
The spoken consent brief, scope limits, referral and insurance discipline
Being a practitioner people can safely report, and what you owe when it is you
What to do when it is already happening

sentences: I say what I am about to do before I do it, every time, out loud.
I name my training and its limits without being asked.
A yes from before the medicine does not cover during the medicine.
I do not integrate someone I have a personal stake in. I refer.
If somebody raises something about me, the first job is not defending myself.

scenarios.archetype: The Unverifiable Credential / Borrowed Authority
scenarios.clinical: Credential Fabrication / Appeal to Unfalsifiable Lineage
scenarios.who: Speaks with total calm certainty about where the work came from. Names a teacher, a region, a tradition, a number of years. Everything he says is structurally impossible to check, and he chose it for that reason.
scenarios.scene: He says he trained for nine years with a lineage holder in a place you would have to fly to, whose name he gives softly, as though saying it too loudly would be disrespectful. Nobody in this tent is going to fact-check that. Nobody in this tent could. And you notice, as he says it, that the reverence in his voice is doing all the work that a certificate would otherwise have to do.
tells: Credentials that cannot be verified by design — remote, oral, or a deceased teacher
Reverence used to make questions feel rude
No insurance, no professional body, no supervisor, no complaints route
Scope that expands to whatever you need — trauma, grief, fertility, diagnosis
Vague about the parts a trained person is precise about: contraindications, referral, limits
Gets cooler toward anyone who asks a second question
scenarios.happening: Every regulated healing profession is built on three things a false practitioner cannot supply: a checkable qualification, a body that can remove you, and a named limit to your scope. Unverifiable lineage is chosen precisely because it substitutes for all three at once — authority without accountability. It is the single most common structure in this scene's abuse cases, and the reason is not mysticism, it is architecture. The honest practitioners with real traditional training are usually the easiest people in the world to ask about it; they will tell you their teacher, their years, what they do not do, and who they refer to. Precision is the tell in both directions.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “E” CHECK: “Can I name this person's training, their limits, and who they answer to?” Three blanks is not a lineage. It is a costume.
scenarios.darkTitle: Unfalsifiable Is The Feature
scenarios.dark: Pay attention to what the claim is built out of: every element is unfalsifiable on purpose. Far away, long ago, orally transmitted, teacher deceased, tradition that does not certify. A person inventing a credential does not pick a claim you could check, and the ones who pick unfalsifiable claims are not being humble about the ineffable — they are engineering a position where doubting them is a spiritual failing rather than due diligence. That inversion is the actual product, because it is what makes the later stuff survivable: once questioning him reads as your resistance, the room will help him. Ask the second question. His temperature when you do is more informative than the answer.
scenarios.move: Ask three plain questions in a friendly voice: who trained you, what do you not do, and who would I talk to if I had a problem with a session. Ask them in front of other people. Write down what he says.
scenarios.say: Love the sound of that — who did you train with, and what's outside your scope? And if I had a concern afterwards, who's the person I'd raise it with?
scenarios.truth: Real practitioners answer credential questions with relief. Only a costume is insulted by them.

scenarios.archetype: Scope Creep On The Table / The Session That Keeps Extending
scenarios.who: Booked for one thing, doing a slightly different thing by minute twenty. Narrates it as responsiveness — the body asked for it, the energy moved there. Never quite announces the change, which is how you end up somewhere you did not agree to.
scenarios.scene: You booked a shoulder session. Forty minutes in, his hands are on your ribs and then lower and he is saying something about where the grief is held, and you are running an internal calculation about whether objecting would make you the person who does not understand the work. He has not done anything you could name. He has moved four times, and each individual move was two inches.
tells: Contact moves to new areas without being named beforehand
Changes framed as the body's request rather than a practitioner's decision
Draping, positioning, or clothing renegotiated mid-session
Session runs long without being re-agreed
Objecting is pre-framed as not understanding the modality
Each step is small enough to be deniable; the sequence is not
scenarios.happening: Progressive boundary erosion is the documented mechanism in the overwhelming majority of bodywork and therapeutic misconduct cases, and it works because a body on a table is passive, undressed, prone, and socially committed to trusting the person touching it. Each two-inch move is individually defensible, which is the design — the practitioner is not testing whether you consent, he is testing whether you will interrupt. That is why the professional standard in every legitimate manual therapy is spoken permission before each new region, every session, regardless of history. It removes the thing being exploited, which is your reluctance to be the one who makes it weird.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “H” CHECK: “Did they say what they were about to do, before they did it?” Unannounced contact is the violation, whatever it turns out to be.
scenarios.darkTitle: They Are Testing The Interrupt, Not The Consent
scenarios.dark: Understanding this changes what you watch for. He is not building toward a moment where you agree — he is establishing that you do not interrupt, because a person who did not object at two inches is statistically less likely to object at four, and he knows it. That is also why the recovery from this is so hard afterwards: you will interrogate your own silence rather than his sequence. Put it down. The obligation was never on the person lying face-down and half-dressed to narrate the boundary. It was on the trained professional to announce the next move, and he chose not to, repeatedly, which is the finding.
scenarios.move: Interrupt early and cheaply, because the first interruption is the whole thing — it costs almost nothing at minute five and everything at minute forty. Sit up. Sitting up ends the physical frame, and you can be polite from upright.
scenarios.say: Stop there — I booked shoulders, I want to stay on shoulders. — I'm going to sit up for a minute.
scenarios.truth: You do not owe a practitioner the benefit of the doubt while they are touching you. That is exactly the wrong moment for generosity.

scenarios.archetype: Spiritual Framing As A Consent Override
scenarios.clinical: Ceremonial Coercion / Consent Override in Altered States
scenarios.who: Holds the container, poured the cup, and is the only person in the room who is not altered. Interprets what is happening for everyone, including for you, including about you. Is never wrong inside the frame he built.
scenarios.scene: You are four hours into something and the room has stopped having edges. He sits down close and says the medicine has shown him that you and he are meant to work together more deeply, that your resistance is the thing the work is for, and that this is the part where people either open or run. You cannot currently construct a sentence. He knows that. That is the reason this conversation is happening now and not on Tuesday.
tells: The pitch arrives while you are altered and not before
Your hesitation is renamed as resistance, fear, or ego
He is the sole interpreter of what the experience means
Pre-ceremony agreements about touch are revised mid-ceremony
Nobody sober is in the room who is not him
Leaving is framed as spiritually dangerous or as abandoning the work
scenarios.happening: This is the single most important line in this guide: a consent given before an altered state cannot cover what happens inside it, and a consent given during one is not consent, because capacity is the thing the substance removed. Every serious ceremonial ethic in the world states it — no romantic or sexual contact with participants, no revision of agreements mid-state, a sober second person present. The reason is not squeamishness, it is that the facilitator holds total interpretive authority over someone who cannot currently evaluate interpretations. Any framework where your objection is proof the framework is working is not a spiritual technology. It is a closed loop, and closed loops are what this book calls a cage.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “A” CHECK: “Is this being asked of me now because now is when I cannot assess it?” Timing is the tell. A real invitation survives Tuesday.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Loop Where Your No Is Evidence
scenarios.dark: The structure to name is the unfalsifiable loop: agreement proves the medicine is working, and refusal proves you have more work to do. Once that loop is running there is no answer you can give that exits it, which means the conversation was never a request. It is the same architecture as the unverifiable lineage on the first page of this guide and it is built by the same person for the same reason. This is also where the room turns — other participants, sincerely, will help, because they are inside the frame too and your resistance genuinely looks to them like fear. That is why the protection has to be structural and installed beforehand: a sober ally physically present, an agreement in writing, and someone outside the ceremony expecting to hear from you.
scenarios.move: Set it before you sit down, in writing, and give a copy to someone not in the room: no touch beyond what is named, no agreements revised during, and a sober person of your choosing present. If you are already in it — you are allowed to say nothing, stand up, and walk to the sober person. You do not have to win the argument.
scenarios.say: Before we start: nothing gets renegotiated once I've drunk. Anything you want to propose, propose it on Tuesday. — [in the moment] I'm not discussing this now. I'm going to sit with Nadia.
scenarios.truth: Anything that is only true while you are altered is not true. It is just unopposed.

scenarios.archetype: The Integrator / Dependency After The Fact
scenarios.who: The same person who facilitated, now offering to be the one who helps you make sense of it — for a fee, or for closeness, or both. Often kind. Almost always the wrong person for the job.
scenarios.scene: The ceremony was enormous and you are not okay and he is the only person who was there and understands. He offers weekly calls. Then he offers to have you stay. Then there is a retreat he thinks you should be at, and a role in his organization, and at no point was there a moment where you decided any of this — there was a moment where you needed help and he was standing there.
tells: The facilitator is also the integrator, the landlord, the employer, or the partner
Your understanding of your own experience routes entirely through him
Cost escalates — money, time, proximity, loyalty
He discourages outside therapy, framed as it not understanding the work
Leaving the relationship would mean losing your sense of what happened to you
Nobody independent has ever spoken to you about that ceremony
scenarios.happening: Dual relationships are prohibited in every clinical code for one reason: each additional role removes an exit. When your facilitator is also your integrator, you cannot process a bad experience of him with anyone but him, and a person's interpretation of their own most vulnerable hours becomes something another person authors. Post-ceremonial suggestibility is real and elevated for a meaningful period afterwards, which makes that window the highest-leverage one that exists. An honest practitioner treats it as the most dangerous part of their work and refers out. That referral is the single clearest marker of a real one.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “L” CHECK: “How many roles does this person hold in my life?” One is a relationship. Three is an enclosure.
scenarios.darkTitle: Who Authors What Happened To You
scenarios.dark: The lasting damage here is not financial and it is not even always sexual — it is authorship. If the only person who can tell you what your ceremony meant is the person who ran it, then a harm that occurred inside it is uninterpretable to you without his help, and he will help. People come out of these arrangements years later describing the disorientation of realizing they had no independent memory of their own experience, only his account of it. The counter is boringly practical and it has to be arranged in advance, while you still think you will not need it: a separate integrator, booked before the ceremony, who has never met the facilitator.
scenarios.move: Separate the roles before you go in — book your integration with someone unconnected, ideally a licensed therapist familiar with this territory. Keep one relationship outside the whole ecosystem. If you are already inside it, the first move is one outside conversation, not a confrontation.
scenarios.say: I've got integration booked with someone separate — I keep those roles apart on principle. Can you send me your notes for them?
scenarios.truth: Nobody should be both the person who took you in and the only person who can bring you back.

scenarios.archetype: The Page For Your Own Practice
scenarios.who: You. Honest, well-trained, in this for the right reasons, and holding more power in every session than the frame of healing makes it easy to notice.
scenarios.scene: A client tells you, three weeks later, that something in a session did not sit right. Your entire body wants to explain — what you actually did, what the modality is, what they may have misread. That impulse is normal, it is human, and it is the exact moment where good practitioners become bad ones. What you do in the next sixty seconds is your whole ethics, and it is not a feeling, it is a procedure.
tells: You are the only one who could say what happened in that room
Your client was undressed, prone, altered, or grieving — sometimes all four
Attraction to a client has arisen and you have not told a supervisor
You have extended a session, or a role, because it felt right in the moment
You have no supervisor, no insurance, and no complaints route
Your first instinct on hearing a concern is to explain rather than to hear
scenarios.happening: The power differential in this work does not switch off because your intentions are good. You control the room, the interpretation, the duration, and the narrative afterwards, and your client is frequently in a state they cannot fully assess. That is why every regulated profession requires supervision, insurance, a scope statement, and a complaints route that does not run through you — not because practitioners are assumed to be predators, but because an unsupervised practitioner cannot self-detect drift. The false shaman this guide opens with relies on the entire field being unregulated. The way honest practitioners take that cover away is by visibly having the things he cannot have.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “L” CHECK: “If a client wanted to complain about me, could they — to someone who is not me?” If not, you are running the same structure as the person you would never want to be.
scenarios.darkTitle: Nobody Decides To Become That Person
scenarios.dark: Read the misconduct literature and the pattern is remarkably consistent: almost nobody sets out to do it. It goes one session long, then one region unannounced, then one dual relationship, then a rationalization that the work required it — and each step was taken by somebody who believed themselves to be a good practitioner, because they were, right up until they were not. Supervision exists because that drift is invisible from inside. If you are reading this and one specific session came to mind: that is not proof you are a bad practitioner, it is the ordinary early warning this whole page is for. Take it to a supervisor this week. The ones who never take anything to anyone are the ones this ends badly for.
scenarios.move: Build what the false ones cannot fake: insurance, a named supervisor you actually use, a written scope with limits, a spoken consent brief every session, and a complaints route that bypasses you — published. If a concern comes to you, the first response is thank you for telling me, and the second is a referral to that route. Not an explanation.
scenarios.say: Thank you for telling me — that took something. I'm not going to defend myself at you. Here's the person you can take it to independently, and I'll cooperate with whatever they ask.
scenarios.truth: The practitioner people can safely complain about is the one worth going to. Be the one with a route that does not run through you.

scenarios.archetype: The Ninety Seconds Before Any Hands
scenarios.who: For practitioners, and for anyone about to get on a table, into a container, or under someone's hands. Ninety seconds, said out loud, every session, including with the client you have seen forty times.
scenarios.scene: The brief is the thing that makes the rest of this guide unnecessary. It is also the thing that gets skipped first, because it feels clinical and the work is supposed to feel sacred — and that feeling is precisely what every pattern in this guide has been exploiting. Said once, it converts an unspoken understanding into a shared agreement, and unspoken understandings are the medium predators swim in.
tells: Name the modality and what it actually involves, in plain words
Name every area you will work on, and what stays covered
Name what is outside your scope and who you refer to
Say how long, and that any extension gets re-agreed out loud
Say that stop ends it instantly, with no explanation owed and no cost
Say who they can raise a concern with who is not you — and mean it
scenarios.happening: Every documented mechanism in this guide — scope creep, unannounced contact, sessions that extend, agreements revised mid-state — fails against a brief that was given out loud beforehand. Not because a bad practitioner will not try, but because the client now has a stated baseline to notice the departure from, and noticing is the whole difficulty. This is the same logic as the pre-burn check in F.L.O.W. and the access plan in A.C.C.E.S.S.: front-load the decisions to a moment when everyone is clear-headed, so the moment of pressure only requires recognition rather than judgment.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “H” CHECK: “Was the brief given out loud this session — not implied, not last time?” If it was skipped, that is the first departure, and it happened before anything else did.
scenarios.darkTitle: Who Objects To Ninety Seconds
scenarios.dark: There is diagnostic value in offering it. Honest practitioners are glad of the brief — it protects them as much as the client, and most will tell you it has saved them from a misunderstanding at some point. A practitioner who finds it cold, clinical, unnecessary between people who trust each other, or contrary to the flow of the work is telling you that they prefer the ambiguity, and ambiguity has exactly one beneficiary in a room where one person is dressed and standing. You are allowed to ask for it as a client. The answer you get is worth more than the ninety seconds.
scenarios.move: Practitioners: write yours, six lines, and say it every time until it is automatic. Clients: if nobody gives you one, ask — what will you be working on, what stays covered, how long, and who do I talk to if something feels off.
scenarios.say: Before we start: shoulders and upper back only, everything else stays covered, fifty minutes, and if I want to go anywhere else I'll ask you first. Stop ends it immediately, no explanation needed. And if anything sits badly afterwards, here's who you can talk to who isn't me.
scenarios.truth: Ninety seconds of plain speech removes most of what is in this guide. That is why the people in this guide skip it.

scenarios.hook: THE CLIENT WHO BOOKS YOU EVERY DAY
scenarios.archetype: When You Are The One Being Targeted
scenarios.who: Books repeatedly, discloses heavily and fast, and treats the session as a relationship rather than an appointment. Sometimes genuinely in distress. Sometimes using the one structure on site where a stranger will touch you alone in a tent for an hour.
scenarios.scene: Third booking in two days. He has started arriving early and staying after, and the disclosures have moved from his shoulder to his marriage to the fact that you are the only person who has ever really understood him, and today he asked whether you would have dinner, and when you said no he apologized so thoroughly that you ended up reassuring him.
tells: Books far more often than the presenting issue warrants
Rapid, heavy personal disclosure aimed at building intimacy
Arrives early, stays late, wants to be in your space outside the session
Gifts, or paying over the rate
Tests small boundaries and apologizes elaborately when they hold
You have started dreading the booking and have not told anyone
scenarios.happening: The therapeutic frame is unusually exploitable in this direction: a practitioner is alone, often in a soft-walled space, professionally committed to warmth and non-judgement, and financially motivated to keep a repeat client. All four of those work against you. This is a known pattern in massage, bodywork and complementary practice, and the festival version is worse because there is no reception, no colleague next door, no booking system, and no employer — just you, a tent and somebody who booked an hour of unobserved access.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “L” CHECK: “Is this a client, or is somebody building a relationship inside an appointment?” Frequency, disclosure and after-time are the three that tell you.
scenarios.darkTitle: Your Training Is Being Used Against You
scenarios.dark: Notice which of your professional instincts are working for him. Non-judgement stops you naming it. Holding space keeps you in the tent. Not wanting to shame a client stops you saying no plainly. Needing the booking stops you cancelling. Every one of those is a good quality and all four are load-bearing for him, which is why practitioners are so slow to act on this and why by the time they do it has usually escalated. Break it with structure rather than with a judgement about him: somebody else on site knows your schedule, the tent flap stays open, and the booking pattern is capped. You do not have to decide he is dangerous to stop being alone with him.
scenarios.move: Cap repeat bookings and say the cap is policy. Tell one person your schedule and have them walk past at the end of each session. Keep the space semi-open. End the after-time at the door rather than inside, and write down what happened the same day.
scenarios.say: I keep it to one session a day per person so everyone gets a slot — book you in Sunday. — I'm going to wrap it there, I've got Mira coming in. [walking out with him]
scenarios.truth: Warmth is your professional tool. It is not an obligation to be alone with somebody who is using it.

scenarios.archetype: A Crisis Arrives On Your Table / Knowing Your Own Edge
scenarios.clinical: Scope of Practice / Crisis Recognition and Referral
scenarios.who: A client who came in for tension and is now in the middle of something much larger — a flashback, a panic attack, a disclosure of abuse, or a psychiatric emergency — in your tent, on your table, with you.
scenarios.scene: Bodywork opened something and she is not in the room any more. She is shaking, breathing badly, somewhere in her own history, and telling you something she has clearly never said out loud. You are a massage therapist. You have ninety seconds to decide what you are and are not going to try to do, and every instinct you have is pulling you toward staying with it.
tells: Dissociation, flashback, or panic on the table
A disclosure of abuse, self-harm or suicidal thinking
Signs of a psychiatric emergency rather than emotional release
You are considering doing something you were never trained to do
The session has run long because stopping feels like abandonment
You have no referral route and did not find one before the event
scenarios.happening: Bodywork and altered-state contexts surface trauma routinely, and the single most consequential skill a practitioner has is knowing where their own edge is. Attempting to process trauma without that training can deepen it, and the moment where it feels most compassionate to continue is the moment it is most likely to do harm. The competent response is small and unglamorous: stabilize, ground, do not excavate, and hand over to someone whose job it is. Every large festival has welfare, and most have psychedelic support services staffed by people trained for precisely this.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “E” CHECK: “Am I still inside what I was trained to do?” The honest answer arrives fast, and it is usually no, and no is the correct place to stop.
scenarios.darkTitle: Staying Is Not Always The Kind Thing
scenarios.dark: The mistake almost never looks like negligence — it looks like a caring practitioner who did not want to abandon somebody mid-crisis, and who therefore attempted trauma work they had no training for, in a tent, on a stranger, at a festival. That is how people are left more destabilized than they arrived, and it is committed by good practitioners with good intentions every season. Handing over is not abandonment, and it is worth saying out loud to the client that it is not, because they will experience it that way if you do not. Walk them there. Do not send them.
scenarios.move: Stop the bodywork. Ground them — upright, feet on the floor, breathing, orient to the room and the day. Do not ask for more detail and do not interpret. Then walk them to welfare or the psychedelic support tent yourself, and debrief afterwards with your own person.
scenarios.say: I'm going to stop the massage. Feet on the floor, sit up with me, look at the doorway. You're at a festival, it's Saturday afternoon, you're safe. — This is bigger than what I'm trained for, and that's not me leaving you. I'm going to walk over to welfare with you and stay while you get someone who does this properly.
scenarios.truth: Knowing where your training stops is your training. Walking somebody to the right person is competence, not failure.

scenarios.archetype: Barter, And The Deal That Stops Being A Deal
scenarios.clinical: Undefined Exchange / Boundary Ambiguity in Barter
scenarios.who: Everyone, at every festival, because the gift economy is real and beautiful and almost entirely undocumented — which means every trade has terms nobody said out loud.
scenarios.scene: You will do a session and he will sort you out for the weekend. It is a fair trade and you both meant it kindly. Then it is unclear whether one session covered it or three, and he keeps appearing, and on Saturday when you say you are done for the day there is a silence, and you realize that neither of you ever said what the deal was and he has been keeping a different tally.
tells: A trade agreed in a sentence, with no scope and no end point
Value on both sides assumed rather than stated
The other party's side arrives first, creating an open obligation
Being traded substances, which ties your work to a supply
The deal is renegotiated afterwards, upward
You are doing sessions you do not want to do and cannot say why
scenarios.happening: Barter is not the problem — vagueness is. An undefined trade creates exactly the open-ended obligation that the reciprocity pages elsewhere in this book describe, with the additional feature that professional work is now entangled with a personal relationship and nobody can point to the terms. Trading for substances is the version worth refusing outright: it makes your practice dependent on a supply and a supplier, it is the clearest route to a dual relationship, and it converts a professional service into something you can be leaned on for.
scenarios.check: H.E.A.L. — “L” CHECK: “Does this trade have a stated scope and an end?” If not, it is not a trade, it is an account somebody else is keeping.
scenarios.darkTitle: An Open Account Is A Hold
scenarios.dark: The damage is not the specific trade, it is the self-editing that starts once you believe you owe somebody something you cannot quantify. You do the extra session. You do not raise the thing that annoyed you. You keep the appointment you wanted to cancel. That is the same quiet accommodation the gift-with-a-ledger pages describe, and in a practitioner it is worse, because the currency you are paying in is unobserved physical access to your own time and body. Close the account explicitly, even at the cost of seeming transactional in a scene that prizes not being.
scenarios.move: Say the terms out loud and keep them small and closed — one session for one named thing, done, settled. Never trade for substances. Write the trade in a message so it exists. If an account has already opened, close it deliberately rather than letting it run.
scenarios.say: Happy to trade — one session for the [x], and then we're square, yeah? Just so neither of us is keeping score. — I don't trade for anything you consume, but I'll do you a mate's rate.
scenarios.truth: A trade with no end point is not generosity, it is an open account. Say the number, even when it feels unspiritual.

guides.intro: Your music is the power. Don't let anyone else hold the switch.

checks.name: Sign Before You Play
checks.desc: No contract, no soundcheck. Your performance has value. Protect it in writing. Every time.

checks.name: Own Your Masters
checks.desc: Who owns the recordings made of your set? Who owns the footage? Find out before you go on, not after it's posted.

checks.name: Understand The Room
checks.desc: Who's in the green room? Who has access? The most dangerous situations happen in spaces that feel private and protected.

checks.name: No Is A Full Sentence
checks.desc: To the promoter. To the superfan. To the manager. No explanation required. No is complete.

checks.name: Document Everything
checks.desc: Agreements, payments, incidents, communications. Screenshots. Paper trail. Your memory is not evidence.

outline.desc: Promoter traps, false management, industry gatekeeping
Road isolation, superfan dynamics, substance pressure
Contract manipulation, revenue skimming, reputation threats
Contracts, rights, green room safety, touring survival
Fame as a responsibility — the page about your own power

sentences: The stage gives me power. Power requires responsibility.
My music's value is not determined by whoever is booking me.
Green room access is a privilege, not an invitation.
Document it now or lose it later.

scenarios.archetype: The Promoter Who Books and Controls
scenarios.who: The promoter with the network, the stages, the bookings. Positions themselves as the gatekeeper to your next level. Uses that position to extract below-rate fees, free promotion work, personal access, and silence. The next level stays perpetually 3 months away.
scenarios.scene: "I'm building something with your sound specifically in mind — I need you for three dates this summer and if those go well we're talking main stage next year. We don't need a formal contract yet, this is about building a relationship first." Three shows later: you've covered your own travel, been paid 60% of what was agreed verbally, done promotional content for free, and the main stage conversation has vaporized.
tells: Future opportunity always slightly out of reach — dependent on your continued compliance
Contract discussions deflected as premature or as signs of distrust
Payment consistently below what was agreed verbally, framed as temporary
Any friction triggers implicit threat to the whole relationship and future bookings
scenarios.happening: The festival and music industry has a specific power structure that predatory promoters exploit: artists need bookings, bookings require promoter relationships, and challenging a promoter feels like risking your entire access to the scene. The "building something together" frame removes professional clarity while the promoter retains all the structural power. A legitimate promoter makes money when you get paid fairly.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “S” CHECK: “Is there a signed contract — or just a verbal promise and a sense that questioning it risks the whole opportunity?” — that feeling is the leverage working exactly as intended.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Minimum Performance Contract
scenarios.dark: Every booking needs in writing: performance fee, payment timeline (50% deposit before, 50% at show is standard), cancellation terms, accommodation and travel responsibilities, set time and length, technical rider requirements, who owns live recordings or footage, and promotional obligations on both sides. American Federation of Musicians (afm.org) has standard contract templates. Music attorneys offer one-time consultations. A legitimate promoter will sign. The ones who won't are giving you your answer.
scenarios.move: No contract, no soundcheck. This is a full sentence and a complete policy.
scenarios.say: I'm excited about these dates — let's get the agreement in writing so we're both protected. I can send my standard rider tonight.
scenarios.truth: Any promoter who won't put it in writing is showing you what the deal actually is.

scenarios.archetype: Predatory Management / The Isolation Manager
scenarios.who: The manager who positions themselves between you and every other industry relationship. "Let me handle this" becomes "let me control this" becomes "I am the only person who understands your vision." By the time you see it, most of your independent contacts are gone.
scenarios.scene: She approached you after a set that went off. Clearly connected. "I think you're three months away from something major and I want to be the person who gets you there." No management contract yet. A year later: she takes 25% of everything including merch you handle yourself, discourages direct relationships with bookers ("let me handle it, it's cleaner"), and when you question any of it the conversation turns to everything she's done for you.
tells: Discourages direct relationships with bookers, labels, promoters — "let me handle it"
Commission structure expands beyond agreed terms without renegotiation
Questions about finances or terms received as betrayal or ingratitude
Industry contacts you had before have been quietly replaced by her relationships
scenarios.happening: Predatory management isolates artists from their industry network under the cover of professionalism. When your entire industry network runs through one person, that person has complete leverage. Standard management commission is 15-20% of gross income from work THEY source — not your merch, not your pre-existing relationships. Know that standard before any conversation.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — "N" CHECK: "Can I talk directly to my booker or label — or does everything go through them first?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Management Contract Basics
scenarios.dark: A legitimate management contract specifies: commission rate and what it applies to, term length (1–2 years standard — not open-ended), sunset clause (they earn commission on deals they originated after the contract ends, for a defined period), and termination conditions for both parties. No management contract should give them power of attorney or control over your bank accounts. California Talent Agencies Act and similar state laws regulate management. Music attorney consultation before signing — non-negotiable.
scenarios.move: Maintain direct relationships with at least 3 industry contacts independently of any manager. Always.
scenarios.say: "I appreciate you handling things — I also keep direct relationships with my bookers. That's just how I work."
scenarios.truth: A manager who needs to be your only industry contact needs to be your former manager.

scenarios.archetype: The Bait and Switch Booking
scenarios.who: The booking that changes significantly between offer and show — stage size, set time, payment, production support — revealed after you've committed flights, accommodation, and your promotional energy to announcing the show.
scenarios.scene: "We're really excited to have you — you'll be on the Garden Stage, Saturday evening set, solid slot." You announce it, post it, your fans make plans. Two weeks before the show: "there have been some lineup adjustments — we've moved you to the Morning Stage, Sunday 11am." The ticket buyers for your slot have already made travel plans. Pulling out now costs you more than accepting the downgrade.
tells: Details confirmed verbally don't match the written confirmation when it arrives
"Adjustments" happen after you've publicly announced and promoted the show
Changes arrive late enough that backing out carries significant cost
Each change is framed as minor — the cumulative impact is significant
scenarios.happening: Bait and switch bookings work by getting your public commitment before you have the details in writing. Once you've announced a show to your audience, backing out has real social and professional cost — which the promoter counts on. The protection is simple: nothing goes on your social media until you have the booking confirmation in writing, with all material details (stage, set time, date, fee) confirmed. No exceptions.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “S” CHECK: “Have I confirmed every material detail of this booking in writing before I announce it to my own audience?” — once you’ve announced it, the leverage in the negotiation is gone, and it’s gone in their favor.
scenarios.darkTitle: Announce Only After Written Confirmation
scenarios.dark: The sequence for any festival booking: (1) Verbal offer received. (2) Written confirmation requested — stage, set time, date, fee, production details. (3) Contract signed. (4) Deposit received. (5) Announcement made. Skipping any of these steps removes your leverage. Promoters who push you to announce before paperwork is signed are using your audience as collateral. Your fans are excited to see you — that excitement belongs to you, not to a promoter who hasn't put anything in writing yet.
scenarios.move: Nothing gets announced until you have written confirmation of every material detail.
scenarios.say: I'd love to announce this — can you send me the written confirmation with stage, set time, and fee first?
scenarios.truth: Your audience's excitement is yours. Don't let it become someone else's leverage.

scenarios.archetype: Green Room Access as Grooming / Post-Show Vulnerability
scenarios.who: The post-show window is one of the highest-risk periods for performing artists. Adrenaline crash, endorphin flood, crowds wanting proximity — and a specific category of person who knows exactly how to exploit that window.
scenarios.scene: You just came off a set that felt transcendent. Everyone backstage is warm and electric. Someone from the crowd has somehow gotten backstage — through who, you're not sure. They're beautiful and clearly want to be near you and the attention feels like an extension of the performance high. Two hours later, in a much quieter context with a much clearer head, you're trying to reconstruct how the decisions of the last two hours happened.
tells: People in backstage spaces you don't know how they got there
The post-show adrenaline state is specifically targeted — decisions here are impaired
Someone who zeroes in on you immediately post-performance before you've landed
An entourage that appears after every show and gradually never leaves
scenarios.happening: The post-performance state is a genuine altered state — high adrenaline, endorphin flood, identity in flux between performer-self and regular-self. Predatory fans and industry people know this window intimately and specifically target it. As the performer you're also in the position of power in that space — which means your responsibility is higher, not lower. This page is simultaneously about protecting yourself AND about not using the post-show window to cover your own behavior.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — "U" CHECK: "Who is actually in this space — do I know how they got here and what they want?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Green Room Protocol — Yours To Set
scenarios.dark: As the artist, you set the terms of your backstage space. Legitimate protocols: explicit guest list with named individuals only (not "plus whoever"), a trusted person who manages access, a minimum 30-minute closed cooldown after you come off before socializing, and a clear policy communicated to promoters before the show about who can be back there.
