Your rider can include backstage access requirements. Use it.
scenarios.move: Land first. Decompress with your core people. Then decide who you want in your space from a clearer head.
scenarios.say: [To your team before the show]: "30-minute closed cooldown after we come off — then we open the room. Can you hold that?"
scenarios.truth: The post-show high is real and beautiful. It is also the window people have been waiting all night to exploit.

scenarios.archetype: When Admiration Becomes Stalking
scenarios.who: Most superfans are genuinely loving people your music has meant something real to. Some are not. The ones who aren't operate with a sense of relationship and entitlement that your actual relationship with them does not support.
scenarios.scene: She's been at six of your shows in three cities. Knows your setlist changes before you announce them. Has your tour schedule memorized. Shows up at the venue during soundcheck. DMs you daily — long, personal, detailed. When you don't respond she escalates. At the last show she got backstage and stood close in a way that felt like pressure. Your team dismisses it: "that's just a dedicated fan." Your body is saying something different.
tells: Attendance at multiple shows in multiple cities without your invitation
Knowledge of non-public information: hotel, soundcheck time, private schedule
Access to backstage or personal spaces that should have been controlled
Communication that escalates when you don't respond or engage
scenarios.happening: Parasocial relationships — where a fan experiences genuine emotional intimacy with an artist who doesn't know them — are a normal feature of music fandom. They become dangerous when the fan can't hold the asymmetry and begins operating as though the relationship is mutual. The music industry often fails artists here by treating obvious stalking as enthusiasm. Your discomfort is data. Your body's signal about someone is data.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “D” CHECK: “Have I documented this person’s behavior with dates, locations, and screenshots — solely so I have a record if this escalates?” — a fan’s dedication is not a reason to skip documenting once it stops feeling safe.
scenarios.darkTitle: Documenting And Reporting Stalking
scenarios.dark: Documentation: screenshot every message, note dates and locations of every appearance, keep a written log. When to report: when they appear at non-public locations, when they attempt physical contact you haven't invited, when communication escalates after you stop responding, when they contact people in your personal life. Report to: venue security (who can issue trespass notices), local police (a report creates a record even if no immediate action), Stalking Prevention Awareness and Resource Center (stalkingawareness.org). Report early rather than late.
scenarios.move: Trust your body's signal. Document. Tell your team. Report early.
scenarios.say: [To your tour manager]: "I need you to document this person's appearances and pull their backstage access. I want a record."
scenarios.truth: "Dedicated fan" is not a category that overrides your safety. Your discomfort is data.

scenarios.archetype: How Touring Disconnects You From Everyone Who Knows You
scenarios.who: Touring creates a specific kind of isolation — from your home community, your support network, and the people who knew you before the music. That isolation makes you more dependent on the people immediately around you, which creates leverage for anyone on tour with you who wants to exploit it.
scenarios.scene: You're four weeks into a run and you haven't had a real conversation with anyone from home in two weeks. The tour manager controls the schedule, the transport, the accommodation, and by extension a lot of how your days feel. The sound engineer has been making comments about your decisions. Your bandmate has a habit that's starting to affect the shows and nobody will address it. You feel completely dependent on the very people who are causing friction.
tells: Your home support network feels increasingly remote and unreachable
One person on tour controls multiple aspects of your daily logistics and wellbeing
Decisions about your career are being made without your input during the run
You're too exhausted and too far from home to push back on anything
scenarios.happening: Road isolation is structural — touring literally removes you from your support network and puts you in a temporary closed system where the people with you have enormous power over your daily experience. This is not inherently predatory but it creates conditions that are easily exploited. Maintaining active connection to your home network, having at least one person on tour who is genuinely in your corner, and preserving your own decision-making authority are the protections.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — "U" CHECK: "When did I last have a real conversation with someone who knew me before the music?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Maintaining Connection On The Road
scenarios.dark: Practical steps for staying connected during extended tours: (1) Weekly scheduled call with your most trusted person at home — protected in the schedule. (2) At least one person on tour who is genuinely your person, not the promoter's or label's. (3) Keep your own record of all agreements, all financial terms, all incidents — don't rely on tour management's records as your only documentation. (4) If something is happening on tour that feels wrong: name it to a trusted person at home who can help you think through it with outside perspective.
scenarios.move: Maintain active connection to your home network throughout the tour. Schedule it.
scenarios.say: [To your most trusted person at home]: "Can we do a weekly call on Sundays for the duration of this run? I need someone external to check in with."
scenarios.truth: The road is a closed system. Keep one door open to the outside.

scenarios.archetype: Live Recording Rights / Who Owns Your Festival Set
scenarios.who: Every festival set you play is potentially being recorded — audio, video, professional and amateur. Who owns those recordings is determined by what's in writing before you play. If nothing is in writing: probably not you.
scenarios.scene: Your set went viral — 400,000 views on the festival's YouTube channel. The recording is incredible. Fans are using it everywhere. The festival is now licensing it to a streaming platform for a compilation. You receive nothing because when you signed the booking confirmation — buried in the terms — you assigned all recording rights to the festival for all formats in perpetuity.
tells: Booking confirmation or contract contains a recording rights clause you didn't negotiate
"Standard terms" applied to recording rights without specific discussion
Festival recording professionally without having discussed rights with you
Live recordings appear on streaming platforms or in commercial contexts without your knowledge
scenarios.happening: Live recording rights are one of the most commonly overlooked and most valuable assets in a musician's career. Festival organizers routinely include sweeping rights grabs in standard booking paperwork. Your performance is a copyrightable work. Your likeness in those recordings is yours. A simple rider clause reserves your recording rights or requires negotiation. Without it, you're playing the show and handing them a product.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “O” CHECK: “Who owns the recordings being made of me tonight — and is that in writing before I go on stage?” — know who owns the product before you create it, not after.
scenarios.darkTitle: Recording Rights Rider Language
scenarios.dark: Add to your standard rider: "Artist retains all rights to audio and video recordings of the performance. Any recording by Presenter requires written agreement specifying format, distribution, compensation, and Artist approval rights prior to the event." For streaming: separate sync licensing fees apply. ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC collect performance royalties — make sure your set is registered. SoundExchange collects digital performance royalties. If a festival has a streaming deal, your performance may generate royalties you're entitled to but not receiving.
scenarios.move: Add recording rights language to your rider. Always. Non-negotiable.
scenarios.say: Before I confirm — I need to add my standard recording rights clause to this agreement. I can send the language tonight.
scenarios.truth: Your performance is a product. Know who owns it before you create it.

scenarios.archetype: Payment Delays / Revenue Skimming
scenarios.who: Getting paid what you were promised, on the timeline agreed, is the baseline. It is also one of the most commonly violated terms in festival and live performance. Your leverage decreases dramatically after you've performed.
scenarios.scene: "The accounting is still getting sorted — it'll be in your account by end of month." End of month: "we had some unexpected costs with the event, we're going to need to adjust the final payment." Or: the merch sales from your table were handled by their team and the reconciliation is $800 short of what you counted. Or: your 50% deposit never arrived but your show is tomorrow and the flights are booked.
tells: Deposit due before show hasn't arrived and you're too committed to pull out
Final payment delayed past agreed date without prior communication
Merch or door split reconciliation doesn't match your own count
"Unexpected costs" appear after the show as reasons for reduced payment
scenarios.happening: Cash flow manipulation benefits the promoter while your leverage decreases once you've performed. That's why deposits exist. Get them before you travel. Count your own merch. Send a payment reminder email with terms on Day 1 after the show. Paper trail everything. Most non-payers rely on artists being too tired or too non-confrontational to pursue it.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “D” CHECK: “Do I have documentation of everything agreed financially — so I have something to point to when the money doesn’t show up on time?” — you performed. You get paid what was agreed. This is completely enforceable.
scenarios.darkTitle: When They Don't Pay — Your Options
scenarios.dark: Step 1: written demand email with contract attached, specific payment deadline (7-14 days). Step 2: small claims court handles disputes up to $10,000-$25,000 depending on state — filing fee usually under $100. Step 3: music attorney demand letter ($150-300) frequently resolves it. Step 4: American Federation of Musicians (afm.org) has a Claims & Collections department. Step 5: publicizing non-payment in musician communities (Indie on the Move, local music forums) is legal and effective. Document everything before going public.
scenarios.move: 50% deposit before you travel. Count your own merch. Send payment follow-up in writing the morning after.
scenarios.say: Per our agreement — the remaining balance of [X] is due within 7 days of the show. Please confirm receipt of this.
scenarios.truth: You performed. You get paid what was agreed. This is completely enforceable.

scenarios.archetype: Reputation Threats / Blacklisting
scenarios.who: The implicit or explicit threat that pushing back on a promoter, a manager, or an industry figure will result in being blacklisted, badmouthed, or frozen out of the circuit. One of the most effective control mechanisms in the music industry.
scenarios.scene: You stopped working with the promoter who wasn't paying you. Two months later you start hearing through the circuit that you're "difficult to work with" and "unreliable." Your booking inquiries from other promoters in that network have slowed. You didn't do anything wrong. But the narrative is already in circulation and you don't know how to counter something you're not supposed to know is being said.
tells: Implicit or explicit threats to your reputation when you exercise independence
Negative characterizations begin circulating after you end a bad deal
Professional contacts who were previously warm become suddenly distant
The person spreading the narrative directly benefits from your compliance
scenarios.happening: Reputation threats work because the music and festival circuit is small, relationship-driven, and operates heavily on word of mouth. The goal is to make the cost of pushing back higher than the cost of compliance. It often works. The counter is: document everything before any dispute escalates, build independent relationships across the industry, and proactively communicate your version of events to people who matter to you. Being blacklisted by predatory promoters is often a feature, not a bug.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “D” CHECK: “Have I documented the facts of this situation so I have something to point to if my version of events gets challenged later?” — the people worth working with will believe the documentation over the rumor.
scenarios.darkTitle: When Your Reputation Is Being Attacked
scenarios.dark: (1) Document: exactly what is being said, where, by whom, and when. (2) Communicate directly with your most important professional relationships — not to spin but to share facts. "I wanted to reach out directly because I understand there may be things being said about me — here's what actually happened." (3) Let your work speak. Predatory promoters lose credibility over time as more artists share experiences. (4) Musician-specific reputation defense: being known as someone who stands up for fair pay makes you MORE attractive to legitimate promoters.
scenarios.move: Document the dispute. Communicate directly with people who matter to you. Let your work speak.
scenarios.say: [To a trusted industry contact]: "I'm reaching out directly because I understand there may be things being said — I wanted you to have the facts."
scenarios.truth: Being blacklisted by predatory promoters is often a feature, not a bug. Your real advocates will know the difference.

scenarios.archetype: Internal Financial Exploitation / Band Dynamics
scenarios.who: The financial and power dynamics within a band or creative partnership are one of the most commonly neglected protection areas for musicians. Exploitation by a bandmate or creative partner is just as real as exploitation by a promoter — and harder to name because the relationship is closer.
scenarios.scene: You write most of the songs. You book most of the shows. You handle most of the promotion. The split has always been equal. You never thought to question it — you're a band, you're family. Then a manager offers you a solo project and you realize that without you the band doesn't function, and with the band you're sharing everything you generate equally with people who generate a fraction of what you do.
tells: Contributions to the band's output and income are significantly unequal but compensation isn't
One member controls band finances, social media, or industry relationships
Leaving the band feels like losing ownership of work you created
Creative credit doesn't reflect actual creative contribution
scenarios.happening: Band agreements are one of the most neglected legal documents in independent music. Who owns the name? Who owns the masters? What's the songwriting split? What happens when someone leaves? Who controls social media? Without answers in writing, whoever controls the logistics controls the band — and the person who does the most work often has the least formal protection. This isn't just about money. It's about who owns your creative legacy.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — "O" CHECK: "Do I know what I actually own in this creative partnership — in writing?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Band Agreement Basics
scenarios.dark: A band agreement should address: (1) who owns the band name and what happens to it if someone leaves. (2) Songwriting and publishing splits — and whether they're per-song or blanket. (3) Who owns the master recordings. (4) Revenue split for touring vs recording vs publishing vs merch. (5) Decision-making process — majority vote, unanimous, or designated authority. (6) Exit terms — what a departing member takes with them. Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts has band agreement templates. A music attorney review costs a fraction of what disputes cost later.
scenarios.move: Get your band agreement in writing before you have a dispute about what you each own.
scenarios.say: I think we should get our band agreement written down so we're all protected — I can get a template and we can go through it together.
scenarios.truth: The band feels like family until there's money involved. The paperwork is how you protect the family.

scenarios.archetype: What to Include, How to Use It
scenarios.who: Your rider is not just technical requirements. It is the document that defines your professional terms, protects your rights, and sets the expectations for every engagement before you arrive. Most musicians don't use it fully. This page changes that.
scenarios.scene: You've been showing up to gigs and figuring things out on arrival — the recording situation, the merch arrangement, the accommodation, the payment timing. Each thing individually seems manageable to negotiate in person. Collectively, negotiating all of these while you're also trying to prepare for a performance means you're always behind and always slightly at a disadvantage. Your rider is supposed to solve this before you arrive.
tells: Technical requirements: sound system specs, monitoring, load-in time, soundcheck time
Financial terms: fee, payment method and timing, deposit requirements and deadline
Recording and broadcast: explicit statement that Artist retains all recording rights
Accommodation and hospitality: what's provided, what's not, quality standards
scenarios.happening: A comprehensive rider serves two functions: it communicates your professional requirements AND it creates a paper trail of what was agreed. When things don't match the rider at the venue, you have documentation of what was promised. When recording happens without your agreement, you have documentation of what your rights are. The rider is not a diva document — it's a professional standard that protects both parties.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “S” CHECK: “Does my rider include recording rights language, payment terms, and all my technical requirements, spelled out in writing?” — the rider is not arrogance. It’s professionalism, and it protects both sides of the booking.
scenarios.darkTitle: What A Complete Rider Covers
scenarios.dark: Technical rider: stage plot, input list, monitoring requirements, backline requirements, load-in/soundcheck/show times. Business rider: fee and payment terms, deposit amount and deadline, cancellation policy, accommodation and transportation specs, press photo and bio requirements. Rights rider: recording rights clause (you retain all), broadcast rights, how your name can be used in promotion. Hospitality rider: green room requirements, food and beverage, guest list. Template riders are available from AFM (afm.org) and from music attorney blogs. Customize and use yours consistently.
scenarios.move: Send your rider with every booking confirmation. Update it annually. Use it as your baseline.
scenarios.say: I'll send my rider along with the signed contract — let me know if anything needs discussion before the show.
scenarios.truth: The rider is not arrogance. It is professionalism. It protects you and it protects the promoter.

scenarios.hook: BUYING AND SELLING SAFELY ON THE CIRCUIT
scenarios.archetype: Legal Risk, Undercovers, and Festival Transactions
scenarios.who: Musicians and touring artists face specific legal risks at festivals around buying, selling, and the substance culture of the touring life. This page is practical harm reduction for people who live on the circuit.
scenarios.scene: After the show, in the green room, someone offers you something. You're still running on the set, the green room feels safe and private, and the person seems completely trustworthy — they've been on tour with you for weeks. The substances have been tested this run, you know what you're getting. Two hours later you're in a situation that's more complicated than the green room felt.
tells: Green room transactions feel safer because they're "backstage" — they're not legally safer
Someone you trust on tour can still put you in a position of legal exposure
Substances offered in the context of a close working relationship still carry risk
The touring lifestyle normalizes substance use in ways that can gradually erode risk-assessment
scenarios.happening: Artists on tour are subject to the same drug laws as everyone else regardless of backstage location. Green room status does not create legal protection. The touring lifestyle creates normalization of substance use that can gradually erode your assessment of what's risky. Know what you're taking (test it), Know your legal exposure, and be aware that the people around you on tour have their own legal exposure to consider — which may or may not align with your interests.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “U” CHECK: “Do I understand who is actually in this space and what the legal implications of this transaction actually are?” — backstage is not a legal gray zone just because it feels like one.
scenarios.darkTitle: If You're Detained At A Festival Or Venue
scenarios.dark: Know this before you need it: (1) You have the right to remain silent — use it. "I'd like to speak with a lawyer." (2) Your manager or label does not automatically have the right to make legal decisions for you — that's your call. (3) Your tour rider and performance contract are your documents — you have the right to a copy of any contract you've signed. (4) Know the National Lawyers Guild (nlg.org) — they have observer programs at many major events. (5) Good Samaritan laws protect people seeking overdose help in most states — always call for medical help in an overdose situation.
scenarios.move: Know your legal exposure before any situation requires you to think about it.
scenarios.say: I'd like to speak with a lawyer before I answer any questions.
scenarios.truth: The backstage is not a legal gray zone. Know your rights.

scenarios.hook: THE STAGE IS NOT A CONSENT BYPASS
scenarios.archetype: Fame, Access, and Your Responsibility With Both
scenarios.who: This page is for every musician and touring artist regardless of level. The stage gives you power — social, sexual, financial, reputational. Power requires responsibility. This is the one nobody puts in the welcome packet.
scenarios.scene: You're coming off a strong set and you're still buzzing. Someone backstage is clearly interested — has been sending signals all night. They're consenting adults, everything feels mutual. Here's what's also true: you just performed to thousands of people, you have a team and access they don't have, you are in your element and they are in yours — and that power differential is real whether you acknowledge it or not.
tells: The post-show high and stage power can distort your read of consent signals
Someone in your green room may feel unable to say no to you — that's real whether you intend it or not
Your access to substances and role as host creates a power dynamic you're responsible for
Fame makes people want to be chosen by you — that want is not the same as uninhibited consent
scenarios.happening: The music industry has a long and documented history of artists using stage power and access to override or bypass consent. This is not ancient history — it is ongoing. You don't have to be a predator to contribute to this dynamic. The post-show adrenaline state impairs your judgment. The power you hold in that space is real even when you're not wielding it deliberately. The ask is simple: slow down, check in with words, receive the answer, and respect it completely.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — "N" CHECK: "'No' from someone in my space is a full sentence. It requires nothing further from me."
scenarios.darkTitle: If You've Crossed A Line
scenarios.dark: If you've done something — in an altered state, in the post-show window, under pressure, or deliberately — that you know wasn't okay: the accountable path is not silence. Reaching out to acknowledge what happened, through a trusted intermediary if direct contact might cause more harm, is the beginning of actual accountability. RAINN has resources for people who have caused harm (rainn.org). The music community is small. The reckoning always comes. Being ahead of it with honesty is better than being caught by it.
scenarios.move: Ask with words. Receive the answer. Respect it completely. This is the whole job.
scenarios.say: "I'm feeling this — is this okay with you?" Then honor whatever comes next. Fully.
scenarios.truth: The artists who build lasting careers are the ones their community can actually trust. Be that artist.

scenarios.archetype: Using Your Platform for Actual Safety
scenarios.who: If you have a stage, you have a microphone. If you have a microphone, you have an opportunity to make the space safer for everyone in it. This page is about using that opportunity.
scenarios.scene: You're two songs into your set and you can feel the energy of the crowd — fully in it, totally open. You have their complete attention. A lot can happen in that crowd tonight. Some of it will be beautiful. Some of it won't be. You have an actual ability to influence which way it goes. The question is whether you choose to use it.
tells: Stating consent expectations from the stage normalizes them in the crowd
Pointing to Harm Reduction resources from the stage reduces the stigma of using them
Calling out behavior you see from the stage carries enormous weight
Creating moments of grounding and community check-in is part of what great performers do
scenarios.happening: Artists with stage platforms have a specific ability to shape the culture of a crowd that most people in that crowd don't have. Stating consent expectations, pointing to safety resources, calling out behavior you see — these are not political statements. They are basic community care that is within your power to provide. The artists who do this are often the ones whose shows feel different — where people feel safer to be fully present.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — "N" CHECK: "What does my platform allow me to contribute to the safety of this community right now?"
scenarios.darkTitle: From Stage — What To Actually Say
scenarios.dark: Simple, real, effective stage interventions: "Before we go any further — look around you. Everyone here deserves to have a great time. If you see something that doesn't look right, say something." "If you need support tonight, Harm Reduction is [location]. No judgment, no questions, just help." "Hands to yourself unless someone has specifically invited them — and if you're not sure, ask." These take 20 seconds. They change the energy of a room. They make the artists who say them more trustworthy, not less cool.
scenarios.move: Use your platform. Even one sentence from the stage can change someone's night.
scenarios.say: [From stage]: "Before we get into this — look out for each other tonight. Harm Reduction is [location], no questions asked. Hands to yourself unless someone said yes. Now let's go."
scenarios.truth: Your platform is a privilege. Using it for community safety is one of the most powerful things you can do with it.

scenarios.hook: THE MENTAL HEALTH REALITY OF TOURING
scenarios.archetype: What Nobody Talks About and What Actually Helps
scenarios.who: Touring is one of the most mentally demanding sustained experiences a person can undertake. The highs are extraordinary. The lows are real and they're often invisible — because the expectation is that you're living the dream and therefore shouldn't be struggling.
scenarios.scene: You're three weeks into a six-week run. The shows have been incredible. The audiences have been extraordinary. You're also sleeping in different places every two days, eating inconsistently, performing at high emotional output nightly, and haven't had a genuine conversation with someone who isn't on tour with you in three weeks. You feel both full and completely empty. You don't know how to explain that to anyone.
tells: Simultaneous emotional fullness from performance and depletion from everything else
No stable environment, schedule, or routine for weeks or months at a time
High public performance combined with very little genuine private connection
The expectation that "living the dream" means you shouldn't have struggles
scenarios.happening: Touring mental health is a serious and underaddressed issue in the music industry. The combination of sleep disruption, dietary inconsistency, emotional performance demands, social isolation, and substance exposure creates conditions that are genuinely hard on mental health — regardless of how much you love the music. Acknowledging this is not weakness. It is professional self-care. The musicians who sustain long careers are the ones who take their mental health as seriously as their technical craft.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “N” CHECK: “What does my actual wellbeing need right now — not what does the tour schedule need from me?” — those are two different questions, and only one of them is actually yours to answer.
scenarios.darkTitle: Mental Health Resources For Musicians
scenarios.dark: MusiCares (grammy.com/musicares): free mental health referrals and financial assistance for music professionals. Sweet Relief Musicians Fund (sweetrelief.org): financial assistance for touring musicians in crisis. Musicians Foundation (musiciansfoundation.org): emergency assistance grants. Backline (backline.care): free mental health and wellness resources specifically for music industry professionals. 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988, 24/7. The music industry is increasingly building mental health infrastructure — use it. Reaching out is not a career-ending move. Burning out silently is.
scenarios.move: Treat your mental health with the same professionalism you bring to your craft.
scenarios.say: [To your most trusted person]: "I'm struggling on this run and I need to say that out loud to someone who isn't on tour with me."
scenarios.truth: You can love the music AND acknowledge that the life is hard. These are not opposites.

scenarios.archetype: Hearing Damage / The Injury That Ends The Career Quietly
scenarios.who: The job itself. Monitors, the pit, load-in, the bus, three hundred nights a year, and a culture where asking for in-ears or wearing plugs still occasionally reads as not being committed.
scenarios.scene: The ringing after a show used to last an hour and now it lasts until the afternoon. You have started asking people to repeat themselves in bars. You mix your own tracks slightly brighter than you used to, which is your ears telling you something you are choosing to hear as a preference.
tells: Tinnitus that persists longer after each run
Struggling with speech in noisy rooms
Turning monitors up across a tour rather than down
No custom moulded plugs, or a pair you have stopped using
Ear fatigue changing the mixing decisions you make
The idea that plugs would ruin the experience, which is the belief that costs the most
scenarios.happening: Noise-induced hearing loss and tinnitus are the defining occupational injuries of this trade, they are cumulative, and they are permanent — there is no treatment that restores what is gone. The specific cruelty for musicians is that the damaged faculty is the instrument: the loss is not merely a disability, it degrades your ability to do the work, and it does so gradually enough that you will adjust to it rather than notice it. Custom moulded musicians' plugs attenuate evenly rather than muffling, which is the objection most people have and the one that is not true.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “D” CHECK: “How long does the ringing last now compared with a year ago?” Write it down. Trend is the measurement that matters.
scenarios.darkTitle: It Does Not Come Back
scenarios.dark: There is no recovery arc here and that is the whole point of the page. Hair cells do not regenerate, tinnitus that becomes permanent is permanent, and the endpoint for a significant number of people in this industry is a career ended by an injury that was completely preventable with a piece of equipment costing less than a single flight case. It is also the injury least likely to be taken seriously in the moment, because it does not hurt and there is nothing to see. Get a baseline audiogram now, get moulded plugs, use them at load-in and in the pit as well as on stage, and treat the trend as data rather than as ageing.
scenarios.move: Get custom moulded musicians' plugs with interchangeable filters, and a baseline audiogram you repeat annually. Wear protection at load-in, soundcheck and in the crowd, not just on stage. Push for in-ears in your rider. Give your ears two quiet days after a run.
scenarios.say: In-ears are on my rider and they're not a nice-to-have — I'm protecting the thing I work with. — I've got moulded plugs in, I can hear you fine, they're flat.
scenarios.truth: Your ears are the instrument and they do not heal. The plugs cost less than one flight case.

scenarios.archetype: Gear Theft On The Road / The Night The Tour Ends
scenarios.who: Organized and specific. People who know what a band's van looks like, which hotels touring acts use, and that a vehicle packed after a show and parked overnight contains everything the act owns.
scenarios.scene: You loaded out at two, drove forty minutes, parked outside the travel lodge like always, and in the morning the side door is open and the van is empty. Instruments, laptops with the stems, merch, the lot. You have a show tomorrow, the insurance certificate is in a folder somewhere, and nobody wrote down a single serial number.
tells: A packed vehicle left overnight in an unsecured car park
Band or crew branding on the van, which advertises the contents
No serial numbers, no photographs, no itemized inventory
Insurance that does not cover unattended vehicles overnight — most do not
Backups of session files kept only on the stolen laptops
Predictable routine: same venues, same hotels, same parking
scenarios.happening: Van theft is a specialist activity aimed at touring musicians precisely because the value density is extraordinary and the routine is predictable. The part most bands get wrong is the insurance: a great many policies exclude theft from an unattended vehicle overnight, which means the cover people believe they have does not apply to the single most likely way they will lose everything. The second thing is documentation — without serials and photographs a claim is slow and a police recovery is effectively impossible even when the gear surfaces.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “D” CHECK: “Could I list every serial number and produce a photograph of each item today?” If not, you do not have a claim, you have a list of regrets.
scenarios.darkTitle: Read The Overnight Exclusion Before The Tour
scenarios.dark: Do this one thing this week: find the clause about unattended vehicles. Bands discover it at the worst possible moment — after the theft, mid-tour, with dates they cannot play and a claim that will be declined. Alongside it, keep the session files somewhere that is not in the van: a cloud backup of stems and masters costs almost nothing and is the only part of the loss that is genuinely irreplaceable, because instruments can be re-bought and a year of unreleased recordings cannot. Everything else on this page is inconvenience; that part is the career.
scenarios.move: Photograph and serial-number everything into a shared document before you leave. Unload the critical items into the accommodation every night — tedious, and it is the whole prevention. Use an unbranded van, vary parking, fit a secondary lock and a tracker. Check the overnight exclusion and back up your files off the vehicle.
scenarios.say: Small gear and laptops come in with us every night, no exceptions — it's twenty minutes and it's the difference between a bad night and no tour. — Can you send me the policy wording for unattended vehicles?
scenarios.truth: Twenty minutes of carrying flight cases into a hotel is the cheapest insurance on the road, and the only one with no exclusions.

scenarios.archetype: The Promoter Who Supplies / Hospitality As A Hook
scenarios.clinical: Substance Provision as Leverage / Dependency Cultivation
scenarios.who: The promoter, the tour manager, or the local fixer whose hospitality is unusually comprehensive and who never seems to want paying for that part of it.
scenarios.scene: The rider is fine and there is something else on the table that was not on it, and he says it is sorted, and this happens at every one of his shows. By the fourth booking you are aware that you look forward to his shows for a reason that is not the audience, and that the conversation about the fee has become a conversation you are less inclined to have.
tells: Substances provided as hospitality, routinely and unasked
Never itemized, never charged, never discussed
Availability increases around contract or payment conversations
Supply is tied to continuing to work with this person specifically
Your consumption has escalated in a way that tracks the touring schedule
You have stopped pushing on money and cannot say exactly when that started
scenarios.happening: Supply is one of the oldest forms of leverage in this industry and it works without a single explicit exchange being proposed. It creates reciprocal debt, it degrades judgement during exactly the conversations where your judgement matters commercially, and it establishes a dependency that is tied to one relationship. It also builds an accumulating hold: somebody who has supplied you for two years knows things about your consumption that they can allude to, and that hold does not require any intention at the time to be usable later.
scenarios.check: S.O.U.N.D. — “N” CHECK: “Would I push as hard on this contract if the hospitality stopped?” If the answer is yes, the hospitality is doing business.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Supply Is A Record Of You
scenarios.dark: The part that arrives years later is the knowledge. A person who has supplied you routinely has a detailed, private account of your use, and at the point where you want to leave, renegotiate, or raise something about their conduct, that account exists and both of you know it. Nothing has to be said explicitly; the industry is full of artists who simply found it easier not to push. Keep your own supply if you use, decline provided substances as a flat policy rather than a judgement, and keep the money conversation in writing and in daylight where the hospitality cannot reach it.
scenarios.move: Make it a standing policy and say it early so it is not about anyone: your rider is your rider, and you do not take anything else from promoters. Do contract and money conversations by email, sober, before the show rather than after it.
scenarios.say: Appreciate it, I keep it to what's on the rider — blanket rule for me, nothing personal. — Let's do the fee by email in the morning rather than tonight.
scenarios.truth: Hospitality that is never itemized is not hospitality. It is an account being opened in your name.

guides.intro: Your booth is your business. Your inventory is your livelihood. Protect both.

checks.name: Money Moves First
checks.desc: Cash, Venmo, Square — you set the terms. Never extend credit to strangers or accept payment you cannot verify.

checks.name: Access Is Earned
checks.desc: Booth placement, electricity, water — whoever controls these controls your event. Know who holds that leverage.

checks.name: Record Everything
checks.desc: Every fee paid, every agreement made, every incident. Your paper trail is your only real protection.

checks.name: Know Your Circuit
checks.desc: The traveling vendor circuit has a memory. Predatory promoters get named. Learn who they are before you book.

checks.name: Exit Costs Nothing
checks.desc: A bad vendor agreement costs more to stay in than to leave. Know your exit terms before you sign.

checks.name: Travel Safely
checks.desc: Solo travel with inventory and cash is one of the highest-risk situations in the vendor world. Plan it like it matters.

outline.desc: Promoter traps, false opportunity, the circuit scam
Camp pressure, romantic entanglement, partner control
Booth retaliation, consignment traps, design theft, cash safety
Contracts, payment protection, travel safety, legal resources
Real vendor solidarity vs competitive sabotage

sentences: My inventory is my livelihood. I protect it accordingly.
A verbal agreement is not an agreement.
Someone who controls my booth placement has leverage I need to account for.
My cash on hand is not community property. Neither is my inventory.

scenarios.archetype: The Bait-and-Switch Promoter
scenarios.who: The event promoter who controls your placement, electricity, water, foot traffic, and your access to the event. Starts with a perfect pitch. Delivers something different. Uses your sunk costs to keep you from pushing back.
scenarios.scene: The pitch was perfect: high-foot-traffic spot near the main stage, 2,000 attendees, electricity included. You paid the $800 vendor fee two months out. You arrive to find your spot is behind the food trucks, electricity needs an additional $150 hookup fee nobody mentioned, and the 2,000 attendee number was from three years ago. When you raise it he reminds you with a smile that the vendor fee is non-refundable.
tells: Placement promises made verbally — not written into the vendor agreement
Additional fees appear after you have committed and payment is non-refundable
Attendance or traffic numbers are from a different year or simply made up
Complaints are met with the reminder that you have already paid
scenarios.happening: Vendor fee manipulation relies on the non-refundable deposit to eliminate your leverage once you have committed. The bait-and-switch is a known and widespread practice on the festival vendor circuit. Your only real protection is what is written down before you pay. If it is not in the vendor agreement it did not happen and you have no recourse. Research every promoter in Facebook vendor groups and Indie Craft Experience forums before you commit. The circuit has a long memory for bad promoters.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “M” CHECK: “Is the placement, the attendance number, and every fee in writing — or just verbally promised by someone with every reason to over-promise?” — a great pitch that isn’t in writing is just a story.
scenarios.darkTitle: Vendor Agreement Must-Haves
scenarios.dark: Before paying any vendor fee, the written agreement must include: exact booth location or tier with a map, all fees fully itemized including electricity and water hookups, minimum attendance guarantee or clear as-is disclaimer, refund policy under specific conditions including event cancellation, your sales category and exclusivity protections, and setup and breakdown time windows. Research every promoter on Facebook vendor groups before committing.
scenarios.move: If it is not in the written agreement it does not exist. Pay only what the paper says.
scenarios.say: I would love to participate — can you send me the vendor agreement with placement details and all fees before I commit?
scenarios.truth: A great pitch that is not in writing is just a story.

scenarios.archetype: Terms Shifted After You Are Fully Committed
scenarios.who: The promoter who confirms your spot, collects your fee, then changes material terms after you are too invested to walk away without serious loss. Each change seems small. The cumulative impact is significant.
scenarios.scene: You confirmed spot 14 near the main entrance with electrical hookup in writing two months ago. You arrive to find spot 14 has been given to a premium sponsor and you are now in spot 47 near the back fence with no electricity. When you protest: "We sent an email about changes last week" — to an address you had not checked. The show opens in four hours and your inventory is on the truck.
tells: Material terms change after full payment and you are completely committed
Changes communicated through easily missable channels at the last minute
Your leverage is zero because your inventory is already there
Each individual change is presented as minor or outside their control
scenarios.happening: Last-minute term changes exploit the sunk cost of your presence. You have traveled, brought inventory, and made plans that are hard to reverse. The cost of walking away feels higher than accepting the change — and that is exactly the calculation the promoter is banking on. Documenting the original agreement in writing and responding to every change in writing creates a paper trail that supports a refund claim or small claims filing after the event.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “R” CHECK: “Do I have written documentation of what was originally agreed so I can actually point to it when the terms shift?” — the paper trail you build before the event is the only thing that protects you at it.
scenarios.darkTitle: When They Change Your Terms After Arrival
scenarios.dark: (1) Document immediately — photograph your contracted spot vs where they have put you. (2) Send a written objection via email before the event opens: "This placement does not match our agreement. I am proceeding under protest and reserving the right to seek a refund." (3) After the event: small claims court handles disputes up to $25,000 depending on state, filing fee usually under $100, you represent yourself. Your written agreement is your evidence. Most promoters will settle rather than face a filing.
scenarios.move: Document the original agreement. Document every change. Respond to all changes in writing immediately.
scenarios.say: This placement does not match our agreement. I am setting up under protest and will follow up in writing.
scenarios.truth: The paper trail you build before the event is the only thing that protects you at the event.

scenarios.archetype: The Camp Host Who Expects Inventory as Rent
scenarios.who: The camp or collective that offers housing, infrastructure, or event access in exchange for vague contribution — which expands over time to include gifting your inventory, free labor, and staying quiet about how the arrangement works.
scenarios.scene: The camp offered you a booth placement and a campsite. "We just ask that everyone contributes to the community." By the second event you have gifted $400 of inventory, worked 12 hours of camp setup and breakdown, and contributed $200 cash to camp costs. You are making less per event than you were before you joined the family. When you raise it, the response is a hurt look and a reminder of everything they have done for you.
tells: Contribution expectations are vague at start and expand with each event
Gifting your inventory positioned as community participation not a cost to your business
Access to placement tied to your continued compliance with camp demands
Raising the financial impact of the arrangement is received as not being a good community fit
scenarios.happening: Camp-based vendor arrangements can be genuinely mutually beneficial and they can be a systematic way to extract inventory, labor, and compliance from traveling vendors who need the infrastructure. The tell is always whether terms are defined and mutual. Real community has reciprocity both parties can articulate. When your contributions keep expanding and the camp contributions stay stable — that is feudalism with better branding.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “E” CHECK: “What would it actually cost me to leave this arrangement — and is that cost getting bigger the longer I stay quiet about it?” — an undefined cost that grows with your silence is not community. It’s a bill you didn’t agree to.
scenarios.darkTitle: Calculate Your Actual Camp Arrangement Cost
scenarios.dark: Write this down: (1) Vendor fee or equivalent you are paying. (2) Value of inventory gifted at your wholesale cost. (3) Value of your labor hours at your day rate. (4) Cash contributions to camp costs. Now compare to what a solo vendor spot at the same event would cost and what your actual net sales were. If the camp arrangement costs more than going independently — you are paying for the privilege of working for them. Name that clearly before committing to another season.
scenarios.move: Calculate every camp arrangement in actual dollars before you commit to another event.
scenarios.say: I want to understand what the arrangement looks like financially before I commit — can we talk through what is expected specifically?
scenarios.truth: Community costs should be defined, mutual, and agreed to in advance. Anything else is uncompensated labor.

scenarios.archetype: Peer Guilt Pressure / Inventory Extraction
scenarios.who: The pressure from fellow vendors — framed as community solidarity — to give discounts, free products, or special arrangements. Real community exists. So does community being used as cover for extracting commercial value from you.
scenarios.scene: The vendor two booths over has been friendly all weekend and helped you with a few things. Now she wants $200 of your inventory for $80 "because we take care of each other here." The festie culture frames this as normal generosity. But $120 of lost margin on a slow sales day is not a gift you can afford. When you hesitate she mentions how she helped you with the tent stakes yesterday morning.
tells: The "we are family" frame used specifically in commercial transactions
Reciprocity invoked one-sidedly — their help earlier, your discount now
Declining is framed as being un-community or not understanding how the circuit works
The pressure arrives when you are already depleted or in a vulnerable moment
scenarios.happening: Festival vendor culture has genuine traditions of mutual aid. The predatory version uses that cultural norm to extract commercial value — discounts, free inventory, special pricing — framed as solidarity. Real community support does not require you to absorb losses to prove you belong. A discount is a business decision. So is not giving one. You are allowed to make that decision based on your actual financial situation.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — "M" CHECK: "Is this exchange actually mutual — or am I absorbing a loss to avoid a social cost?"
scenarios.darkTitle: How To Decline Gracefully And Firmly
scenarios.dark: You do not need a lengthy explanation to decline a discount request. Simple responses that work: "I keep my pricing consistent across the weekend — I cannot do discounts." "My margins are pretty tight this event — I appreciate you asking though." "I am not in a position to do discounts right now." You do not owe anyone your cost breakdown or a justification for your pricing. A fellow vendor who responds to a firm but kind no with guilt or withdrawal was not being community with you.
scenarios.move: Your pricing is your pricing. You are allowed to hold it regardless of social pressure.
scenarios.say: I keep my pricing consistent all weekend — I am not able to do discounts. I appreciate you though.
scenarios.truth: Your margin is your livelihood. Protecting it is not being anti-community. It is being a sustainable business.

scenarios.hook: I CAN GET YOU IN ANYWHERE
scenarios.archetype: Romantic Entanglement With Access Holders
scenarios.who: The promoter, camp lead, or circuit organizer who becomes romantically involved with a vendor and uses that relationship to control business access. Starts as genuine connection. Becomes leverage when the relationship gets complicated.
scenarios.scene: You met him at the winter market and the connection was real. By spring he was helping you get into better events and your bookings genuinely improved. By summer you are in a relationship that has become complicated and painful — and every conversation about ending it carries an unspoken freight of what happens to your bookings and circuit relationships when you do. The personal and professional are completely entangled and you have less power in both.
tells: Romantic relationship develops with someone who controls your business access
Professional benefits and relationship status feel tied — both rise and fall together
Contemplating ending the relationship includes calculating professional costs
They reference your bookings or placement during relationship conflicts
scenarios.happening: Romantic entanglement with access holders is a specific and common vendor vulnerability because the festival circuit is small and relationship-driven. The problem is not the relationship. The problem is when the relationship becomes the mechanism of professional control. If you cannot evaluate your relationship independently of what it costs your business — the entanglement has already become control. Your professional access should never live inside a romantic relationship.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “A” CHECK: “Does my business access depend on this relationship — and what does that mean for me the day this relationship ends?” — access that depends on one relationship was never really yours.
scenarios.darkTitle: Building Access Independent Of Any One Person
scenarios.dark: Your vendor circuit access should run through multiple independent relationships. Practical steps: join at least two vendor Facebook groups and participate so people know you independently. Apply to events directly rather than through an intermediary whenever possible. Build relationships with multiple promoters independently of any romantic partner. Document your own sales history and reviews so your reputation is yours — not borrowed from someone else's endorsement. The goal is that your access to the circuit survives any single relationship ending.
scenarios.move: Keep your professional relationships independent of your romantic ones. Build your own circuit reputation.
scenarios.say: I am going to apply to this one directly — I want to build my own relationship with the organizer.
scenarios.truth: Your business access is yours. It should never live inside someone else's hands.

scenarios.archetype: When Your Road Partner Controls the Vehicle or Money
scenarios.who: The traveling vendor partner who controls the shared vehicle, the shared float, or the shared logistics — and uses that control to manufacture compliance, silence about problems, or tolerance of exploitation.
scenarios.scene: You share a van and travel costs with her. It made the circuit financially viable for the first time. Six months in you realize: she sets the travel schedule without your input, she manages the shared float with accounting you never see, and she decides which events you attend based on criteria that seem to benefit her inventory over yours. The van is hers. Leaving means losing the whole circuit arrangement.
tells: One partner controls transportation and the other is fully dependent on it for the circuit
Financial decisions — shared float, joint purchases, event fees — made unilaterally
Event selection appears to systematically favor one partner's inventory or relationships
Raising concerns triggers the implicit threat of losing the arrangement entirely
scenarios.happening: Travel partnerships on the vendor circuit are economically valuable and structurally vulnerable to exploitation when one party holds more resource control. The vehicle, the float, the event relationships — each creates leverage. Without a written partnership agreement defining decision-making, financial access, and exit terms, the person with more physical control has more power regardless of what was verbally agreed at the start.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — "A" CHECK: "Do I have independent access to the money and transportation in this arrangement?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Traveling Vendor Partnership Agreement Basics
scenarios.dark: Every traveling vendor partnership needs in writing: who owns the vehicle and what the other partner's rights are, how travel costs are split and documented, how event selection decisions are made and by whom, how the shared float is managed and who has access to records, how revenue and costs are reconciled after each event, and exit terms — what happens if one partner wants to stop. This is not distrust. This is the document that makes the partnership sustainable. A one-page agreement prevents years of resentment.
scenarios.move: Never enter a traveling vendor partnership without a written agreement covering money, transport, and exit.
scenarios.say: I am really excited to do this together — let us get the basic terms in writing so we are both protected.
scenarios.truth: The partnership that starts as family needs the same paperwork as a business partnership. Because it is both.

scenarios.archetype: Social Proof Sabotage / Competitor Gossip
scenarios.who: The fellow vendor who uses the tight-knit circuit to spread reputation damage — questioning your craft authenticity, poaching your customers, or running whisper campaigns to promoters about why they should not book you.
scenarios.scene: Sales started dropping at your third event of the season without obvious reason. A promoter friend tells you she has been hearing your work is not really handmade — she does not know where it is coming from but multiple people have mentioned it. You trace it back to a vendor two spots over who you have been outselling for three seasons. Nothing being said is true. But it is already in circulation and you do not know how to correct something you are not supposed to know is being said.
tells: Sales drop or bookings thin without clear cause — investigate the social layer
Promoters who previously booked you easily are now vague or unresponsive
Other vendors seem to have information about your business you did not share
A specific competitor directly benefits from the narrative circulating about you
scenarios.happening: The festival vendor circuit is small, relationship-driven, and operates heavily on reputation. Smear campaigns are highly effective because the market is interconnected — a few well-placed doubts can close doors quietly without you knowing they were closing. The most effective counter is documented proof: photos of your process, behind-the-scenes content, certificates of authenticity for materials, and direct relationships with promoters that are independent of any one person.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — "K" CHECK: "Do I have documentation of my process and materials that speaks for itself?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Document Your Process — This Is Your Defense
scenarios.dark: Build a documentation library: time-lapse or process videos of your making, raw material photos with supplier tags, works-in-progress shots, and studio photos. Post these regularly — not just finished pieces. This creates an independent timestamped record that no smear campaign can erase. When you hear something is being said: address it directly with your promoter contacts with evidence. "I heard there is a question about my process — I wanted to share my documentation directly with you." Confident and documented beats defensive every time.
scenarios.move: Let your process documentation be louder than anyone's whisper campaign.
scenarios.say: I make everything myself and I have the receipts — happy to share my process documentation if that would be helpful.
scenarios.truth: You cannot control what people say. You can make the truth undeniable.

scenarios.archetype: The Organizer Who Moves You When You Push Back
scenarios.who: The promoter or market organizer who uses booth placement as a reward and punishment system — giving prime spots to compliant vendors and moving anyone who raises concerns or exercises independence to low-traffic locations.
scenarios.scene: You raised concerns about an electricity fee discrepancy in a vendor group last season — politely, with documentation, requesting the refund you were owed. This season's placement confirmation arrives: spot 52, far corner, partial shade, foot traffic rated poor on the organizer's own map. Last season you were in spot 8. Nothing has changed about your product or professionalism. Everything has changed about your willingness to be quiet.
tells: Placement quality drops significantly after you raised a legitimate concern
The explanation for the change is vague or contradictory
Other vendors who also raised concerns have also received worse placements
You feel that raising future concerns would cost you even more placement quality
scenarios.happening: Placement retaliation is a control mechanism that works because it is hard to prove and because the cost of fighting it feels higher than the cost of compliance. The organizer has plausible deniability — placement decisions involve many factors. The counter is documentation of the pattern across multiple events and multiple vendors, and building relationships with other organizers so your circuit access does not depend on any one event.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “K” CHECK: “Am I staying quiet about legitimate concerns because I am afraid of what it will cost my placement next season?” — an organizer who punishes standards is telling you exactly who they are.
scenarios.darkTitle: Building Circuit Independence
scenarios.dark: The most effective protection against any single organizer's retaliation is a circuit that does not depend on them. Practical steps: apply to at least three times more events than you plan to attend so you have real options. Build direct relationships with multiple organizers independently. Document your sales performance and vendor reviews so your reputation exists independently. Participate in vendor communities so other organizers know your work before they see your application. Independence is the protection.
scenarios.move: Build circuit access that does not depend on any single organizer's approval.
scenarios.say: I am going to continue applying to a range of events so I always have real options each season.
scenarios.truth: The organizer who punishes you for having standards is telling you they are not the right partner for your business.

scenarios.archetype: Solo Travel With Inventory and Cash
scenarios.who: Traveling vendors are a specific target: you arrive with known valuable inventory, leave with known cash, are often solo, and festival environments give people multiple days to observe your patterns, schedule, and vehicle.
scenarios.scene: Sunday breakdown. Strong weekend — the cash box is full. You are loading your van alone in the dim hour before dawn, moving merchandise in multiple trips. The spot next to you is empty. You have been so focused on the physical work of loading that you have completely stopped being aware of who is around. This is the window. It is the one experienced thieves specifically wait for.
tells: Loading and unloading solo in low-traffic hours with visible valuable inventory
Cash box visible during transactions and during breakdown
Same parking location over multiple days — your vehicle and patterns become known
Arrival time, departure time, and cash handling routine all become observable
scenarios.happening: Festival vendor robbery targets specific patterns: the breakdown window when you are tired and often solo, visible cash after a strong sales day, and known vehicle location. It is not always strangers — sometimes it is other vendors or people with festival access who have been watching your patterns all weekend. Cash management, breakdown protocol, and travel companions are not paranoia. They are the professional infrastructure of the traveling vendor life.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — "T" CHECK: "Am I traveling and breaking down in a way that minimizes my visibility as a target?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Traveling Vendor Physical Safety Protocol
scenarios.dark: Cash management: bank deposits same-day when possible, never keep full weekend cash in the vehicle overnight, use a money belt or hidden pouch during breakdown. Vehicle: do not leave inventory visible in a parked vehicle overnight, park in well-lit areas, share your spot location with someone not at the event. Breakdown: break down with at least one other vendor present whenever possible, load valuables last when you are ready to drive immediately. Travel: share your route and ETA with someone. Check in when you arrive.
scenarios.move: Never break down solo with a full cash box. Build the protocol and use it every time.
scenarios.say: Hey — want to watch each other's spaces during breakdown? I will help you load if you help me.
scenarios.truth: The most experienced vendors on the circuit are also the most careful ones. That is not a coincidence.

scenarios.archetype: Work Left Behind, Payment Never Comes
scenarios.who: The shop, gallery, boutique, or pop-up that wants your work on consignment — and then does not pay, goes out of business with your inventory inside, or loses the reconciliation. Consignment is legitimate. Unprotected consignment is a gift.
scenarios.scene: "We would love to carry your line — we do 60/40 in your favor, you would be in great company." You drop off $1,800 of wholesale inventory. Three months later you are still waiting for the first check. The shop is still open. Your work is still on the shelves. Phone calls go unanswered. Emails get vague responses. Six months in you have recovered $600 of $1,800 in product and the shop just posted new arrivals on Instagram.
tells: No written consignment agreement with payment terms and reconciliation schedule
First payment arrives late or partial — this sets the pattern for everything that follows
No inventory tracking system or signed receipt for what you left
The owner becomes progressively harder to reach as time goes on
scenarios.happening: Consignment fraud is one of the most common forms of vendor exploitation because artists feel awkward being professional with people who seem enthusiastic about their work. The enthusiasm is real — your work is valuable. The payment intention varies. A consignment agreement is not distrust — it is the thing that makes the relationship honest and enforceable. Without it, recovering your inventory or your payment requires legal action that costs more than the inventory is worth.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — "M" CHECK: "Do I have a signed agreement with payment terms — or just a handshake and a hope?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Consignment Agreement Minimum Terms
scenarios.dark: Every consignment placement needs in writing: itemized list of pieces with your price and the split, payment schedule (monthly reconciliation is standard), what happens to unsold pieces and when (90-day return clause), who is responsible for lost or damaged inventory, and what access you have to check on your pieces. Bring a printed agreement to every drop-off and do not rely on theirs. If a shop will not sign your agreement — take your inventory back. That is your information about their payment intention.
scenarios.move: No signed consignment agreement, no inventory drop-off. This policy saves you every time.
scenarios.say: I use a standard consignment agreement for all my placements — I have one here for us both to sign before I leave anything.
scenarios.truth: Enthusiasm about your work is not a payment plan. A signed agreement is.

scenarios.archetype: Design Theft / Your Work Sold by Someone Else
scenarios.who: Your designs, your photographs, your product images appearing on someone else's booth, Etsy shop, or social media — without your permission, without credit, and often in direct competition with you on the same circuit.
scenarios.scene: A customer at your booth holds up their phone: "I saw something almost identical to this at the booth down the way — they are selling it for less." You go look. It is not almost identical. It IS identical — your photo, your design, printed by a drop-ship service. The vendor shrugs: "I found the image online, how was I supposed to know?" Your image has a watermark. It was cropped out. This is not an accident.
tells: Your product photos appearing on other vendors' social media without credit
Your designs appearing in physical or digital products from another seller
Drop-ship or print-on-demand versions of your work sold at lower prices on your circuit
Your business name or brand elements used by someone else in your market space
scenarios.happening: Design theft and image theft are endemic in the handmade marketplace — the internet makes copying easy and enforcement feels difficult. But copyright protection is automatic the moment you create original work and you have real options. The key is documentation: timestamp your original files, watermark everything you post publicly, maintain a creation file with original dated drafts. US Copyright registration ($65) enables enforcement with statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per infringement.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “R” CHECK: “Do I have timestamped documentation of my original designs that establishes my ownership before anyone else’s does?” — your designs are copyrighted the moment you create them. You get to enforce that.
scenarios.darkTitle: When Your Work Is Stolen — Your Options
scenarios.dark: Documentation first: screenshot everything, note dates, save original files. DMCA takedown: file with the platform — Google, Etsy, and Instagram all have processes and take these seriously. Etsy: file an Intellectual Property infringement report — they will remove listings. Legal: small claims for amounts under your state limit. Copyright registration ($65 at copyright.gov) opens the door to statutory damages and attorney fees — making enforcement financially viable. Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts offers free consultations in most major cities.
scenarios.move: Watermark everything. Document your creation dates. Enforce your copyright.
scenarios.say: That is my image and my design. I need you to remove it from your inventory today. I have documentation of the original.
scenarios.truth: Your designs are copyrighted the moment you create them. You get to enforce that.

scenarios.archetype: Legal Risk, Undercovers, and Festival Transactions
scenarios.who: Transactions at festivals — substances, goods, services, tickets — carry real legal risk that vendors often underestimate because the festival environment feels safe and familiar. Undercover officers work festivals and look exactly like attendees.
scenarios.scene: He has been browsing your booth for twenty minutes asking thoughtful questions about your process. The conversation shifts — he mentions he knows people who might be interested in other things you might have access to, winks included. It feels casual. It feels like a fellow festie making a sideways inquiry. Something about the specificity of the questions feels slightly rehearsed. You cannot put your finger on it. But something is off.
tells: They approach YOU with an inquiry that moves from your products to something else entirely
Unusual specificity about quantities, prices, or sourcing that goes beyond normal customer curiosity
Wants to move the conversation somewhere more private or away from your booth
Something about the interaction feels slightly scripted — you cannot articulate why but it is there
scenarios.happening: Undercover officers at festivals are specifically trained to blend in and they are often very good at it. As a vendor with a public booth you are particularly visible and accessible. The behavioral tells are in the conversation pattern itself: they redirect from legitimate commerce to other things, they guide toward isolation, and they push for specificity. You are never obligated to complete any conversation or transaction. "I am just focused on my product today" ends it cleanly.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “A” CHECK: “Am I proceeding with this conversation because I actually want to — or because saying no feels riskier than it is?” — no transaction at a festival is worth your freedom, and no conversation is worth your business.
scenarios.darkTitle: If You Are Approached By Police Or Detained
scenarios.dark: Know this before you need it: (1) You have the right to remain silent — use it. "I would like to speak with a lawyer" is the only thing you say. (2) You can ask if you are being detained or free to go — if free to go, go. (3) You can decline to consent to a search. (4) Do not physically resist any police interaction. (5) Write down badge numbers and details as soon as possible. (6) Contact a lawyer or the National Lawyers Guild (nlg.org) which has observer programs at many major festivals. Good Samaritan laws protect people seeking overdose help in most US states.
scenarios.move: "I am just focused on my product today" ends any sideways conversation. Clean and done.
scenarios.say: I am just focused on my booth today — thanks for stopping by.
scenarios.truth: No transaction at a festival is worth your freedom. No conversation is worth your business.

scenarios.archetype: Your Options When Payment Does Not Come
scenarios.who: You did the event. You delivered the inventory. You completed the commission. The payment did not come. This page covers what you actually do next — step by step — because most predatory promoters and buyers rely on vendors being too tired or too non-confrontational to pursue it.
scenarios.scene: It has been six weeks since the event. You have sent three polite emails. You have received two vague replies and one promise of "by end of week" that came and went. The promoter is still posting about upcoming events on Instagram. Your follow-up messages are being read but not replied to. You are owed $1,200 and you are running out of patience and confidence that it is coming.
tells: Payment delayed past agreed date without proactive communication from their side
Replies become progressively vague, slow, or one-word as time passes
"Accounting issues" or "cash flow" appear as explanations without a concrete resolution date
They are visibly active on social media and running their business while ignoring your payment
scenarios.happening: Most non-payment situations resolve at the written demand stage because most bad-faith payers are not prepared to actually face legal consequences — they are relying on vendors giving up. A written demand with a specific deadline and a reference to your legal options is the trigger that moves most situations to resolution. The ones who still do not pay after a written demand are the ones you take to small claims. The process is simpler than most people think.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — "R" CHECK: "Do I have documentation of everything agreed and every follow-up I have sent?"
scenarios.darkTitle: The Non-Payment Escalation Sequence
scenarios.dark: Step 1: Formal written demand email with your contract attached, a specific payment deadline of 7-14 days, and a statement that you will pursue legal remedies if unpaid. Step 2: small claims court — handles disputes up to $10,000-$25,000 depending on state, filing fee usually under $100, you represent yourself. Step 3: attorney demand letter for larger amounts ($150-300 one-time) frequently resolves it immediately. Step 4: publicizing non-payment in vendor communities is legal and effective. Document everything before going public. Most situations resolve at Step 1 or 2.
scenarios.move: Send the written demand. Most situations resolve there. Be prepared to file if they do not.
scenarios.say: Per our agreement, payment of [X] was due on [date]. Please remit by [new date] or I will pursue this through small claims court.
scenarios.truth: You did the work. You get paid. This is completely enforceable and simpler than they want you to think.

scenarios.archetype: The Documents and Resources That Protect You
scenarios.who: This is the reference page. The documents, resources, and practices that mean you are protected before any problem starts — not scrambling to protect yourself after it already has.
scenarios.scene: The vendors who have long and sustainable careers on the festival circuit are not the ones who never get taken advantage of. They are the ones who built the infrastructure early, put things in writing consistently, and stopped apologizing for having professional standards inside a culture that frames everything as love and vibes. You can love this community AND operate professionally within it. These are not opposites.
tells: Standard vendor agreement — one page, covers placement, fees, refund policy, and exclusivity
Standard consignment agreement — covers inventory list, split, payment schedule, and returns
Invoice template with payment terms, late fees, and your legal remedies clearly stated
Process documentation library — timestamped photos and videos of your making process
scenarios.happening: Professional infrastructure is not about distrust — it is about making every relationship honest from the start. Vendors with clear written terms attract the promoters and buyers who are comfortable with clear written terms, which turns out to be exactly the promoters and buyers you want to work with. The ones who resist paperwork are showing you their payment intentions. Let paperwork be the filter. It saves enormous amounts of time and energy.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — "R" CHECK: "Do I have the documents I need to protect myself before I need them — not after?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Vendor Legal And Business Resources
scenarios.dark: Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts (vlany.org): free and low-cost legal help for artists and makers on contracts, copyright, and business disputes. US Copyright Office (copyright.gov): automatic copyright on creation, registration $65 enables enforcement. SCORE (score.org): free business mentoring from experienced business owners — very useful for pricing and business structure. Small Business Development Centers (sba.gov/sbdc): free consulting on business plans, finances, and legal structure. Indie Craft Experience and similar vendor communities: peer knowledge about specific promoters and events.
scenarios.move: Build the documents before you need them. They are the filter that attracts the right partners.
scenarios.say: Here is my standard vendor agreement — I use this for all my events so we are both protected.
scenarios.truth: Professional standards do not push the right people away. They push the wrong people away. That is the point.

scenarios.archetype: How to Tell the Difference and Build the Real Thing
scenarios.who: The vendor circuit at its best is one of the most genuinely supportive professional communities that exists — people who share leads, warn each other about bad promoters, help each other during breakdown, and celebrate each other's success. This page is about building that and protecting it from the extractive version.
scenarios.scene: The vendor two booths over comes by mid-morning on Saturday: "Hey I noticed you are running low on bags — I have extras, take some." No reciprocity mentioned. No ledger. Later she tells you she heard a rumor about next year's event moving to a smaller venue — thought you should know before you committed your spot fee. Later still she helps you carry your tent poles to the car. None of it was transactional. All of it was real.
tells: Real vendor community: sharing information freely including about bad promoters and difficult buyers
Real vendor community: helping during load-in and breakdown without keeping score
Real vendor community: celebrating each other's success including when a neighboring booth has a great day
Real vendor community: honest feedback about your work and business when you ask for it
scenarios.happening: Real vendor solidarity is built through repeated small interactions where each person is free to give or not give without social cost either way.
