It looks like sharing information, helping during the hard moments of setup and breakdown, warning each other about problems on the circuit, and genuinely celebrating when someone in the community thrives. It does not look like keeping score, invoking community as leverage in commercial transactions, or using shared history as a reason you owe someone something.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “K” CHECK: “Is this interaction genuinely mutual — or is community being invoked to extract something one direction only?” — real community runs both ways. Extraction only runs one.
scenarios.darkTitle: How To Build Your Real Vendor Network
scenarios.dark: Real vendor community is built through: sharing information generously including about bad promoters — this is the most valuable thing you can do for each other. Participating in vendor Facebook groups not just to ask questions but to answer them. Introducing yourself to neighboring vendors at every event with genuine curiosity about their work. Helping during breakdown even when you are exhausted. Giving honest referrals and honest warnings. The vendors who build the longest and most sustainable careers are almost always the ones who invest most genuinely in the community around them.
scenarios.move: Invest in real vendor community. It is the best business development and the best protection at the same time.
scenarios.say: I heard something about that promoter you should know before you commit — let me tell you what happened to me.
scenarios.truth: The real vendor community is out there and it is extraordinary. Protect yourself from the extractive version so you have the energy to find it.

scenarios.hook: THE PAYMENT SAYS IT WENT THROUGH
scenarios.archetype: Card Fraud, Fake Transfers And Counterfeit Notes
scenarios.who: Somebody who has worked out that a vendor at hour nine, in bad light, with a queue forming and no signal, cannot verify anything and will not hold up the line to try.
scenarios.scene: He shows you the screen. It says sent, with your name on it and a tick. It is half past eleven, the signal has been dropping all day, your banking app will not load, and there are four people waiting behind him holding things they want to buy. You hand over the piece.
tells: A screenshot of a transfer rather than money in your account
Payment claimed at the exact moment your signal is worst
A card that declines and is retried on a different reader
Large notes for small items, late at night, in poor light
Hurrying you, with a queue behind, and a reason it must be now
Refunds requested in cash for a card transaction
scenarios.happening: Every one of these relies on the same three conditions a festival supplies reliably: bad connectivity, bad light and social pressure from a queue. A transfer screenshot proves nothing and is trivial to fake; a pending or unsettled card payment is not a payment; and counterfeit notes at a market stall late at night are an old trade that persists because nobody wants to be the vendor who holds up the line over a twenty. The cash-refund version is the cleanest fraud of the lot, and the answer to it is that a refund goes back the way the money came, always.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “M” CHECK: “Has the money arrived in my account, or have I been shown a picture of money?” Those are not the same event.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Queue Is The Weapon
scenarios.dark: Notice what is actually being used against you, because it is not technology. It is your reluctance to make four other paying customers wait while you check. That pressure is manufactured, it is often manufactured deliberately, and it is the reason this works at eleven at night and never at eleven in the morning. Decide the policy in advance so there is no decision to make in the moment: no goods leave the stall until the money is confirmed in your account or the terminal says approved, and if the signal is down you take cash or you take a name and hold the item. Losing one sale is not a cost. Losing four pieces across a weekend is.
scenarios.move: Set the rule before the event and put it on a small card on the stall. Keep a UV pen and check large notes. Never refund cash on a card payment. Take a deposit and hold the item if you cannot verify. Reconcile takings nightly rather than on Monday.
scenarios.say: I'll hold it for you — I just can't let it go until it lands my end, signal's awful. Two minutes and it'll come through. — Refunds go back to the card, not in cash, sorry.
scenarios.truth: A screenshot is not a payment. The queue behind him is the pressure, and it is doing exactly what it was arranged to do.

scenarios.archetype: Weather, Loss And The Insurance Nobody Bought
scenarios.who: The forecast, and a pitch fee that bought you a square of grass and no guarantees whatsoever.
scenarios.scene: It went at four in the morning. The frame is in three pieces, half the stock is in a puddle, the rest blew toward the fence, and the event is running as normal at ten. Nobody is going to reimburse you, your pitch fee is not coming back, and you have just discovered that your policy covers theft but not weather.
tells: Gazebo weights instead of ground anchors, on a forecast you did not check
Stock stored at ground level in a field
No stock insurance, or a policy that excludes weather and unattended loss
No written terms about cancellation or refund with the organizer
No contingency float to survive a wiped weekend
Everything you own on the circuit is in this one gazebo
scenarios.happening: Vendors carry all the risk at an outdoor event and almost none of the protection. Pitch fees are near-universally non-refundable, organizers rarely take liability for weather, and the standard trader policy people buy often excludes exactly the two things most likely to happen in a field — storm damage and loss from an unattended stall overnight. The result is a business that can lose a season's stock in one night with no route to recovery, sitting next to an event that continues around it.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “R” CHECK: “If my stall was destroyed tonight, what would I actually recover?” Read the policy now, not at four in the morning.
scenarios.darkTitle: Concentration Is The Real Exposure
scenarios.dark: The structural danger is concentration rather than weather. Most makers put their entire inventory into one vehicle, one gazebo, one weekend, and a single night removes the business rather than a weekend's takings. Split the stock: keep a reserve in the van, and a reserve at home that never travels, so the worst night costs you an event instead of a livelihood. Then read the policy wording for storm and unattended exclusions, ask the organizer in writing what happens to the pitch fee if the event is cancelled or a trading day is lost, and keep a float that covers one wiped weekend. None of this is pessimism; it is the difference between a bad weekend and starting again.
scenarios.move: Ground-anchor properly and check the forecast daily. Stock off the ground, in lidded boxes. Split inventory across stall, van and home. Get a policy that covers storm and unattended stock, and get the organizer's cancellation terms in writing before you pay the pitch fee.
scenarios.say: Before I pay the pitch — what are the terms if the event's cancelled or we lose a trading day to weather? Can you put that in the email? — Half the stock stays in the van, always.
scenarios.truth: The pitch fee buys you grass. Everything that happens on it is yours, so split the stock and read the exclusions.

scenarios.archetype: The Physical Cost Nobody Budgets For
scenarios.who: The schedule. Four days, fourteen-hour trading days, a build at either end, no chair because standing sells better, and no break because a break is a closed stall.
scenarios.scene: Day three. You have not sat down since seven, you have eaten one thing, you cannot leave because there is nobody to cover you, and you have started making decisions — about pricing, about a wholesale enquiry, about whether that transfer really went through — with a brain that has been standing up in the sun since dawn.
tells: No cover, so no breaks, so no meals and no toilet trips
Standing all day on hard ground with no anti-fatigue matting
Dehydration because drinking means needing the toilet you cannot go to
Business decisions being made at hour twelve
Lifting the whole build alone, twice per event
Recovery time between events that is shorter each season
scenarios.happening: Vendor fatigue is an economic problem before it is a health one. Every transaction on this page's neighbours — the fake transfer, the renegotiated deal, the wholesale offer that is worse than it sounds, the pressure to drop a price — arrives at the end of a long day and lands on a depleted person, and depleted people concede. The physical toll is real and cumulative too, but the immediate cost is commercial: you are making your most consequential decisions in your worst condition, by design, several times a weekend.
scenarios.check: M.A.R.K.E.T. — “E” CHECK: “Am I about to make a real decision at hour twelve?” Defer it to the morning. Everything that is genuinely good will still be there.
scenarios.darkTitle: They Come At You At Closing Time
scenarios.dark: Notice the timing of the difficult conversations across a weekend. The wholesale enquiry, the request for a discount, the organizer wanting to change your pitch, the payment that cannot quite be verified — these cluster late, and not entirely by accident. Some of it is simply when people wander past, and some of it is people who have learned that a vendor at closing on day three will agree to things they would refuse on Friday morning. So make the policy, not the judgement: no deal over a set value, no contract, no wholesale terms and no price change is agreed after a certain hour. You will never regret the sentence, and the good ones come back in the morning.
scenarios.move: Rota real breaks with a neighbour — mutual stall cover is the most valuable trade on any circuit. Anti-fatigue mat, a stool, water on a schedule. Set a cut-off hour after which no significant decision is made, and say so cheerfully.
scenarios.say: Can we cover each other? Twenty minutes each, twice a day — I'll do yours first. — That sounds great and I don't do deals after seven — come back at ten tomorrow and we'll sort it properly.
scenarios.truth: Your worst decisions happen at hour twelve, and the people asking know it. Defer anything that matters to the morning.

guides.intro: You hold the event together. This guide holds you together while you do it.

checks.name: Hold Your Limits
checks.desc: Caregiver roles create specific pressure to keep giving past empty. Your limit is the line that keeps you useful.

checks.name: Observe the Pattern
checks.desc: One incident can be chance. Two is a pattern. Three is a system. Name what you are seeing out loud.

checks.name: Log Everything
checks.desc: If it was worth noticing it is worth writing down. Date, time, location, what you saw. Your notes outlast your shift.

checks.name: Debrief After
checks.desc: Hard shifts require processing. You cannot pour from an empty vessel. Decompression is part of the job, not extra.

outline.desc: Attendees who target staff, false volunteer premises, recruitment traps
Compassion fatigue, burnout as control, participant manipulation
Reporting suppression, staff hierarchy abuse, being blamed
Your rights, how to report, bystander activation, exit from a role
Using your access responsibly — the page about your own power

sentences: I can care deeply about this community AND have limits in my role.
Reporting harm is not drama. It is the job.
My wellbeing is not optional. It is what makes me effective.
The predator who knows where the safe space tent is — that is not hypothetical.

scenarios.archetype: The Attendee Who Romantically Targets Staff on Duty
scenarios.who: The attendee who identifies that you are caring, available, and emotionally present in your role — and targets those qualities specifically as a hook for romantic or sexual access. Your caregiving energy is real. It is also visible and exploitable.
scenarios.scene: You have been doing back-to-back shifts at the Harm Reduction tent and you are tired but still fully present with everyone who comes in. He has come by three times today — each time with a small question, each time staying a little longer to talk. The third time he says "I just feel so safe with you, I have never met anyone who listens like you do." He asks if you want to get a drink after your shift. Something about the sequence feels off but you cannot name it. You are also exhausted and the attention feels kind.
tells: Multiple visits to your station with escalating personal rather than service-related conversation
Compliments that specifically target your caregiving qualities — your presence, your listening, your safety
Asking about your schedule, when your shift ends, or what you are doing after
The line between appreciating your support and pursuing you personally starts to blur
scenarios.happening: Staff and volunteers in caregiving roles at festivals — Harm Reduction, Rangers, medics, counselors — are specifically targeted by people who recognize that your role signals emotional availability, safety, and care. Those are genuine qualities. They are also qualities that certain people learn to use as a vector for access. The caregiving role creates a power dynamic you need to be aware of: you are in your element, you are giving, and some people use that specifically to get close.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — "H" CHECK: "Am I maintaining the boundary between my care role and my personal availability?"
scenarios.darkTitle: The On-Duty Boundary — Why It Exists
scenarios.dark: The on-duty boundary — not pursuing personal relationships with people you are supporting in your role — exists to protect both of you. It protects attendees from the power imbalance of a caregiver becoming a romantic pursuit. It protects you from the legal and professional risk of mixing your role with personal relationships. And it protects your ability to be effective — because once personal attraction enters the caregiver role the caregiving quality changes. "I am on duty right now" is a complete sentence and a professional standard, not a personal rejection.
scenarios.move: Maintain the on-duty boundary. Warm, caring, and professionally boundaried are completely compatible.
scenarios.say: "I am on shift right now so I keep things professional during my role — I hope you have a great rest of your festival."
scenarios.truth: Your caregiving presence is a professional skill. Not everyone who benefits from it is entitled to more of you.

scenarios.archetype: Recruited Under False Premises / Scope Creep in Your Role
scenarios.clinical: Manufactured Dependency / Bait and Switch Role
scenarios.who: The volunteer role that is described as one thing and becomes something significantly different once you have committed and are on site. Your transportation, accommodation, and schedule are now controlled by the event and walking away has real costs.
scenarios.scene: The volunteer description said: two four-hour shifts managing crowd flow, accommodation provided, meals covered, full festival access. You arrive to find: you are actually needed for six to eight hours a day, the accommodation is a tent in a staff area with no amenities, meals are inconsistent, and your festival access is conditional on covering gaps in the schedule. The festival organizer is warm and grateful and every time you raise a concern she reminds you how much the event needs you.
tells: The role as described and the role as experienced are materially different
Schedule, accommodation, or compensation change after you have committed and are on site
Your transportation home is tied to completing a schedule that keeps expanding
"We need you" and "after everything we have set up for you" used when you raise concerns
scenarios.happening: Volunteer exploitation at festivals is widespread and normalized under the cover of community contribution and festival love. The bait-and-switch works because by the time you discover the real terms you are already there, your transportation is tied to the event, and walking away feels like abandoning people who need you. That feeling of obligation was manufactured by the structure of the arrangement. Your labor has value. Volunteer exploitation is still exploitation.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — "O" CHECK: "Is what I am being asked to do now what I agreed to do before I arrived?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Volunteer Agreement Basics Before You Commit
scenarios.dark: Before accepting any festival volunteer role, get in writing: exact hours and number of shifts, what accommodation is provided and its actual standard, meal coverage — exactly what and when, whether festival access is during non-shift hours only or all access, what happens if the schedule changes after you arrive, and how you get home if you need to leave before the event ends. A legitimate organization will have this in writing. One that resists writing it down is showing you their intentions for your labor.
scenarios.move: Get your volunteer terms in writing before you commit. They are not asking too much. You are not asking too much.
scenarios.say: "I am excited to help — can you send me the written volunteer terms including schedule, accommodation, and meals before I confirm?"
scenarios.truth: Volunteer labor is still labor. It deserves clear terms and honest expectations.

scenarios.hook: THE PREDATOR KNOWS WHERE THE TENT IS
scenarios.archetype: Bad Actors Who Target Safe Spaces
scenarios.clinical: Position of Trust Exploitation / Predatory Access
scenarios.who: The reality that some people who seek positions of access at festivals — as staff, as volunteers, as practitioners in Harm Reduction or healing spaces — are specifically motivated by the access those positions provide to vulnerable people. This is not hypothetical.
scenarios.scene: He has been volunteering in the Harm Reduction tent for three seasons. Everyone trusts him. He knows the layout, the protocols, the staff schedule, and most importantly he knows who comes in — who is most vulnerable, who is most altered, who is alone. He is warm, knowledgeable, and consistently present. He is also using that position and that knowledge in ways that the team has not yet named even though some of them have felt something was off.
tells: A staff or volunteer member who shows unusual interest in specific attendees beyond the care role
Someone who seeks ongoing contact with attendees they supported after their interaction in the role
A pattern of being present when vulnerable attendees are alone in the space
Discomfort among other staff about a specific person that has not yet been formally named
scenarios.happening: People who want access to vulnerable people at festivals will seek roles that provide that access. Harm Reduction tents, medical stations, safe spaces, and security roles all provide access to people who are at their most vulnerable. This is a known and documented pattern in safeguarding contexts. If you have a gut feeling about a colleague in your space — that feeling is data. Name it to a supervisor. Document it. The culture of "but they have been here for years" is specifically what these patterns rely on.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “L” CHECK: “Have I documented the specific behaviors that are making me uncomfortable about this person in an access role, with dates and specifics?” — the team looking out for each other matters as much as the team looking out for attendees.
scenarios.darkTitle: Safeguarding In Festival Staff Contexts
scenarios.dark: Basic safeguarding practices for festival staff spaces: no staff or volunteer should have unsupervised one-on-one access to impaired or vulnerable attendees. Staff contact with attendees ends when the support need ends — ongoing personal contact is a red flag. Any staff member who is seeking out specific attendees after interactions should be reported to a supervisor. All concerns about staff behavior should be documented in writing with date, time, and specific observed behavior. A genuine organization will take these concerns seriously. One that dismisses them is protecting the wrong person.
scenarios.move: Name what you see to a supervisor. Document it in writing. The culture of silence is what protects predators in these spaces.
scenarios.say: I want to document a concern about a colleague's behavior — can I speak with a supervisor privately?
scenarios.truth: The most important safeguarding the team does is looking out for each other as much as for attendees.

scenarios.archetype: Compassion Fatigue / Giving Until Empty
scenarios.who: The slow drain of giving at high emotional intensity for extended periods without adequate recovery. Compassion fatigue in festival caregiving roles is real, it affects your effectiveness, and the culture often makes it hard to name.
scenarios.scene: You are into your third consecutive shift covering for a no-show. You have supported four difficult situations today — one overdose response, two bad trips, one assault disclosure. You are still showing up fully for every person who comes in. But something has shifted in how you are receiving their experiences — they are landing differently. You feel numb where you used to feel present. You are performing care rather than actually giving it. And you have not told anyone because there is nobody to cover you.
tells: Emotional numbness in situations that would previously have moved you
Performing care rather than actually experiencing presence and connection
Physical symptoms: headache, fatigue, muscle tension that persists between shifts
Intrusive thoughts about difficult situations encountered during your shifts
scenarios.happening: Compassion fatigue is a recognized occupational hazard for anyone in sustained caregiving roles. It is not weakness. It is a physiological response to extended high-intensity emotional labor. Festival caregiving compresses what might be a week of a therapist's caseload into a single shift. The culture that says "just one more shift" and "the event needs you" is the same culture that burns out its best volunteers. Your wellbeing is not optional. It is what makes you effective.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “H” CHECK: “Am I actually present with the people I am supporting — or am I running on empty and performing presence I don’t actually have?” — you cannot give what you do not have. Recovery is the job, not a luxury outside it.
scenarios.darkTitle: Compassion Fatigue Recovery Protocol
scenarios.dark: During an event: take your full breaks even when the space is busy, eat real food even when you are not hungry, drink water before you are thirsty, step outside the tent for ten minutes between difficult interactions. After a difficult shift: do not go directly to the main festival environment — give yourself a 15-30 minute transition in a quiet space. After the event: give yourself 3-5 days before processing difficult experiences, talk to someone outside the festival context about what you carried, and if intrusive thoughts or emotional numbness persist beyond two weeks contact a mental health professional.
scenarios.move: Take your breaks. Eat. Drink water. Step outside between difficult interactions. Your depletion serves nobody.
scenarios.say: I need to step out for ten minutes — can someone cover the tent briefly?
scenarios.truth: You cannot give what you do not have. Your recovery is not a luxury. It is the job.

scenarios.hook: THE PARTICIPANT WHO MANIPULATES YOUR CARE
scenarios.archetype: When Your Support Role Gets Exploited
scenarios.who: The attendee who uses your caregiving role to access resources, information, or proximity that they are not seeking for genuine support needs. Your care is real. Not every person using the space is there for the reasons they present.
scenarios.scene: He has been to the Harm Reduction tent four times this weekend. Each time presenting a slightly different version of a support need. He is articulate, charming, and good at presenting in ways that trigger your care response. You have given him supplies, information, quiet space, and two extended conversations. On his fourth visit you notice: he is gathering information about other attendees who have come through, he is asking about staff schedules, and his affect when he thinks he is not being observed is different from his affect when he is.
tells: Multiple visits with shifting or evolving presentations of their support need
Interest in other attendees who have used the space or in staff schedules
Requests that go beyond the scope of your role — information, introductions, personal contact
Noticeably different presentation when they think they are not being directly observed
scenarios.happening: Most people who access Harm Reduction or support spaces at festivals are there for genuine reasons. Some are not. People who want to gather information about vulnerable attendees, access resources beyond what is appropriate, or build proximity to staff will use the care space to do it because the care space is specifically designed to receive people without judgment. Noticing patterns is not being judgmental. It is being a good safeguarder.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “O” CHECK: “Is the pattern of this person’s engagement consistent with genuine support seeking — or does it track more closely with something else entirely?” — discernment is as much a part of this role as compassion.
scenarios.darkTitle: What To Do When Something Feels Off
scenarios.dark: Trust your gut. If something about a repeated visitor feels off — name it to a colleague quietly during a transition. Document: how many visits, what they requested each time, anything that seemed inconsistent. You do not need certainty to document a concern. Documentation is not accusation — it is creating a record in case the pattern becomes clearer later. If the behavior is actively concerning — someone gathering information about other attendees, someone following up with specific attendees after interactions — that goes to your supervisor immediately and in writing.
scenarios.move: Trust the pattern. Name it to a colleague. Document it. That is what good safeguarding looks like.
scenarios.say: I want to flag something I have noticed about a repeated visitor — can we talk privately for a minute?
scenarios.truth: Your care role requires discernment as much as compassion. Both are part of doing it well.

scenarios.archetype: Being Kept Too Depleted to See Clearly
scenarios.who: The event structure or leadership that keeps staff and volunteers so busy, so sleep deprived, and so short on basic resources that the capacity to notice problems, raise concerns, or exercise independent judgment is systematically eliminated.
scenarios.scene: By Saturday afternoon you have been on since 6am, you have not had a proper meal, the staff communication channel is so full of urgent requests that you have stopped reading it, and the supervisor you would report concerns to is also clearly running on empty. Something happened in the camping area last night that three people have mentioned in passing but nobody has formally reported. You know you should do something about it. You genuinely do not have the capacity to figure out what.
tells: Staffing is so thin that there is never a moment to observe, think, or raise concerns
Basic needs — food, sleep, breaks — are systematically not being met for staff and volunteers
Reporting channels are so overwhelmed that nothing non-urgent gets processed
Leadership is also depleted — there is no functional escalation path for concerns
scenarios.happening: Systematic depletion of staff and volunteers is sometimes accidental and sometimes deliberate. When everyone is too exhausted to notice patterns or raise concerns — problems that would otherwise be caught and addressed do not get caught and addressed. If you are in an event structure where your basic needs are not being met and there is no functional path for raising concerns — that is information about the organization, not just about the event. Name it. Document it. And protect yourself accordingly.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “H” CHECK: “Do I have the basic resources I need to do this role safely — food, sleep, breaks, a way to say when I’ve hit my limit?” — a depleted volunteer isn’t a martyr, they’re a liability to everyone they’re trying to protect.
scenarios.darkTitle: When The Reporting Structure Is Broken
scenarios.dark: If your direct supervisor is unavailable, overwhelmed, or is the source of the problem: escalate to the next level up. If there is no functional next level: document your concern in writing and send it to the organization in writing — email creates a timestamp. If the issue involves immediate safety: contact festival medical or emergency services directly, bypassing the organizational structure. After the event: formal written feedback to the organization and to any professional bodies or associations that oversee the event. Your concern being hard to hear does not make it wrong.
scenarios.move: Meet your own basic needs first. You cannot report-effectively from a place of complete depletion.
scenarios.say: "I need to take my break before I can cover anything else — where can I get food?"
scenarios.truth: A depleted volunteer is not a martyr. A depleted volunteer is a liability for everyone including the people they are trying to protect.

scenarios.hook: DON'T RUIN THE VIBE OF THE EVENT
scenarios.archetype: Reporting Suppression / Don't Be the Problem
scenarios.who: The direct or indirect pressure on staff and volunteers not to formally report incidents because it would create problems for the event, upset attendees, attract unwanted attention, or disrupt the experience. Your report becomes the problem rather than the incident.
scenarios.scene: You witnessed something between two attendees in the camping area that you are fairly sure was not consensual. You reported it to your supervisor. She took it seriously in the moment. An hour later the event director came to you: "I know you reported something and I appreciate that you care, but we need to think about how we handle this — a formal report right now would be really complicated for the event. Can we just make sure the people involved are okay and handle this internally?" You feel the pressure of a hundred things at once.
tells: Informal resolution is proposed for situations that require formal reporting
"The event" or "the community" invoked as reasons not to formally document an incident
You are asked to handle it yourself rather than escalating through proper channels
Pressure to wait, consider, or discuss rather than document and report immediately
scenarios.happening: Reporting suppression protects the organization and the event at the expense of the people harmed. When incidents are handled informally at the request of event leadership — no report, no documentation, no formal process — the people harmed lose their ability to seek redress, the pattern goes untracked, and the organization avoids accountability. Your role is to report. The decision about how to handle the report is not yours alone. Make the report and let the process work.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “L” CHECK: “Have I documented this incident in writing regardless of what the organization is asking me to prioritize instead?” — reporting harm is the job. Anyone telling you otherwise is protecting the wrong thing.
scenarios.darkTitle: What To Do When Told Not To Report
scenarios.dark: If you are asked not to formally report an incident: (1) Document the incident yourself in writing regardless — date, time, location, what you witnessed, what you reported, and what response you received including the instruction not to formally report. (2) If the incident involves assault, harassment, or a crime — you may have independent legal obligations to report depending on your role and jurisdiction. (3) If the organization is suppressing reports: that is reportable to relevant authorities and professional bodies after the event. (4) RAINN (rainn.org) has guidance for bystanders and witnesses as well as victims.
scenarios.move: Make your report. Document everything including the response. The organization's comfort is not your responsibility.
scenarios.say: I hear you and I understand the concern — I am still going to document this formally. I will send it to you in writing.
scenarios.truth: Reporting harm is not drama. It is the job. Anyone who tells you otherwise is protecting the wrong thing.

scenarios.archetype: When the Power Is Above You and Points at You
scenarios.who: The supervisor, event director, or senior staff member who uses their position in the staff hierarchy to create sexual pressure on those below them. The power differential makes saying no feel like a professional risk.
scenarios.scene: Your supervisor has been warm and supportive all weekend. He has also made several comments that felt personal rather than professional. Saturday night he asks if you want to come back to the staff area after your shift to "debrief." Something about the way he says it makes the invitation feel less professional than the word suggests. You also know he controls your schedule, your access, and your reference if you volunteer here again next year. Saying no feels complicated in a way it should not.
tells: Comments from a supervisor that feel personal, sexual, or designed to gauge your interest
Invitations that are framed as professional but feel personally motivated
The awareness that this person controls something you need — your schedule, your reference, your access
A feeling that saying no directly would create professional consequences
scenarios.happening: Sexual pressure within staff hierarchies is a specific form of workplace sexual harassment regardless of the festival context. The power differential is real: supervisors control schedules, references, access, and the experience of working in that role. That power makes genuine consent complicated and makes declining feel costly. You do not owe a supervisor access to you personally in exchange for a good volunteer experience. The harassment is the problem — not your response to it.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — "L" CHECK: "Have I documented this interaction so I have a record if I choose to report it?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Reporting Staff Hierarchy Sexual Pressure
scenarios.dark: Options for reporting: (1) To a supervisor above the person who harassed you — skip the chain if the harasser is your direct supervisor. (2) To the event's designated safeguarding lead if one exists. (3) In writing directly to the event director or organization — this creates a timestamp. (4) After the event: to any professional bodies, associations, or regulatory bodies that oversee the event or the organization. (5) RAINN (1-800-656-4673) supports people who have experienced harassment in workplace contexts including volunteer roles. You do not have to have experienced assault for your experience to be worth reporting.
scenarios.move: Document it. Report it through the highest available channel. Your experience in this role should not cost you this.
scenarios.say: "I am going to keep things professional — I need to head back to my station."
scenarios.truth: Your access to a good volunteer experience should not require tolerating sexual pressure from anyone above you.

scenarios.archetype: Being Blamed When Something Goes Wrong on Your Watch
scenarios.who: The organizational dynamic where front-line staff and volunteers are held responsible for systemic failures — inadequate staffing, poor training, unclear protocols — that were set in motion by leadership decisions long before your shift began.
scenarios.scene: An incident happened during your shift. You responded as best you could with the training and resources you had. Afterward, the event director calls you in and the tone is very different from the supportive one you experienced all weekend. Suddenly the focus is on what you did or did not do. The staffing shortage that left you covering an area alone, the training gaps, the protocol that was unclear — none of that is part of the conversation. You are.
tells: Post-incident conversation focuses exclusively on your actions rather than systemic conditions
Systemic failures — understaffing, training gaps, resource shortfalls — are not part of the review
You are asked to sign statements or acknowledgments that implicitly accept responsibility
The framing shifts from "what happened" to "what did you do" in ways that feel like assignment of blame
scenarios.happening: Front-line workers are the easiest people to blame for systemic failures because they were physically present when things went wrong. Organizations that do not want to examine their own structural failures direct accountability downward onto the people least able to defend themselves. You are not required to accept blame for conditions you did not create. Document your version of events in writing immediately after any incident. Do not sign anything you do not fully understand and agree with.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “L” CHECK: “Have I documented my version of events in writing immediately — before organizational framing has a chance to reshape it?” — you’re responsible for your actions, not for the systemic conditions you were placed in.
scenarios.darkTitle: Protecting Yourself After An Incident
scenarios.dark: Immediately after any significant incident: (1) Write your own account in as much detail as possible — what you observed, what you did, what resources and training you had, what the conditions were. Include timestamps. (2) Do not sign any organizational documentation before you have had time to read it carefully and compare it to your own account. (3) If asked to participate in a formal review: you have the right to have someone present with you. (4) If you feel you are being scapegoated for systemic failures: contact a lawyer or the National Lawyers Guild before signing anything.
scenarios.move: Write your own account immediately. Do not sign anything before reading it carefully against your own record.
scenarios.say: I want to cooperate fully with any review — I am also going to document my own account of what happened. Can I have until tomorrow to do that?
scenarios.truth: You are responsible for your actions. You are not responsible for the systemic conditions you were placed in.

scenarios.archetype: What You Do In The Moment You See Something
scenarios.who: As staff or a volunteer you have visibility, authority, and access that most attendees do not. You also have the specific responsibility to use it. This page is about what that looks like in practice — not in theory.
scenarios.scene: You are doing a walk-through of the camping area mid-afternoon and you see a woman sitting with a man who seems agitated. Her body language is closed and she is looking at the ground. You are in your staff vest. You have radio access. You have the authority to intervene in ways that most attendees do not. You also have the very human impulse to not want to make it worse, not want to assume wrong, not want to create a scene. The impulse is real. So is your responsibility.
tells: Your staff vest and radio change the social dynamics of an intervention — use that
You can ask directly: "Is everything okay here?" — your role gives you standing to ask
You can radio for support before approaching — you do not have to handle it alone
Documentation after any intervention is part of the job, not optional
scenarios.happening: Staff and volunteers have a fundamentally different role in bystander intervention than attendees — you have authority, visibility, backup, and a professional obligation to act that most attendees do not. The threshold for intervention is lower for you. The tools available are better. The accountability for not acting is higher. See something, do something — and document what you did and why.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “O” CHECK: “What am I observing right now, and what does my role require me to do with that observation, in this exact moment?” — your vest and your radio are the tools for this moment. Use them.
scenarios.darkTitle: Staff Bystander Toolkit
scenarios.dark: What staff have that attendees do not: (1) Radio — you can call for backup before approaching. Use it. (2) Authority — "Is everything okay here?" from someone in a staff vest lands differently than the same question from an attendee. (3) Known safe spaces — you know where Harm Reduction and medical are. You can offer to walk someone there. (4) Incident reporting — everything you witness and act on gets documented. That documentation protects people, creates patterns, and holds the organization accountable. (5) Colleagues — you are not alone. Use your team.
scenarios.move: Use your radio, your authority, your access, and your colleagues. You have more tools than anyone else here.
scenarios.say: "Hey — I am staff. Is everything okay here?" Then radio for support if needed.
scenarios.truth: Your vest and your radio are the tools for this moment. Use them.

scenarios.archetype: What You Can Refuse and What You Are Owed
scenarios.who: Volunteers have rights. Not the same rights as employees in every jurisdiction but real rights nonetheless — the right to safe working conditions, the right to refuse unsafe tasks, the right to leave a role that is causing harm, and the right to documentation of what you were promised.
scenarios.scene: You are being asked to cover a solo overnight shift in a remote area of the festival with no radio contact and no clear protocol for what to do if something happens. Your gut says this is not safe. Your supervisor says everyone does it and there is nobody else. You want to be helpful. You also want to go home in one piece. The question is whether you have the right to say no — and the answer is yes.
tells: Being asked to work alone in unsafe conditions without adequate communication or support
Being asked to cover tasks that are outside your training, role description, or competency
Being pressured to continue working when you have raised a safety concern about your conditions
Basic needs — food, water, breaks, sleep — being systematically denied for operational reasons
scenarios.happening: Festival volunteer culture often blurs the line between genuine community contribution and labor exploitation. The "we are all in this together" framing can make it feel selfish or disloyal to refuse unsafe tasks or insist on basic working conditions. It is not. Volunteers who are placed in unsafe conditions and something goes wrong face real consequences — personal harm, trauma, and sometimes legal exposure. You have the right to refuse conditions that put you at unreasonable risk.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “H” CHECK: “Am I being asked to do something that my training, my safety, or my basic needs require me to say no to?” — saying no to an unsafe task isn’t letting the team down. It’s doing the job correctly.
scenarios.darkTitle: Volunteer Rights In Practice
scenarios.dark: In practice, volunteer rights include: the right to know what your role involves before you commit, the right to refuse tasks outside your role description or competency without losing your position, the right to safe working conditions including adequate communication, support, and backup, the right to leave a role that is actively harmful to you without legal consequence in most jurisdictions, and the right to documentation of what was agreed. After the event: formal feedback to the organization and to any bodies that oversee the event. Your experience matters and your feedback improves conditions for future volunteers.
scenarios.move: Know your rights before you need them. Refusing unsafe conditions is not abandonment — it is professional judgment.
scenarios.say: "I am not comfortable covering that alone without radio contact — what backup can you provide or what is the alternative?"
scenarios.truth: Saying no to an unsafe task is not letting the team down. It is doing the job correctly.

scenarios.hook: THE DEBRIEF IS PART OF THE JOB
scenarios.archetype: Processing After a Hard Shift or Difficult Incident
scenarios.who: Festival caregiving roles expose you to a concentration of difficult human experiences in a very short time. Decompressing from that exposure is not optional — it is what prevents the experiences you carry home from becoming experiences that stay with you.
scenarios.scene: You supported an overdose response, two assault disclosures, and a mental health crisis in the same shift. All of them resolved as well as they could. You did your job well. It is now Sunday evening and the festival is winding down and you are sitting in your car in the parking area before driving home and you realize you have not actually stopped moving since Thursday. You are not sure what you feel. You are not sure you feel anything. That numbness is the thing to pay attention to.
tells: Emotional numbness or flatness after a shift involving difficult incidents
Intrusive mental replaying of difficult situations you witnessed or supported
Difficulty transitioning out of the staff role back into your regular self
Physical symptoms — tension, headache, fatigue — that persist well after your shift ends
scenarios.happening: Secondary traumatic stress — also called vicarious trauma — is a recognized occupational hazard for people in caregiving and emergency response roles. It develops from repeated exposure to other people's traumatic experiences. Festival caregiving compresses this exposure dramatically. Debrief is the professional standard for managing it — named processing of what you experienced, with colleagues or a professional, before it gets metabolized as unprocessed trauma.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “D” CHECK: “Have I actually stopped and processed what I experienced today — or am I just pushing through to the next shift?” — what you process becomes wisdom. What you don’t becomes weight.
scenarios.darkTitle: What An Effective Debrief Looks Like
scenarios.dark: At minimum after any difficult shift: 15-30 minutes of quiet transition before driving or going to the main festival. Name — out loud to at least one colleague — the most difficult thing you experienced this shift. After the event: talk to at least one person outside the festival context about what you carried. If multiple difficult incidents happened: consider a session with a therapist who works with first responders or emergency services. Resources specifically for caregivers: Zendo Project (zendoproject.org) trains staff and can refer to ongoing support. Psychology Today (psychologytoday.com) has therapist finders by specialty.
scenarios.move: Name what you experienced out loud to at least one colleague before leaving. That is the minimum.
scenarios.say: Before we all head out — can we take ten minutes just to name what today was like? I need to say some of it out loud.
scenarios.truth: The experiences you process become wisdom. The ones you do not process become weight. Debrief is how you choose which is which.

scenarios.hook: YOUR ACCESS IS NOT YOUR PERMISSION
scenarios.archetype: Using Your Role Responsibly
scenarios.who: Staff and volunteer roles at festivals come with access — to sensitive information, to vulnerable people, to spaces and resources that most attendees do not have. This page is about using that access in ways that are genuinely in service of the people you are there to protect.
scenarios.scene: You are a Ranger and someone came to you in genuine distress about a situation in their camp. You helped them, you supported them, you were exactly what the role is supposed to be. You also now know specific private information about them — who they were with, what happened, where their camp is, what their vulnerable moment looked like. The question is not whether that information is real. The question is what you do with it after they walk away from your care.
tells: Information shared with you in a care context belongs to the person who shared it — not to you
Access to the festival layout, staff areas, and resources is for the role — not for personal use
Ongoing contact with people you supported in your role is a boundary issue in most contexts
The power of your role continues to exist even when you are off duty at the same event
scenarios.happening: The access that comes with festival staff and volunteer roles creates real power over people who are in vulnerable moments. That power is a tool for service — it is not a benefit of the role. Information shared in a care context is confidential. Access to spaces and resources is role-specific. Ongoing personal contact with people you supported in your role raises the same issues as any therapist-client boundary — the power imbalance does not disappear when the immediate support need does.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “H” CHECK: “Am I using my access in service of the people I am there to protect — or for my own convenience, curiosity, or gain?” — the access isn’t yours, it belongs to the role. Use it accordingly.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Ethics Of Your Access
scenarios.dark: Ethical use of staff access: information shared with you in a care context stays in the care context — it does not get shared with other staff except on a need-to-know basis and not at all outside the organizational context. Physical access to secure or restricted areas is for role purposes only. Contact with people you supported ends when the support need ends — seeking ongoing personal contact is a boundary violation regardless of how the connection felt. If you are unsure whether something is within bounds: ask your supervisor before doing it, not after.
scenarios.move: Use your access for the people you are there to serve. Full stop.
scenarios.say: "I want to check before I do this — is this within the scope of my role?"
scenarios.truth: The access is not yours. It belongs to the role. Use it accordingly.

scenarios.archetype: What Healthy Staff Culture Actually Looks Like
scenarios.who: The culture of a festival's staff team is one of the most important determinants of how safe the event actually is for everyone. This page is about what healthy staff culture looks like — and how to build it from wherever you are in the organizational structure.
scenarios.scene: The briefing before gates open sets the tone. The lead says: "Our job this weekend is to hold the space so everyone can have the experience they came for. That means we take every concern seriously, we report what we see, we take care of each other so we can take care of everyone else, and we never dismiss a gut feeling. If something feels off — name it to your team. There are no bad reports. There are only missed patterns." That briefing changes how the whole weekend goes.
tells: Leadership explicitly states that all concerns will be taken seriously — not managed down
Staff are encouraged to name gut feelings and concerns without requiring certainty
Debrief and staff wellbeing are treated as operational priorities not afterthoughts
Accountability runs in all directions — leadership is held to the same standards as front-line staff
scenarios.happening: Healthy staff culture is built from the first briefing and maintained through how leadership responds to the first concern that is raised. Organizations where leadership takes concerns seriously, supports staff wellbeing, and holds itself to the same standards it holds front-line workers create genuinely safer events. Organizations that suppress concerns, burn out volunteers, and deflect accountability downward create events where harm is more likely and less likely to be addressed.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “O” CHECK: “Does the culture of this staff team make it easy or hard to raise concerns?” — that tells you a great deal about how safe this event actually is.
scenarios.darkTitle: How To Build Healthy Staff Culture From Your Position
scenarios.dark: Regardless of where you sit in the organization: (1) Model taking gut feelings seriously by naming yours out loud. "Something about that felt off to me — I am going to document it." (2) Celebrate colleagues who raise concerns rather than treating them as troublemakers. (3) Debrief after difficult shifts even when leadership does not require it. (4) Give honest post-event feedback to the organization about what worked and what did not. (5) If you are in leadership: the first time a concern is dismissed sets the culture for every concern that follows. Take them all seriously.
scenarios.move: Build the culture you want to work in. It starts with how you respond to the first concern you hear.
scenarios.say: I want to hear about that — tell me what you saw and let us figure out together what to do with it.
scenarios.truth: The safest events are the ones with staff teams who look out for each other as fiercely as they look out for attendees.

scenarios.hook: YOU'RE OFF SHIFT BUT YOU'RE STILL STAFF
scenarios.archetype: The Dual Role / Volunteer By Day, Attendee By Night
scenarios.who: Everyone on a volunteer-for-a-ticket arrangement, which is most of the workforce at most festivals — you are staff for eight hours and a punter for sixteen, wearing the same wristband and known to the same people.
scenarios.scene: You finished at six. At eleven, in the crowd, somebody recognizes you from the welfare tent and starts telling you about their night, and then somebody else asks you where the medical tent is, and then an actual incident happens four feet away and everyone nearby turns to look at you, and you have had three drinks.
tells: People bring you work problems when you are off shift
You are identifiable as staff even out of hi-vis
You have intervened in something while off duty and impaired
Your camp is staff camping, so there is no off-site to go to
Management treats you as available for the whole event
You cannot say where the shift ended and the weekend started
scenarios.happening: The volunteer-for-a-ticket model produces a genuinely ambiguous role and almost no organizations address it. Two specific risks follow. First, liability: intervening while off duty and impaired is not covered by any briefing or insurance, and it is where volunteers get hurt or get someone else hurt. Second, depletion: a person who is never fully off shift does not recover, and the compassion-fatigue pages elsewhere in this guide describe what that turns into by day three. Neither is your fault; both are yours to manage, because the event almost certainly has not.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “H” CHECK: “Am I on duty right now — and does everyone around me know the answer?” If it is ambiguous to you, it is ambiguous to them.
scenarios.darkTitle: Impaired And Intervening Is The Worst Combination
scenarios.dark: Picture the incident report. A volunteer, off shift, three drinks in, restrained somebody or made a medical call or walked an attendee somewhere — and it went wrong. There is no briefing that covers it, no insurance that applies, and the organization's position afterwards will be that you were not working. This is also the exact scenario where genuinely well-meaning volunteers cause harm, because the instinct to help does not switch off with the shift and the judgement does switch off with the drinks. Make it visible instead: wristband off, lanyard away, and one sentence that hands it to whoever is actually on duty.
scenarios.move: Make off-duty physically visible — lanyard off, hi-vis away, and say it out loud when asked. Hand every off-shift request to the on-duty team by radio or in person rather than handling it. Leave staff camping for part of each day if you can, because being permanently among colleagues is what makes the role never end.
scenarios.say: I'm off shift and I've had a drink, so I'm not the right person — but I'll walk you to the welfare tent right now and hand you to whoever's on.
scenarios.truth: A wristband that never comes off is a shift that never ends. Being off duty only counts if the people around you can tell.

scenarios.hook: COME BACK TO OURS AFTER, EVERYONE DOES
scenarios.archetype: The After-Shift Party And The Person Who Signs Your Hours
scenarios.who: A supervisor, a team lead, or a long-standing crew member with informal authority — who is not asking you for anything explicit, and who also decides your shifts, your reference, and whether you are asked back.
scenarios.scene: The crew party is a real thing and it is where the bonding happens and where next season's roles get informally decided, and the person suggesting you come is the person who writes your hours. Going means drinking with somebody who has power over you, in their camp, at three in the morning. Not going means being the one who does not join in, and both of you know which one is easier.
tells: Social attendance is where progression and rota decisions actually happen
The invitation comes from someone in your reporting line
Declining is noticed and mentioned later
Alcohol, staff camping, and no HR of any kind
Other volunteers have had a bad experience nobody wrote down
There is no reporting route that does not run through this person
scenarios.happening: Festival crews have workplace power structures and almost none of the workplace protections — no HR, no written complaints route, no contracts for volunteers, and a supervisor who controls access to next season. The after-shift party is where that power operates informally, and the risk is not the party itself, which is often genuinely one of the best parts of the job. It is that declining has a cost and attending has a different one, and that there is nobody to report to if something happens, because the person you would report is the person you would report to.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “O” CHECK: “Who could I report this person to, by name?” Ask on day one. If there is no second name, the hierarchy has no floor.
scenarios.darkTitle: Find The Second Name Before You Need It
scenarios.dark: The structural fix is one question asked in your first hour, when it is completely neutral: who handles a concern about a supervisor. Ask it of the volunteer coordinator as a routine induction question and write the answer down. Almost every event has a safeguarding or welfare lead outside the line hierarchy, and almost nobody tells volunteers who they are — which means the information exists and simply is not distributed. Asking on Thursday costs nothing and is forgettable. Asking on Sunday, after something, is an accusation before you have even described it.
scenarios.move: Get the out-of-line reporting name on day one. Go to the party if you want to and take a crew mate, or decline warmly and without a reason and let the relationship prove itself. Keep your own notes of shifts and any incident, dated, on your own phone.
scenarios.say: Who handles it if someone's got a concern about a supervisor — is there someone outside the team? Just like to know where things go. — I'm knackered, I'll catch you tomorrow — have a good one.
scenarios.truth: Ask who the complaint goes to while nothing has happened. On Thursday it is admin; on Sunday it is an accusation.

scenarios.hook: WHEN YOU HAVE TO PUT HANDS ON SOMEONE
scenarios.archetype: Physical Intervention Without The Training For It
scenarios.who: Every volunteer who has ever had to stop somebody walking into a road, hold a stretcher, move somebody who is unconscious, or get between two people who are fighting — with a two-hour briefing and no qualification whatsoever.
scenarios.scene: He is unconscious and needs moving out of the crowd, or he is trying to climb something, or two people are going at it and you are the nearest person in hi-vis and everybody has turned to look at you. You have never been trained in any of this and you are about to do it anyway because nobody else is going to.
tells: No restraint or manual-handling training, and no licence
You are the nearest hi-vis and that has become an instruction
Someone unconscious being moved by well-meaning bystanders
Face-down or compressed positioning, which is the lethal one
No radio call made before hands went on
Nobody has told you what you are and are not permitted to do
scenarios.happening: Untrained physical intervention is the highest-consequence thing an unqualified volunteer can do, and it happens constantly because the hi-vis creates an expectation the training never met. Two specifics are worth knowing above everything else. Positional asphyxia — holding or leaving someone face-down or folded, especially if they are intoxicated, large, or struggling — kills people, and it is the single most documented cause of restraint-related death. And an unconscious person who is breathing goes into the recovery position on their side, not face-up and not face-down, because the airway is the whole problem.
scenarios.check: H.O.L.D. — “H” CHECK: “Am I trained for what I am about to do?” If not, the intervention is a radio call and a presence, not a hold.
scenarios.darkTitle: Face Down Is The One That Kills
scenarios.dark: If you remember one line from this guide, make it this. Never hold or leave anybody face-down, and never fold somebody forward while restraining them, and never sit or kneel on a back or a chest. Positional asphyxia gives almost no warning: the person stops struggling, and everyone present reads that as calming down when it is the opposite. If someone is unconscious and breathing, they go on their side. If they are struggling, you get a trained responder and you keep space rather than keeping hold. Your job in every one of these is to call it in fast, keep the area clear, and stay — presence and a radio have saved far more people at festivals than grip ever has.
scenarios.move: Radio first, always, before hands. Use presence and space rather than contact. If someone is unconscious and breathing, recovery position and stay with them. Never face-down, never weight on a torso. Ask your supervisor on day one exactly what you are authorized to do physically, and get the answer.
scenarios.say: Control, I need a medic and security at the north bar now, one male unconscious but breathing, I'm with him. — [to bystanders] Give us room please, don't move him, I've got help coming.
scenarios.truth: A radio and your presence are the intervention. Hands are the part you were never trained for and the part that kills people.

guides.intro: You are on site two weeks before anyone else and you leave after the lights go. This guide is for the part of the festival nobody photographs.

checks.name: Barter Is Still A Contract
checks.desc: Wristband, food, a bunk, a credit — if you are working for it, it has terms. Get them in writing before the first shift.

checks.name: Unsafe Is A Full Stop
checks.desc: You are allowed to refuse a task. Fatigue, missing PPE, bad rigging, no banksman. The site's schedule is not your liability.

checks.name: Isolation Is The Risk Multiplier
checks.desc: Half-empty site, night shift, no medical yet, no phone signal. Everything in this book gets more dangerous when nobody is around.

checks.name: Log It While It Is Fresh
checks.desc: Hours, incidents, changes to the deal, who said what. Build runs on memory and goodwill, and both get rewritten at settle-up.

checks.name: Danger Of The Ninety-Sixth Hour
checks.desc: Most build injuries happen late in a long stretch to experienced people. Tiredness is the hazard, not inexperience.

outline.desc: Recruitment by passion, the deal that changes, crew as family
Fatigue, unsafe tasks, night-shift isolation, PPE that never arrives
Wages withheld, accommodation as leverage, blacklisting
The written deal, the hours log, the refusal script, the buddy rule
Real crew solidarity versus a family that only takes

sentences: If I am working for it, it has terms, and the terms are written down.
I can refuse an unsafe task and keep my place. If I cannot, that is the whole problem.
Nobody works at height or with plant alone on a dark site.
I log my hours the day I work them, not at settle-up.
Crew who only call it family when they are asking are not family.

scenarios.hook: WE'RE NOT A COMPANY, WE'RE A FAMILY
scenarios.archetype: The Crew That Pays In Belonging
scenarios.who: Warm, genuinely bonded, and absolutely running on unpaid hours. Recruits on love of the work. Uses family language exactly where a normal employer would use a contract, and only ever in the direction of asking.
scenarios.scene: The build crew is the best group of people you have ever worked with and the first four days are the happiest you have been in a year. On day five you realize nobody has mentioned money since the first conversation, the sixteen-hour days have become the schedule rather than the exception, and when you ask about the rate the lead says, kindly, that this is not really that kind of thing, that everybody here is doing it for the same reason, and that the family looks after each other.
tells: Family language appears exactly where terms should be
No written agreement, and asking for one reads as a trust problem
Hours expand without the deal changing
Asking about money is treated as a character flaw rather than a question
Looking after each other is invoked when asking, never when paying
Everyone senior has a real job title in the outside world
scenarios.happening: Familial framing is the most efficient way to extract labor, because it converts a commercial question into a loyalty question — and once that conversion has happened, asking about your rate makes you the person who does not love the thing, in front of people whose respect you now depend on. Build crews are especially exposed because the work is genuinely joyful, the bonds are genuinely real, and the culture genuinely is one of mutual aid. All of that is true and none of it is a contract. The test is directional: notice whether family gets invoked when something is being asked of you, or also when something is owed to you.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “B” CHECK: “If I could not work another shift from tomorrow, what would I actually be owed — in writing?” If the answer is a feeling, you do not have a deal.
scenarios.darkTitle: Family Is Load-Bearing In One Direction
scenarios.dark: Watch what happens at the edges, because that is where the frame reveals itself. Somebody gets injured on a family crew and discovers there is no insurance, no sick pay, and no employer, because they were never an employee — they were family, and family has no legal standing. Somebody raises a concern about a senior member and discovers the family closes, because a family protects its own and you are the newest one. That is the same mechanism the cult chapter of this scene's literature describes, arriving in work boots. It does not mean the warmth is fake. It means warmth is not a substitute for terms, and the crews that have both are the ones worth staying with.
scenarios.move: Get the deal in a message before the first shift — hours, what you get, what happens if you are injured, who pays for the ferry home. A text is a written agreement. Then keep working and enjoy the crew, which is genuinely one of the best things in this scene.
scenarios.say: Love it here, in for the full build. Can you drop me a quick message with the hours and what the deal covers — mostly so I know where I stand if I get hurt.
scenarios.truth: A real family will write it down without being wounded about it. Only the extractive version treats the question as an insult.

scenarios.archetype: Fatigue As The Actual Hazard
scenarios.who: Nobody. This one is the schedule. Day nine of a build, fourth consecutive sixteen-hour day, everybody running on catering coffee and the fact that the gates open Thursday whatever happens.
scenarios.scene: You have been awake for nineteen hours and you are about to make a cut you have made a thousand times. The thing is you have made it a thousand times, which is why you are doing it now instead of stopping, and which is also why your hands are doing it while your attention is somewhere else. Everyone around you is in the same state and nobody is going to be the one who says the crew should stand down, because the schedule is the schedule.
tells: Consecutive long shifts with no rostered rest
Experienced people making basic errors and laughing about it
Microsleeps, dropped tools, losing the thread mid-sentence
Safety-critical work scheduled at the end of shifts rather than the start
Nobody empowered to stop the job without it being a confrontation
The build is behind and that has quietly become everyone's justification
scenarios.happening: Sustained sleep restriction degrades reaction time, judgment, and risk assessment measurably, and past roughly seventeen to nineteen hours awake the impairment is comparable to being over the legal driving limit — with the extra problem that self-assessment degrades alongside performance, so the more impaired you are the more confident you feel. Occupational injury data across construction and events points the same way: serious incidents cluster late in long stretches, among experienced workers, on routine tasks. The hazard is not the dangerous job you were nervous about. It is the easy one you have done a thousand times, at hour nineteen.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “D” CHECK: “How long have I been awake, and is this task one I would let a drunk person do?” If you would not, the honest answer is that the site currently has one.
scenarios.darkTitle: Competence Is Why It Gets You
scenarios.dark: The cruel part is that skill is the risk factor here, not the protection. Novices are slow and frightened, which keeps their attention on the task. Experienced hands run the cut on autopilot, which is exactly the faculty fatigue takes first, and it is why the amputations and the falls in this industry belong overwhelmingly to people who had done that job for years. There is a second layer specific to build: the incident happens on a site with no medical yet, no public, thin signal, and everyone else also exhausted. The margin you are relying on is not there. Stopping is not weakness on a build crew — it is the only intervention with any evidence behind it.
scenarios.move: Name it as a crew rather than as an individual, because the social cost is what keeps it running: agree a hard stop hour for safety-critical work, and agree that anyone can call fatigue on anyone without argument. Schedule the height work, the plant, and the blades for the start of a shift.
scenarios.say: I'm nineteen hours in — I'm not cutting tonight, I'll do it first thing and it'll be better work. Anyone else past it should say now, nobody's keeping score.
scenarios.truth: The most experienced person on site is the one most likely to be hurt at hour ninety-six. That is not an insult. It is the data.

scenarios.hook: IT'S JUST YOU OUT THERE TONIGHT
scenarios.archetype: The Half-Built Site / Isolation Before The Festival Exists
scenarios.who: The site itself, during load-in. Dark, enormous, mostly empty, with the medical tent not up yet, security not started, no public, patchy signal, and people you have never met driving plant around in the dark.
scenarios.scene: You are finishing a run of cable at the far end of a field at eleven at night. There is one work light. The nearest other human is about four hundred metres away and does not know exactly where you are. Your phone has one bar. Every single protection this festival will have by Friday — rangers, medical, welfare, crowds of witnesses — does not exist yet, and will not for six days.
tells: Lone working at night with nobody holding your location
Medical, welfare, and security not yet operational on site
Plant moving in the dark without a banksman
No radio, or a radio on a channel nobody is monitoring
Accommodation shared with people who have not been vetted at all
No headcount — nobody would notice by morning
scenarios.happening: Everything else in this book assumes a populated festival: witnesses, a medical tent you can walk to, rangers, other people's phones. Build phase has none of that, and it is also when the workforce is smallest, least known to each other, and most exhausted. Two separate risks stack in that gap — the industrial one, where an ordinary injury becomes serious because nobody finds you for two hours, and the interpersonal one, where every pattern in this book operates without any of the infrastructure that usually constrains it. Crew accommodation in particular is often a field of strangers with no vetting and no lock, which is not a comment on crew, it is a description of the conditions.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “I” CHECK: “Does one named person know where I am and when I am due back?” Not the crew. A person, with a time.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Six Days Before Anyone Is Watching
scenarios.dark: Say the plain version: the safest time to harm someone at a festival is before it is a festival. No public, no cameras, no rangers, no welfare tent, a small pool of people who all outrank you in tenure, and a culture that will close ranks around the build because the build is behind. The people this lands on hardest are new crew, and especially young or lone women and anyone who needed this gig — because raising anything means losing the accommodation you are currently sleeping in, on a site you cannot leave without a lift. That is the structural problem, and it is why the buddy rule is not fussiness. Two people, a stated return time, and one person off-site who expects to hear from you.
scenarios.move: Buddy anything at height, with plant, with blades, or after dark — no exceptions, arranged as a crew norm rather than a personal request. Put a location and a return time to one named person every night. Know where the first-aider is, and where the vehicle keys live.
scenarios.say: Buddy rule after dark, I'm not doing the far field on my own. — Back by half eleven, if I'm not, come find me, I'm at the north cable run.
scenarios.truth: The festival's safety net goes up on Wednesday. You have been on site since the Thursday before. Build your own until then.

scenarios.archetype: The Deal That Shrinks At The End / Payment As Leverage
scenarios.who: The production manager with a spreadsheet and a cash-flow problem. Pleasant all build. Becomes hard to find on the Monday, and when found, remembers the arrangement differently and has the advantage of being the one who writes it down.
scenarios.scene: The agreement was a day rate and expenses. It is Monday, the site is half struck, and the number he says now is lower — because the days you did were partly travel, because the accommodation counts against it, because the original figure was always a best case. You have no contract. You have a fortnight of sixteen-hour days, a van you paid the diesel for, and no leverage at all, because the work is already done.
tells: Terms agreed verbally and never confirmed in writing
Payment scheduled entirely after the work is complete
Deductions appearing at settle-up that were never mentioned
Your accommodation or transport home is in their gift
Other crew have had the same conversation and did not compare notes
The implication that complaining costs you next season
scenarios.happening: All the leverage in a build arrangement sits at the end, which is why unscrupulous production will schedule payment there and why the honest ones pay staged. Once your labor is spent it cannot be withdrawn, and the threat that does the real work is rarely stated: next year's booking. In a scene where work comes by reputation and relationship, being known as difficult about money is a genuine cost, and everybody doing this knows you have done that arithmetic. It is the same structure as the vendor non-payment page in M.A.R.K.E.T., with one addition — they may also control whether you have a bed tonight and a way home tomorrow.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “L” CHECK: “Do I have the agreed terms in writing, and a dated log of hours I actually worked?” Memory loses to a spreadsheet, every time.
scenarios.darkTitle: Next Year Is The Threat Nobody Says
scenarios.dark: The unspoken sentence doing all the work is that there is always next season, and you want to be on it. That is what keeps crews quiet about underpayment for years at a time, and it is why the problem is almost never one bad payer — it is a whole circuit where everybody has been shorted and nobody compared figures, because comparing figures is exactly what the threat prevents. The single most effective move available is the one that costs nothing and feels the most awkward: ask two other crew what they were paid. Wage secrecy is the mechanism. Breaking it is the counter, and crews that talk openly about rates do not have this problem.
scenarios.move: Get the terms in a message before shift one and stage the payment — something up front, something mid-build. Log hours daily in a dated note with photographs of the work. Keep your own route home so your exit is never in their gift. Afterwards: a dated written demand, politely, with the log attached, beats a phone call every time.
scenarios.say: Before I start — can you confirm the rate, the days, and what's covered, just in a text? And I'd want a third up front. Standard for me, nothing personal.
scenarios.truth: Your labor is only leverage before you spend it. Write the terms down while you still have some.

scenarios.archetype: The Five Things That Make A Build Survivable
scenarios.who: For anyone taking a build gig, at any level, on any crew — including the good ones, because the good ones do all of this already and will respect you for it.
scenarios.scene: You are packing. What goes in the bag now is what you will have at hour ninety-six on a dark field with no signal and a production office that has gone home. Everything on this page takes ten minutes to arrange before you travel and is impossible to arrange afterwards.
tells: The deal in writing: rate, days, what's covered, injury, transport home
A dated hours log you fill in daily, with photos of the work
Your own PPE — boots, gloves, hi-vis, glasses, ear protection, head torch
Your own route home that nobody else controls
One off-site person with the site address who expects a daily check-in
The name of the site first-aider and where the trauma kit actually is
scenarios.happening: Every pattern in this guide is defeated by something arranged in advance rather than negotiated in the moment, and the moment is always the worst time — you are tired, you are isolated, the work is already done, and the other party holds the leverage. Bringing your own PPE is the clearest example: it removes the most common coercive sentence on any site, which is that there is not a spare and the job still needs doing. Owning your route home removes the second. These are not signs of distrust. Experienced crew arrive with all of it, and the crews worth working for notice and think better of you.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “U” CHECK: “Can I refuse a task right now without losing my bed or my lift?” If not, fix that before you need to refuse anything.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Kit Is What Makes No Possible
scenarios.dark: Every item on that list exists to make one sentence survivable: no, I am not doing that. Your own boots mean nobody can tell you the job goes ahead in trainers. Your own transport means refusing does not strand you. The written deal means walking away does not cost you a fortnight's pay. The check-in means somebody notices. Refusal is not a matter of courage on a build site, it is a matter of what refusing costs — and everything on that list is there to lower the price until it is something you can actually afford to say.
