scenarios.move: Pack the kit, send the deal message, name your off-site person, and find the first-aider and the trauma kit in your first hour on site. Then do the work, which is some of the best work there is.
scenarios.say: Got my own PPE and my own van, so I'm sorted. Who's the first-aider this build, and where's the trauma kit living?
scenarios.truth: Every bit of that kit buys you the same thing: the ability to say no and still have a bed, a lift, and a wage.

scenarios.archetype: Real Solidarity Versus A Family That Only Takes
scenarios.clinical: Authentic Crew Culture vs Extractive Belonging
scenarios.who: The real thing is unglamorous and specific: people who tell each other their rates, who cover a shift without a ledger, who stop the job when somebody is unfit, and who back the newest person over the most senior one when the newest person is right.
scenarios.scene: Two crews. On the first, a lad two days in says he is not comfortable going up in that wind, and the lead says fine, get the ground kit, and nothing else is ever said about it. On the second, the same sentence produces a silence, and then a joke, and then somebody else goes up instead — and everybody learns what happens if you say it.
tells: Real: refusing an unsafe task costs nothing, visibly, in public
Real: people talk openly about rates and compare them
Real: the newest person is listened to when they flag something
Extractive: family gets invoked only when something is being asked
Extractive: raising a concern about a senior member closes the group
Extractive: everyone has been shorted and nobody has compared figures
scenarios.happening: Build crews produce some of the most genuine solidarity in this scene — shared hardship, real skill, work that would be impossible alone — and that is exactly why the extractive version is so effective, because it is wearing the same clothes. The difference is not warmth, both have warmth. The difference is what the group does when somebody's interests conflict with the schedule: a real crew absorbs the cost, an extractive one transfers it to the person with the least standing. Watch one refusal and one complaint and you will know which one you are on, usually within the first week.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “U” CHECK: “What happened the last time somebody here said no to a task?” That answer is the crew's actual culture, whatever the culture says about itself.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Silence After The Refusal
scenarios.dark: It is worth knowing how a crew goes bad, because it is rarely a decision. It is one refusal met with a silence, and then a joke, and everybody present filing that away. After that the unsafe tasks get done by whoever needs the gig most, which is always the youngest, newest, most precarious person there, and the crew genuinely believes it has no safety problem because nobody says no any more. If you are senior on a crew: the most protective thing available to you is to publicly accept the next refusal you get, immediately and without comment. Everyone watching learns what it costs, and the answer is nothing, and that is how a crew that holds gets built.
scenarios.move: Talk about rates out loud. Accept refusals without comment, especially if you are senior. Buddy the newest person on their first night shift. Cover a shift for somebody without starting a ledger, and let that be the culture rather than the exception.
scenarios.say: Fair enough, grab the ground kit. — What are you on for this one? I'm on two-forty, worth knowing if they're paying people differently.
scenarios.truth: Watch what happens after one person says no. That is the whole crew, revealed in about four seconds.

scenarios.archetype: The Most Dangerous Hour Of The Whole Build
scenarios.who: You, on the Monday, after a three-week build and a two-day strike, with a van full of kit and four hours of motorway between you and a bed.
scenarios.scene: Everything is loaded. The site is a field again. You have slept eleven hours in the last three days and you are going to drive home now because that is what everybody does and because the alternative is another night in a field. You will be fine for the first hour. The one that gets people is the third.
tells: Driving at the end of a long build or a full strike
Fewer than five hours' sleep in each of the preceding nights
Driving in the window your body expects to be asleep
Loaded van, unfamiliar route, motorway
The whole crew leaves at once, so nobody is checking on anybody
“I'll stop if I get tired”, which is the belief that does the damage
scenarios.happening: Fatigue is a leading cause of fatal road collisions and the risk profile matches this exact moment: sustained sleep debt, monotonous roads, and driving at a time of day when the body is trying to shut down. The specific danger is the microsleep — a few seconds of sleep with the eyes open, which the driver does not experience as having happened, which is why “I'll know when I'm too tired” is false. At seventy miles an hour, four seconds is a hundred and twenty metres of unattended vehicle.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “D” CHECK: “How many hours have I slept in the last three nights?” If it is under fifteen, you are not driving tonight. That is arithmetic, not opinion.
scenarios.darkTitle: Crews Lose People On The Monday
scenarios.dark: This is the one that actually kills build crew, and it happens after the dangerous work is finished, which is exactly why nobody plans for it. The whole site has spent weeks being careful about heights and plant and blades, and then everybody gets in a vehicle in the worst physiological state of the entire job and drives home alone. Budget the extra night the way you budget fuel — sleep on site and leave Tuesday morning, or put the money for a room in the quote. If you are running the build, build it into the schedule and say out loud that nobody drives on Monday, because a crew will not do it individually if the culture expects the Monday drive.
scenarios.move: Sleep before you drive — one more night on site is cheaper than any alternative. Share the driving and stop every two hours regardless of how you feel. Caffeine buys twenty minutes, not four hours. Text somebody when you arrive so a missing message means something.
scenarios.say: I'm not driving tonight, I've had about four hours a night all week — I'll go first thing. — Crew rule this year: nobody drives on the Monday. Put the extra night in the budget.
scenarios.truth: The build did not hurt you. The drive home is the part that kills people, and it happens after you think the job is over.

scenarios.hook: STRIKE IS WHEN IT ALL GOES WRONG
scenarios.archetype: Teardown / The Phase Nobody Briefs
scenarios.who: The last forty-eight hours, when the audience has gone, the production office has half packed, most of the supervisors have left, and whoever is still on site is dismantling in the dark with the fewest people and the least oversight of the entire job.
scenarios.scene: Everyone is exhausted, the structures are coming down in reverse order by people who did not put them up, half the crew are new faces brought in for the teardown, and the person who would have said no to something is already on a train. There is no briefing for strike. There never is.
tells: No strike briefing, though there was a build one
Structures dismantled by people who did not erect them
Supervisors and safety leads already departed
New casual crew with unverified experience
Everyone at their most fatigued, working at speed to finish
Payment and paperwork also leaving the site, with you unpaid
scenarios.happening: Teardown concentrates every risk factor in this guide into the shortest window: maximum fatigue, minimum supervision, unfamiliar crews, and a strong collective incentive to be finished. Dismantling is more dangerous than erecting, because loads shift unpredictably when a structure comes apart and because the people taking it down often do not know how it went together. It is also when the money leaves — the production company is closing the site down, and a worker who is owed and has not been paid is now chasing an organization that has physically gone.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “U” CHECK: “Who is supervising strike, and who am I handing this structure to?” If nobody can answer, that is the finding, on day one of teardown.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Money Leaves With The Site
scenarios.dark: Two things walk off during strike and both matter. The first is competence: the people who know how each structure was built leave before it comes down, so ask for a handover from whoever erected it and do not guess a load path. The second is your wage. Payment at settle-up is bad enough; payment at settle-up during a teardown, when the office is packing and the crew is dispersing, is how people go home unpaid with no one left to ask. Get your hours signed before strike begins, not after, while there is still somebody on site whose job it is to sign them.
scenarios.move: Insist on a strike briefing, even a five-minute one. Get a handover from whoever built a structure before you take it down. Get your hours signed and confirmed before teardown starts. Keep the buddy rule and the fatigue rule harder in strike than in build.
scenarios.say: Before we start pulling this down — who put it up, and can they walk me through it? — Can you sign off my hours today rather than Monday, while there's still an office?
scenarios.truth: Strike has the most fatigue, the fewest supervisors and the least oversight of the whole job, and nobody briefs it. Ask for the briefing.

scenarios.hook: YEAH, I'VE DRIVEN ONE OF THESE
scenarios.archetype: Faked Competence / The Ticket Nobody Checked
scenarios.who: Somebody who needs the work and has said yes to a question they should have said no to — usually not out of recklessness, but because admitting it on a site where everyone else seems to know what they are doing feels impossible.
scenarios.scene: He is on the telehandler moving a two-tonne load over a walkway and his movements are not right and everybody can see it and nobody is saying anything, because saying something means calling a man a liar in front of the crew. You are standing in the area he is swinging over.
tells: Nobody has asked to see a ticket, licence or certification
Hesitant, jerky or improvised operation of plant or lifting equipment
Vague or deflecting answers about where and when they trained
No banksman, no exclusion zone, no lift plan
The crew has noticed and is communicating about it by eye contact
The site has no record of anybody's qualifications
scenarios.happening: Plant, lifting and height work are ticketed for a reason and festival builds are one of the last places where nobody asks to see the ticket. The pressure runs both ways: an operator who overstates their experience is usually somebody who could not afford to lose the gig, and a crew that will not challenge it is protecting a man's dignity at the expense of everyone standing underneath. Neither of those is malice, and the outcome is the same as if it were.
scenarios.check: B.U.I.L.D. — “U” CHECK: “Has anybody actually seen this person's ticket?” Assumed competence is not competence, and you are standing in the swing radius.
scenarios.darkTitle: Say It To The Supervisor, Not To The Man
scenarios.dark: The reason this persists is entirely social, so the fix has to be social too. Challenging the operator directly in front of the crew is humiliating and will be resisted, which is why nobody does it and why the situation runs for days. Take it to the supervisor as a question about paperwork rather than about a person — have we got tickets on file for the plant operators — and it becomes an administrative matter with no one accused of anything. And remember the other half: if you are the one who said yes to something you cannot do, saying so now costs you a job, and saying so after costs somebody a life. Nobody on a site has ever been fired for saying they need a hand with a machine they do not know.
scenarios.move: Ask the supervisor for tickets to be on file as a site-wide matter, not about an individual. Stay out of swing and drop zones regardless. Insist on a banksman for every lift. And if it is you: say so, today, to one person.
scenarios.say: Have we got plant tickets on file for everyone? Worth having if anything happens. — [if it's you] I've not run one of these before, I said yes when I shouldn't have. Can I get shown properly or put somewhere else?
scenarios.truth: Nobody wants to call a man a liar in front of the crew. Make it a question about paperwork and it stops being about him.

guides.intro: You hold the space that holds everything. This guide holds you.

checks.name: Capacity Has a Limit
checks.desc: You cannot pour from an empty vessel. Your depletion is not a badge. It is a risk to the people you serve.

checks.name: Accountability Goes Both Ways
checks.desc: You are accountable to the people you serve. Your organization is accountable to you. Know both directions.

checks.name: Red Flags Are Data
checks.desc: Your gut is an instrument. When something feels off about a participant or a colleague — log it, don't dismiss it.

checks.name: Exit and Debrief Always
checks.desc: Hard shifts require processing. What you carry out of the tent without naming becomes what you carry for years.

sentences: My wellbeing is not optional. It is what makes me effective.
The participant manipulating my care role is not my failure to spot. It is a pattern to document.

I hold space for others. Someone needs to hold space for me.

scenarios.hook: YOU ARE SO SAFE TO BE AROUND
scenarios.archetype: When Your Care Energy Becomes a Hook
scenarios.who: Harm Reduction volunteers radiate something that most festival attendees are genuinely seeking — calm, presence, non-judgment, safety. These are real and valuable qualities. They are also specifically targeted by people who mistake your professional care for personal availability.
scenarios.scene: He has been to your tent three times today. Each visit has a slightly different stated reason but the pattern of the conversation is the same — he lingers, he asks questions about you, he says things like "I have never felt so comfortable talking to someone." The fourth visit he asks if you want to get food after your shift. You are tired and his attention has felt kind throughout a difficult day. Something in you wants to say yes. Something else notes the pattern.
tells: Multiple visits with escalating personal rather than support-related conversation
Compliments that specifically target your care qualities — your presence, your listening, your safety
Questions about your schedule, when your shift ends, what you are doing after
The line between appreciating your support and pursuing you personally has started to blur
scenarios.happening: The Harm Reduction role creates a specific dynamic: you are at your most professionally present and emotionally available while participants are at their most open and vulnerable. Some participants experience the care you provide in your role as personal connection. Some deliberately target that dynamic for access. Maintaining the on-duty boundary — warm, caring, and professionally boundaried — protects both of you.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — "C" CHECK: "Am I maintaining the distinction between my care role and my personal availability?"
scenarios.darkTitle: The On-Duty Boundary And Why It Exists
scenarios.dark: The on-duty boundary exists because: the power differential between a care provider and someone receiving care makes genuine consent complicated. Your ability to provide care effectively depends on maintaining the distinction between professional and personal. Crossing the boundary exposes you to real professional and sometimes legal risk. And it exposes the participant to the experience of someone they trusted professionally pursuing them personally — which is a harm regardless of your intentions. "I am on duty right now so I keep things professional during my role" is a complete and professional response. It is not a rejection.
scenarios.move: Warm, caring, professionally boundaried. All three at the same time. That is the standard.
scenarios.say: "I am on shift right now so I keep things professional during my role — I hope you have a great rest of your festival."
scenarios.truth: Your care is a professional skill. Not everyone who benefits from it is entitled to more of you.

scenarios.hook: THE PARTICIPANT WHO RUNS A PATTERN
scenarios.archetype: When Someone Is Using the Space for Something Other Than Support
scenarios.who: Most people who come to a Harm Reduction tent are there for genuine reasons. Some are not. Recognizing the difference is a specific skill and a safeguarding responsibility.
scenarios.scene: He has been to the tent four times this weekend. Each visit, the stated reason shifts. He is articulate and charming and good at triggering the care response. You have given him supplies, information, quiet space, and extended conversations. On the fourth visit you notice: he is asking detailed questions about other participants who have come through the tent. He seems interested in the staff schedule. His affect when he thinks nobody is watching is different from his affect when he is being supported.
tells: Multiple visits with shifting or evolving presentations of the support need
Interest in other participants who have used the space or in staff schedules and rotations
Requests that go beyond the scope of the Harm Reduction role
Noticeably different affect when they think they are not being directly observed
scenarios.happening: People who want to gather information about vulnerable attendees, access resources beyond what is appropriate, or build proximity to care staff will use the Harm Reduction tent to do it because the tent is specifically designed to receive people without judgment. Noticing patterns is not being judgmental. It is safeguarding. Your gut when something is off is data. Document it and name it to your team lead.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “R” CHECK: “Is the pattern of this person’s engagement consistent with genuine support seeking — or does it track more closely with something else entirely?” — discernment is as much a part of this role as compassion.
scenarios.darkTitle: Documenting Concerning Patterns
scenarios.dark: When something feels off about a participant: (1) Note the visit — time, brief description of what was requested, anything that seemed inconsistent. (2) Share your observation with a colleague quietly during a transition — "I want to flag something about a repeat visitor." (3) If the behavior is actively concerning — gathering information about other participants, following up with specific participants after interactions — report to your team lead immediately and in writing. You do not need certainty to document. Documentation is not accusation. It is creating a record in case the pattern becomes clearer.
scenarios.move: Trust the pattern. Note it. Share it with a colleague. Document it. That is what good safeguarding looks like.
scenarios.say: I want to flag something I have noticed about a repeat visitor — can we talk privately for a minute?
scenarios.truth: Your care role requires discernment as much as compassion. Both are part of doing it well.

scenarios.archetype: Compassion Fatigue and Secondary Traumatic Stress
scenarios.who: Harm Reduction volunteers encounter a concentration of difficult human experiences in a very short time. Compassion fatigue and secondary traumatic stress are not personal failures. They are occupational hazards of sustained high-intensity emotional labor.
scenarios.scene: You have supported four difficult situations today — one overdose response, two sexual assault disclosures, one severe psychological crisis. You are still showing up fully for every person who comes in. But something has shifted in how you are receiving their experiences. They are landing differently. You feel numb where you used to feel present. You are performing care rather than actually giving it. You have not told anyone because the tent is busy and there is nobody to cover you.
tells: Emotional numbness in situations that would previously have moved you
Performing care rather than experiencing genuine presence and connection
Physical symptoms that persist between interactions: tension, headache, dissociation
Intrusive thoughts about difficult situations you have witnessed during your shifts
scenarios.happening: Secondary traumatic stress develops from repeated exposure to other people's traumatic experiences. Harm Reduction work at festivals compresses what might be a week of a therapist's caseload into a single shift. The culture that says "just one more" and "people need you" is the same culture that burns out its best volunteers and leaves participants being supported by someone running on empty. Your depletion is not noble. It is a risk to the people you are trying to help.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “C” CHECK: “Am I actually present with the people I am supporting — or am I performing presence from a tank that’s already empty?” — you cannot give what you do not have, and your recovery is what makes the giving possible.
scenarios.darkTitle: Recognizing And Responding To Compassion Fatigue
scenarios.dark: During a shift: step outside for ten minutes between difficult interactions even when the space is busy. Eat something before your shift and during it. Drink water. Name what you are carrying to a colleague before taking the next participant. After a difficult shift: do not go directly to the main festival environment — give yourself 15-30 minutes in a quiet space. Name the most difficult thing from the shift out loud to at least one colleague before leaving. After the event: if intrusive thoughts or emotional numbness persist beyond two weeks — contact a mental health professional. Zendo Project (zendoproject.org) provides training and ongoing support specifically for Harm Reduction volunteers.
scenarios.move: Your recovery is part of the job. Take your breaks. Eat. Drink water. Name what you are carrying. Debrief.
scenarios.say: I need to step out for ten minutes — can someone cover briefly?
scenarios.truth: You cannot give what you do not have. Your recovery serves the people you are trying to help.

scenarios.archetype: Confidentiality Weaponized / Organizational Reporting Suppression
scenarios.who: Confidentiality in Harm Reduction work is a genuine and important value. It can also be weaponized — used to suppress reporting of staff behavior, organizational failures, or incidents that should be escalated beyond the tent.
scenarios.scene: You witnessed something that happened between a staff member and a participant that you believe was a violation. When you raised it with your team lead, the response was: "What happens in the tent stays in the tent — we cannot breach participant confidentiality." The confidentiality framing is being applied to suppress a report about staff behavior rather than to protect participant information. These are not the same thing.
tells: Confidentiality invoked specifically when you try to report staff behavior or organizational failures
The line between protecting participant information and suppressing accountability is blurred
"What happens here stays here" applied to situations that clearly require escalation
You feel that reporting would violate your role when it actually falls within your safeguarding responsibilities
scenarios.happening: Confidentiality in Harm Reduction protects participant information — not staff behavior, not organizational failures, and not incidents that require escalation to protect others. These are distinct categories. A team lead or organization that uses confidentiality language to suppress reports about staff behavior or organizational accountability is misusing the concept. Your safeguarding responsibilities include reporting when you witness harm, regardless of where it occurred.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “A” CHECK: “Is confidentiality being applied to protect the people we serve — or to protect the organization from accountability?” — confidentiality protects participants. It was never meant to protect an organization from consequences.
scenarios.darkTitle: What To Do When The Reporting Structure Is Broken
scenarios.dark: If your team lead is suppressing a report: escalate to the next level of the organization in writing. If there is no functional next level: document the incident yourself in writing with date, time, and exactly what you witnessed. Send that documentation to the organization in writing — email creates a timestamp. If the incident involves assault or a crime: you may have independent obligations to report regardless of organizational direction. After the event: report to any professional bodies or associations that oversee the event or the Harm Reduction organization. RAINN (rainn.org) has guidance for witnesses and bystanders.
scenarios.move: Your safeguarding responsibilities include reporting harm you witness — that is not a breach of confidentiality.
scenarios.say: I understand the confidentiality concern but what I witnessed involves staff behavior that I believe requires escalation. I am going to document it formally.
scenarios.truth: Confidentiality protects participants. It does not protect organizations from accountability for harm.

scenarios.archetype: Being Blamed for Systemic Failures
scenarios.who: Harm Reduction volunteers are sometimes held responsible for outcomes that were determined by organizational failures — inadequate staffing, poor training, unclear protocols — that were set in motion long before your shift began.
scenarios.scene: A participant had a serious adverse event during your shift. You responded as well as you could with the training and resources you had. Afterward the organizational debrief focuses almost entirely on your response rather than the systemic conditions: the understaffing that left you alone with a participant who needed two-person support, the training gap that meant you were not prepared for this specific situation, the protocol that was unclear. You are the person who was there. You are becoming the story.
tells: Post-incident debrief focuses on your actions rather than the systemic conditions you were placed in
Staffing ratios, training gaps, and resource shortfalls are not part of the organizational review
You are being asked to sign documentation that implies individual responsibility for systemic failures
The framing has shifted from "what happened" to "what did you do" in ways that assign blame downward
scenarios.happening: Front-line Harm Reduction volunteers are the easiest people to blame for systemic failures because they were physically present when things went wrong. Organizations that do not want to examine their structural failures direct accountability toward the people least able to defend themselves. You are not required to accept responsibility for conditions you did not create. Document your own account of events immediately after any incident. Do not sign anything without reading it carefully against your own record.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “A” CHECK: “Have I documented my own account of events immediately — before organizational framing has a chance to reshape it?” — you’re responsible for your actions, not for the systemic conditions you were placed in.
scenarios.darkTitle: Protecting Yourself After An Incident
scenarios.dark: Immediately after any significant incident: (1) Write your own detailed account — what you observed, what you did, what resources and training you had, what the conditions were. Include timestamps. (2) Do not sign organizational documentation before comparing it to your own account. (3) If asked to participate in a formal review: you have the right to have someone present with you. (4) If you feel you are being scapegoated for systemic failures: contact a lawyer or advocate before signing anything. (5) Keep copies of all documentation you receive from the organization. Your account is the evidence that protects you.
scenarios.move: Write your account immediately. Do not sign anything before reading it against your own record.
scenarios.say: I want to cooperate fully with any review. I am also going to document my own account of what happened and what conditions I was working in.
scenarios.truth: You are responsible for your actions. You are not responsible for the systemic conditions you were placed in.

scenarios.archetype: Processing What You Carry So It Does Not Carry You
scenarios.who: Debrief is not extra. Debrief is part of the job. What you name and process from a difficult shift becomes wisdom. What you do not name becomes weight you carry into the next shift and beyond.
scenarios.scene: The shift ends and the tendency is to immediately transition back to the festival or to crash into sleep. The transition period — the ten to thirty minutes between the end of a shift and the next thing — is when the debrief happens. Not in a formal structured way necessarily. Just: what was the hardest thing from this shift, said out loud, to at least one colleague. That is the minimum. And it changes everything about what you carry out.
tells: Name the hardest thing from the shift out loud to at least one colleague before leaving
Physical transition: change out of your shift vest, eat something, drink water
If multiple difficult incidents happened: 20-30 minutes of quiet before re-entering the festival
Weekly or post-event check-in with a mental health professional if this is regular work for you
scenarios.happening: Secondary traumatic stress accumulates when difficult experiences are not processed. The processing does not have to be elaborate — naming what was hard, in plain language, to someone who was also there or who understands the context, is often sufficient for immediate decompression. It is the naming that matters. What stays unnamed stays active. Harm Reduction volunteers who debrief consistently report lower rates of burnout and secondary trauma than those who do not.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “E” CHECK: “Have I actually stopped and named what I am carrying from this shift — or am I just pushing it down to deal with later?” — what you name, you can put down. What you don’t, you carry.
scenarios.darkTitle: What Undebriefed Weekends Turn Into
scenarios.dark: The people who leave harm reduction rarely leave because of one terrible night. They leave because of forty ordinary ones that were never processed, stacked up until the work started costing more than it gave. The documented pattern is specific: accumulated vicarious trauma turns into intrusive memory, then into sleep loss, then into the thing nobody in this field likes saying out loud, which is that a meaningful number of burned-out harm reduction workers end up using in ways they would flag instantly in a participant. You will be the last person to notice it in yourself, because your whole skill set is pointed outward. That is exactly why the debrief is scheduled rather than optional, and why it has to be with someone whose job is you — not the participant, not the org, not the friend who also worked the shift.
scenarios.move: Name what was hard. Out loud. To someone. Before you leave the tent. That is the minimum.
scenarios.say: Before we all head out — can we take ten minutes to say what today was like? I need to name some of it out loud.
scenarios.truth: What you name, you can put down. What you do not name, you carry. Name it.

scenarios.archetype: What You Bring, What You Set, What You Do After
scenarios.who: For everyone working a harm-reduction, welfare or sober-support shift — paid, volunteer, or the person who just ended up doing it because they were the one who was up.
scenarios.scene: You will spend this shift giving people your full attention at the worst moment of their weekend. Everything on this page is what makes that sustainable past year two, and it is all arranged before the shift rather than during it, because during it you will be entirely focused on somebody else.
tells: Your own water, food and a break time somebody else knows about
A named shift partner — nobody works a tent or a walkout alone
The escalation line: who you call, for what, and their actual number
Your personal scope, decided sober: what you do and what you hand on
No lone walkouts to a tent or a vehicle, ever, regardless of the request
A debrief booked for after — a named person and a time, not a vague intention
scenarios.happening: Harm-reduction workers occupy a role that is simultaneously high-exposure and low-protection: physical proximity to impaired people, emotional weight, long hours, and frequently no supervision, no insurance and no handover. The two failure modes are burnout and boundary drift, and they feed each other — a depleted worker is worse at holding a line, and a worker who has been holding no lines depletes faster. Everything here is structural rather than attitudinal, because attitude is exactly what goes first at hour nine of a shift.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “E” CHECK: “Do I have a shift partner, a break time, and a debrief booked?” Three answers before you start, or you are improvising your own protection while looking after somebody else.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Are A Target In This Role, Too
scenarios.dark: Worth saying plainly because the role's framing makes it easy to miss: being the calm helpful person in the welfare tent at four in the morning makes you visible to exactly the people this book is about. The care role attracts them — it is reliably staffed by empathetic people, it involves private conversations, it happens at night, and it comes with a strong professional instinct not to judge anyone. Participants who target the care role are a documented pattern, not a paranoid one, and the lone walkout is where it happens. Two people, always, for every escort and every tent visit. It is not distrust of the person you are helping. It is the same reason ambulance crews are crewed.
scenarios.move: Set the three before the shift — partner, break, debrief — and write your personal scope down while you are sober. Never do a walkout alone. Take the break even when it feels indulgent, especially then.
scenarios.say: I'm not doing that walkout on my own — grab Sam and we'll both go. — I'm off at four and I'm debriefing with Mara at ten tomorrow, it's in the diary.
scenarios.truth: You cannot hold a tent full of people from an empty tank. The kit is not self-indulgence, it is the equipment.

scenarios.archetype: The Critical Incident And The Weeks After It
scenarios.who: Nobody did anything wrong. This page is for the hours and the months after the worst night, and it is written because almost nobody in this role is prepared for it and it happens every season somewhere.
scenarios.scene: You did everything right. You did CPR, you called it in, the medics came, and it did not matter. It is four in the morning and the tent is still open and there are eleven people outside who need things, and somebody is asking you where the water is.
tells: You kept working, because the tent was still open
You are recounting the timeline compulsively, looking for the error
Nobody senior has formally stood you down
There is no organizational debrief scheduled, only a gap
You have not told the people at home, to protect them
You are fine, loudly, and have started sleeping badly
scenarios.happening: A death on shift is a critical incident, and the response to it is well established even though this sector rarely provides it: stand down immediately rather than finishing the shift, a factual operational debrief within twenty-four hours that is separate from any emotional processing, and follow-up over weeks rather than a single conversation on the night. What does not help, and is the standard offering, is an unstructured group conversation at four in the morning with everyone still activated. What helps is sleep, food, being stood down, and a scheduled conversation later with somebody trained.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “E” CHECK: “Am I still working?” If yes, that is the first thing to change. You are not a resource tonight.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Review Will Find You Did Not Fail
scenarios.dark: The thing that hurts people in this role is not the death, it is the replay — the compulsive re-examination of the timeline looking for the two minutes where it could have gone differently. Almost always there is no such moment, and being told that by somebody who knows the clinical picture is enormously more useful than being told it by a friend. Ask for the operational debrief and ask to be walked through what actually happened medically, because unanswered questions are what the replay feeds on. And put the follow-up in the diary for three and six weeks, when everyone has gone home and it gets much louder. Bereaved-by-suicide and critical-incident support services exist for responders and volunteers, not only for family.
scenarios.move: Stand down now, not at the end of the shift — hand over and say you are unfit to continue, which is a clinical statement rather than a request. Eat, hydrate, sleep. Ask for a factual operational debrief within a day and book a proper one for three weeks out. Tell one person at home something true.
scenarios.say: I'm standing down — I'm not fit to be on this tent tonight, someone needs to take over. — I want an operational debrief in the next day, and I want to be walked through what happened clinically.
scenarios.truth: Finishing the shift is not resilience. Standing down is the first piece of clinical judgement you make about yourself.

scenarios.archetype: Police And Security At The Harm Reduction Tent
scenarios.who: An officer, a security supervisor, or an event manager standing at the entrance of your tent asking a question you should not answer, usually politely, and usually believing they are entitled to.
scenarios.scene: There is a young woman in the corner who came in twenty minutes ago in a bad state and is only just settling, and there is now a uniform at the door asking what she took and whether he can have a word. Everybody in the tent has gone quiet and is watching what you do, and what you do in the next ten seconds determines whether anybody uses this tent again this weekend.
tells: Uniformed presence at or inside the service space
Requests for names, substances, or details about a participant
Being asked to identify who is holding, or to point somebody out
Security using the tent as an observation post
An event manager asking for information to manage reputation
Participants stopping at the door, looking in, and walking away
scenarios.happening: The entire clinical value of a harm reduction service rests on one thing: people believing they can come in without consequence. That belief is fragile, it is community knowledge rather than individual knowledge, and it is destroyed by a single visible interaction — one person seen speaking to police at the tent door ends the service's usefulness for the rest of the weekend, because the word travels faster than anything you can say to correct it. Protecting the boundary is not obstruction; it is the operational requirement that makes the service work at all.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “A” CHECK: “What does this look like to the people watching from inside my tent?” That perception is the service, and it is what you are protecting.
scenarios.darkTitle: Agree It In Writing Before The Gates Open
scenarios.dark: The failure is almost always a planning failure rather than a confrontation. Services that get this right have a written agreement with the event and with police before the event opens — where the boundary is, what is and is not shared, and who to escalate to — and services that get it wrong are improvising it at two in the morning with an officer at the door and a frightened participant behind them. Get the memorandum in advance, get the senior officer's name, and brief every volunteer on the single sentence they use so that nobody has to invent one under pressure. Nobody should be working out an organization's information-sharing policy while somebody watches from a beanbag.
scenarios.move: Step outside to speak rather than letting the conversation happen in the space. Give one clear sentence, escalate to your coordinator, and do not disclose participant information. Afterwards, tell the room plainly what did and did not happen.
scenarios.say: I'll come out to you — let's talk out here. We don't share participant information; if you need something formally, my coordinator is the person for that and I'll get them now. — [to the room] Nobody's name was given and nobody's getting spoken to. You're fine here.
scenarios.truth: A single conversation at your door can close the service for the whole weekend. Step outside and protect what the room believes.

scenarios.archetype: The Line Between Harm Reduction And Medicine
scenarios.who: For everyone on a harm reduction or welfare shift, holding a role with no clinical registration and a queue of people whose conditions you are not qualified to assess.
scenarios.scene: He has been sitting with you for an hour and is not improving, and you are not sure whether this is a long comedown, dehydration, a reaction, or something genuinely medical. Walking him to the medics feels like escalating, and you have a specific fear of being the volunteer who overreacts and looks green in front of the medical team.
tells: Not improving, or getting worse, over time you would expect improvement
Temperature: very hot and not sweating, or cold and clammy
Breathing that is slow, irregular, snoring or noisy
Unrousable, or rousable only briefly, or seizing
Chest pain, a head injury, or an unexplained one-sided weakness
You are debating it with yourself, which is itself the threshold
scenarios.happening: Harm reduction and welfare workers are the first point of contact for a great many situations and are not clinicians, and the most consequential skill in the role is a low, pre-decided threshold for escalation. Every serious festival incident review finds the same thing: the delay happened because somebody was not sure it was serious enough. The thresholds above are not judgement calls and should not be treated as any — temperature extremes, breathing changes, unrousability, seizures and head injuries go to medical immediately, every time, without a discussion about whether it warrants it.
scenarios.check: C.A.R.E. — “R” CHECK: “Am I debating whether this is medical?” The debate is the answer. Escalate while you are still discussing it.
scenarios.darkTitle: Nobody Was Ever Criticized For The Early Call
scenarios.dark: Name the fear, because it is what causes the delay: you do not want to be the volunteer who walked someone over and was told it was nothing. Ask any festival medic and they will tell you the opposite — early calls are welcome, they would far rather see ten people who were fine than one an hour late, and the ones that go badly are always the late ones. The specific pattern to watch for is the person who is quietly deteriorating while the tent is busy, because a quiet person gets less attention than a loud one and deterioration is quiet by nature. Set a review time for everybody you are holding, and check them even when nothing has changed.
scenarios.move: Pre-decide the thresholds and escalate on any of them without deliberating. Set an explicit review time for every person you are holding. Walk them to medical rather than sending them. Hand over factually: what they took if known, when, what you have observed, what has changed.
scenarios.say: I'm walking you over to the medics — not because it's dramatic, just because it's their call and not mine. — [handing over] Male, about twenty-five, in with us ninety minutes, reports MDMA around ten, temperature's up and he's not sweating, and he's less responsive than he was.
scenarios.truth: If you are debating whether it is medical, it is medical. No medic has ever complained about being called early.

guides.intro: The power you hold in your camp is real. Use it to protect people, not to own them.

checks.name: Lead With Accountability
checks.desc: The standard you walk past is the standard you set. What you allow in your camp becomes what your camp is.

checks.name: Earn Trust, Don't Assume It
checks.desc: Your role gives you authority. Authority is not the same as trust. Trust is earned through what you do when it costs you.

checks.name: Access Creates Responsibility
checks.desc: You control housing, resources, placement, belonging. That control is a tool for protection — or a lever for harm.

checks.name: Debrief and Reflect
checks.desc: Hard situations happen in every camp. What you do with them afterward shapes whether they happen again.

outline.desc: How camps attract and collect people — including predatory dynamics
How camp culture gets built and what builds it badly
Power abuse camp leads may not recognize in themselves
Accountability practices, conflict resolution, reporting
Building a camp that is genuinely safe for everyone in it

sentences: The standard I walk past is the standard I set.
My role gives me authority. Authority is not the same as trust.
I use my access to protect people, not to create dependency.
A camp that cannot hear hard things cannot protect its people.

scenarios.archetype: Camp Recruitment and What It Signals
scenarios.who: Camps recruit new members every season. The pitch — community, infrastructure, belonging, access — is real when the camp is genuine and a trap when the camp is extractive. Understanding which kind of camp you are running starts with honest assessment.
scenarios.scene: You recruited twelve new members this season. The pitch was warm, the infrastructure is real, and most of them are having a genuinely good experience. Three of them are doing significantly more camp labor than others and seem reluctant to raise concerns. One new member has been spending most of their time with a senior camp member in ways that look more like dependency than connection. You have not looked closely at these dynamics because camp is running well overall.
tells: New members doing disproportionate labor compared to senior members without discussion
New members who seem reluctant to raise concerns or push back on anything
Dependency dynamics forming between new members and specific senior members
Camp culture that treats questioning the leadership as disloyalty rather than healthy input
scenarios.happening: Camp leaders are often the last to see problematic dynamics because they are managing the whole operation and because the overall experience is positive. The patterns to watch for in your own camp are the same ones that signal predatory structures in other contexts: unequal contribution without discussion, reluctance to raise concerns, dependency dynamics, and cultures that treat questioning as betrayal. Your camp is only as healthy as what you are willing to look at.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — "L" CHECK: "What dynamics in my camp am I avoiding looking at because things are running well overall?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Camp Health Self-Assessment
scenarios.dark: Honest questions to ask yourself about your camp: (1) Can any member raise a concern with me without social cost? (2) Is labor distributed equitably and has that been discussed explicitly? (3) Are there specific senior members whose relationships with new members I should look at more closely? (4) Do members feel free to leave the camp during the festival without it affecting their standing? (5) Has anyone ever pushed back on a camp decision and how was that received? (6) If I am honest, do any members seem afraid of me or of consequences from me? Your answers to these questions tell you what kind of camp you are running.
scenarios.move: Look honestly at the dynamics you have been avoiding. The health of your camp depends on what you are willing to see.
scenarios.say: "I want to do a camp culture check-in before the festival — I want to hear honestly from everyone about how things are going."
scenarios.truth: You cannot protect your camp from dynamics you are not willing to look at.

scenarios.archetype: When Someone in Your Camp Is Causing Harm
scenarios.who: Someone in your camp is causing harm to other members or to festival attendees. They may be a long-standing member. They may be well-liked. The situation is complicated. This page is about what you do anyway.
scenarios.scene: A newer member comes to you with a concern about someone who has been in the camp for four years. She is specific about what she observed and what happened to her. You believe her. You also know that the person she is describing is one of your most reliable camp contributors, is well-liked, and has been part of the community for years. The situation has no easy resolution. But it does have a right next step.
tells: A member with concerns is coming to you directly — this is the outcome of the trust you built
The person being reported is well-integrated into the camp — this is what makes it hard
The temptation to manage it informally to protect the camp's cohesion
The understanding that how you respond right now defines your camp culture permanently
scenarios.happening: Every camp leader will eventually face a situation where a trusted and integrated member has caused harm. The response to that situation defines the camp culture more than any other single event. Camps that protect long-standing members at the expense of the people they harmed build a culture where harm is tolerated when the person causing it is valuable enough. Camps that hold everyone to the same standard build a culture where people feel genuinely safe to report.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “L” CHECK: “Am I responding to this in a way that protects the person who came to me — or the person the report is about?” — the standard you set when it’s hard is the only standard that actually matters.
scenarios.darkTitle: Responding To Harm Reports In Your Camp
scenarios.dark: When someone brings you a concern: (1) Believe them enough to take action, even if you cannot verify everything immediately. (2) Document what they told you in writing, with their knowledge and consent. (3) Separate the accused person from access to the reporting person immediately and without drama. (4) Consult with the event's safety or security team — this should not be handled entirely within the camp. (5) Do not share the reporter's identity with the accused person without the reporter's explicit consent. (6) Follow up with the reporter. (7) Make a decision about camp membership that reflects the seriousness of the report. There is no version where you do nothing and maintain the trust of your community.
scenarios.move: Believe enough to act. Document. Separate. Consult. Follow up. Make a decision. In that order.
scenarios.say: Thank you for telling me. I am going to take this seriously. Here is what happens next.
scenarios.truth: The standard you set when it is hard is the only standard that matters.

scenarios.hook: THIS IS HOW WE DO THINGS HERE
scenarios.archetype: Camp Culture and What Builds It Badly
scenarios.who: Camp culture is built by what you reward, what you tolerate, and what you address. It is built more by your behavior in difficult moments than by your stated values in calm ones. This page is about the specific ways camps build cultures that hurt people.
scenarios.scene: Your camp has a norm of not talking about what happens in camp outside camp. It started as a way to protect privacy and maintain a sense of internal safety. Over time it has also functioned as a way to prevent accountability — things that happen in camp stay in camp because "that's our culture." Someone who was harmed by a camp member felt they could not report it externally because of this norm. The norm that was meant to protect people is now protecting the person who harmed them.
tells: Privacy norms that function as reporting suppression
Loyalty norms that equate questioning the camp with betrayal of the community
Contribution norms that create unpayable debt for new or less senior members
Norms that make it harder rather than easier to raise concerns or exit the camp
scenarios.happening: Every camp norm was created for a reason and serves a function. The question is whether the function it currently serves is the one it was created for — or whether it has evolved into a protection mechanism for the camp's reputation rather than its people. Privacy norms that prevent reporting, loyalty norms that suppress dissent, contribution norms that extract labor — all of these start somewhere reasonable and can drift somewhere harmful. Examining your norms honestly is camp leadership.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “E” CHECK: “Do my camp’s norms make it easier or harder for members to raise concerns and seek help when something has gone wrong?” — the norms you build in calm times are the ones that show up in the hard ones.
scenarios.darkTitle: Camp Norm Audit
scenarios.dark: Take each of your camp's major norms and ask: (1) What was this norm created for? (2) Is it currently serving that purpose? (3) Who does this norm protect when there is conflict? (4) Does this norm make it easier or harder for harmed people to seek help? Specific norms to examine: confidentiality norms, loyalty norms, contribution expectations, seniority hierarchies, and any norms around how conflict is handled. If your honest audit reveals that a norm is primarily protecting the camp's reputation or the comfort of senior members at the expense of accountability — it needs to change.
scenarios.move: Audit your camp norms honestly. Change the ones that protect the camp at the expense of its people.
scenarios.say: "I want us to look at our camp norms together and be honest about whether they are serving the people in this camp or protecting the camp itself."
scenarios.truth: The norms you build in calm times define what happens in the hard ones.

scenarios.archetype: Founder Syndrome / When Leadership Becomes Ownership
scenarios.who: The specific dynamic where a camp founder or long-standing leader begins to treat the camp as personal property — where their vision overrides community input, their comfort overrides member wellbeing, and accountability flows downward but not upward.
scenarios.scene: You have run this camp for seven years. You have poured extraordinary amounts of time, money, and love into building it. You know the infrastructure better than anyone. You also notice that your decisions rarely get questioned, that members seem careful about how they raise concerns with you, and that the last two people who pushed back significantly on a camp decision are no longer in the camp. You tell yourself they were not a good fit. You have not considered whether there is a pattern.
tells: Decisions are made unilaterally and questioning them is received as ingratitude or disloyalty
People who push back on decisions tend to leave or be pushed out
Your comfort and vision consistently override member input in conflicts
The camp's accountability structures apply to members but not clearly to you
scenarios.happening: Founder syndrome in camp culture is the accumulation of unchecked authority over time — a process so gradual it is often invisible to the person experiencing it. The camp leader who started with genuine community intention can become, through years of carrying the weight of the camp, someone who confuses their investment in the camp with ownership of it and ownership of the people in it. The antidote is structural: accountability that includes you, decision-making that includes others, and the willingness to hear things about yourself that are hard.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — "E" CHECK: "Am I accountable to my camp in the same ways my camp members are accountable to me?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Structural Accountability For Camp Leadership
scenarios.dark: Practical accountability structures for camp leads: (1) At least one other person in the camp has authority to raise concerns about your behavior without social cost. (2) Major camp decisions involve input from members before they are made, not just communication after. (3) There is a clear process for raising concerns about camp leadership specifically. (4) Camp finances are transparent to at least two members beyond yourself. (5) Exit from the camp is genuinely free — members can leave without social consequences. (6) You actively seek honest feedback after events rather than only welcoming positive feedback. These structures do not diminish your leadership. They make it trustworthy.
scenarios.move: Build accountability structures that include you. The camp that cannot hold its leader accountable cannot protect its members.
scenarios.say: I want to create a formal way for camp members to raise concerns about my decisions and my leadership. Here is what I am proposing.
scenarios.truth: The camp you built belongs to the community in it as much as to you. Lead accordingly.

scenarios.archetype: When What You Provide Becomes Control
scenarios.who: Camp leads who provide housing, infrastructure, or festival access control something that members genuinely need. That control becomes leverage — sometimes deliberately, sometimes not — when members feel they cannot exercise independence or raise concerns without risking what you provide.
scenarios.scene: You provided accommodation and festival access to six members of your camp. You did this generously and genuinely. You also notice that the members whose accommodation you control raise concerns less often, agree with your decisions more consistently, and seem to navigate their interactions with you more carefully than others. You have not used housing as leverage explicitly. But the dynamic it creates is real regardless of your intentions.
tells: Members whose accommodation or access you control behave differently from those who are independent
Concerns from accommodation-dependent members are rare even when issues exist
The implicit threat of losing housing is present even when you have never voiced it
Your decisions as a camp lead are harder to push back on when members depend on you for basics
scenarios.happening: Resource control creates leverage regardless of intent. When members depend on you for housing, festival access, or other basics, the power differential is real even if you never use it deliberately. People who need something from you will navigate that need carefully — which means raising concerns carefully, agreeing more often than they might otherwise, and staying in situations they might leave if they were independent. Acknowledging this dynamic is the beginning of mitigating it.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “A” CHECK: “Do the members who depend most on what I provide feel the most or least free to push back on me when something’s wrong?” — generosity that creates dependency isn’t generosity. It’s leverage that happens to be warm.
scenarios.darkTitle: Managing Resource Dependency Ethically
scenarios.dark: If you provide housing, access, or other resources to camp members: (1) Make explicit that their place in the camp and in the accommodation is not conditional on agreeing with your decisions. Say this out loud at the start of each season. (2) Create separate channels for concerns about camp decisions that do not go through you directly. (3) Be more careful about your behavior with members who depend on you, not less — the power imbalance means your actions land harder. (4) Never reference housing or access in conversations about camp disagreements or member behavior — even implicitly. (5) If someone wants to leave the camp, support that — the accommodation does not bind them.
scenarios.move: Acknowledge the leverage your resources create and actively work against it rather than ignoring it.
scenarios.say: Your place here is not conditional on agreeing with me. I want to be clear about that and I want you to feel free to push back.
scenarios.truth: Generosity that creates dependency is not generosity. It is leverage that happens to be warm.

scenarios.archetype: When Camp Membership Becomes a Control Structure
scenarios.clinical: High Control Group Dynamics / BITE Model
scenarios.who: This page is for camp leads who may be running — without full awareness — a camp that functions more like a high-control group than a genuine community. The signs are specific and worth examining honestly.
scenarios.scene: You care deeply about your camp and your members. You also have high standards for participation and strong views about what it means to be a good member of the community you have built. You have removed members who were not a good fit. You discourage members from talking about camp dynamics with people outside the camp. You feel that deep loyalty to the camp is an important value. These individually can be reasonable. Together they warrant examination.
tells: Leaving the camp carries significant social cost — former members are characterized negatively
Talking about camp dynamics with outsiders is discouraged as a loyalty issue
Questioning camp leadership is framed as a character issue rather than legitimate input
Deep loyalty to the camp is valued above members' individual wellbeing and judgment
scenarios.happening: High-control group dynamics in camps develop gradually and are usually invisible from the inside. The characteristics — discouraging outside input, penalizing exit, equating questioning with disloyalty, valuing camp loyalty above individual judgment — serve a genuine function for the person running the camp: they reduce conflict and maintain cohesion. They also prevent the accountability and self-correction that healthy communities require. If several of these are present in your camp, it is worth examining honestly.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “L” CHECK: “Can members of my camp leave freely, talk to outsiders freely, and question decisions freely, without a cost attached to any of it?” — a community that needs control to hold together isn’t a community. It’s a structure.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Bite Model — A Self-Assessment Tool
scenarios.dark: The BITE Model (Behavior, Information, Thought, Emotional control) is used to assess high-control groups. Applied to camps: Behavior control — are member behaviors controlled beyond what the camp function requires? Information control — is information about the camp restricted from outsiders? Thought control — is questioning the camp framed as a thought problem in the member? Emotional control — are members' emotions managed through guilt, shame, or fear of loss? Answering yes to any of these is worth examining. freedomofmind.com has resources on high-control group dynamics that apply to informal communities as well as formal organizations.
scenarios.move: Examine your camp honestly against these criteria. Make changes where the examination reveals them.
scenarios.say: "I want to make sure our camp is a place people feel genuinely free in — including free to leave, free to question, and free to talk to outsiders."
scenarios.truth: A community that requires control to maintain cohesion is not a community. It is a structure.

scenarios.archetype: Practical Structures That Make Your Camp Genuinely Safe
scenarios.who: This page is practical. Specific structures that make the difference between a camp that talks about safety and a camp that actually provides it.
scenarios.scene: The briefing before gates open is the most important ten minutes of the festival. What you say in that briefing — and what structures you establish in it — shapes what members feel able to do and say for the entire weekend. The camps with the best safety records are not the ones with the most rules. They are the ones where the culture of safety is established before anything difficult has happened.
tells: Pre-festival briefing: consent expectations, reporting process, code words, daily check-in times
Designated safety contact who is not you — someone members can go to with concerns about camp leadership
Clear, simple reporting process that does not require members to confront the person they are concerned about
Post-festival debrief: what happened, what worked, what needs to change next season
scenarios.happening: The structures you build before the festival are the ones that work during it. A reporting process established in a calm briefing is infinitely more useful than one improvised in a crisis. A designated safety contact who is not you means members have a path for concerns about your behavior as well as others. A code word system means members can signal for help without having to explain themselves in the moment. These are not elaborate systems — they are ten minutes of planning that change everything.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — "A" CHECK: "Have I built safety infrastructure into my camp that works even when I am the problem?"
scenarios.darkTitle: The Pre-Festival Camp Safety Briefing Template
scenarios.dark: Cover in your briefing: (1) Consent expectations — specific, not just "be cool." (2) Reporting process — how to raise a concern, who to go to, what happens next. (3) Code word — one word that means "I need help right now, come find me." (4) Daily check-in time — when and how. (5) Exit is free — anyone can leave the camp any time for any reason with no social cost. (6) What to do if something goes wrong and you are not sure who to tell. (7) Resources: Harm Reduction tent location, Ranger station location, medical tent location. Ten minutes. Do it before gates open. Every season.
scenarios.move: Build the safety infrastructure before you need it. Run the briefing before gates open. Every season.
scenarios.say: Before gates open — ten minutes for our safety briefing. This is how we take care of each other this weekend.
scenarios.truth: The camps with the best safety records are the ones that built the infrastructure before anything went wrong.

scenarios.hook: THE CAMP LEAD WHO DOES THE WORK
scenarios.archetype: What Genuine Leadership in This Context Looks Like
scenarios.who: This final page is about what it looks like when camp leadership is done right — not as a set of rules but as a practice of genuine care that includes accountability, humility, and the willingness to be wrong.
scenarios.scene: The best camp leads you know have several things in common: they take concerns seriously regardless of who brings them. They hold themselves to the same standards they hold their members. They have built ways for members to push back on their decisions. They have removed people from their camps when those people caused harm — even when it was complicated. They are honest about the limits of their own judgment. They debrief after hard weekends and make changes.
tells: Takes concerns seriously and follows up on every single one regardless of who brought it
Holds themselves to the same behavioral standards as every other camp member
Has built accountability structures that include themselves not just their members
Makes decisions about camp membership based on behavior not on seniority or contribution
scenarios.happening: Genuine camp leadership is a practice of consistent accountability — to your members, to the community, and to yourself. The camp leads who build the safest camps are not the ones who have the best rules. They are the ones who model what accountability looks like, who take the same risks with their own behavior that they ask their members to take, and who treat every person in the camp as someone whose wellbeing they are genuinely responsible for.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “D” CHECK: “When I look at my camp honestly — am I the kind of leader I would want my members to describe honestly, if they were asked?” — the best camp lead isn’t the one who never gets it wrong. It’s the one who keeps working to get it more right.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Ongoing Practice Of Accountable Leadership
scenarios.dark: Ongoing practices for camp leaders: (1) Post-event honest debrief with at least one person who will tell you the truth. (2) Annual review of camp norms — are they still serving the people in the camp? (3) Regular check-ins with members specifically about how safe they feel in the camp. (4) Seek out critical feedback actively — not just welcome positive feedback. (5) When you get it wrong, say so and change. Out loud. To your members. (6) Invest in your own learning about group dynamics, safeguarding, and consent culture. The work of being a good camp lead is not finished when the event ends. It continues in how you build for the next one.
scenarios.move: Do the ongoing work of accountable leadership. It is never finished and it is always worth it.
scenarios.say: After every event I want to hear honestly about what worked and what I could do better. I mean that.
scenarios.truth: The best camp lead is not the one who never gets it wrong. It is the one who keeps doing the work to get it more right.

scenarios.archetype: The Conversation Camp Leads Avoid For Years
scenarios.who: You, holding a decision you have already made and have been postponing for eleven months because you do not know how to do the next part without it becoming a scene.
scenarios.scene: You know he cannot come back. You have known since August. What you do not have is a way of saying it that does not turn into a two-hour argument in front of the camp, or a group chat meltdown, or him turning up anyway because nothing was ever said clearly enough to be enforceable.
tells: The decision is made and only the delivery is missing
You are waiting for one more incident to make it defensible
The camp is quietly organizing itself around avoiding him
People have started not coming, and you know which people
There is no written camp agreement to point at
You are planning to do it in person, alone, at the event
scenarios.happening: Most camp exclusions go badly for procedural reasons rather than emotional ones: delivered verbally, at the event, by one person, with no written basis and no defined scope, which makes them arguable, unenforceable and humiliating for everyone present. Every organization that does this well does the same four things — decide off-site, deliver in writing, be specific and short about what and for how long, and do not debate. The last one is the hardest and the most important: the decision is not being negotiated, it is being communicated.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “A” CHECK: “Is this decided, and is it written down?” If it is not written, it is a disagreement rather than a decision, and it will be treated as one.
scenarios.darkTitle: Do It Before The Event, Not At It
scenarios.dark: Doing it on site is the mistake that produces every bad outcome. He arrives having paid, packed and travelled, in front of an audience, with nowhere to go and nothing to lose — and that is the version that becomes a confrontation, or a scene the whole camp remembers, or a safety issue at two in the morning. Send it weeks out, in writing, and tell the event's safeguarding lead that you have done it so somebody official knows before he turns up. Also protect the person who raised it: never name them, and never let the reasoning be specific enough to identify them, because the single biggest deterrent to anyone else ever reporting anything is watching what happened to the last person who did.
scenarios.move: Decide with two other people, not alone. Send it in writing weeks before the event, short, specific, with a clear scope and no invitation to discuss. Tell the event's safeguarding lead. Brief the camp on what is happening without the detail and without names.
scenarios.say: You're not camping with us this year. This is a decision, not a discussion, and I'm not going to debate it over messages. If you turn up, we'll be asking the event to handle it.
scenarios.truth: Waiting for one more incident means one more person gets hurt. Decide off-site, write it down, and do not debate it.

scenarios.hook: TWO OF MY PEOPLE, ONE STORY EACH
scenarios.archetype: A Report About Somebody Inside Your Own Camp
scenarios.clinical: Internal Report Handling / Conflict of Interest
scenarios.who: You, holding a disclosure from one camp member about another, both of whom you like, in a structure with no process, no training and no separation of roles whatsoever.
scenarios.scene: She told you what happened on Friday. He has been your friend for nine years. You are now the investigator, the judge, the friend of both parties and the person who has to keep this camp functioning for another two days, and you have no idea what you are doing.
tells: You are close to both parties and there is no independent person
Your first instinct is to get them in a room together
You are trying to establish what really happened
The camp has begun taking sides before anything is decided
No notes have been taken and it is already three days ago
The reporting person has asked you not to do anything
scenarios.happening: Camp leads are handed reports with none of the structure that makes handling them possible, and the two most common instincts are both wrong. Mediation — getting both parties in a room — is actively harmful where there is any power imbalance or alleged harm, because it requires the person who was harmed to negotiate with the person who harmed them. And investigating, in the sense of establishing the truth, is not your role and you are not equipped for it; your role is immediate safety, accurate notes, and routing it to someone independent.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “L” CHECK: “Am I trying to find out what really happened?” That is not the job. Safety, notes, and handing it on is the job.
scenarios.darkTitle: What The Reporting Person Controls And What They Do Not
scenarios.dark: Two things have to be held together and it is uncomfortable. The reporting person controls their own disclosure — who they tell, whether they make a formal report, whether they involve police — and you do not override that. But you do control your camp, and if there is an ongoing safety risk you can act on that without their consent, as long as you do it in a way that does not identify them. Separating sleeping arrangements, changing a rota, or removing somebody can all be done as a camp decision rather than as a response to a specific report. And write the notes tonight, factual and dated, because in four months this will come back and memory is not evidence.
scenarios.move: Ask what she wants and what she needs to be safe tonight, and do the safety part immediately. Take dated factual notes the same day. Separate them physically without announcing why. Route it to the event's safeguarding lead. Do not mediate, do not investigate, and do not tell the camp.
scenarios.say: Thank you for telling me. Two things: what do you need tonight to feel safe, and what do you want to happen next — that part's yours to decide. I'm going to move some sleeping arrangements either way, and I won't say why to anyone.
scenarios.truth: You are not an investigator and you are certainly not a mediator. You are safety tonight, notes today, and a handover tomorrow.

scenarios.archetype: Dues, Floats And The Quiet Financial Hold
scenarios.who: Whoever collects for the generator, the truck, the food, the sound system and the pitch — often the founder, often for years, often with no accounting anybody has ever seen.
scenarios.scene: Everyone pays in two hundred at the start of the season and nobody has ever seen a spreadsheet. It is almost certainly fine. It is also the reason that when somebody wants to leave the camp, or disagrees with him about something, there is an unspoken question about what happens to what they have put in, and nobody asks it out loud.
tells: One person collects and spends with no reporting
No receipts, no ledger, no statement at the end of the season
Members do not know what they have collectively paid for
Assets — the shade structure, the sound system, the truck — are in one name
Leaving the camp means losing money nobody can quantify
Asking about it would be treated as an accusation
scenarios.happening: Camp money is usually handled by a trusted person acting in good faith, and the problem is structural rather than moral: unaccounted collective funds create an exit cost that nobody can name, and an exit cost is leverage whether or not anybody intends to use it. It compounds with the housing-as-leverage dynamic elsewhere in this guide — if the same person controls where you sleep, what you have paid in, and the assets you helped buy, then disagreeing with them has a price that is real and unquantifiable, which is the worst combination.
scenarios.check: L.E.A.D. — “E” CHECK: “Could any member see where the money went, without asking a favour?” If not, trust is doing a job that a spreadsheet should be doing.
scenarios.darkTitle: Transparency Protects The Person Holding It
scenarios.dark: If you are the one holding the money, the accounting is for you before it is for anybody else. The moment a camp has a falling-out — and camps do — an unaccounted fund becomes the thing people reach for, and years of genuine generosity get reinterpreted in a group chat by people doing arithmetic from memory. A shared sheet, receipts photographed into a folder, and a five-minute end-of-season summary makes that impossible. And put the significant assets somewhere collective, because a shade structure everybody paid for that lives in one person's garage is an ownership question waiting for a bad year.
scenarios.move: Run a shared spreadsheet anybody can open, photograph receipts into a shared folder, and post a short end-of-season summary without being asked. Name a second signatory. Write down who owns the major assets and what happens to them if the camp splits.
scenarios.say: Putting the camp finances on a shared sheet this year — not because anything's wrong, just so it's never a question. Anyone want to be second pair of eyes on it?
scenarios.truth: Unaccounted money is an exit cost nobody can name, and it is leverage even when nobody means it to be.

guides.intro: You create the conditions. Everything that happens at your event is shaped by your choices.

checks.name: Environment Is Yours To Set
checks.desc: The physical and social environment of your event is a choice. Safety features, lighting, staffing — all of it is yours.

checks.name: Vendor and Artist Contracts
checks.desc: Written agreements are not distrust. They are the thing that makes every professional relationship honest.

checks.name: Enforce Your Standards
checks.desc: The standards you state and do not enforce are not standards. They are decoration.

checks.name: No Means No From Your Staff
checks.desc: Your staff saying no to unsafe conditions is not insubordination. It is the system working.

checks.name: Transparent Financials
checks.desc: Pay what you agree, on the agreed timeline. Every time. This is the baseline of a business worth working with.

outline.desc: Promoter behaviors that cause harm — named directly
What you owe the people who make your event possible
Consent, safety infrastructure, and enforcing your own policies
Contracts, financial practices, staff protection, reporting
The event you are known for is the one you actually ran

sentences: The standard I walk past is the standard I set.
My event is only as safe as what I am willing to enforce.
Pay what I agreed, on the timeline I agreed. Every time.
The reputation I build is the one I deserve.

scenarios.archetype: Promising What You Cannot Deliver
