scenarios.who: This page is written directly to you. Not about bad promoters. To you. About the specific behaviors that cause harm to artists, vendors, staff, and attendees — and what accountability for those behaviors looks like.
scenarios.scene: You pitched a vendor on a premium spot near the main stage, 2,000 attendees, electricity included. You knew when you pitched it that the numbers were optimistic and the electricity situation was complicated. She paid $800 and planned her whole season around it. She arrived to a spot behind the food trucks and an electricity bill she had not budgeted for. You told yourself it was close enough. It was not close enough. She lost money because of information you provided that was not accurate.
tells: Attendance numbers and traffic projections should be accurate and from the current event context
Placement commitments belong in writing before payment is collected — not described verbally
All fees including conditionals like electricity hookups belong in the written agreement
The vendor cannot make an informed decision based on optimistic projections that serve your pitch
scenarios.happening: Misrepresentation in vendor and artist pitches is widespread because the incentive structure rewards it — you get the fee and the performer, and the consequences arrive later and are diffuse. The vendor absorbs the loss. The artist absorbs the gap between what was promised and what was delivered. Your reputation absorbs it slowly. Accurate representation of what your event offers is not just ethical — it is how you build the relationships and reputation that sustain your events long-term.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “V” CHECK: “Would I be comfortable if every vendor and artist I have worked with saw this pitch in writing, side by side with what actually happened?” — the reputation you’re building is the accurate one, not the one in your pitch.
scenarios.darkTitle: What Honest Representation Looks Like
scenarios.dark: In your vendor and artist agreements: use attendance numbers from the equivalent prior event, clearly noted as historical. Specify booth placement as a location tier with a map, not a verbal description. List all fees including conditionals before collecting any payment. Include a refund policy that covers material misrepresentation. Make your production details — stage size, sound system, streaming arrangements — specific and accurate. An agreement that accurately represents your event is the foundation of a reputation that lasts. An agreement that oversells it is a debt you will pay in reputation and relationships.
scenarios.move: Represent your event accurately in every agreement. Every time. That is the baseline.
scenarios.say: "Here is what our event actually delivered last year and what we are realistically planning for this year."
scenarios.truth: The reputation you are building is the one that is accurate — not the one in your pitch.

scenarios.archetype: Financial Accountability to Artists and Vendors
scenarios.who: You agreed to a fee. You agreed to a payment timeline. Those agreements are binding regardless of how the event went, what your costs were, or what complications arose. Pay what you agreed, on the timeline you agreed. This is the entire baseline of a professional reputation.
scenarios.scene: The event cost more than projected. The attendance was lower than you hoped. The performer you agreed to pay $2,000 is now getting a message that you can only do $1,200 "given how the event went." She had no say in how the event went. She delivered her performance. She incurred the travel costs. She fulfilled her side of the agreement. The event's financial performance is your risk, not hers.
tells: Post-event financial "adjustments" are contract violations — not conversations to negotiate
The event's costs and revenue are your business risk — not a risk that transfers to your artists
Payment timelines in contracts are enforceable — "end of month" is a legal commitment
Offering future booking as compensation for current non-payment is not compensation
scenarios.happening: Late payment and post-event fee adjustments are so normalized in the independent event world that many promoters do not register them as the contract violations they are. They are. When you agree to a fee and a payment timeline, that agreement is binding. The event's financial performance does not change your obligation. Artists and vendors who absorb your losses are subsidizing your events with their own labor and financial risk. That is not a sustainable or ethical business model.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — "T" CHECK: "Am I paying what I agreed, to whom I agreed, on the timeline I agreed — every time?"
scenarios.darkTitle: What Professional Payment Practice Looks Like
scenarios.dark: Professional payment practice: (1) Pay deposits on the agreed timeline before the event — not when you get around to it. (2) Reconcile and pay final amounts within the agreed timeframe after the event — 7-14 days is standard. (3) If you genuinely cannot pay on time: communicate proactively before the deadline, not after you have already missed it. (4) Do not offer future booking, exposure, or "a better deal next time" as substitutes for agreed payment. (5) If you had to adjust fees due to genuine crisis: negotiate BEFORE the event, not after. Late adjustment is a unilateral contract change. That is not how agreements work.
scenarios.move: Pay what you agreed, on the agreed timeline. Every time. This is the whole standard.
scenarios.say: "The payment will be in your account by [agreed date]. Let me know if you do not receive it by then."
scenarios.truth: Your financial reputation is built one payment at a time. It is also destroyed one payment at a time.

scenarios.archetype: What You Owe the People Who Run Your Event
scenarios.clinical: Labor Obligation / Operational Duty of Care
scenarios.who: Your event runs because people show up to make it run. Staff and volunteers who work your event are owed specific things — clear terms, safe working conditions, basic resources, and the knowledge that raising concerns will be taken seriously rather than cost them their position.
scenarios.scene: Your volunteer briefing says "this is a family" and "we are all in this together." It does not say what the actual shift hours are, what accommodation is provided, what meals are covered, what happens if someone needs to leave early, or how to raise a concern about another staff member. By Saturday your Harm Reduction team is short-staffed, two volunteers have left without explanation, and a concern that was raised Friday morning has not been acted on. The family framing did not substitute for the operational clarity that was needed.
tells: Volunteer agreements should specify hours, accommodation, meals, and exit terms in writing
Staff should have a clear reporting process for concerns about other staff members
Basic needs — food, water, breaks, sleep — should be structurally provided not assumed
Concerns raised by staff should be documented and acted on within a defined timeframe
scenarios.happening: Festival promoters who treat staff and volunteers as family while providing no operational clarity are using the emotional frame to avoid the practical obligations. Family framing does not substitute for written agreements. Community language does not provide food and rest. And a culture where concerns are raised but not acted on is a culture where the next concern does not get raised — until something goes seriously wrong.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “N” CHECK: “Do my staff have what they need to do their jobs safely — and do they have a clear path to raise a concern without it costing them?” — your event runs on other people’s labor. You owe them clarity, safety, and a path that actually works.
scenarios.darkTitle: Staff And Volunteer Minimum Standards
scenarios.dark: For every event: (1) Written volunteer agreements specifying hours, accommodation, meals, and exit terms before the event. (2) Pre-event briefing covering reporting process, code words, daily check-in expectations. (3) Designated staff welfare role — someone whose job includes checking that staff are okay. (4) Documented process for raising concerns about other staff members that does not require going to their direct supervisor. (5) Post-event debrief for staff that includes honest assessment of what could be improved. These are not extras. They are the baseline of running an event with people in it.
scenarios.move: Provide clear written terms, safe conditions, and a functioning reporting process for every person who works your event.
scenarios.say: Here is your written volunteer agreement — read it carefully. Here is how to raise concerns. Here is what I am committed to providing.
scenarios.truth: Your event runs on the labor of other people. You owe them clarity, safety, and the knowledge that concerns will be heard.

scenarios.archetype: Consent Culture That Is Real, Not Decorative
scenarios.who: Many events have consent policies. Fewer events enforce them consistently. The gap between a stated policy and its enforcement is not just a failure of follow-through — it is the active message that the policy is decorative rather than real.
scenarios.scene: Your event's consent policy is posted at the entrance. It is in your promotional materials. Your team briefing included it. On Saturday night a security staff member reports a consent violation to the team lead. The team lead, who knows the person being reported, decides to handle it informally. The person stays at the event. By Sunday morning two more people have had experiences with the same individual. The policy did not fail. The enforcement did.
tells: Consent violations handled informally when formal processes exist
Known violators who remain at events because of their connections or contributions
Different enforcement standards applied based on who the violator is
Reports that are received and not acted on within a defined timeframe
scenarios.happening: Inconsistent enforcement of consent policies does more damage than no policy at all — because it signals to potential violators that the policy is navigable through the right relationships, and to potential reporters that reporting may not be worth the cost. Consistent enforcement regardless of who the violator is — including people who are connected, contributing, or beloved — is the only thing that makes the policy real. The first time you fail to enforce it is the moment you define what the policy actually is.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — "E" CHECK: "Am I enforcing my consent policy consistently — regardless of who the violator is?"
scenarios.darkTitle: What Real Consent Policy Enforcement Looks Like
scenarios.dark: Real enforcement means: (1) Every reported consent violation is documented and reviewed by a designated safety lead — not handled informally by whoever is available. (2) The safety lead has actual authority to remove people from the event. (3) Removal decisions are made based on the report, not on the violator's connections or contributions. (4) The person who made the report is updated on what happened. (5) Patterns are tracked — one report about a person is an incident, two is a pattern that changes the response. (6) Post-event review includes analysis of consent-related reports and how they were handled. This is what enforcement looks like. Anything less is decoration.
scenarios.move: Enforce your consent policy consistently. The first exception defines what the policy actually is.
scenarios.say: This person has been reported for a consent violation. Here is our process and here is what happens next regardless of who they are.
scenarios.truth: A consent policy you do not enforce is not a consent policy. It is a liability.

scenarios.archetype: What You Actually Own From Your Event
scenarios.who: Your event produces content — video, audio, photography, social media. The question of what you own and what your artists and performers own is both a legal question and an ethical one. This page is about being honest about both.
scenarios.scene: Your festival set videos are performing well on your YouTube channel. They are driving discovery for your next event. They are also generating streaming revenue through the platform's music content system. The artists in those videos were paid for their performance. They were not paid for the recording, the distribution, or the streaming revenue. Your standard booking confirmation contained a rights clause they did not negotiate. The content that is building your brand was created by people who are not sharing in its returns.
tells: Sweeping recording rights clauses in standard booking confirmation language
Live recordings generating streaming or licensing revenue without artist participation
Photography and video of artists used in commercial contexts without their agreement
Social media content featuring artists used to promote future events without compensation
scenarios.happening: The gap between what promoters legally own through standard contracts and what they ethically owe the artists who created the content is significant. Artists whose performances are recorded, distributed, and monetized are entitled to participate in that revenue. A recording rights clause buried in a booking confirmation is not the same as a negotiated agreement. The ethical standard is transparency about what you are doing with the content and fair participation for the people who created it.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “V” CHECK: “Are the artists whose recordings I am using being compensated fairly for the commercial use I am putting that footage to?” — the content that builds your brand was created by artists. Treat their contribution accordingly.
scenarios.darkTitle: Ethical Recording Rights Practice
scenarios.dark: Ethical practice for event recordings: (1) Be explicit in booking agreements about what recording will happen and for what purpose. (2) Distinguish between archival recording (no commercial use) and commercial recording (streaming, licensing, promotion) — these are different agreements. (3) Share streaming and licensing revenue with performing artists — this is both the legal standard in many contexts and the ethical one in all contexts. (4) Use artist images and recordings for event promotion only with their explicit agreement. (5) When in doubt: ask before you use. The conversation is easier before the content is published than after.
scenarios.move: Be transparent about what you record, how you use it, and share revenue with the people who created it.
scenarios.say: Here is what we record at our events and how we use it. Here is how we share revenue with performing artists.
scenarios.truth: The content that builds your brand was created by artists. Treat their contribution accordingly.

scenarios.archetype: Practical Standards for Honest Event Production
scenarios.who: This page is the practical one. Specific practices and standards that distinguish events built on ethical foundations from ones built on the exploitation of artists, vendors, staff, and attendees.
scenarios.scene: The promoters you respect — the ones whose names on a lineup or a market mean something — have all built reputations over time through the same things: they pay what they agreed. They represent their events accurately. They enforce their own standards regardless of who is involved. Their staff know what to expect and have somewhere to go with concerns. Their artists are glad to come back. None of this is complicated. All of it is a choice.
tells: Written agreements with all artists, vendors, and staff before any money changes hands
Accurate representation of attendance, placement, and production in all pitches and agreements
Clear, functional reporting processes for safety concerns with named responsible parties
Post-event financial reconciliation completed and communicated within agreed timelines
scenarios.happening: Ethical event production is not a higher bar than most promoters can reach. It is a set of consistent practices that most promoters know they should follow and some do not. The ones who do build reputations that compound over time — artists want to play their events, vendors want placement at their markets, staff want to work their shows. The ones who do not build reputations that also compound — and the circuit has a very long memory.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “T” CHECK: “Would the artists, vendors, and staff who worked my last event describe it the way I just did?” — ethical production isn’t complicated. It’s a set of choices made consistently. Make them.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Ethical Promoter Checklist
scenarios.dark: Before every event: (1) All agreements in writing and signed before any performance or payment. (2) Attendance and placement representations accurate and documented. (3) All fees including conditionals listed in written agreements. (4) Staff and volunteer agreements specify hours, accommodation, meals, and reporting process. (5) Safety infrastructure plan in place and staffed. (6) Consent policy in writing with enforcement process named. After every event: (7) Financial reconciliation within agreed timeline. (8) Feedback collected from artists, vendors, and staff. (9) Post-event safety review including analysis of any incidents and their handling. (10) Changes made based on what the review reveals.
scenarios.move: Run the checklist before and after every event. The reputation you build is the one that is accurate.
scenarios.say: Here is our event agreement. Here is our safety plan. Here is how to raise concerns. Here is when payment will arrive.
scenarios.truth: Ethical event production is not complicated. It is a set of choices you make consistently. Make them.

scenarios.archetype: The Documents And Structures That Make An Event Safe
scenarios.clinical: Operational Infrastructure / Duty of Care Implementation
scenarios.who: For anyone putting on an event, from a four-hundred-capacity warehouse to a field with three stages. This page is the difference between believing your event is safe and being able to show it.
scenarios.scene: Everything here is arranged in the planning months, when it is cheap and nobody is under pressure. None of it can be improvised on the Saturday, which is when you will find out whether you did it — and the finding out is always somebody's worst night.
tells: A written code of conduct, published, with named consequences
A reporting route that does not run through the person most likely to be reported
Two named safeguarding leads, on the site map, contactable by radio and in person
Written contracts with artists, vendors and crew — rates, terms, and payment dates
Staff and volunteer briefing that covers reporting, not just wristbands and bins
An incident log kept properly, and read afterwards rather than filed
scenarios.happening: The gap between an event that says it takes safety seriously and one that does is almost entirely paperwork done in advance — and the single most load-bearing item is a reporting route that bypasses seniority. Most festival safeguarding failures are not the absence of a policy; they are a report that went to somebody with a relationship to the person being reported. Naming two independent leads and publishing how to reach them is cheap, and it is the thing that determines whether you find out about a problem in year one or in year four when it reaches social media.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “E” CHECK: “Can somebody report a senior person at my event without that report reaching them first?” If not, you do not have a reporting process, you have a filter.
scenarios.darkTitle: You Will Be Judged On The First One
scenarios.dark: Every event that has come apart publicly over this has come apart the same way: a first report that was handled informally, by someone close to the subject, with no record kept — and then a second and a third, and by the time it is undeniable the story is no longer about the individual, it is about an organization that knew. The incident log is what makes the difference, and not because it protects you legally, though it does. It is because a pattern is invisible without one: three separate reports across three years, each individually ambiguous, are obviously a pattern on one page and obviously nothing at all in three people's memories. Keep the log. Read it before every event.
scenarios.move: Publish the code of conduct and the reporting route before tickets go on sale. Name two safeguarding leads and put them on the site map. Get every artist, vendor and crew agreement in writing with payment dates. Keep the incident log and actually read it back each year.
scenarios.say: Reporting goes to Priya or Mo directly, not through me and not through the stage managers — that's published, and it's on the map. If it involves me, it goes to them and I'm not in that conversation.
scenarios.truth: Safety at an event is not a value, it is a set of documents and two names. You either did it in March or you did not.

scenarios.hook: THE REPORT IS ABOUT YOUR HEADLINER
scenarios.archetype: When Acting Costs You The Event
scenarios.who: You, holding a credible report about the one person on the bill you cannot replace, forty-eight hours out, with six thousand tickets sold on their name.
scenarios.scene: It came through welfare last night and it is specific, it is not the first thing you have half-heard about him, and he is on at ten tomorrow. The maths is doing itself in your head before you have finished reading: refunds, the agent, the insurance, next year's booking relationships, and a field full of people who bought tickets for him.
tells: The commercial cost of acting is immediately obvious and the cost of not acting is not
You are looking for reasons the report might be unreliable
You are thinking about handling it quietly, after the event
The agent's likely reaction is in your reasoning
You have heard something before and it did not go anywhere
Nobody outside your commercial interest is involved in the decision
scenarios.happening: This is the decision that defines an event, and the pattern of failure across the industry is consistent: not a promoter who decided to protect a predator, but a promoter who decided to handle it after the weekend, and then after the season, and then not at all. Everything about the moment pushes one way — the cost of acting is concrete and immediate, the cost of not acting is diffuse and deferred — and that asymmetry is the whole trap. The counter is structural: a decision rule written when nothing is at stake, and a person outside the commercial line who makes the call.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “E” CHECK: “Would I act on this identical report if it were about a volunteer?” If yes, then the only variable is money, and you already know that is not a reason.
scenarios.darkTitle: Everything Comes Out Eventually, With Your Name On It
scenarios.dark: Every event that has been publicly destroyed by this was destroyed by the cover-up rather than by the incident. It surfaces two or three years later, with the timeline, and the sentence that ends the organization is always that they knew and booked him anyway — because that is provable from a welfare log and an email. The decision looks commercial in the moment and reputational in retrospect, and the reputational version is always the larger number. Act on it now, document the decision and the reasoning, and accept the refunds, because the refunds are the cheap option and you will not believe that until it is too late to choose them.
scenarios.move: Take the decision out of the commercial line — your safeguarding lead decides, not you. Act on the current event: remove, or supervise and separate with named conditions. Document the report, the decision and the reasoning the same day. Tell the agent factually and in writing. Write the rule into next year's contracts before you need it again.
scenarios.say: This goes to our safeguarding lead and their decision stands, including if it costs us the headline slot. — [to the agent] We've received a report we're acting on. He's not performing. I'm putting the decision and the reasons in writing to you today.
scenarios.truth: The refund is the cheap option and it will never feel like it. What ends events is not the incident, it is the email showing you knew.

scenarios.archetype: Density, Surges And The Thing That Kills People At Festivals
scenarios.who: Physics. Not a bad actor, not a decision anybody made — a density figure, a pinch point, and a moment when a crowd stops being people and becomes a fluid.
scenarios.scene: It is the headline act, the barrier is full, there is a surge from the back, and somewhere in the middle of it a person goes down and the people around them cannot bend to help because there is no room to bend. Nothing about this looks dangerous from the mixing desk and it is the single most lethal thing that happens at music events.
tells: Density above roughly four to five people per square metre
Pinch points, narrowing barriers, or one exit route into a viewing area
Crowd movement that propagates as waves rather than as individuals
No spotters at the barrier and no view from the front looking back
No agreed show-stop authority, or one nobody will use
Late-arriving surges toward a single popular act
scenarios.happening: Deaths in crowds are almost never trampling, which is the popular misconception — they are compressive asphyxia, where density becomes high enough that people cannot expand their chests, and it is survivable for only a few minutes. It is entirely a design and management problem: density limits, monitoring from a position that can see the front, spotters at the barrier, and crucially a named person with unambiguous authority to stop the show. The single factor that turns a dangerous crowd into a fatal one is hesitation about stopping.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “E” CHECK: “Who can stop the show, right now, without asking anybody?” If that person is not named and briefed, you do not have a crowd safety plan.
scenarios.darkTitle: Somebody Must Be Able To Stop It Without Permission
scenarios.dark: Every crowd disaster review finds the same failure: people could see it and nobody stopped it, because stopping meant overriding a headline performance and nobody was sure they were allowed. Name the person, tell them in writing that they have the authority, tell the artist and their management in advance that a show-stop may happen and that they are to stop when asked, and rehearse the call. Give your spotters the same authority to escalate. It costs a few minutes of a set and the alternative is the thing that ends people's lives and organizations. Nobody has ever regretted a show-stop.
scenarios.move: Set and monitor density limits with a competent crowd safety adviser. Put spotters at the barrier facing the crowd. Name the show-stop authority in writing and brief artists that it exists. Design out pinch points and single-route viewing areas. Rehearse the stop.
scenarios.say: Show-stop authority tonight is Kerry, and it is not subject to anyone's approval including mine. If she calls it, the band stops mid-song. — [to management] Please brief the artist that a show-stop is possible and what it sounds like.
scenarios.truth: People do not get trampled, they get compressed, and it takes minutes. Name the person who can stop it without asking.

scenarios.hook: YOU HIRED THEM, YOU OWN THEM
scenarios.archetype: The Security Contractor Is Your Responsibility
scenarios.who: A security company that you engaged, whose staff you did not select, did not brief on your values, and whose conduct the public will attribute entirely to your event.
scenarios.scene: Two complaints come through about the same door team — a search that was handled badly, and someone spoken to in a way that was not acceptable. They are not your employees. They are wearing lanyards with your logo on them, and to everybody who was there they are your festival.
tells: No briefing given beyond capacity and ejection procedures
No shared standard on searches, gender, or trans attendees
Complaints about security route to the security company, not to you
No mechanism for an attendee to report a guard
The same complaints recur each year with no record kept
You have never checked licensing, or spoken to the guards yourself
scenarios.happening: Security are the most physically interventionist people on site and usually the least integrated into the event's stated values, because they arrive as a contracted service rather than as part of the team. Attendees do not distinguish: a bad search or an aggressive ejection is remembered as something your festival did. The fix is contractual and procedural — brief them as staff, set the standards in the contract, and provide a complaints route that does not run through the company being complained about.
scenarios.check: E.V.E.N.T. — “N” CHECK: “Can an attendee complain about a guard to someone who does not work for the security company?” If not, you will never hear about it and it will continue.
scenarios.darkTitle: Searches Are Where This Actually Goes Wrong
scenarios.dark: The specific, recurring failure is the search, because it is the one moment where a stranger in a uniform makes physical contact with every single person who enters. Get it in writing in the contract: same-gender searching offered as standard, a stated option for trans and non-binary attendees including a private space and an officer of their choosing, no searching of minors without a guardian present, and a stated protocol for assistance dogs, mobility equipment and medication. None of that is exotic and almost no event specifies it, which is why it is improvised at the gate by whoever is on that morning — and improvisation at a gate is how a person's weekend starts badly and how your festival acquires a reputation.
scenarios.move: Brief security as staff, in person, on your values and your consent policy. Put the search standards, licensing requirements and conduct expectations in the contract. Publish a complaints route that bypasses the contractor. Log every complaint and review it before renewing.
scenarios.say: You're briefed with our team, not separately — our consent policy applies to your staff. Same-gender searches offered as standard, private option available, and complaints come to our welfare lead, not to your supervisor.
scenarios.truth: They wear your logo and the public cannot tell the difference. Brief them like staff, or accept what they do in your name.

guides.intro: The guide for looking out for yourself and everybody around you all weekend.

checks.name: See Something Say Something
checks.desc: You notice something before it becomes a crisis. That moment — right there — is the one that matters.

checks.name: Ask Before You Consume
checks.desc: Know what it is. Test it. Start small. Have a sober buddy. These four things together save lives.

checks.name: Find the Resources First
checks.desc: Medical tent. Harm Reduction tent. Ranger station. Know where all three are before your first night.

checks.name: Everyone Gets Home Safe
checks.desc: This is the goal. Not just you. Everyone in your crew. Buddy system, code words, check-ins.

outline.desc: Water, electrolytes, heat, food, sleep — the physical basics
Testing, dosing, mixing, overdose response, Narcan
Bystander activation, reading a situation, how to help
Medical tent, Rangers, overdose response, missing persons
Difficult experiences, crisis support, decompression
Buddy system, group check-ins, the morning after

sentences: By the time you feel thirsty you are already behind. Drink now.
Test your stuff. Every time. No exceptions. Full stop.
See something? You have three options. Pick one and do it.
Everyone in your crew gets home safe. That is the only finish line.

scenarios.archetype: Hydration, Electrolytes, and Heat Safety
scenarios.who: By the time you feel thirsty at a festival you are already behind. The combination of dancing, heat, sun exposure, and many substances means your hydration needs are significantly higher than your normal daily baseline — and your body's thirst signal is often suppressed or delayed.
scenarios.scene: It is 2pm Saturday and it is hot. You have been dancing since 11am. You have had one bottle of water and three sips from someone else's hydration pack. You feel fine — energized actually, slightly euphoric. That feeling is not a reliable indicator of your hydration status. By the time the headache hits and you start feeling off your balance you are already significantly behind. The medical tent is about to get busy because you are not the only one.
tells: Drink water consistently throughout the day — at least 500ml per hour in heat and while dancing
Electrolytes matter as much as water — plain water alone can cause hyponatremia in high volumes
Signs of heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, cool pale skin, weakness, nausea, headache
Signs of heat stroke — EMERGENCY: hot red dry skin, no sweating, confusion, loss of consciousness
scenarios.happening: Festivals combine multiple dehydration risk factors simultaneously: physical exertion from dancing, sun and heat exposure, alcohol and stimulant use (both increase fluid loss), and environments that make stopping to drink feel inconvenient. Heat exhaustion is common and treatable. Heat stroke is a medical emergency that kills people. The difference between them is speed of treatment. Know the signs. Act early. The medical tent is there specifically for this.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — "F" CHECK: "Do I know where the medical tent is — and have I actually had enough water in the last hour?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Heat Stroke Is A Medical Emergency
scenarios.dark: Heat stroke signs: hot, red, dry skin with no sweating. Confusion, slurred speech, loss of consciousness. Body temperature above 104F. This is life-threatening and requires immediate medical attention. What to do right now: call for medical help immediately, move the person to shade and cool them with water or ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin, do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious. Festival medical teams are trained for this. Get them immediately. Do not wait to see if it gets better.
scenarios.move: Drink water now. Take an electrolyte packet. Find shade for ten minutes. Do it before you need to.
scenarios.say: Hey — when did you last have water? Come on, let us both drink something right now.
scenarios.truth: Every medical tent at every festival sees preventable heat illness every day. Do not be that story.

scenarios.hook: FOOD, SLEEP, AND YOUR ACTUAL BODY
scenarios.archetype: The Physical Infrastructure That Makes Everything Safer
scenarios.who: Festivals are designed for endurance — multiple days, extended hours, high stimulation. Your body has limits regardless of how good the music is and how much you want to keep going. The people who have the best full-weekend experiences are the ones who treat their physical needs as seriously as their social ones.
scenarios.scene: It is Sunday morning. You have slept a total of six hours over three nights. You have eaten intermittently and mostly festival food. You have consumed substances that have both depleted your body and masked the signals it is trying to send you. You are running on a combination of adrenaline, social excitement, and genuine will. You feel okay. You are not okay. And the decisions you make today — about substances, about consent, about safety — will be made from this state.
tells: Eat at least two real meals per day even when the music is calling — your judgment depends on it
Sleep deprivation after 36 hours significantly impairs decision-making even when you feel fine
Sunscreen reapplication every two hours — sunburn on top of everything else is genuinely dangerous
Foot care matters — blisters become infections, infections at festivals are hard to treat
scenarios.happening: Sleep deprivation is one of the most consistently underestimated risk factors at festivals. After 36 hours without sleep, cognitive impairment is equivalent to a 0.10 blood alcohol level. After 48 hours it is significantly higher. Combined with substances, heat, and social pressure this creates a state where the very judgment systems you need to make good decisions about your own safety are significantly compromised. Rest is not weakness. Rest is strategy.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “A” CHECK: “Am I making decisions right now with my full judgment — or with a significantly depleted version of it?” — rest isn’t missing the festival. It’s what makes you available to actually be in it.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Case For Actually Sleeping
scenarios.dark: You will remember more of your festival if you sleep. Genuine experiences integrate better when your brain is functioning. You will be more present in conversations, more able to receive music, more connected to the people around you. The FOMO of missing a few hours by sleeping is almost always outweighed by the quality of the hours you are present for. Plan for at least one solid sleep block in a 72-hour event. Bring earplugs and an eye mask. Tell your campmates you are sleeping and not to disturb you. This is not weakness. This is how you have the festival you actually came for.
scenarios.move: Eat something real. Sleep when you can. Your experience of the festival depends on your body being functional.
scenarios.say: I am going to get a couple hours — wake me up for the set I marked. I will be more here for it if I sleep.
scenarios.truth: Rest is not missing the festival. Rest is what makes you available to actually be in it.

scenarios.archetype: Fentanyl Strips, Reagent Kits, and Why This Is Non-Optional
scenarios.who: Fentanyl is in the supply. It is in pills, powders, and substances where people are not expecting it. It is invisible, odorless, and a lethal dose is smaller than a few grains of salt. Testing is the single most effective harm reduction step you can take.
scenarios.scene: "Someone in our camp tested their MDMA Saturday morning and it came back as something completely different." This happens at every major festival. Not occasionally — every festival, every season. The person who handed it to you may not have known either. Testing is not about distrust of the person who gave it to you. It is about knowing what is actually in what you are consuming. You would not eat a wild mushroom without identifying it first. Same exact energy. Same exact stakes.
tells: Fentanyl test strips: dissolve a tiny amount in water, dip — ONE line means fentanyl present, do not use
Reagent kits (Marquis, Mecke, Simon's): color reactions identify MDMA, MDA, amphetamines, and adulterants
Start with a much smaller amount than you think is the dose — festival environments intensify everything
Wait before redosing — onset times vary and stacking doses before you feel the first one is how people get in trouble
scenarios.happening: The recreational drug supply has been contaminated with fentanyl and fentanyl analogues at a scale that makes testing not optional — it is a basic safety step equivalent to checking that your tent stakes are in the ground before it rains.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “A” CHECK: “Have I tested this — and does everyone in my group know what to do if something goes wrong?” — two minutes of testing is the difference between a good night and a medical emergency.
scenarios.darkTitle: Every Time Means The Batch You Already Trust
scenarios.dark: Fentanyl and its analogues have turned up in pressed pills sold as MDMA, in cocaine, in ketamine, in counterfeit prescription tablets — substances where nobody in the chain intended an opioid to be present at all. Contamination is not evenly mixed: two pills pressed in the same batch can differ, so a strip that came back clean on Friday’s half says nothing about Saturday’s. This is the specific reason “it’s from a friend” is not a safety measure — your friend is not the chemist, he is another customer, and he is testing nothing either. Two strips and a reagent kit cost less than a night of parking. Carry naloxone even if you never touch an opioid on purpose, because the overdose you reverse will most likely belong to somebody who also thought they never had.
scenarios.move: Test your stuff. Carry Narcan. Know the overdose signs. These three things save lives.
scenarios.say: Hold on — let me test it first. I have strips in my kit. Two minutes.
scenarios.truth: The two minutes it takes to test is not inconvenience. It is the difference between a good night and a medical emergency.

scenarios.archetype: What Not to Mix and Why It Matters
scenarios.who: Most serious adverse events at festivals involve combinations of substances rather than any single substance. Festival environments where multiple substances are available and social pressure normalizes consumption make accidental dangerous combinations common.
scenarios.scene: You took MDMA earlier. Someone offers you something they describe as a downer to take the edge off. You do not know exactly what it is. You are already altered and the offer feels casual and the person seems trustworthy. This specific combination — a stimulant and a CNS depressant — is one of the most common contributors to serious adverse events at festivals. Not because either thing alone is necessarily fatal but because the combination creates unpredictable interactions that your altered state makes it hard to assess.
tells: MDMA plus alcohol: dramatically increases dehydration and cardiovascular strain
Stimulants plus depressants (including alcohol): mask each other's effects and create unpredictable states
MDMA plus other serotonergic substances: risk of serotonin syndrome which can be life-threatening
Any substance plus another substance from an unknown or unverified source: compounded unknown risk
scenarios.happening: Polydrug use — using more than one substance — is extremely common at festivals and the risk profile of combinations is not intuitively obvious. Substances that seem to balance each other out are often actually masking warning signals from your body. The feeling of being okay is not reliable information when two substances are creating competing effects. The Harm Reduction tent has staff trained in polydrug risk assessment. When in doubt — go there before you take something else.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “A” CHECK: “Do I know what I have already taken and do I actually know what I am being offered right now, specifically?” — the combination is where most of the risk lives. Know what you’re mixing before you mix it.
scenarios.darkTitle: Harm Reduction Tent — Use Them For This
scenarios.dark: Harm Reduction tents at major festivals have staff trained in substance interaction risk. You can walk in and say "I took X a few hours ago and someone is offering me Y — is that a problem?" and receive factual, non-judgmental information. This is confidential. They are not the police. They are not going to take away your substances or report you. They are there specifically to help you make safer choices. TripSit (tripsit.me) also has a free online drug combination checker that works on mobile. Check before you mix.
scenarios.move: Know what you have taken before taking anything else. When unsure — ask the Harm Reduction tent.
scenarios.say: What is that exactly? I need to know before I decide — I already took something earlier.
scenarios.truth: The combination is where most of the risk lives. Know what you are mixing before you mix it.

scenarios.archetype: Overdose Response and Getting Help Without Fear
scenarios.who: The most important thing to Know about someone in trouble from substances is that you call for help immediately — and that Good Samaritan laws in most US states protect you from prosecution when you do. The call saves the life. The delay kills.
scenarios.scene: Your campmate is not responsive. You called their name. You shook their shoulder. They are breathing but slowly — it sounds wrong. Their lips look slightly blue. You do not know exactly what they took. You are scared. You are also the person standing there right now and you are the only thing standing between this situation and a very different outcome. You have about two minutes to make a decision that matters enormously.
tells: Unresponsive or very difficult to rouse — this is the clearest emergency sign
Slow, shallow, or stopped breathing — count breaths if unsure, fewer than one per 5 seconds is critical
Blue or purple tinge to lips or fingertips — indicates oxygen deprivation
Gurgling or snoring sounds from airway — roll them to recovery position on their side immediately
scenarios.happening: Opioid overdose is the most immediately life-threatening substance emergency at festivals and Narcan reverses it. But stimulant overdose, serotonin syndrome, and heat stroke can also present as altered consciousness and require different emergency responses. The common thread is this: if someone is unresponsive or their breathing is wrong — call for medical help immediately and administer Narcan if you have it, because if it is an opioid overdose the Narcan will help and if it is not it will not harm them.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — "F" CHECK: "Do I know where the medical tent is and do I have Narcan in my camp right now?"
scenarios.darkTitle: The 60-Second Overdose Response Protocol
scenarios.dark: Step 1: Try to rouse them — call their name, rub knuckles firmly on their sternum. Step 2: Call for medical help immediately — festival medics, 911, anyone with a radio. Do this NOW, do not wait. Step 3: If you have Narcan — one puff in each nostril. Repeat in 2-3 minutes if no response. Step 4: Roll them into recovery position on their side so they do not choke on vomit. Step 5: Stay with them until medical help arrives. Good Samaritan laws protect you. Making the call is always the right choice. Always.
scenarios.move: Call for help first. Narcan second. Recovery position third. Stay with them. Do not leave.
scenarios.say: "Someone is unresponsive — I need medical help at [your location] right now!" Then do not hang up.
scenarios.truth: The call you make in the next 60 seconds is the difference. Make it.

scenarios.archetype: How to Actually Intervene When Something Looks Wrong
scenarios.who: At some point this weekend you will see something that does not look right. A situation. A person. A dynamic. The bystander effect is real — in groups, individuals are less likely to act because everyone assumes someone else will. You are the someone else.
scenarios.scene: You are walking between stages and you see a woman sitting with a man who seems agitated. Her body language is closed. He is leaning into her space and she is looking at the ground. You are not sure if it is anything. You almost keep walking because you do not want to assume, do not want to make it weird, do not want to be wrong. But something caught. This is the moment. This is the one. You have three options and they all take less than two minutes.
tells: THE DISTRACTION: walk up like you know her — "Oh my god, there you are! I have been looking everywhere for you!"
THE RESOURCE: find a Ranger or Harm Reduction worker, describe location and exactly what you saw
THE CHECK-IN: wait for a private moment and ask her directly — "Hey — are you okay?"
You do NOT have to confront the person causing concern — that is not required and not always safe
scenarios.happening: The most effective bystander interventions are the subtle ones — the distraction approach changes the social dynamic without confrontation and gives the person an exit without escalation. You do not have to be certain something is wrong to intervene. You do not have to be a hero. You just have to be the person who showed up. The festival community is only as safe as what each individual does in the moment they notice something.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. —"S" CHECK: "What did I actually see — and which of the three moves fits this situation?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Reading A Situation Quickly
scenarios.dark: Signs a situation may need intervention: someone who seems significantly more impaired than their companions and is being directed or moved somewhere. Body language that is closed, small, or fearful in contrast to the other person's open or dominant posture. Someone who looks uncomfortable when you make eye contact with them and then looks away quickly. Someone being separated from their group by another person. A transaction that looks pressured or coerced. You do not need certainty to intervene with a distraction or to alert a Ranger. You just need a gut feeling. Trust it.
scenarios.move: Pick one of the three moves and do it. Doing something imperfectly is always better than doing nothing perfectly.
scenarios.say: Oh my god, there you are! I have been looking everywhere — come on, everyone is at the stage.
scenarios.truth: You do not need to be certain. You need to be the person who showed up.

scenarios.archetype: Reading Impairment and Knowing When to Stay
scenarios.who: Being altered is a normal part of many festival experiences. Being so altered that you cannot take care of yourself, communicate clearly, or make safe decisions is a different situation — and the people around you are your safety net when you are in that state.
scenarios.scene: Your friend is having a bigger night than she intended. She is not in medical trouble but she is very out of it — she cannot navigate independently, she is making decisions that she would not make with clearer judgment, and she is attracting attention from some people who seem very interested in being helpful in ways that feel off to you. This is the moment where the buddy system is not a suggestion. It is the thing that determines how her night ends.
tells: Cannot navigate or find their way without help — beyond just being unfamiliar with the layout
Communication is significantly impaired — not just slow but unable to form coherent sentences
Making decisions that are completely out of character — especially about people or locations
Others are clustering around them in ways that feel more predatory than supportive
scenarios.happening: Severe impairment in a festival environment is a specific vulnerability state that predatory people specifically target. The person who cannot walk straight, cannot communicate clearly, and cannot make coherent decisions cannot consent to anything and cannot protect themselves from anyone. If your friend or someone near you is in this state — stay with them. Get them to a safe space. If they need medical attention get it without hesitation. Good Samaritan laws exist for exactly this situation.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — "E" CHECK: "Can this person take care of themselves right now — and if not, who is actually with them?"
scenarios.darkTitle: When To Go To Medical Or Harm Reduction
scenarios.dark: Go immediately: if they are unresponsive or semi-conscious, if their breathing is wrong, if their lips or fingertips are blue, if they had a seizure, if they have a high fever with no sweating. Go sooner rather than later: if they are significantly confused and getting more so, if they took something unknown and are reacting badly, if they are very distressed and not calming down, if you are worried and not sure why. The Harm Reduction tent is specifically for situations where you are not sure — they will help you assess. You will not get in trouble for bringing someone for care. You might regret not doing it.
scenarios.move: Stay with them. Get them to a safe space. Go to Harm Reduction or medical if you are unsure. Do not leave them alone.
scenarios.say: I am staying with you — we are going to find somewhere quiet. Come on.
scenarios.truth: The buddy who stays is the reason the story has a good ending. Be that person.

scenarios.hook: KNOW THESE LOCATIONS BEFORE NIGHT ONE
scenarios.archetype: Medical Tent, Harm Reduction, Rangers — Before You Need Them
scenarios.who: The single most effective thing you can do for your safety this weekend — before any substance, before any adventure, before anything — is to physically locate the medical tent, the Harm Reduction tent, and the Ranger station. Do this before your first night. With your whole group. Together.
scenarios.scene: It is Thursday afternoon and you have just arrived. Your camp is set up. The festival has not really started yet. Everything feels calm and oriented. This is the moment to walk the grounds with your group and find the three locations. Not Saturday night when you need them. Right now. The ten minutes you spend orienting yourselves right now are the ten minutes that could determine how a difficult situation on Saturday night resolves.
tells: Medical tent: equipped for physical emergencies, serious injury, overdose, and heat illness
Harm Reduction tent: equipped for substance-related distress, difficult experiences, non-judgmental support
Ranger station: event-specific safety response, less clinical, often better for social or interpersonal situations
Note the nearest water stations and shade structures to all three locations
scenarios.happening: The gap between knowing where help is and not knowing where help is is the difference between a situation that gets addressed quickly and one that escalates because nobody knows what to do or where to go. In a medical emergency at a festival, every minute matters. Pre-mapping your resources is the preparation that costs nothing and is worth everything.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “F” CHECK: “Have I physically located the medical tent, Harm Reduction tent, and Ranger station with my own feet, not just on the map?” — knowing where help is before you need it is the preparation everything else builds on.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Five-Minute Group Orientation
scenarios.dark: Before your first night — as a group: (1) Walk to the medical tent together. Note the route and a visual landmark nearby. (2) Walk to the Harm Reduction tent. Note the route. (3) Walk to the Ranger station. Note the route. (4) Identify the nearest water station to your camp. (5) Choose a physical meeting spot for if you get separated — not a GPS location, a physical landmark. "The big wooden arch at the east entrance." (6) Set a daily check-in time. "We touch base at 2pm every day no matter what." This is ten minutes that changes the whole weekend.
scenarios.move: Do the five-minute group orientation before your first night. Every member of your group. Together.
scenarios.say: "Before we get into it tonight — let us all walk to the medical tent and Harm Reduction together so we know where they are."
scenarios.truth: Knowing where help is before you need it is the preparation. Everything else builds on that.

scenarios.archetype: What to Do and How Fast to Do It
scenarios.who: Someone in your group is missing and you have not been able to reach them. This happens at festivals and it is almost always fine — and it is also sometimes not fine. The protocol for the first category and the second category is the same: act early, not late.
scenarios.scene: It is 4am and your campmate said she was going to the bathroom two hours ago and has not come back. Her phone is going to voicemail. You have checked the spot where you usually meet up. You have asked around the camp. Nobody has seen her. You are torn between assuming she is fine and having a good time somewhere and the feeling in your gut that something is wrong. The feeling in your gut is data.
tells: Report to festival security or Rangers as soon as you are concerned — there is no minimum time to wait
Have her photo available on your phone before you go to report — full face, what she is wearing today
Know what she was last wearing — write it down when you last saw her, not when she is missing
Check the medical tent and Harm Reduction tent before assuming the worst — she may already be safe there
scenarios.happening: There is no required waiting period before reporting a missing person at a festival. The idea that you must wait 24 hours is a myth and in a festival context is actively dangerous. Report as soon as you are concerned. Festival security, Rangers, and medical teams all have protocols for missing persons. The earlier you report, the better the resources available, and the better the outcomes. Your concern is sufficient reason to make a report.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “E” CHECK: “Have I already checked medical and Harm Reduction tents — and do I have her photo on my phone, ready to show people?” — there’s no minimum wait time to report someone missing. Report when you’re concerned, not after.
scenarios.darkTitle: Missing Person Information To Have Ready
scenarios.dark: When you report: (1) Full name and age. (2) Physical description including height, approximate weight, hair color. (3) What she was wearing the last time you saw her — be specific including shoes. (4) Last known location and time. (5) Phone number and whether it is going to voicemail. (6) Her relationship to alcohol and substances this weekend and any medical conditions. (7) A clear recent photo from your phone. Write some of this down when you last see members of your group each day — not when they are missing and you are panicking.
scenarios.move: Check medical and Harm Reduction tents first. If not found — report to Rangers immediately with photo and description.
scenarios.say: I need to report a missing person — she has been gone for two hours and is not answering her phone.
scenarios.truth: There is no minimum wait time to report a missing person at a festival. Report when you are concerned. Not after.

scenarios.archetype: What They Look Like and What Actually Helps
scenarios.who: Difficult psychological experiences at festivals — sometimes called bad trips, sometimes genuine mental health crises — are common, often preventable, and very treatable when handled correctly. The wrong response can make them significantly worse.
scenarios.scene: Your friend took something three hours ago and for the first two hours he was having the time of his life. Now something has shifted. He is very frightened — he cannot articulate why exactly but everything feels threatening. He is trying to leave the area but you are not sure where he wants to go or if he should be alone right now. He is not in physical danger but he is clearly in real psychological distress and getting more so.
tells: Intense fear or panic without a clear external cause
Disorientation or confusion about what is real vs not real
Wanting to escape urgently without a clear destination or reason
Physical symptoms accompanying the psychological distress: rapid breathing, shaking, sweating
scenarios.happening: Difficult psychedelic or substance-induced experiences are almost always temporary and almost always respond well to calm, quiet, grounded support. The worst things you can do: try to talk them out of their experience, argue with them about what is real, leave them alone, or take them to a loud and stimulating environment. The Zendo Project specializes specifically in difficult psychedelic experience support and has trained staff at many major festivals. Get them there if available.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “F” CHECK: “Do I know where the Zendo or Harm Reduction tent is — and can I get us both there calmly, without rushing them?” — a calm presence is the most powerful intervention there is, and you already have it.
scenarios.darkTitle: What Actually Helps In A Difficult Experience
scenarios.dark: What helps: move to a quieter, lower-stimulation space. Sit with them on the ground. Speak calmly and slowly. Remind them where they are and that they are physically safe. "You took something, it will pass, I am right here, you are safe." Do not try to fix or solve the experience — just be a calm presence in it. What does not help: arguing about what is real, leaving them alone, taking them to a loud or crowded space, giving them more substances, or panicking yourself. Zendo Project (zendoproject.org): specifically trained for this. Get them there if you can.
scenarios.move: Get to a quiet space. Sit down together. Stay calm. Get to Harm Reduction or Zendo if it is not resolving.
scenarios.say: I am right here. You are safe. You took something and it will pass. I am not going anywhere.
scenarios.truth: A calm presence is the most powerful intervention in a difficult experience. You have that.

scenarios.hook: SIGNS OF A GENUINE MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS
scenarios.archetype: When It Is More Than a Difficult Trip
scenarios.who: Festival environments can precipitate genuine mental health crises in people who may have underlying vulnerabilities — the combination of sleep deprivation, substances, emotional intensity, and social pressure can tip someone into a state that requires more than peer support.
scenarios.scene: Your campmate has been quiet and withdrawn since Saturday morning. He came out once, said he was fine, went back in. It is Sunday and you have knocked twice and he said he was okay but something in his voice did not match the word. He has not eaten anything you know of. He made a comment last night about not being sure why he came. You are sitting with the question of whether to push harder to check on him. Push harder.
tells: Withdrawal from the festival for an extended period when they came to engage
Saying they are fine in a way that does not match their voice, energy, or behavior
Comments that sound like they feel hopeless, purposeless, or like they should not have come
Not eating, not sleeping, not coming out — for longer than exhaustion alone explains
scenarios.happening: Mental health crises at festivals are underreported and underidentified because the expectation is that everyone is having a good time and should be having a good time. The signs can be subtle and easy to attribute to tiredness or a difficult trip. If your gut says something is wrong with someone in your group — check on them again. Ask directly. "Are you actually okay — because I am asking for real." The question asked with genuine care and real eye contact is a different question than the passing "you okay?"
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — "S" CHECK: "What is my gut actually telling me about this person — and am I acting on it?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Crisis Resources At Festivals
scenarios.dark: Zendo Project (zendoproject.org): difficult psychedelic experiences and mental health crisis — present at many major festivals. Festival medical tents: handle mental health crises as well as physical ones. 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988, 24/7, trained crisis counselors. Crisis Text Line: text HOME to 741741 — useful when a voice call feels too hard. If someone says anything that sounds like they are thinking about hurting themselves: take it seriously, stay with them, get help. "I am just going to make sure you are okay — come on, let us go find somewhere quiet together."
scenarios.move: Knock again. Ask directly. Stay with them. Get help if needed. Do not normalize what your gut is flagging.
scenarios.say: I am asking for real — are you actually okay? Because I am not going anywhere until I know.
scenarios.truth: Checking on your people is not being dramatic. It is being a real friend.

scenarios.archetype: Processing Difficult Experiences Without Shame
scenarios.who: Something happened this weekend. Or you watched something happen. Or you supported someone through something. Or you are sitting with something you cannot fully name yet. This page is for Sunday — the quiet one when everything gets real.
scenarios.scene: It is Sunday afternoon and the festival is winding down and you are sitting with something heavy. You are not sure if you are being dramatic. You are not sure who to tell. You are exhausted and overwhelmed and every feeling is louder than normal. Here is what is true: you do not have to have it figured out to deserve support. You do not need a perfect story. You do not need certainty about what happened or what to call it. You just need to reach out.
tells: You do not need a perfect memory or perfect certainty to deserve support — reach out anyway
Harm Reduction tents are confidential and are not required to report to law enforcement
RAINN hotline (1-800-656-4673) is 24/7 and supports all genders and all types of experiences
Crisis Text Line: text HOME to 741741 if talking feels too hard right now
scenarios.happening: Post-incident processing is hard enough without the additional weight of deciding whether your experience is bad enough to matter. It is. Whatever level of severity it sits at — it matters. You do not have to be okay by the time you load the car. You do not have to have it figured out before you talk to someone. Give yourself the first 48-72 hours for basic recovery — sleep, food, low stimulation — before trying to process fully. Then talk to someone you trust.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “E” CHECK: “What does my body actually need right now — not what does the situation require me to perform?” — you don’t have to be okay yet. Support exists, and you deserve it.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Week After The Festival
scenarios.dark: Post-festival blues are real — the crash from social intensity, sleep debt, and substances can feel significant and last several days. What helps: sleep, real food, gentle movement, low stimulation, reconnecting with people you trust. What makes it harder: immediately jumping back into intensity, isolating, making major decisions in the first week. If you are carrying something heavy from the weekend: give yourself 3-5 days before trying to process it fully. If the weight does not lift after a week or two — reach out to a therapist. Psychology Today (psychologytoday.com) has a therapist finder by specialty including trauma.
scenarios.move: Eat. Sleep. Tell one trusted person. Reach out to resources if you need more. You deserve support.
scenarios.say: Something happened this weekend I am still processing. I do not need you to fix it — I just need you to hear it.
scenarios.truth: You do not have to be okay yet. Support exists. You deserve it.

scenarios.archetype: How to Actually Run One That Works
scenarios.who: The buddy system is not childish. It is the single most effective community safety tool at a festival and the people who use it consistently have better and safer experiences than the people who do not. Here is how to actually run one.
scenarios.scene: Friday morning before the festival opens your group sits down for ten minutes. Everyone says who their buddy is for the weekend. You set a check-in time — 2pm every day, you physically find each other or send a specific text. You choose a code word that means "come find me right now, no questions." You agree on a meeting spot for if you get separated. You agree that if anyone does not check in on time someone comes looking. Ten minutes. That is the whole investment.
tells: Name your buddy before gates open — not organically during the festival
Set a specific daily check-in time with a specific response expected, not just "stay in touch"
Choose a code word that means "come find me immediately" — something you would not say normally
Agree on a physical meeting spot that does not require phone signal to find
scenarios.happening: The buddy system works because it creates accountability before you need it — not after something has already gone wrong. The check-in time means that if something is wrong you know within hours, not days. The code word means you can signal for help in any situation without making a scene. The meeting spot means you can reconnect without phone signal. These are not elaborate safety measures. They are ten minutes of planning that changes the entire risk profile of your weekend.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “E” CHECK: “Does everyone in my group have a buddy, and do we all have the code word and the meeting point, agreed before we split up?” — ten minutes spent on this before the festival is the preparation that matters most.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Full Buddy System Checklist
scenarios.dark: Before gates open: (1) Every person has a named buddy. (2) Daily check-in time agreed — specific time, specific expected response. (3) Code word chosen — something normal-sounding that means "come get me now." (4) Physical meeting spot chosen — a Specific landmark, not a GPS point. (5) One person not at the festival has the names and phone numbers of everyone in the group. (6) Everyone writes two emergency numbers in pen on their arm — their buddy and one person at home. (7) Offline festival map downloaded on at least two phones. Ten minutes. Do it before the music starts.
scenarios.move: Do the buddy system setup with your whole group before gates open. All of it. Ten minutes.
scenarios.say: Before we go in — ten minutes to sort the buddy system. Who is with who? What is the code word? What is the meeting spot?
scenarios.truth: The ten minutes you spend on this before the festival is the preparation that matters most.

scenarios.hook: THE BATHROOM BUDDY AND NIGHT WALKS
scenarios.archetype: Simple Habits That Significantly Reduce Risk
scenarios.who: Some of the simplest safety habits in festival culture are also the most consistently overlooked — especially as the weekend progresses and everyone gets more comfortable and more tired. These are the ones worth making non-negotiable.
scenarios.scene: It is 3am Saturday. You need the bathroom and your campmate is finally asleep and your buddy is at a set you did not want to see. The walk to the bathroom is maybe four minutes through a part of the festival that is less busy at this hour. You almost go alone. The almost is the moment. The almost is where the simple habit matters.
tells: Bathroom buddy rule: someone walks with you to the bathroom after dark, every time, no exceptions
Walking each other back to tents after late sets — do not let altered friends navigate alone in the dark
Phone charging as safety infrastructure — share chargers freely, a dead phone is a vulnerability
The quiet check-in: "you good?" before splitting up is two seconds and it matters
scenarios.happening: Most adverse incidents at festivals happen in low-visibility, low-traffic situations in the later hours of the night — on walks between stages, in bathroom queues, in the paths between camping areas. The simple habit of not being alone in those moments is one of the most effective risk reductions available. It does not require elaborate systems. It just requires the group norm that you do not let people walk alone after dark.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — "E" CHECK: "Is anyone in our group alone right now in a situation where they should not be?"
scenarios.darkTitle: Night Navigation Safety Basics
scenarios.dark: After dark at festivals: bring a headlamp or phone torch — being able to see and be seen is basic safety. Stay on lit paths between stages when possible. If you are going somewhere unfamiliar or less trafficked, tell your buddy where you are going and when you expect to be back. If you feel uncomfortable on a walk — trust that. Change direction, find a busier path, head toward lights and sound. Ranger patrols concentrate on darker and less trafficked areas — if you see a Ranger and feel unsafe, walk with them or near them. You do not have to explain why.
scenarios.move: Bathroom buddy rule. Walk each other back. Share your charger. Two seconds to check in before splitting up.
scenarios.say: I am going to the bathroom — come with me? I will walk you back after.
scenarios.truth: The simplest habits are the ones that matter most. Make them non-negotiable in your group.

scenarios.archetype: Looking Out for Strangers as Well as Your People
scenarios.who: The festival community is only as safe as what each person does when they see something that does not involve their own crew. This page is about extending your care beyond your group — because the stranger you help might be someone else's buddy who needs exactly what you have to offer.
scenarios.scene: You are at the water station and a woman comes up alone and asks if you can spare a phone charger for ten minutes. She says she got separated from her group and cannot reach anyone. She seems okay but uncertain. You have a portable charger. The ten minutes it takes to help her reconnect with her group might be the ten minutes that means her story has a good ending. This is what community care actually looks like — not grand gestures, small ones.
tells: Share your phone charger freely — a charged phone is safety infrastructure for everyone
If someone seems lost or uncertain — ask if they need help finding something
If you see someone alone and very impaired — check in, do not assume someone else will
If you are leaving a set and see someone alone at the edge who looks uncomfortable — the distraction approach works on strangers too
scenarios.happening: Community safety at festivals is not the responsibility of staff and Rangers alone — it is a distributed responsibility across every person there. The small acts of community care — sharing a charger, asking if someone is okay, walking someone to the Harm Reduction tent, using the distraction approach for a stranger in a difficult situation — these are what make the difference between a festival where harm happens and goes unaddressed and one where the community catches things before they escalate.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — "E" CHECK: "Am I extending care beyond my own group — or only looking out for the people I know?"
scenarios.darkTitle: What Festie Community Care Actually Looks Like
scenarios.dark: Real community care in practice: share your charger without being asked. Ask the person sitting alone if they are waiting for someone or need help. Walk someone to a resource if they seem unsure where to go. Give your extra water to someone who clearly needs it. Use the distraction approach for a stranger in a situation that looks off. Tell a Ranger what you saw. These are not heroic acts. They are the distributed infrastructure of a safe festival. When everyone does the small things the big things happen less often.
scenarios.move: Extend your care beyond your camp. The small acts of community care are the infrastructure of a safe festival.
scenarios.say: "Hey — do you need help finding something? I have a charger if your phone is dead."
scenarios.truth: The festival is only as safe as what each person does when they see something. That includes you.

scenarios.hook: IF THE CROWD GETS TOO TIGHT
scenarios.archetype: Crowd Crush / What To Actually Do Inside One
scenarios.who: Nobody. This is physics, and it is the most lethal thing that happens at music events, and almost nobody in a crowd knows the three things that keep them alive in one.
scenarios.scene: You are forty rows back and the crowd has stopped feeling like people. You are being moved without walking. Your arms are pinned. There is a wave that goes through from behind and you feel your feet leave the ground briefly, and you cannot get your chest to expand fully on the in-breath.
tells: You are being carried by the crowd rather than choosing your steps
You cannot raise your arms or take a full breath
Waves of pressure travelling through the crowd rather than individual movement
You are shoulder-to-shoulder on all four sides with no gaps at all
People near you have gone quiet
You cannot see a gap, a barrier gate, or an edge
scenarios.happening: Crowd deaths are compressive asphyxia, not trampling: the pressure of bodies prevents the chest from expanding and a person suffocates upright, frequently while nobody around them realizes what is happening. It becomes dangerous above roughly five people per square metre and the window is short. The three things that matter are simple and completely counterintuitive, which is why they have to be known in advance rather than worked out at the time.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “S” CHECK: “Can I raise my arms and take a full breath?” The moment the answer is no, you are in a crush and you start moving out now, not later.
scenarios.darkTitle: The Three Things That Keep You Breathing
scenarios.dark: Memorize these now. One: get your arms up in a boxer's guard, hands in front of your chest, elbows out — this creates the few centimetres of space in front of your ribs that lets you keep breathing, and it is the single highest-value action. Two: do not push, do not fight the wave, and above all do not bend down for anything, including a phone or a person — going down in a dense crowd is how people do not come back up, and you cannot help anyone from the floor. Three: move diagonally and with the surges, not against them, using the moments of give to gain half a metre toward an edge; going against a crowd achieves nothing and exhausts you. And if somebody goes down near you, shout, and make a wall with the people around you rather than bending into the gap alone.
scenarios.move: Arms up in a guard, protect your chest. Stay upright at all costs. Move diagonally toward an edge during the moments of slack. Shout if somebody goes down and form a wall with the people beside you. If you can, leave before it gets to this — density builds visibly for minutes beforehand.
scenarios.say: Arms up! — Somebody's down, make a wall! Don't bend, hold the space! — Back this way, move with it, not against it.
scenarios.truth: People suffocate standing up, and it takes minutes. Arms up, stay upright, move diagonally with the wave.

scenarios.archetype: Storms, Heat And Evacuation In A Field
scenarios.who: The weather, at a site made of temporary metal structures, canvas, and eighty thousand people with nowhere indoors to go.
scenarios.scene: The stage goes dark mid-set and a voice says something you cannot make out over the PA, and the crowd starts to move in a direction, and it is beginning to rain properly. Nobody around you knows whether this is a five-minute pause, a storm hold, or a full evacuation, and the field is already becoming a single large moving mass.
tells: Stages held or dark with no clear announcement reaching you
Lightning visible, or thunder inside thirty seconds of a flash
Standing water, mud, or wind moving temporary structures
Crowds converging on one route out of an arena
Extreme heat with no shade and long queues for water
You do not know where your site's shelter or muster points are
scenarios.happening: Weather is the likeliest cause of a mass evacuation at an outdoor event and every festival has a plan for it that attendees have almost never read. The two lethal versions are lightning — a field of temporary metal structures with no substantial buildings is close to the worst possible place — and the crowd movement that an evacuation itself produces, which is where the injuries actually happen. Heat is the slower one and it kills more people than storms do, usually through people who have been dancing in sun for hours without shade or salt.
scenarios.check: S.A.F.E. — “F” CHECK: “Do I know where my shelter is and where my camp's muster point is?” Find both on Thursday, because there is no time to find them on Saturday.
scenarios.darkTitle: Vehicles, Not Tents, And Move Early
scenarios.dark: Two specifics worth having in advance. In lightning, a tent is worse than useless — it offers no protection at all and its poles are the tallest thing in a flat field. A hard-topped vehicle is genuine shelter and so is a substantial permanent building; a gazebo, a marquee and a stage structure are not. Get away from metal, from the highest ground and from lone trees, and use the thirty-second rule: if thunder follows the flash within thirty seconds, the storm is close enough to be dangerous.
